Approaches

The theoretical inspirations, concepts and methods of the 77 books and articles on museums this site is built from, grouped into 11 families: where each idea comes from and, above all, how the works use it. 594 concepts are recorded, each with the author's definition, how it is put to work, a quotation, and a page reference.

How this was made: each text's introduction, conclusion and theoretical passages were read by machine and its concepts recorded with line references; every quotation was checked by script to occur in the text. The thematic essays were then written from those records. Nothing here was checked by a person, and the readers did not read every chapter of every book. Definitions report how each author uses a term in that text, which may differ from the theorist's own usage. "Carrying it over" and "Possible use elsewhere" are suggestions for research, not findings. References lead to the text's entry on the contents page; page boxes give the printed page where it could be established, otherwise the page of our PDF.

Power, knowledge and the governing of publics

Foucault's discipline and governmentality, Bennett's exhibitionary complex, and other ways of treating the museum as an instrument of the state, of reform and of knowledge. 53 concepts from 40 texts

This family of approaches treats the museum as an instrument of the state, of reform and of knowledge: a place where authority is displayed and visitors are shaped. Its question is how display and public access govern conduct (Hooper-Greenhill 1992p. 190; Bennett 1995p. 8). Foucault stands behind most of it, usually through Tony Bennett, whose 'exhibitionary complex' and 'liberal government' are the common points of departure (Denton 2014p. 12; Bennett 1995p. 20). Gramsci's hegemony enters through Coombes and Bennett (Coombes 1994p. 6; Bennett 1995p. 91), while Bourdieu's habitus, Elias's civilising body and Laclau and Althusser's discourse enter through Lu, Black and Sem (Lu 2014p. 135; Black 2000p. 34; Fromm 2014p. 104).

The texts at the centre are Bennett's The Birth of the Museum (Bennett 1995), Hooper-Greenhill's Museums and the Shaping of Knowledge (Hooper-Greenhill 1992), Sherman and Rogoff's Museum Culture (Sherman & Rogoff 1994) and Hill's Culture and Class in English Public Museums (Hill 2005), with Denton (Denton 2014) and Guy, Williams and Wintle (Guy 2024) as the main extensions and critiques. The approach is strongest where a state's role is visible and weakest where the archive shows little planning (Longair & McAleer 2012p. 5; Hill 2005p. 91).

Bennett's exhibitionary complex

The exhibitionary complex is Bennett's model of display as a state technology that makes power visible to the public and invites visitors to regulate themselves by seeing as the state sees (Denton 2014p. 12). Denton applies it to Chinese state history museums but adapts it: control is negotiated among curators, cadres and officials, and visitors receive the displays differently, so it is not a simple transfer of ideology (Denton 2014p. 12; Denton 2014p. 13). Leahy uses it more broadly, placing the National Gallery and the Society of Arts exhibitions among commercial and popular spectacles, so that regulating the visitor's body appears as part of a wider display culture (Rees Leahy 2012p. 20). Stokes-Rees applies the term to the fixed route of The Hong Kong Story, which enforces one storyline on visitors who are expected to be passive viewers (Knell et al. 2011p. 345). Guy, Williams and Wintle treat the concept as the paradigm of a critical museum studies that analysed finished exhibitions, and criticise that literature for leaving out designers and technicians (Guy 2024p. 3). Cvetkovski uses the term for the cultural-geographical arrangement of the 1910 Russian ethnographic exhibition, names no source for it, and tests whether that display carried an imperial message (Cvetkovski & Hofmeister 2014p. 213).

Foucault: discipline, surveillance and the visitor's body

Discipline is the second Foucauldian strand, used to read architecture, routes and bodies. Hooper-Greenhill calls the public museum an apparatus of discipline and surveillance, dividing the hidden work of stores and offices from public galleries, one of the apparatuses "that created 'docile bodies' through disciplinary technologies" (Hooper-Greenhill 1992p. 190; Hooper-Greenhill 1992p. 183). Barrett takes Foucault through Bennett and Hooper-Greenhill to call public museums disciplinary spaces, then uses heterotopia to explain how counter-publics coexist within one institution (Barrett 2011p. 100). Black applies the panopticon to Kipling's Lahore Museum as a total survey, and Elias's civilising body to Laurie's displays of the human body (Black 2000p. 155; Black 2000p. 31). Hill measures this claim on ground plans and finds that most municipal layouts followed existing buildings, scarce budgets and donors' prestige, so that only Liverpool approached a one-way evolutionary route (Hill 2005p. 91). Brady uses Foucault's problematization to explain the NMAI Act and NAGPRA as answers to earlier collecting practices, and asks why the Mall museum was never itself questioned (Sleeper-Smith 2009p. 134).

Foucault: discourse, master narratives and power-knowledge

Discourse and master narratives give a second, textual strand. Coombes applies Foucault's discursive formation to show how scientific and popular rhetoric produced 'Africa' as a body of truth for the British public, but pairs Foucault with Gramsci because Foucault leaves little room for dissent (Coombes 1994p. 6). Sem applies discourse theory, drawing on Laclau and Althusser, to show that veterans held the recognised subject positions in the Falstad debate, so that counter-narratives were treated as meaningless deviations (Fromm 2014p. 104). Sherman and Rogoff take Foucault's model of epistemic structures and argue that choosing one cultural tendency as a period's expression sustains a master narrative (Sherman & Rogoff 1994PDF p. 13). Yanni tests that reading against the buildings and finds that close architectural history is "surprisingly resistant to Foucauldian analysis", since the displays held several co-existing theories rather than one narrative (Yanni 1999p. 8). Conn rejects the critique outright, arguing that Foucauldian critics analyse power without the knowledge that power produced (Conn 1998p. 11).

Gramsci and negotiated hegemony

Gramsci's hegemony, understood as maintained by bargaining rather than imposed from above, is the lens used to temper Foucault. Coombes uses it to explain why exhibitions of colonial material maintained the myth of a unified colonial Britain, and treats the dialogue between coloniser and colonised as real but circumscribed by violence (Coombes 1994p. 6). Bennett combines Gramsci's state as educator with Foucault's disciplinary power, using each to correct the other, so that museum politics must address institutional properties and not only the content of displays (Bennett 1995p. 91). Hill takes a narrower point from Bennett, that museum authority was "modified by negotiations among classes and groups", and makes inconsistency and failure the premise of the English case studies (Hill 2005p. 5). Denton's account of negotiated control among curators and officials makes the same move for a Chinese setting (Denton 2014p. 13).

Neutrality as a claim to test

Several texts treat museum neutrality as a claim to be tested rather than a fact. Sherman and Rogoff take Haacke's idea, drawn from Enzensberger's 'consciousness industry', that sponsorship, layout and labels make museums "managers of consciousness" (Sherman & Rogoff 1994PDF p. 16). Greenhalgh argues that "political neutrality is a fiction", setting the open politics of the great international exhibitions against the artificial neutrality of English museums, and tests the claim by the exhibitions' popular success (Vergo 1989p. 94). Janes applies the 'fallacy of authoritative neutrality' to corporate and foundation funding, arguing that sponsors are themselves special interest groups (Janes 2009p. 59). Yanni applies the claim to architecture, finding that modernist plain forms look objective, while Victorian buildings legitimated particular science without trying to appear neutral (Yanni 1999p. 159).

Colonial rule and cultural technologies of the state

The last strand asks whether museums were planned instruments at all. Longair and McAleer take MacKenzie's phrase that museums were 'tools' of empire and qualify it: the editors argue that we should "move beyond the interpretation of museums as part of some overarching imperial project" (Longair & McAleer 2012p. 5). Basu takes Cohn and Dirks's 'cultural technologies of rule' as the thesis to test against British West Africa, finds the museums to be the pet projects of individual enthusiasts, and concludes that the concept fails as a description (Longair & McAleer 2012p. 145). MacKenzie says the surveillance model does not fit the colonial setting, where control lay in collecting and display rather than in watching visitors (MacKenzie 2009p. 16). Lu defines heritage as something that depends on who controls the discourse and the museum, and uses Bourdieu's habitus to explain why curators adapt to Party frameworks (Lu 2014PDF p. 16; Lu 2014p. 135).

Debates and limits

The disagreements are sharpest where authors test the model against archives. Basu finds that colonial West African museums were not shaped by the imperial policy the concept assumes, and Hill finds English municipal layouts unplanned rather than uniformly disciplinary (Longair & McAleer 2012p. 145; Hill 2005p. 91). Conn and Yanni go furthest against the Foucauldian reading, Conn on the ground that its critics analyse power without the knowledge it produced (Conn 1998p. 11; Yanni 1999p. 8). What the approach tends to leave out, by the texts' own account, is visitor reception: Lu concedes too little evidence of how visitors received displays (Lu 2014p. 88), and Hill notes that how far messages were accepted cannot be shown (Hill 2005p. 145).

Carrying it over to a new case

  • Ask whether a state museum's founding documents show a plan or a personal initiative, to test any claim that it served a government; the editors' emphasis on peripheral, individually founded museums makes the question concrete (Longair & McAleer 2012p. 5; Longair & McAleer 2012p. 145).
  • Trace who speaks with recognised authority in a local dispute over a contested exhibition, and which voices never reach print, as Sem does at Falstad (Fromm 2014p. 104).
  • Read a regional museum's route and room order as disciplinary space, asking what conduct the layout was built to produce, as Barrett does for the public museum (Barrett 2011p. 100).
  • Test a master-narrative reading against a museum's building history and labels to see whether it presents one story or several, as Yanni does for the Natural History Museum (Yanni 1999p. 8).
  • Ask whose interests a claim to political neutrality protects in a state- or sponsor-funded museum, following Janes's fallacy of authoritative neutrality (Janes 2009p. 59).
  • Trace the sponsorship credits and interpretive panels of a museum to see which interests they make visible or hide, using Sherman and Rogoff's managers of consciousness (Sherman & Rogoff 1994PDF p. 16).

Where to start reading

  • Denton, Kirk A. (2014). Exhibiting the Past: Historical Memory and the Politics of Museums in Postsocialist China. Honolulu: University of Hawai‘i Press. Denton, for the adaptation of Bennett's model to negotiated state control.
  • Bennett, Tony (1995). The Birth of the Museum: History, Theory, Politics. London: Routledge. Bennett, for liberal government and the political rationality of reform.
  • Guy, Kate; Williams, Hajra; Wintle, Claire (eds.) (2024). Histories of Exhibition Design in the Museum: Makers, Process, and Practice. London: Routledge. Guy, Williams and Wintle, for the critique of the exhibitionary complex as a study of finished displays.
  • Hooper-Greenhill, Eilean (1992). Museums and the Shaping of Knowledge. London: Routledge. Hooper-Greenhill, for the museum as an apparatus of discipline.
  • Hill, Kate (2005). Culture and Class in English Public Museums, 1850–1914. Aldershot: Ashgate. Hill, for negotiated power and the limits of disciplinary space in municipal museums.
  • Yanni, Carla (1999). Nature’s Museums: Victorian Science and the Architecture of Display. Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press. Yanni, for a test of the master-narrative reading against architectural history.
  • Coombes, Annie E. (1994). Reinventing Africa: Museums, Material Culture and Popular Imagination in Late Victorian and Edwardian England. New Haven: Yale University Press. Coombes, for discursive formation paired with Gramsci.
  • Sherman, Daniel J.; Rogoff, Irit (eds.) (1994). Museum Culture: Histories, Discourses, Spectacles. Minneapolis: University of Minnesota Press. Sherman and Rogoff, for master narratives and managers of consciousness.

Alberti, Samuel J. M. M. (2009). Nature and Culture: Objects, Disciplines and the Manchester Museum. Manchester: Manchester University Press.
museums as political instruments and machines for making meaningAlbertiadaptstheoretical framing

Museums are cast as political instruments and machines for making meaning that impose particular behaviours on their visitors, a framing developed in the early 1990s museum studies. (Alberti 2009p. 1)

Draws on Eilean Hooper-Greenhill; Susan Pearce; Tony Bennett

How it is used Alberti places the book in this lineage and then adapts it. Where studies of state-level governance look at national museums, he looks at an intermediary, local level of control, examining individuals and institutions in provincial England and their audience constituencies. He presents the book as complementing the Foucauldian and post-colonial agenda rather than extending it.

“instruments, machines for making meaning and imposing particular behaviours on” p. 2
Manchester Museumprovincial civic collections

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The local-level focus invites a comparison between a provincial museum's governance and a national museum's, asking which level of control shaped its displays of non-European material.

Barrett, Jennifer (2011). Museums and the Public Sphere. Chichester: Wiley-Blackwell.
disciplinary space and heterotopiaBarrettappliesanalytic concept

Foucault's account of institutions as disciplinary spaces that shape social life and subjectivity, and of heterotopias as places that act as counter-sites, reflecting other real places in social life. Barrett uses both to show that the museum displays state power and also hosts publics that form within it. (Barrett 2011p. 100)

Draws on Michel Foucault; Tony Bennett; Eilean Hooper-Greenhill

How it is used Barrett takes Foucault through Bennett and Hooper-Greenhill to argue that public museums are disciplinary spaces that shape the public, and then uses the heterotopia to explain how contradictory functions and publics, including counter-publics, can coexist within one institution. The concept lets her treat the space of the museum, not only its texts, as a discourse of the public sphere.

“these spaces become disciplinary spaces of social life, with a direct” p. 100
the nineteenth-century public museumthe museum as an institution of the state

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could read the route and room order of a colonial or provincial museum as disciplinary space, asking what conduct the layout was built to produce in its visitors.

Bennett, Tony (1995). The Birth of the Museum: History, Theory, Politics. London: Routledge.
liberal governmentBennettappliestheoretical framing

A form of government that works at a distance by shaping individuals' capacities for self-monitoring and self-regulation rather than by increasing coercive state power. Culture is the resource through which this government operates, and the museum is one of its cultural technologies. (Bennett 1995p. 8)

Draws on Foucault

How it is used Bennett applies Foucault's concept to the rational recreation movement and to Cole's and Goode's arguments for museums, showing that the case for public culture rested on governing the working man's leisure by inner discipline. The concept lets him explain why reformers wanted public museums at all, rather than reading museums only as sites of ideological display, and it ties museum policy to the wider field of cultural government.

“It is, then, in the view of high culture as a resource that might be used to regulate the field of social behaviour” p. 20
the rational recreation movementHenry Cole's museums opened to the working manGoode's 'passionless reformers'

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask whether a municipal library, zoo or botanic garden in another city was justified in the same terms of self-regulating conduct, and what its founders expected visitors to learn about restraint.

political rationalityBennettappliesanalytic concept

The specific logic by which an institution exercises power, which may differ from the reforming rhetoric it claims for itself. Bennett borrows the term from Foucault's account of the prison, and uses the mismatch between rhetoric and function to explain why demands for museum reform recur. (Bennett 1995p. 89)

Draws on Foucault

How it is used Bennett applies the prison model to the museum: demands for access and for representational adequacy are read as products of a gap between a democratic rhetoric and a museum that works to reform manners. The argument lets him say that repeated reform does not threaten the museum's existence, and it sets up the politics he advocates in the final chapter of Part I.

“its political rationality, a term I borrow from Foucault. The development of” p. 89
nineteenth-century public museumsdemands for public accessdemands for representational adequacy

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could test whether access campaigns for a museum in another country show the same pattern of recurring reform demands without change, using visitor figures and annual reports from several decades.

Gramscian hegemony and counter-hegemonyBennettcombinesanalytic concept

The idea that museums display the values of ruling groups through a rhetorical incorporation of the people, so that cultural politics aims to build a counter-hegemony by changing displays. Gramsci's account of the state as educator is the source, and Bennett uses it alongside Foucault rather than in place of him. (Bennett 1995p. 91)

Draws on Gramsci

How it is used Bennett combines Gramsci's account of the state as educator with Foucault's account of disciplinary power, using each to correct the other: Gramsci explains how the museum incorporates the people, while Foucault shows that museum politics cannot be reduced to ideological display. The combination supports the claim that museum politics must address the museum's institutional properties and not only the content of its displays.

“generally are, museums are represented as instruments of ruling-class” p. 91
nineteenth-century public museums as pedagogic institutionsmuseum displays of the nation's history

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): One could ask whether a museum in a newly independent state is best read as an educator of citizens in Gramsci's sense, or as an institution whose own rules limit what any counter-display can achieve.

Black, Barbara J. (2000). On Exhibit: Victorians and Their Museums. Charlottesville: University Press of Virginia.
museum as panopticon and utopia of surveillanceBlackappliescritique

The museum as a space that watches and orders its visitors and the colonised, a total survey in which the museum goer sees all but the museum official sees more. In Kim the Lahore Museum is the example that makes this concrete. (Black 2000p. 155)

Draws on Jeremy Bentham; John McClure; Benedict Anderson

How it is used Black applies the panopticon to Kipling's Lahore Museum, which he reads as a front for the British secret service, and links it to Anderson's account of census, map and museum as systems of colonial surveillance. The reading lets him show that Kim's training in collecting is training for imperial rule, in which knowing the colonised is a form of power. Black sets this against McClure's view of Kim as Kipling's richest dream.

“Kipling’s museum emerges a utopia based on surveillance” p. 156
the Lahore Museum in Kipling's Kim

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could read a colonial or post-colonial museum in East or Southeast Asia against the same question: what its catalogues, cataloguing staff and visitor controls were for, and whom they watched.

regulating the body through civilising displayBlackappliestheoretical framing

Elias's account of civilisation as a long process of disciplining the body, which Black applies to museums as places that teach visitors how to stand, look and move, and that regulate the body along with the mind. (Black 2000p. 31)

Draws on Norbert Elias

How it is used Black applies Elias to the Bethnal Green branch and to Laurie's display of the human body, where the museum's displays of the athlete's arm, the drunkard's stomach and the bound Chinese foot are read as instruction in the disciplined body. Black argues that the museum's role in perpetuating culture is to regulate the body, and that the visitor learns the codes of conduct by example. The concept links museum visiting to the wider civilising project of the state.

“the museums role in perpetuating culture is to regulate the body” p. 34
Thomas Laurie's display of the human bodythe Bethnal Green branch of the South Kensington Museum

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask how a museum in an East or Southeast Asian country used display to discipline the body, for example in hygiene, dress or posture campaigns, and whether the same Eliasian reading holds.

Conn, Steven (1998). Museums and American Intellectual Life, 1876–1926. Chicago: University of Chicago Press.
Foucauldian power-knowledge critiqueConncriticisescritique

The view that museum classifications and displays were exercises of power, so that the categories of knowledge museums presented were contingent and their visitors were brought to accept them. Conn presents it as the position he argues against, while accepting that the categories were not timeless truths. (Conn 1998p. 11)

Draws on Michel Foucault; Tony Bennett; Eilean Hooper-Greenhill; Paul DiMaggio

How it is used Conn sets this position against the historical record. Conn argues that Foucauldian critics analyse power without the knowledge that power produced, and that museum builders needed categories to make knowledge possible at all. Conn cites Bennett's exhibitionary complex and the claim that museums made the public complicit with power, and in the closing chapter concedes that the walls around knowledge were not immutable while proposing a pragmatic, Jamesian sense in which the museums' ideas became true by being displayed. The critique frames the whole book's method, which is to take the museums' intellectual claims seriously.

“Among the problems with a Foucauldian analysis, as I see it, is that” p. 11
museums of the late nineteenth century generallythe museums of Philadelphia in 1926

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could use the critique to ask of a state or colonial museum whether its classifications were powerful in practice, and then what knowledge its curators believed they were producing.

Coombes, Annie E. (1994). Reinventing Africa: Museums, Material Culture and Popular Imagination in Late Victorian and Edwardian England. New Haven: Yale University Press.
hegemony as maintained through negotiationCoombesadaptstheoretical framing

Gramsci's idea of hegemony is taken as a relation maintained by constant bargaining between social groups, not imposed from above, so that colonial culture is a field of negotiated consent and dissent rather than straightforward propaganda. (Coombes 1994p. 6)

Draws on Gramsci

How it is used The author uses the idea to explain the ambivalence of anthropology's position and why exhibitions of colonial material were a potent means of maintaining the myth of a unified colonial Britain. It lets her treat the dialogue between coloniser and colonised as real but circumscribed by violence, and it supports the argument that African and Irish critics could expose the contradictions of imperial unity.

“In particular, Gramsci’s concept of hegemony as maintained” p. 6
Franco-British Exhibition (1908)ethnographic museums and popular exhibitions, 1890-1913

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The idea could frame a study of how a state museum in Asia negotiated its national narrative with visiting publics and with local communities rather than simply imposing one.

discursive formation and regimes of truthCoombesappliestheoretical framing

Foucault's notion of discursive formation is used to show how scientific and popular rhetorics about race and culture together produced 'Africa' for different parts of the British public as a body of truth. (Coombes 1994p. 6)

Draws on Foucault

How it is used The author applies the concept to relate scientific and popular accounts of race, so that she can treat the Benin narratives, the exhibitions and the museums as one field of statements. Her stated reservation is that Foucault leaves little room for dissent, which is why she pairs him with Gramsci.

“Foucault’s concept of discursive formation has also enabled me to think through the” p. 6
Benin expedition press accountsLiverpool Mayer Museum classificationStanley and African Exhibition

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The same concept could be used to ask how the racial vocabulary of a Western museum of Asian objects was built from scientific and popular statements, and which regimes of truth it addressed.

Cvetkovski, Roland; Hofmeister, Alexis (eds.) (2014). An Empire of Others: Creating Ethnographic Knowledge in Imperial Russia and the USSR. Budapest: Central European University Press.
exhibitionary complexCvetkovskitestsanalytic concept

The idea that museum display is an instrument through which objects are arranged to communicate social and political order. The chapter uses the term for the cultural-geographical arrangement of the 1910 exhibition and sets it against the registration system behind the displays. The text does not name a source for the term. (Cvetkovski & Hofmeister 2014p. 213)

How it is used The chapter tests whether ethnographic objects could carry an imperial message. It shows that the exhibition's cultural-geographical arrangement, centred on the Great Russians, was undercut by a registration system that did not follow imperial territory. The chapter also shows the exhibition as a place where objects 'simply displayed the Other' rather than the empire's self-image.

“Emphasizing its exhibitionary status,” p. 213
1910 trial exhibition, Russian Ethnographic Museum

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The question could be applied to other ethnographic museums in Asia or to European collections of Asian objects, asking whether a display's order matched the order in which the objects had been registered.

Denton, Kirk A. (2014). Exhibiting the Past: Historical Memory and the Politics of Museums in Postsocialist China. Honolulu: University of Hawai‘i Press.
exhibitionary complexDentonadaptstheoretical framing

The museum as a state technology that makes power visible to the public and invites visitors to regulate themselves by seeing as the state sees. Denton takes it as the base for reading Chinese museums as instruments of the state. (Denton 2014p. 12)

Draws on Tony Bennett; Foucault

How it is used Denton uses Bennett's model to open the introduction and to set the frame for reading state history museums as teaching visitors to internalize party narratives. Denton adapts it by stressing that the state's control is negotiated among curators, cadres and officials, and that visitors receive the displays differently, so it is not a simple transfer of ideology.

“Bennett sees museums as making power visible to the public” p. 12
National Museum of ChinaMuseum of the Chinese Revolution

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could test the complex on a corporate or private museum in Shanghai to ask whether its visitors are still trained to see power from the side of the state.

Fromm, Annette B.; Golding, Viv; Rekdal, Per B. (eds.) (2014). Museums and Truth. Newcastle upon Tyne: Cambridge Scholars Publishing.
discourse and subject positionsSemappliesanalytic concept

A discourse is a system of meaning that makes some statements possible and others not, and it gives speakers subject positions from which they may speak with authority, on condition that they accept the discourse's rules. (Fromm 2014p. 104)

Draws on Laclau; Laclau and Mouffe; Althusser

How it is used Sem applies discourse theory to the Falstad debate and finds that veterans held the occupation and Holocaust discourses, while former borstal boys and pupils of the special school had almost no recognised subject position. Sem uses the concept to explain why counter-narratives were treated as meaningless deviations, and so how the wartime narrative silenced the other eras of the site.

“Althusser has called interpellation (Althusser 1971, 174).” p. 104
Falstad Centre, Norway (exhibition debate 2003-2006)

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could map who speaks, and with what recognised authority, in a comparable local debate over a museum's contested exhibition, and which voices never reach print.

Guy, Kate; Williams, Hajra; Wintle, Claire (eds.) (2024). Histories of Exhibition Design in the Museum: Makers, Process, and Practice. London: Routledge.
exhibitionary complexGuy, Williams, Wintlecriticisestheoretical framing

Bennett's account of museum display as a field of classification and spatial arrangement through which the state and its agendas controlled objects and visitors. The introduction treats it as the paradigm of a critical museum studies that has analysed finished exhibitions. (Guy 2024p. 3)

Draws on Tony Bennett; Michel Foucault

How it is used The introduction sets Bennett's concept as the starting point and then turns against the literature it inspired, arguing that it treats exhibitions as static and that the makers of displays go unseen. Later work, the editors say, works 'after the exhibitionary complex' by crediting curators, donors, trustees and visitors. The volume uses this frame to justify a focus on process rather than on the power of the finished display.

“is perhaps the paradigmatic discussion of” p. 3
Museum of Modern Art, New York (Staniszewski's study)

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The concept can be used as a foil: a researcher could ask, for a given Asian museum's displays, what the exhibitionary complex leaves out, such as the designers and technicians who built the cases and the mannequins.

Hill, Kate (2016). Women and Museums, 1850–1914: Modernity and the Gendering of Knowledge. Manchester: Manchester University Press.
distributed museumHilladaptstheoretical framing

The museum as a network of many people and objects, with dealers, donors, fieldworkers, visitors and committees all producing its meanings, rather than a single institution imposing one effect on its public. (Hill 2016PDF p. 20)

Draws on Gosden and Larson

How it is used Hill uses the model to read donations, visits and patronage as forms of agency inside the museum, and to argue that curators controlled less of what their museums owned or meant than is often assumed. In Chapter 5 she turns the model on its limits, calling the chapter 'about the limits of the distributed museum', since women's gifts were shaped by all-male boards and senior curators.

“The museum, then, needs to be seen as a distributed institution” PDF p. 20
women's donations to a dozen museums, 1880-1914Kate Hall at the Whitechapel MuseumLady Charlotte Schreiber's gifts to South Kensington and the British Museumthe Davies sisters' paintings

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The model could be tested on a provincial museum's receiving book to see which donors, dealers or fieldworkers shaped its holdings, and whether the same network logic holds for an Asian collection assembled through missionaries or traders.

cumulative agencyHillcoinsanalytic concept

Women's influence on museums worked through accumulated gifts, networks and small institutions rather than through leadership, and was often unconscious as well as marginal. (Hill 2016PDF p. 163)

How it is used Hill uses the concept to explain why women shaped museums without leading national ones. Hill reads Schreiber, the Davies sisters and the founders of smaller museums as building influence cumulatively, which is why women were found on the periphery of the distributed network and why all-male boards kept them from the centre.

“Women’s agency was most often cumulative” PDF p. 163
Lady Charlotte Schreiberthe Davies sistersJosephine BowesMarianne North

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The concept could be used to ask how women collectors in a colonial port built influence on a regional museum's holdings without holding its curatorship.

Hill, Kate (2005). Culture and Class in English Public Museums, 1850–1914. Aldershot: Ashgate.
negotiated power in the museumHilladaptsanalytic concept

Museum authority was exercised through negotiation among classes and groups, so that it was inconsistent and contested rather than imposed as one ruling ideology. Hill takes this from Bennett's account of rational recreation and makes it the working premise of the book. (Hill 2005p. 5)

Draws on Tony Bennett

How it is used Hill adopts Bennett's point that reformers were more concerned with habits and manners than with consciousness, and makes it the basis for looking at the inconsistencies and failures of museum power. The cases show uneven results: Liverpool built a coherent evolutionary system, while Preston's Harris Museum relied on donors' statues and little explanation, and councils and curators disagreed over what the museums were for.

“modified by negotiations among classes and groups.” p. 5
Liverpool MuseumPreston Harris Museummunicipal museums in general

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask whether a colonial or provincial museum's display of non-European peoples was negotiated between donors, councils and curators, and whether the same inconsistencies appear there.

disciplinary space and self-surveillanceHilltestsanalytic concept

Galleries, one-way routes and the mutual visibility of visitors are treated as technologies that make the public watch itself and so regulate its behaviour. Hill sets this account, drawn from Bennett and Markus after Foucault, against the plans of English municipal museums. (Hill 2005p. 91)

Draws on Tony Bennett; Thomas Markus; Michel Foucault

How it is used Hill tests the claim that museum architecture disciplined visitors by measuring it on ground plans. Hill finds that most municipal layouts were shaped by existing buildings, scarce budgets and donors' prestige, so that only Liverpool approached a one-way route with an evolutionary narrative. Hill concludes that these museums were unplanned spaces responding to local conditions, not uniform disciplinary machines, and that the layout of Liverpool became less rational as galleries were added.

“But these are big claims, and this chapter will investigate whether this” p. 92
Liverpool Museum 1860 building and 1906 extensionPreston Harris MuseumBirmingham art gallerySheffield Mappin Art GalleryLeicester

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could compare the plans of a regional or colonial museum with the route a visitor could actually take, to see whether the one-way routes and galleries were planned for surveillance or simply followed the building.

Hill, Kate (ed.) (2021). Museums, Modernity and Conflict: Museums and Collections in and of War since the Nineteenth Century. London: Routledge.
total warHillappliesanalytic concept

Modern industrial war that mobilises society and erodes the distinction between military and civilian, which the introduction treats as accelerating from the nineteenth century through the two world wars. Hill uses it as a driver of museum development rather than an external context. (Hill 2021p. 2)

Draws on Chickering; Förster; Strachan

How it is used Hill uses total war to argue that museums took their modern form at the same time as war was modernising, so conflict is part of museum history and not an interruption of it. The idea lets the introduction link Napoleon's confiscations, the Louvre's 1939 evacuation and wartime exhibitions in occupied Europe as one history of museums mobilised by the state. The volume then tests it in its section on the war effort, where propaganda and morale become museum functions. Hill notes in a footnote that the concept has many competing origin dates.

“Sections 2 and 3 of this volume show that total war” p. 2
Napoleonic confiscationsLouvre evacuation of 1939wartime exhibitions in occupied Netherlandsmuseums under Nazi rule in Germany

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask whether a museum's wartime role in a non-European conflict, such as the Sino-Japanese or Pacific wars, followed the same logic of mobilising the public, and whether the 'total war' frame fits it.

Ho, Denise Y.; Li, Jie (2016). “From Landlord Manor to Red Memorabilia: Reincarnations of a Chinese Museum Town”. Modern China.

The idea that the Landlord Manor was designed as a secular temple: its hell-like tableaux, docents and Mao quotations stood in for city god temple sculptures and the magistrate and judge of the netherworld, so that visitors judged the past and were warned against its return. (Ho & Li 2016p. 12)

Draws on Robson; ter Haar; Teiser

How it is used The authors use the temple model to explain the form of the Rent Collection Courtyard, the docent tours and the way Liu Wencai had to be conjured up and exorcised again and again. It links the museum to older popular religious forms and explains its moral effect on visitors, not only its message.

“imparted moral lessons with Mao Zedong quotations as its scripture.” p. 14
Landlord Manor MuseumRent Collection Courtyard and the Xindu arhatsChengdu City God Temple

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask whether other memorial museums on temple sites, or with scripted docents, follow the same pattern, and what visitors actually do in them.

Hooper-Greenhill, Eilean (1992). Museums and the Shaping of Knowledge. London: Routledge.
disciplinary museumHooper-Greenhillappliesanalytic concept

The museum understood as an apparatus of discipline and surveillance. In this account the public museum divides the hidden work of producing knowledge, in stores and offices, from the surveyed public galleries where visitors receive finished knowledge and are shaped as ‘docile bodies’. (Hooper-Greenhill 1992p. 190)

Draws on Foucault

How it is used Hooper-Greenhill applies the idea to the revolutionary Louvre, where confiscations, catalogues in depots, expert agents and guards turned royal and aristocratic property into an instrument of citizenship. Hooper-Greenhill applies it also to the National Gallery and National Portrait Gallery in Britain, which were meant to improve the population through heroic national history. The concept lets her treat the museum’s openness as itself a form of surveillance.

“that created ‘docile bodies’ through disciplinary technologies.” p. 190
LouvreNational Gallery, LondonNational Portrait Gallery, London

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The idea could be tested on a national or ethnographic museum founded in a colonial period, asking which surveillance practices in its galleries, and which hidden cataloguing work, shaped its visitors.

Hopkins, Owen (2021). The Museum: From Its Origins to the 21st Century.

An art practice that exposes what museums usually hide, such as storage, transport and installation, and shows the museum's permanence as a fiction. Hopkins uses it to introduce the question of why the museum keeps its hold even after it has been criticised. (Hopkins 2021)

How it is used Hopkins opens the book with Broodthaers's 1968 Musée d'Art Moderne, Département des Aigles as the seminal case, then turns to Crimp's 1980 essay on Rauschenberg, which he uses to argue that critique can strengthen the museum's hold. The concept lets him set the book's argument against a sceptical reading, so that the museum is treated as a durable authority that critique has not displaced.

“By doing so he revealed the way museums appear as unchanging and eternal as something of a fiction”
Musée d'Art Moderne, Département des Aigles (Brussels, 1968)Rauschenberg's Centennial Certificate (MoMA)

Hudson, Kenneth (1975). A Social History of Museums: What the Visitors Thought. London: Macmillan.

In the nineteenth century art was expected to fill the place of religion, so museums were places of reverence and their directors were treated as priests. Hudson uses the image to describe the authority of the director over the visitor. (Hudson 1975p. 52)

How it is used Hudson links the image to the nineteenth-century idea that art could awaken reverence and devotion, and uses it to explain why directors saw no need to ask visitors what they thought. It frames his later argument that directors' authority, rather than the public's wishes, shaped what visitors were given.

“Museums were temples and their directors priests, to be addressed as such.” p. 52
nineteenth-century European art museumsLeiden ethnographic museum (1837 opening)

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The image could be tested on a museum whose director is also its public face, to ask whether reverence or instruction shapes the visitor's expected role.

Janes uses the phrase for the belief among boards and staff that museums must stay neutral to avoid bias and special interests, and argues that business and corporate sponsors are themselves special interest groups. (Janes 2009p. 59)

How it is used Janes applies the fallacy to the reliance on corporate, foundation and private funding, which he says leaves museums unable to act for fear of alienating sponsors. Janes sets the claim of neutrality against the obvious bias of marketplace ideology and against the historical case of the American Museum of Natural History's eugenics-tinged hall, so that neutrality appears as a choice of interests rather than the absence of one.

“marked by a rigid tribalism grounded in marketplace ideology” p. 59
the American Museum of Natural History's Hall of Human Biology and Evolutionthe Museum of Modern Art's cancelled 1940 exhibition 'For Us, the Living'

The idea that public art museums work like religious ceremonial sites while presenting themselves as secular and neutral, so that their rituals of visiting and display confer identity and legitimise the state. (Karp & Lavine 1991)

Draws on Victor Turner; Alan Wallach

How it is used Duncan applies the idea to the Louvre, reading the decree over the Apollo Gallery, the nineteenth-century ceilings and the Rotunda of Mars as a sequence that ends in France and turns princely treasure into national heritage. Duncan uses the same reading for the Metropolitan Museum of Manila, which Imelda Marcos assembled in 1975 to impress an IMF meeting and which she reads as a display of allegiance to the United States. For the Metropolitan and the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, she shows how newer primitive-art galleries disrupt the older Civilization narrative, and she concludes that controlling a museum means controlling a community's identity.

LouvreRotunda of MarsMetropolitan Museum of ManilaMetropolitan Museum of ArtMuseum of Fine Arts, Boston

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The reading can be applied to a new national museum by asking which sequence of rooms ends in the state's own history, and which ceremony visitors are invited to perform.

Bennett's term for a disciplined display practice that turns visitors' tendency to wander into a directed, sequenced way of looking. Stokes-Rees uses it to explain how the fixed route of the Hong Kong museum makes visitors take in its single storyline. (Knell et al. 2011p. 345)

Draws on Tony Bennett

How it is used Stokes-Rees applies the concept to The Hong Kong Story, arguing that the fixed route enforces the story of transformation from fishing village to metropolis. Visitors are expected to be passive viewers, and she notes that many pass most displays quickly. The concept lets her move from the content of the displays to the way they are walked through.

“Tony Bennett’s ‘exhibitionary complex’” p. 345
The Hong Kong Story, Hong Kong Museum of History

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The same route analysis could be applied to any chronological national gallery, asking where a visitor must pass and what they can skip.

Laurajane Smith's term for the official discourse of governments and experts, institutionalised in law, which determines whose values count as heritage and privileges expert knowledge over community needs. (Logan 2016)

Draws on Laurajane Smith

How it is used Reeves and Plets use the term to explain the Altai Princess dispute in the Altai Republic, where the repatriation demanded by Altaians was refused by archaeologists. Museums often became 'tools' of empire, acquiring knowledge about colonies and providing spaces to display it, but they were not the products of a single imperial plan. (Longair & McAleer 2012p. 5)

They argue that colonial museums were usually founded by peripheral initiatives, were often starved of funds and were physically inadequate, so they cannot be read as parts of an overarching imperial project. “move beyond the interpretation of museums as part of some overarching imperial project” p. 5
Colombo MuseumZanzibar MuseumMadras Museum

How it is used Basu takes this claim as the thesis to be tested against the West African record. Basu finds that colonial-era museums in British West Africa were the pet projects of individual enthusiasts, from education officers to governors, and that the Colonial Office judged antiquities 'very near the bottom of the priority list'. The concept therefore fails as a description of these museums, and he argues that the museum's paternalist assumptions still shape the Sierra Leone collection today.

National Museum of Sierra Leone, FreetownWest African colonial museum policy after the Ife bronzes

Lu, Tracey L-D (2014). Museums in China: Power, Politics and Identities. London: Routledge.

A museum is a stable public institution in which material items of nature, culture and human remains are selectively collected, organised and presented to convey the values of certain social segments and serve their interests. Stakeholders and curators act as agents who select, classify, manage and exhibit objects, and so construct how visitors understand China. (Lu 2014p. 58)

The dispositions, values and tastes formed by a country’s academic, political and ideological discourse, which lead curators and scholars to adapt to the system they work in. (Lu 2014p. 135)

Draws on Bourdieu

How it is used Lu uses habitus to explain why two senior curators in public museums adapt to Party frameworks without formal training in museology, and why Marxist historical materialism has become the habitus of many Chinese scholars, leaving villagers without a role in ecomuseum decisions. It moves the argument from state censorship to the mindset of the people who run museums.

“Bourdieu’s concept of ‘habitus’ (1977) can” p. 135

The effect on visitors of the curator's authority, which is reinforced by the museum's building, its guards and the power networks that boards and cultural agencies form around it. (Lumley 1988p. 222)

Hooper-Greenhill ties the curator's words to the networks of elected boards and cultural agencies, and the architecture and guards to a message of social control and classical culture. The concept lets her argue that visitor numbers do not show how a museum communicates, because the authority effect shapes who comes at all.

Macdonald, Sharon; Fyfe, Gordon (eds.) (1996). Theorizing Museums: Representing Identity and Diversity in a Changing World. Oxford: Blackwell.
context, contest and contentMacdonaldcoinstheoretical framing

The editors' three-part scheme for theorising museums: as contextualizing and contextualized in time and space, as contestable and contested over identity and difference, and as having a content that includes their form and institutional practice. How it is used The scheme lets the editors argue that museums are a process as well as a structure, so that a display must be read as the product of outside forces, of contest, and of its own routines. The editors use it to frame the Enola Gay dispute, the Williamsburg black history tours and the early Tate as cases where content shapes outcome, and they argue that every museum is a statement of position, a theory of the world.

“a museum is a process as well as a structure” PDF p. 11
Enola Gay exhibition, National Air and Space MuseumColonial WilliamsburgTate Gallery and the Chantrey Bequest

MacKenzie, John M. (2009). Museums and Empire: Natural History, Human Cultures and Colonial Identities. Manchester: Manchester University Press.
exhibitionary complex and surveillanceMacKenziecriticisestheoretical framing

Bennett's idea of the exhibitionary complex as a system of surveillance, in building design and in displays that became self-monitoring and incorporated visitors into the controlling vision of power, with its roots in Foucault's concern with discipline and control. (MacKenzie 2009p. 16)

Draws on Tony Bennett; Foucault

How it is used MacKenzie says this model does not fit the colonial setting. Colonial museums seldom welcomed indigenous visitors, so whatever control they exercised lay in collecting and display rather than in monitoring visitors, and the surveillance of whites was diffuse, since many museums did not follow the architectural plan and viewers made of displays what they would. The author uses the critique to justify a narrative approach to colonial museums.

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask who was watched in a museum built for a colonial population, and whether a Southeast Asian museum's displays of local people were meant to discipline visitors or to show them to themselves.

The equation the Crown made in the public eye between the careful conservation of royal art and good government. The museum thus became a sign of the state's competence, and during the Revolution a sign of popular sovereignty and later of military power. (McClellan 1994p. 7)

How it is used McClellan argues that conservation, usually treated as a technical matter, was the political core of the museum from 1750 onwards. McClellan traces how the idea was used first by the monarchy, then by the Republic to counter perceptions of turmoil, and finally to justify confiscation in conquered lands, which lets the book read restoration disputes as political events.

“forging an equation in the public eye between careful conservation of valued art treasures and good government” p. 7
Luxembourg Gallery restorationsRevolutionary Louvre restoration disputeConfiscations after the 1798 convoy

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask whether the conservation of objects from a colonised or recently independent state was presented to foreign or domestic audiences as evidence of the government's competence, and whose restorations were publicised.

politico-historical model of artMcClellanadaptstheoretical framing

The model in which the state of the arts follows the political regime: despotism brings decline and liberty brings renewal. Lenoir presented it in chronological period rooms in which French art rises to the sixteenth century and declines under Louis XIV. (McClellan 1994p. 193)

Draws on Winckelmann

How it is used McClellan shows how Lenoir took Winckelmann's causal link between politics and the arts and used it to make the museum serve successive regimes, first Republican, then Imperial, then royal. The idea lets the author read the Musee des monuments as an argument about the Revolution rather than a simple collection, and explains why the catalogues changed with each regime.

“politico-historical model to suit Republican ideology” p. 193
Musee des monuments francais, period roomsCatalogues of 1809 and 1815

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The model can be used on any museum that narrates a national art history through regime change, asking how a collection of objects from a deposed or displaced polity would be reordered by a successor state.

Morse, Nuala (2021). The Museum as a Space of Social Care. London: Routledge.
non-performativeMorseadaptsanalytic concept

A speech act in which a statement of commitment stands in for the effects it names, so that naming existing work as, for example, community engagement means the institution does not need to change anything. (Morse 2021p. 81)

Draws on Sara Ahmed; John Austin

How it is used Morse adapts Ahmed's model from universities to the museum. Morse applies it to TWAM's mission statement and the claim that 'everything we do is community engagement', arguing that this explains why staff experience resistance even though the institution professes a commitment. It gives her a way to describe institutional power through language rather than through policy failure.

“naming can be a way of not bringing something into effect.” p. 82
TWAM mission statement and 'everything we do is community engagement'the People's Gallery

Pearce, Susan M. (1992). Museums, Objects, and Collections: A Cultural Study. Leicester: Leicester University Press.

Power runs through all social relations, so power and knowledge are closely linked and tied to ideas of truth and reason. Marxist critiques see museums as legitimating the capitalist order, while post-structuralist critiques see power as everywhere and meaning as groundless. (Pearce 1992p. 330)

The Spirit Sings, Glenbow Museum, Calgary (1988)Royal Scottish Museum Evolution galleryRoyal Academy Age of Chivalry (1987-8)

The interpretation of nineteenth-century civic museums as a mechanism by which those in authority maintained social control in newly industrialised cities, which later gave way to an educational rather than an authoritarian approach. (Pearson 2017)

The network of commercial and official displays (private museums, dioramas, panoramas, dealers' galleries, arcades, department stores) within which public museums and exhibitions were placed, and through which the crowd was made visible to itself as a viewing public. (Rees Leahy 2012p. 20)

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The type could be compared with class-based period displays in other national museums, asking which objects were moved to make a historical formation visible and which were left out.

vulgar sociology (vulgarny sotsiologizm)Silinacriticisescritique

The label used from 1932 onwards to condemn the economics-based reading of art in the Marxist displays as an oversimplification of Marxism. Silina shows that it was applied to displays that combined a formalist vocabulary with class sociology. (Silina 2026p. 125)

How it is used Silina treats the label as a verdict of the period that has since shaped historiography. Silina’s argument is that the displays were formally complex, so the charge mis-describes them and hides the formalist analysis behind the labels. The term becomes the object of her criticism rather than a tool she adopts.

Decisions about whose objects are collected and how they are displayed and interpreted include or exclude social groups; museums can open or close historical and cultural possibilities, and can therefore help create or preserve the dominance of some groups. (Silverman 2010p. 20)

Silverman applies the idea to people with disabilities, lesbians and gay men, and the Scottish museums' strategy for removing barriers to participation.

The idea lets her ask why the Mall museum, built for a largely non-Native audience, was never itself questioned, and why the legislation left it in place.

Objects taken from actors in one context of space, time and meaning are made the observer's own in another. The argument is that the museum's power is held by the institution rather than by the observer or by the object. He cites the 1970 Albany and Onondaga wampum dispute as the point at which ownership and the right to represent meaning became contested in American museums.

Greenhalgh compares the Franco-British Exhibition of 1908 with the Victoria and Albert Museum of 1989 to make the point.

He concludes that single master narratives are rare and that close architectural history resists the Foucauldian reading.

Publics, class and taste

Bourdieu's cultural capital and distinction, Habermas's public sphere, Duncan's civilising ritual, and concepts about who visits, how, and what visiting does. 63 concepts from 43 texts

The approaches in this group treat the museum as a place where social position is staged: who is admitted and on what terms, how visitors are expected to look and move, and what the visit does to them. They ask how public institutions reproduce or contest class, gender and national belonging, and whether a visit can be read as ritual or as a public act. Pierre Bourdieu stands behind most of the material, reached through Zolberg, Merriman, Burch, Hill and Barrett (Sherman & Rogoff 1994p. 56; Vergo 1989p. 161; Hill 2012p. 31; Barrett 2011p. 122). Jürgen Habermas's public sphere and Carol Duncan's civilising ritual are the other main supports, the first through Barrett and Hill, the second through Tseng, Koksal and Lu (Barrett 2011p. 15; Duncan 1995p. 21–22; Tseng 2008p. 13; Meyer & Savoy 2014p. 236). The centre of the theme lies in Duncan's Civilizing Rituals, Barrett's Museums and the Public Sphere and Hill's two studies of English and women's museum history (Duncan 1995p. 21–22; Barrett 2011p. 15; Hill 2005p. 9; Hill 2016PDF p. 117).

Bourdieu: distinction and cultural capital

Cultural capital, the taste and schooling that let a visitor feel at home in a museum, comes from Bourdieu's 1960s surveys of European art museums. Merriman finds the account too narrow for general museum visiting and replaces class determination with Kelly's leisure opportunity (Vergo 1989p. 161; Vergo 1989p. 163). Zolberg applies the surveys to the Centre Pompidou and concludes that art education can be treated as a social right (Sherman & Rogoff 1994p. 56). Hill (49) shows Preston's classical casts needing knowledge to be read, while Hill (37) treats women donors as negotiating their gifts rather than being reproduced by the museum's social order (Hill 2005p. 144; Hill 2016PDF p. 19). Burch applies distinction to the Hultén bequest, which turned a donor's taste into the Moderna Museet's legitimacy (Hill 2012p. 31). Barrett argues that free entry is optional entry for those who already hold the capital (Barrett 2011p. 122).

Habermas: the public sphere and counter-publics

Habermas's public sphere, the realm between private life and the state where opinion forms, is reworked by Barrett into a cultural public sphere in which display counts as public discourse, though museums fall short of it (Barrett 2011p. 168). Barrett adds Nancy Fraser's counter-publics: a group admitted to a public that demands reason and decorum must give up what makes it distinct, so Indigenous keeping places are read as counter-publics rather than as one community (Barrett 2011p. 36). Hill (49) rejects the idealised account, arguing that the public sphere was bound up with middle-class hegemony and that competing publics existed (Hill 2005p. 10).

Duncan: the civilising ritual

Duncan reads public art museums as ritual sites with a marked-off space, a script that visitors perform and a promised transformation, drawing on van Gennep, Turner and Douglas (Duncan 1995p. 11–12; Duncan 1995p. 21–22). Tseng applies the frame to the Imperial Museums of Meiji Japan, arguing that the Nara museum moved icons into a different ritual frame from temple airings (Tseng 2008p. 13; Tseng 2008p. 144). Hill (37) tests the visiting script against women's diaries and letters and finds that scripts were ignored or resisted as often as followed (Hill 2016PDF p. 118). Lu adapts the civilising ritual to China, where a revolutionary museum visit is a pilgrimage that builds the myth of the Party (Lu 2014p. 138). Koksal argues that the passage through Istanbul's national displays, not their content, carried the civic message (Meyer & Savoy 2014p. 244). Duncan also takes Turner's liminality, though its non-western origins mean it cannot simply be laid over western aesthetic experience (Duncan 1995p. 11–12; Duncan 1995p. 21–22).

Rational recreation and moral improvement

Hill (49) takes rational recreation as the frame for municipal museums and tests it on visitors: the reform aim largely failed, while the museum's role in defining middle-class status succeeded (Hill 2005p. 137). Hopkins reads the 1851 Great Exhibition and South Kensington as altruistic yet condescending, a civilising instrument that also kept visitors in their place (Hopkins 2021). Sellers ties rational amusement to Peale's instruction through pleasure, and shows the same appeal undone by commercial imitators (Sellers 1980p. 1; Sellers 1980p. 334). Hudson adds the question of entry, since visitors were admitted "as a privilege, not as a right" until the public changed the terms (Hudson 1975p. 6).

Visitor agency and the meaning of the exhibit

Wintle applies Baxandall's model to Brighton, reconstructing audience reactions from press reports because visitor records are scarce; for her, "the agency of the visitor forms a crucial element of how an exhibit is received" (Longair & McAleer 2012p. 48). Baxandall's own model treats an exhibition as a field of three agents, maker, exhibitor and viewer, and argues that exhibitors cannot represent cultures and should offer a pregnant cultural fact instead (Karp & Lavine 1991). MacKenzie, unable to document colonial reception, points to festival visitors to Southeast Asian museums as evidence of identities they found for themselves (MacKenzie 2009p. 277). Silverman replaces the transmission model with meaning-making, in which visitors build meaning from their own relationships (Silverman 2010p. 16). Witcomb uses affect in a "pedagogy of feeling" to reopen received narratives, and Scates and Harris apply Rosenwein's emotional communities to a learners' forum that neither teacher nor curator controlled (Damousi 2020p. 187; Damousi 2020p. 209).

The high-low divide: kitsch, carnival and popular culture

Kirshenblatt-Gimblett treats bad taste as a category made by the arbiters of good taste, unstable as objects circulate and are recoded by subcultures, and sets Greenberg's and Adorno's kitsch against Bakhtin's grotesque body to expose class assumptions (Kirshenblatt-Gimblett 1998p. 276). Bennett grants carnival's signs at Blackpool Pleasure Beach, then rejects the Bakhtinian reading, since carnival is licensed and incorporative (Bennett 1995p. 242). Coombes uses Bennett's popular as an area of exchange between classes to argue that the public helped produce ethnographic knowledge of Africa (Coombes 1994p. 3). Outka shows commerce deploying and dismantling the high-low divide, and argues that the contradictions this produced were constitutive of modernism (Outka 2009p. 12).

Veldkamp: margins of authenticity

Veldkamp's margins of authenticity measure how authentic an object must look for a given viewer to take it as real, and they vary with the viewer and the purpose of the visit (Veldkamp 2014p. 570). He applies them to the Kongju glass cases, where close viewing suits a scholar but not a casual visitor, and to the Leiden celadon replica, where the margins are tighter for specialists (Veldkamp 2014p. 573). His argument is that replica display can serve a general public (Veldkamp 2014p. 573).

Debates and limits

Merriman finds Bourdieu's account too narrow, while Duncan accepts the class division but denies that social distinction exhausts what museums contain (Vergo 1989p. 161; Duncan 1995p. 5–6). Barrett's counter-public objects that inclusion asks the group to surrender its difference, and Grinell adds that bodies can appear in ways an institution does not allow (Barrett 2011p. 36; Fromm 2014p. 178). Several of these texts leave the visitor's side thinly documented: MacKenzie concedes that the view "from below is much less documented than the curators' view, where above is well documented; that from below much less so" (MacKenzie 2009p. 277).

Carrying it over to a new case

  • Ask who was admitted on what terms in a museum's first decades, and when access came to be claimed as a right; apply Hudson's privilege-against-right test to a national museum today (Hudson 1975p. 6).
  • Compare a provincial museum's visitor books with the reform aims in its founding documents, to see which groups came of their own accord and which were channelled by schools or employers (Hill 2005p. 9).
  • Trace the marked-off zones, visitor scripts and promised transformations of a museum in an Asian capital, and ask whether its civic ritual works like the Louvre's (Duncan 1995p. 21–22).
  • Read a national museum's galleries against press reports and visitor comments, as Wintle did, to see what the curators did not control (Longair & McAleer 2012p. 48).
  • Repeat the logic of Bourdieu's survey in a museum of Asian art in a Western city, asking which visitors already have the cultural capital to read its labels (Barrett 2011p. 122).
  • Ask, for a community museum, whether its displays require the group to adopt the museum's terms of address or let it speak in its own terms (Barrett 2011p. 36).
  • Compare a museum's stores, offices and public galleries to see how far Hooper-Greenhill's division between producing and consuming subjects has been bridged (Hooper-Greenhill 1992p. 190).

Where to start reading

  • Duncan, Carol (1995). Civilizing Rituals: Inside Public Art Museums. London: Routledge. Duncan on public art museums as civic ritual, the frame most used in this set.
  • Barrett, Jennifer (2011). Museums and the Public Sphere. Chichester: Wiley-Blackwell. Barrett on the cultural public sphere, counter-publics and cultural capital in open museums.
  • Vergo, Peter (ed.) (1989). The New Museology. London: Reaktion Books. Merriman's test of Bourdieu's distinction against a national visitor survey.
  • Sherman, Daniel J.; Rogoff, Irit (eds.) (1994). Museum Culture: Histories, Discourses, Spectacles. Minneapolis: University of Minnesota Press. Zolberg on habitus and whether art museums can reach a broad public.
  • Hill, Kate (2016). Women and Museums, 1850–1914: Modernity and the Gendering of Knowledge. Manchester: Manchester University Press. Hill on women donors, women visitors and visiting scripts.
  • Longair, Sarah; McAleer, John (eds.) (2012). Curating Empire: Museums and the British Imperial Experience. Manchester: Manchester University Press. Wintle on visitor agency and the reconstruction of audience reaction.
  • Veldkamp, Elmer (2014). “Keeping It Real: The Exhibition of Artifact Replicas in National Museums of Korea”. Acta Koreana, 17.2 (December 2014): 557-581. Veldkamp on the margins of authenticity in replica display.
  • Kirshenblatt-Gimblett, Barbara (1998). Destination Culture: Tourism, Museums, and Heritage. Berkeley: University of California Press. Kirshenblatt-Gimblett on bad taste as a circulating category.

Asma, Stephen T. (2001). Stuffed Animals and Pickled Heads: The Culture and Evolution of Natural History Museums. New York: Oxford University Press.
kinds of spectacle (odd, wonderful, grotesque)Asmaadaptstypology

Spectacle is the common ground of education and entertainment. Asma separates spectacles of the odd, the wonderful and the grotesque, which can lead to reflection, from spectacles that only lead back to themselves and turn the spectacle into the commodity. (Asma 2001)

Draws on Plato; Freud

How it is used Asma applies the typology to the museum edutainment debate: the same spectacle can attract a consumer or a learner, so the question is which kind of spectacle a museum produces. Asma defends the Field Museum's suitcase dioramas as intoxicating but 'companions to the intellect, not combatants', and sets Gould's criticism of commerce beside his own view that the emotions must be addressed.

Barrett, Jennifer (2011). Museums and the Public Sphere. Chichester: Wiley-Blackwell.
cultural public sphereBarrettadaptstheoretical framing

Habermas's bourgeois public sphere, reworked so that the museum counts as a cultural public sphere: a place of public discourse made through display and visual address as well as through print and talk. Barrett argues that museums are necessarily engaged in spatial and visual discourses of the public sphere. (Barrett 2011p. 15)

Draws on Habermas

How it is used Barrett takes Habermas's concept as her starting point, keeps its place between state and private life, and adds the spatial and visual discourses that Habermas largely dismissed, so that display itself becomes a public form. This lets her ask whether a museum can be genuinely public, open to all and democratic, and conclude that museums are a cultural public sphere that falls short of its ideals.

“museums are necessarily engaged in not only spatial discourses of the public sphere but also visual notions of the public sphere” p. 168
the Louvrethe British Museumthe National Museum of Australia

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could test whether a regional or national museum works as a cultural public sphere by comparing its visual display and its visitor address with the publics that form around it.

counter-publicBarretttestsanalytic concept

Alternative publics formed by women, workers and other groups excluded from Habermas's bourgeois public sphere. Barrett uses the term, following Fraser and others, to judge whether inclusion in a public institution means that the excluded group must give up its difference. (Barrett 2011p. 33)

Draws on Nancy Fraser

How it is used Barrett applies Fraser's critique to museums: inclusion in a public that demands reason and decorum brackets difference, so the counter-public must surrender what makes it distinct. Barrett uses this to test the claim that museums are open to all, and reads the alternative publics formed around Indigenous keeping places through counter-publics rather than as a single community.

“the counter-public must surrender its difference” p. 36
museum visitors in generalIndigenous keeping places

cultural capitalBarrettappliesanalytic concept

Bourdieu's concept of the knowledge and manner acquired through class habitus, which lets a person feel at home in a museum. Barrett reads Bourdieu and Darbel's survey of European visitors to show that free entry is optional entry for those who already have it. (Barrett 2011p. 121)

Draws on Pierre Bourdieu; Bourdieu and Darbel

How it is used Barrett uses the survey to show why open museums still exclude: the boundary moved from economic to cultural difference, and free admission does not remove it. Barrett sets Bourdieu against his critics Zolberg and Prior and against visitor metrics, arguing that cultural capital still decides who feels at home, so that museums are open in rhetoric only.

Bennett, Tony (1995). The Birth of the Museum: History, Theory, Politics. London: Routledge.

The aesthetic disposition, learned by the cultivated classes, that treats art as a matter of pure looking and so marks social distinction. Bennett uses it to explain why art galleries exclude visitors who lack the learned competences their displays assume. (Bennett 1995p. 11)

Bennett argues from this that galleries are the least accessible of public collecting institutions, so that access policy has to teach the competences that display takes for granted rather than only opening the doors.

Duncan, Carol (1995). Civilizing Rituals: Inside Public Art Museums. London: Routledge.
art museum as ritual structure (civic ritual)Duncanadaptstheoretical framing

Public art museums are settings for ritual: a marked-off space, a script that visitors perform, and a promised transformation that together carry the museum's central meanings. (Duncan 1995p. 11–12)

Draws on Arnold van Gennep; Victor Turner; Mary Douglas

How it is used Duncan reads each museum as a staged scenario rather than as a container or a building. The Louvre is the prototype civic ritual of the new state (chapter 2), the Met's marked-off rooms are a ritual of civic virtue (chapter 3), and the modern galleries stage a gendered script (chapter 5). The frame lets her treat the museum's values as built into its arrangement rather than as neutral display.

liminality (liminal zone of the museum)Duncanadaptsanalytic concept

A mode of consciousness outside ordinary time and social life, which the museum opens for visitors who step back from their daily concerns. (Duncan 1995p. 11–12)

Draws on Arnold van Gennep; Victor Turner

How it is used Duncan takes Turner's category and applies it to the museum visitor, but modifies it: Turner's data came mostly from non-western cultures, so the concept cannot simply be laid over western aesthetic experience. The idea lets her show the museum as a space that promises renewal of the self, which other writers such as Clark, Bazin and Schildt also describe in different terms.
