Bourdieu's account of cultural distinctionDuncancriticisescritique

Bourdieu's sociology of museum visiting, in which the art museum gives some visitors a feeling of cultural ownership and makes others feel excluded. Duncan admires it but does not accept it in full. (Duncan 1995p. 5–6)

Draws on Pierre Bourdieu; Alain Darbel

How it is used Duncan keeps Bourdieu's point that museums divide visitors by class, then argues that museums also have substantive cultural content that cannot be reduced to social distinction. Duncan uses this qualification to justify reading the museum's rituals and values, not only its class effects, and she states that she does not study real visitors at all.

European art museums (Bourdieu and Darbel's 1960s survey)

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could test whether the class exclusion Bourdieu found also operates in a Western museum of Asian art, and whether its Asian rooms cut across that exclusion.

Findlen, Paula (1994). Possessing Nature: Museums, Collecting, and Scientific Culture in Early Modern Italy. Berkeley: University of California Press.
distinction and accessFindlenappliestheoretical framing

The museum as a means by which collectors displayed status and controlled who could enter, and how the visit was read. Access was graded by gender, social standing and humanist credentials, so the collection expressed the distinctions of early modern society. (Findlen 1994p. 100)

Draws on Pierre Bourdieu

How it is used Findlen takes Bourdieu's account of taste and distinction and applies it to the rules of visiting: collectors set the conditions of access and shaped the meaning of the visit for those eligible to cross the threshold. The idea explains why visitors' records show patrician men of learning rather than women and servants, and it lets her treat the museum as a social setting in which relationships were formed rather than as a neutral store of objects.

“the tendency of early modern society to articulate distinctions.” p. 100
Aldrovandi's visitors' bookCospi's Bologna museumPierre Borel's museum at Castres

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask who was excluded from a museum opened to visitors in a colonial or treaty-port setting, and whether a visitor book or pass system records the same distinction of gender and rank.

Fromm, Annette B.; Golding, Viv; Rekdal, Per B. (eds.) (2014). Museums and Truth. Newcastle upon Tyne: Cambridge Scholars Publishing.
fusion of horizonsGoldingappliesanalytic concept

Dialogue in the museum forum, carried out with the whole person and not only with information, can widen each side's view of its own assumptions and of the other's tradition until the two horizons merge. (Fromm 2014p. 10)

Draws on Gadamer

How it is used Golding takes Gadamer's idea of 'fundamental conversation' into the museum forum and her practice at the Horniman Museum, arguing that objects and emotions, not only information, make the fusion possible. Golding then sets this against relativism, insisting that the museum must also take firm stands against injustice. The idea lets her argue that engaging the body and emotions can widen visitors' horizons in a way that content alone cannot.

“is key to the fusion of horizons” p. 19
Horniman Museum, London (Golding's practice)Work with the English Defence League case study

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could test whether a community programme at a regional museum changes visitors' stated assumptions about a neighbouring group, using the same before-and-after logic as Golding's practice.

public space as space of appearanceGrinelladaptstheoretical framing

Public space is not a container or an institution; it arises only between embodied people who appear to one another. On this account a museum with gates and admission fees is a public institution offering public services, but not a public space in that sense. (Fromm 2014p. 178)

Draws on Judith Butler; Barrett; Habermas; Ranciere

How it is used Grinell adapts Barrett's terminological analysis of 'the public' with Butler's account of embodied appearance and grievability. Grinell uses the distinction to show that the unclear role of the Museum of World Culture in the Jerusalem exhibition was exposed to public critique, and to argue that museums are important spaces where bodies may appear in ways previously denied. The concept lets him separate what a museum is institutionally from where its visitors can actually appear.

“Public space is where we become, or come to be” p. 178
Museum of World Culture, Göteborg (Jerusalem exhibition)

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask, for a given museum, which bodies are visibly admitted to its spaces, and whether entry conditions such as fees, opening hours or dress codes decide who can appear there.

Genoways, Hugh H.; Andrei, Mary Anne (eds.) (2008). Museum Origins: Readings in Early Museum History and Philosophy. Walnut Creek, CA: Left Coast Press.
museum education as informal educationthe editors (Section IV introduction)criticisesanalytic concept

The editors use the term informal education for popular instruction in museums, and treat it as an older practice of museum professionals rather than a movement that began with the 1969 Belmont Report. (Genoways & Andrei 2008p. 153)

How it is used The editors use the concept to challenge the standard origin story of museum education. By pointing to articles from the nineteenth century and to the many women who worked as public educators, they argue that educational thinking was a core part of the profession from the start. It lets the editors present Section IV as a history of early practice, not an introduction to modern programmes.

“museum professionals have been thinking and writing about museums as educational institutions for the last 150 to 200 years” p. 153
Brooklyn Children's Museum (Gallup)museum-school loan collections (Carolyn Rea)Peabody Academy and the Massachusetts public library link (Morse)

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The argument invites a check of when museums in a given region began to make instruction a formal aim, including in East and Southeast Asian museums, before the post-1960s education movement that is usually dated as the start.

Hill, Kate (2016). Women and Museums, 1850–1914: Modernity and the Gendering of Knowledge. Manchester: Manchester University Press.
cultural capital and prestigeHilladaptsanalytic concept

The idea that museums have historically reproduced social prestige through the cultural capital of donors and curators, and that a donation is a negotiation in which donor and curator each bring a social and cultural standing to bear on the object. (Hill 2016PDF p. 19)

Draws on Tony Bennett; Pierre Bourdieu

How it is used Hill takes the Bennett and Bourdieu account of museums as instruments of prestige and adapts it to donation. Hill argues that the outcome of a gift depended on the donor's capital, the curator's need for the object and the object's own value, so that women donors were negotiating rather than simply being reproduced by the museum's social order.

“social prestige through cultural capital” PDF p. 19
donations by women to provincial and London museums, 1880-1914Lady Charlotte Schreiber's ceramics and playing-card gifts

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask which donors to a regional museum in Southeast Asia, such as resident planters or missionaries, had enough cultural capital to get their gifts displayed and how the curator's need for material shaped the negotiation.

visiting scriptHilltestsanalytic concept

The museum visit as a set ritual, its script built into architecture and display, which visitors perform in more or less conforming ways, drawn from Duncan and Wallach's account and extended by Rees Leahy's study of visiting bodies. (Hill 2016PDF p. 117)

Draws on Carol Duncan; Alan Wallach; Helen Rees Leahy

How it is used Hill tests the script against evidence Duncan and Wallach did not use: the diaries and letters of women visitors, and the anxieties about female bodies in museums. Hill finds that scripts were as often ignored or resisted as followed, and that women used the museum for sociability, copying and self-education, and in 1913-14 for suffragette protest.

“scripts were ignored or” PDF p. 118
lady copyists at the National Gallerystudent tickets and conversazionisuffragette attacks at the National Gallery and the National Portrait Gallery, 1913-14

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The script could be tested against visitor letters or diaries from a colonial museum in Southeast Asia, to see whether European women visitors followed or resisted the display's implied account of empire.

feminine public sphereHillcombinesanalytic concept

Women's public life as a partly separate sphere built on service, pleasure and sensibility, set beside the masculine public sphere that Habermas described, and not always a classic public-sphere institution. (Hill 2016PDF p. 118)

Draws on Jürgen Habermas; Megan Smitley; Simon Morgan; Erika Rappaport; Ruth Hoberman

How it is used Hill combines Habermas's public sphere with Rappaport's point that women's pleasure, consumption and service in public were not separate. Hill treats museums as sociable spaces like shops and clubs, not only as places of civic debate, so that visiting became both a pleasure and a claim to feminine citizenship.

“proclaimed women as feminine citizens” PDF p. 120
women's museum visits, especially on weekdays by 1900museum tickets, lectures and conversazioni

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The combined model could ask whether women's visits to a colonial-era museum in Southeast Asia, which were also shopping and social occasions, can be read as public citizenship in a colonial city.

Hill, Kate (2005). Culture and Class in English Public Museums, 1850–1914. Aldershot: Ashgate.
rational recreationHillteststheoretical framing

The mid-nineteenth-century movement that treated leisure and culture as a means of improving the working class, and in which municipal museums became one of the middle-class tactics for reform. Hill uses it as the frame that the visitor evidence has to test. (Hill 2005p. 9)

Draws on Peter Bailey; Tony Bennett

How it is used Hill accepts that municipal museums were part of rational recreation but asks why they were thought to solve class problems. Hill tests the frame against visitors: working-class groups, clubs and schools used some museums, and visitors promenaded and ignored pictures as at music halls and parks. Hill concludes that the aim of reforming working-class behaviour largely failed, while the museum's role in defining middle-class status largely succeeded.

“middle-class tactics for reforming the working class” p. 9
Sheffield Mappin Art GalleryPrestonBirminghamLeicesterHorniman Museum

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could check a provincial or colonial museum's visitor records against the reform aims stated in its founding documents, and identify which visiting groups were self-organised and which were channelled by schools or employers.

public sphereHillcriticisestheoretical framing

The realm between private life and the state where public opinion forms and citizens debate, which the municipal museum offered through universal access. Hill treats it as a historically specific construction tied to middle-class identity and not as an ideal of open debate. (Hill 2005p. 9)

Draws on Habermas; Eley

How it is used Hill uses the concept to explain how a museum could present itself as universal and educational. Against Habermas's idealised account, he argues that the public sphere was bound up with middle-class hegemony, that competing public spheres existed and that some groups were excluded altogether. The museum is then read as one arena in which a contested public sphere was organised, not as an ideal forum for debate.

“to show how this public sphere was very closely bound up with the development of” p. 10
municipal museums in EnglandSheffield Mappin Art Gallery

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask who was excluded from the universal access a colonial or port-city museum advertised, and whether its public sphere was in fact a middle-class or settler one.

cultural capitalHillappliesanalytic concept

The ability to appropriate cultural goods or cultural meaning, which confers status and legitimises the distinction between social groups. Museums, through their objects and displays, both distributed it and made it exclusive. (Hill 2005p. 12)

Draws on Pierre Bourdieu; Paul DiMaggio

How it is used Hill uses cultural capital to show how donors and councils placed objects in museums to display their own taste and status. The clearest case is Preston, where the classical casts and statues were presented with little labelling and needed knowledge to read. He combines the idea with DiMaggio's account of Boston's Fine Art Museum, which moved from education to aesthetic focus and so became impenetrable to those without training, and concludes that the museum offered cultural capital to all while keeping it exclusive in practice.

“worked to increase each other’s cultural and symbolic value” p. 144
Preston Harris Museum statues and castsLiverpool's evolutionary hierarchyJacson and Foster collections, Preston 1894

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask which objects a regional or colonial museum enshrined to display donor taste, and whether its labelling gave visitors any means of reading them as cultural capital.

Hill, Kate (ed.) (2012). Museums and Biographies: Stories, Objects, Identities. Woodbridge: Boydell Press.
Bourdieu’s distinction and the donor’s legitimacyBurchappliestheoretical framing

Bourdieu’s account of taste and cultural capital, in which the inherited possession of art and collections confers legitimacy, so that the donor’s choices become the museum’s authority. Burch reads Hultén’s bequest through this account. (Hill 2012p. 30)

Draws on Pierre Bourdieu

How it is used Burch applies Distinction to Pontus Hultén’s bequest, arguing that the gift turns a donor’s taste into the Moderna Museet’s legitimacy and that the Pontus Hultén Study Gallery keeps the donor present. Burch sets the concept against two episodes that test the bequest: a catalogue that places the donor’s family photographs among the artists, and the Brillo box scandal. Bourdieu’s point about the ‘museum effect’ is used to show why the gallery was named and sited to keep the works embedded in a biography.

“Moderna Museet is just such a ‘social space’.” p. 31
Pontus Hultén Study Gallery, Moderna Museet, StockholmThe Pontus Hultén Collection catalogueBrillo box episode

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The idea could be tested on a donation to a regional Asian art collection in a Western museum, asking whether the donor’s taste became the institution’s legitimacy and how the display kept the donor visible.

Ho, Denise Y.; Li, Jie (2016). “From Landlord Manor to Red Memorabilia: Reincarnations of a Chinese Museum Town”. Modern China.
living spaces (after Robson)Ho, Liadaptstheoretical framing

The claim that museums in China are living spaces that serve their visitors' emotional and ritual needs, building on James Robson's suggestion that museums in Asia function in religious ways. (Ho & Li 2016p. 4)

Draws on James Robson

How it is used The authors take Robson's religious reading and push it further: the Landlord Manor did not only function in religious ways but was based on city god temples. This turns the museum into a secular temple in which visitors are judged and warned, and it gives the article its link between a Mao-era exhibit and older ritual forms.

“museums in China have been living spaces” p. 4
Landlord Manor MuseumRent Collection Courtyard sculptures

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): One could ask whether temples, shrines or ancestral halls supplied the models for other Asian state museums, and check the claim against exhibit planning files.

Hooper-Greenhill, Eilean (1992). Museums and the Shaping of Knowledge. London: Routledge.
producing and consuming subjectsHooper-Greenhillappliesanalytic concept

The division created by the public museum between knowing producers, who work in hidden spaces on catalogues, inventories and installations, and consuming visitors, who receive finished knowledge in surveyed public galleries. The text says the division carries relations of advantage and disadvantage. (Hooper-Greenhill 1992p. 190)

How it is used Hooper-Greenhill uses the division to explain why visitors’ roles have been fixed and why curatorial work has been hidden. Hooper-Greenhill then traces how open storage, offices next to public galleries and participatory exhibitions have begun to bridge it. Hooper-Greenhill’s example is Birmingham’s Gallery 33 project, which she presents as an attempt to let many voices speak; she accepts this as a gain while questioning whether it changes who controls meaning.

“In the public museum the producing subject ‘works’ in the” p. 190
Children’s Museum, BostonGallery 33, Birmingham Museum and Art GalleryThe People’s Story, Edinburgh

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could compare how a museum’s stores, offices and public galleries are arranged, and who is allowed to see the cataloguing work, as a measure of how far the division has been bridged.

Hopkins, Owen (2021). The Museum: From Its Origins to the 21st Century.
public museum as moral improvementHopkinscriticisesanalytic concept

The nineteenth-century idea that museums should educate the working classes and improve their taste, which Hopkins sees as both altruistic and condescending. The museum is a civilising instrument that also keeps its visitors in their place. (Hopkins 2021)

How it is used Hopkins uses the 1851 Great Exhibition and the South Kensington precinct to show the museum becoming an instrument of public education. Hopkins sets the altruism of the project against its paternalism and against fortunes built on exploitation, which lets him argue that the public museum was also a form of social control.

“But on another, it could also be viewed as emerging from a rather condescending view of the working classes for whom education and good taste were seen as vital”
Great Exhibition (1851) and South Kensington Museum (V&A)Frick CollectionMetropolitan Museum and American Museum of Natural History, New York

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask whether public museums built in East or Southeast Asia in the same period were framed as civilising instruments for workers or students, and who the intended audience was.

Hudson, Kenneth (1975). A Social History of Museums: What the Visitors Thought. London: Macmillan.
visitors admitted as a privilege, not a rightHudsonappliesanalytic concept

Eighteenth- and early nineteenth-century museums admitted visitors on the terms of autocratic owners and directors, through tickets, written applications and fees, so that gratitude rather than criticism was expected. Hudson sets this against a later reading of admission as a right. (Hudson 1975p. 6)

How it is used Hudson organises his first two chapters around the contrast, testing it on the British Museum's 1759 Statutes, Hutton's 1784 visit, the Vienna and Dresden galleries and Joseph II's free admission. The contrast lets him show that the change from privilege to right came from the public and from the great exhibitions, not from the collections themselves.

“were admitted as a privilege, not as a right” p. 6
British Museum 1759 StatutesVienna Imperial Gallery and BelvedereDresden galleryCharleston, Peale's and Salem museumsthe 1851 Great Exhibition

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The same test could be applied to a national or regional museum of today: who was admitted on what terms in its first decades, and which admission rules changed when the public began to claim access as of right.

class differences in how visitors see museumsHudsonappliesanalytic concept

Visitors of different social classes give different answers about what a museum is and how it should be visited, so that the public's response to museums varies by class. Hudson presents this through the Bourdieu and Darbel survey. (Hudson 1975p. 113)

Draws on Pierre Bourdieu; Alain Darbel

How it is used Hudson uses the French survey as evidence, not as a model, to show that working-class visitors compare museums to churches and prefer to go round in groups with a guide, while educated visitors avoid guides. Hudson adds British figures from 1973 to show the same middle-class skew in London.

“66 per cent of working class people gave the answer 'a church'” p. 114
art museums in Paris and the provinces (mid-1960s survey)four London museums (1973 survey)

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The church-or-library question could be put to visitors of a regional museum in another country to see whether class differences in its image of museums persist.

several publics and the chief reasons for a visitHudsonappliestypology

A museum serves several publics, and should pick a few main reasons for visiting and arrange its displays to serve them. Hudson takes the typology of aesthetic, romantic and intellectual motives from the director of the Leiden ethnology museum. (Hudson 1975p. 74)

Draws on Peter H. Pott

How it is used Hudson presents Pott's three motives as the basis for arrangement, and links them to the demands each makes on lighting, background and the number of objects shown. It lets him argue that arrangement should follow visitors' purposes rather than the curator's scholarly order.

“Each of these, in Dr Pott's view, makes demands on the way” p. 74
National Museum of Ethnology, LeidenRijksmuseum lighting tests (1898)

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The three motives could be used to classify the visitors of a museum of a single region and to test whether its displays serve each of them.

Janes, Robert R. (2009). Museums in a Troubled World: Renewal, Irrelevance or Collapse?. London: Routledge.
temple, not forumJanesadaptstypology

Janes adopts Duncan Cameron's distinction between the museum as temple, a traditional place of collecting and exhibiting, and the forum, a space for confrontation, experimentation and debate, and argues that the two should coexist rather than be chosen between. (Janes 2009p. 30)

Draws on Duncan Cameron

How it is used Janes uses the duality to diagnose why museums have stayed remote from social problems: practitioners treat the temple and the forum as alternatives, when Cameron wanted both. Janes then reads Cameron's 1971 call for forums against the museums that do exist, arguing that the temple's authority is what makes irrelevance likely.

“the temple and the forum are two sides of the same coin” p. 31
the museum's refusal to take up social and environmental issues in its programmesa museum whose own definition of a forum is questioned in the Canadian context

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The duality could be used to compare an East or Southeast Asian national museum's exhibition practice with its public forum programmes, asking whether one has displaced the other.

civil society and the public sphereJanescriticisestheoretical framing

Janes places museums in the civil society that lies between the family and the state, meaning voluntary and civic associations in liberal societies, and argues that museums have been given little attention as agents of the collective good beyond education and entertainment. (Janes 2009p. 21)

How it is used Janes uses the public sphere as the frame for his thesis, and then criticises a consultant's narrower definition of civil society, in which citizens have equal opportunity to participate in public life, as too general to show what museums should do. Janes insists on the purposeful crafting of missions that enable participation, so the concept becomes a standard for judging museum missions.

“If the thesis of this book can be said to reflect any particular aspect of modern” p. 21
museum mission statements and their role in public lifethe civil-society definition of a consultancy report on museums

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The concept could be used to ask whether museums in Asian cities that depend on state funding can act as civil society organisations, and how that differs from museums that have to earn their own revenue.

Jasanoff, Maya (2005). Edge of Empire: Conquest and Collecting in the East, 1750–1850. London: Fourth Estate.
collecting as self-fashioningJasanoffappliesanalytic concept

Collecting is a way for individuals of any nationality to use objects to advertise, hone or shape their social persona, and so to gain standing in a society they could not enter by office or birth. The author applies it to Europeans in India as well as to Indian princes. (Jasanoff 2005p. 7)

How it is used Jasanoff uses the idea to read collectors such as Polier, whose Lucknow collection was a social investment that opened doors shut to him by Company hierarchies, and Clive, whose collecting aimed at a British peerage. The idea lets her show that a collection could be a route into a social world rather than only a record of conquest. She also uses it to set European and Indian collectors side by side as practising the same habit.

“between collecting and self-fashioning was itself a cross-cultural phenomenon, extending from” p. 7
Antoine Polier's Lucknow collectionRobert Clive's art and Indian objectsIndian princes' collections

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The idea could be tested on a museum founder or donor whose gifts from Asia were meant to build a social position in a metropolitan city. A researcher could ask which collections in a Western museum from East or Southeast Asia were acquired mainly for the collector's own standing.

know-thy-enemy approachJasanoffappliesanalytic concept

A collection formed to educate an audience about the tastes and manners of those who rule them, in which the owner presents a European interior to Indian visitors. The author treats the Marble Palace as a deliberate inversion of the usual collecting of foreign objects. (Jasanoff 2005p. 317)

How it is used Jasanoff applies the idea to Rajendro Mullick's Marble Palace in Calcutta, which she calls a glorious pretender built to instruct Indian visitors. Jasanoff uses it to argue that collecting Western art could be a form of collecting back, parallel to Egyptian attempts to recover their own heritage. The approach gives her a way to read Mullick as neither a mere imitator nor a simple collaborator.

“The Marble Palace in this sense was a glorious pretender” p. 317
Rajendro Mullick's Marble Palace, Calcutta

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The idea could be applied to a museum built by a non-European elite to show its public an outside culture, such as one in Bangkok or Tokyo of the late nineteenth century. It raises the question of who the intended visitor was.

Karp, Ivan; Lavine, Steven D. (eds.) (1991). Exhibiting Cultures: The Poetics and Politics of Museum Display. Washington: Smithsonian Institution Press.
exhibition as a field of three agentsBaxandallcoinstheoretical framing

A model in which an exhibition is a field where the maker of an object, its exhibitor and the viewer each act in different ways, and where the three meet in the space between the object and its label. (Karp & Lavine 1991)

How it is used Baxandall uses the model to analyse a Kota mbulu-ngulu and its label. Baxandall shows that a label explains an object by cause, while the viewer looks for visual interest and then seeks causes, shuttling between the two. From this he argues that exhibitors cannot represent cultures and should instead offer a pregnant cultural fact, or a foreign concept such as pi-i for Chinese painting, and leave the viewer to work at it. The model replaces the idea of an exhibition that represents a culture with one that sets conditions for a viewer's activity.

“a notion of exhibition as a field in”
Kota mbulu-ngulu with a labelFang bieri figure beside itMaori carving with its chips left on the groundChinese painting explained through pi-i

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The model suggests a way of testing a museum label, by asking which causes it offers the viewer and whether a foreign word would make the viewer work harder than an explanation would.

frame analysis of festival participationBauman and Sawinappliesmethod

The idea that festival participants make sense of what they do through frames such as performance, demonstration, instruction, exhibition and work, and must negotiate and test these frames with each other, staff and audiences. (Karp & Lavine 1991)

Draws on Erving Goffman

How it is used Bauman and Sawin apply frame analysis to participants at the 1987 Festival of American Folklife, based on fieldwork with about twenty participants from Michigan. Demonstration proved the most common frame because it tolerated failure and unfinished products, but it caused friction for people who saw their work as occupation, such as Great Lakes fishermen and a cherry grower. The frame lets them show that participants resist the staff's show-must-go-on demands, from private jokes to a staged joke at the folklorists' expense, and they conclude that a fairer politics of representation must treat participants as agents.

“a basic contextualizing question that lies at the heart of frame analysis”
1987 Festival of American FolklifeGreat Lakes fishermen at the festivalMichigan cherry growerEast Lansing festival

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The frames can be used to ask how participants in any living-culture display, such as a craft demonstration or a community performance, understand what they are doing and whether they can refuse the frame set for them.

Kirshenblatt-Gimblett, Barbara (1998). Destination Culture: Tourism, Museums, and Heritage. Berkeley: University of California Press.
bad taste and kitsch as circulating categoriesKirshenblatt-Gimblettcriticisesanalytic concept

Bad taste is a category produced by the arbiters of good taste, and it is unstable: objects circulate through exchange, are recoded by subcultures and return as retro goods. How it is used The author applies the idea to The Encyclopedia of Bad Taste and its twin Quintessence, and to subcultures such as punks and low riders that recode commodities. Setting Greenberg's and Adorno's kitsch against Bakhtin's grotesque body lets her show the class assumptions in the modernist case, and her question about a world of kitsch or a liberating pluralism remains open.

“Kitsch is to taste what superstition is to religion—somebody else's mistake.” p. 276
The Encyclopedia of Bad TasteQuintessence: The Quality of Having Itpunk and low-rider subcultures

Knell, Simon J.; Aronsson, Peter; Amundsen, Arne Bugge; et al. (eds.) (2011). National Museums: New Studies from Around the World. London: Routledge.
symbolic capital transferred through looted objectsBarnesappliesanalytic concept

Bourdieu's notion of the honour, prestige and legitimacy held by an authoritative institution, which Barnes applies to the transfer of Chinese objects into British hands, linking Chinese things to a victorious Britain. (Knell et al. 2011p. 397)

How it is used Barnes uses symbolic capital to explain how the Qianlong lacquered throne, taken from the Nan Yuan hunting park in 1901, gained prestige for its holders. “transference of symbolic capital” p. 397
Qianlong lacquered throne, Victoria and Albert MuseumNan Yuan hunting park

Krech, Shepard, III; Hail, Barbara A. (eds.) (1999). Collecting Native America, 1870–1960. Washington: Smithsonian Institution Press.
cabinet to public museumLeeappliesperiodisation

The shift in the nineteenth century from elite, private cabinets of curiosity to public museums serving a broader audience, which Lee treats as a change in the purpose of displaying objects. (Krech & Hail 1999)

How it is used Lee uses Duncan's argument that the princely cabinet was the antecedent of the public museum to date Jackson's career: the Princeton cabinet was a small select collection, while the Sitka museum and the world's fair exhibits aligned him with a democratizing age. Princeton cabinet (1879)Sheldon Jackson Museum in Sitkaworld's fair exhibits

Logan, William; Nic Craith, Máiréad; Kockel, Ullrich (eds.) (2016). A Companion to Heritage Studies. Chichester: Wiley Blackwell.

The range of intensities in which visitors respond affectively to the same site or exhibition, from intense reactions to traumatic or nationalist histories to a flat, dutiful performance of visiting that reinforces consensus narratives. (Logan 2016)

How it is used Smith and Campbell introduce the term to argue that visitor research should measure affect, not only learning or numbers. They draw on visitor interviews at about 45 museums and sites, and on statements from visitors to the Tenement Museum in New York to show that physically being in the building produced empathy. The concept lets them argue that emotion must be built into interpretation rather than dismissed as commodification.

“We develop the idea of “registers of engagement” to describe this observation.”
Tenement Museum, New Yorkabout 45 museums and sites in England, Australia and the United States

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The term could structure a visitor study of a Southeast Asian war or heritage site, asking where visitors fall between dutiful and intense registers of engagement.

Longair, Sarah; McAleer, John (eds.) (2012). Curating Empire: Museums and the British Imperial Experience. Manchester: Manchester University Press.
visitor agencyWintleappliesanalytic concept

An exhibit's meaning is produced partly by the visitor's own expectations, learning and motives, so a curator's message is one influence among many and not the sole determinant of what audiences understood. (Longair & McAleer 2012p. 48)

Draws on Michael Baxandall; Eilean Hooper-Greenhill

How it is used Wintle applies Baxandall's model to Brighton, where Toms's displays were weakened by high acquisition rates, cramped galleries and understaffing. Because visitor records are scarce, she reconstructs audience reactions from press reports of tours, bazaars and performances, and finds that visitors combined museum messages with stock images of the 'other' drawn from entertainment. Hooper-Greenhill's 'master narrative' is treated as hard to locate in practice.

“the agency of the visitor forms a crucial element of how an exhibit is received” p. 48
Brighton Museum ethnographic galleries (Toms)Brighton bazaars and the Hiawatha performancePress reports of tours through the cannibal man-catchers and tomahawks

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could test the concept on a museum with surviving visitor books, comparing what visitors wrote with what the press reported about the same galleries.

Lu, Tracey L-D (2014). Museums in China: Power, Politics and Identities. London: Routledge.

Museum work gave scholars and curators the means to accumulate cultural capital, the knowledge and standing that let them establish social status and authoritative discourse in their field. (Lu 2014p. 56)

Draws on Bourdieu

How it is used Lu uses cultural capital to explain how the museum work and fieldwork of Licent and de Chardin raised their authority in academic life, and later to describe intellectuals in the Communist period who developed their cultural capital while meeting the needs of the Party. This links the missionary and state chapters across more than a century.

Visiting a museum is a ritual that civilises the visitor; Lu takes the concept from Duncan’s analysis of art museums. (Lu 2014p. 138)

Draws on Duncan

How it is used Lu adapts Duncan’s concept to China. In mainland China a visit to a museum of revolution is a pilgrimage rather than a civilising ritual, and it builds the myth of the Party and of Mao as deities. The adaptation ties museum visiting to the political function of the revolutionary museums, which the book treats as central.

“Duncan (1995) has analysed how visiting art museums is a ‘civilizing ritual’.” p. 138
National Museum of Revolution, Beijing

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask, at a museum in another state with a revolutionary narrative, whether visitors are guided through the displays as a pilgrimage, and what the route and labels direct them to feel.

How it is used Bennett uses Gramsci's warning to judge the post-war folk, open-air and living history museums: 'the people' appear in idealised forms. Bennett applies it to the Beamish tape-slide show, which presents the region's people as cloth-capped and unchanging, and sets the Hyde Park Barracks in Sydney and the People's Palace in Glasgow against it as cases that tie everyday life to political traditions. The concept lets him separate the form of a folk museum from the politics of what it shows.

Fyfe takes this as the starting point of his study of the Tate. (Macdonald & Fyfe 1996PDF p. 206)

How it is used Fyfe accepts the claim that museums institutionalise the cultural arbitrary but qualifies it: subordinate groups may partly penetrate that arbitrary, reproduction may occur through fragmentation, and institutions must be included in the account. Fyfe applies the qualified version to the Chantrey controversy, arguing that the Tate became a contested site where the meaning of British art was decided, not a medium that disclosed the intrinsic Britishness of its collection.

“Bourdieu’s argument is that museums conceal the arbitrariness of” PDF p. 206

Mary Douglas's two dimensions of social ordering: group, the strength of boundaries and of belonging, and grid, the rules that order relations between people across time and space. How it is used The authors map the Cartwright, Brown and Grainger households' relations to museums along grid and group, and use Bourdieu's field of class struggle to account for the moves households make along those dimensions. They find Douglas a more subtle guide to the cultural grammars of their subjects than Bourdieu's Kantian and popular aesthetics, and find that Bourdieu supplies the dynamics that the grid/group thesis lacks. The combination lets visiting be read as a cultural strategy through which class is produced.

MacKenzie cannot document reception across the colonial museums and says so, but he points to Chinese, Indian and Malay visitors to Southeast Asian museums during their religious festivals, and to the growing Chinese New Year attendance at Singapore, as evidence that visitors found identities of their own there. The period phrase for a museum that educated visitors through enjoyment, so that the diffusion of knowledge was pursued as pleasant instruction. Sellers says Peale's museum implemented it, and that commercial imitators later turned the same appeal into cheap entertainment. (Sellers 1980p. 1)

How it is used Sellers ties 'rational amusement' to Rousseau's educational theory, in which visitors are led from familiar objects toward the unfamiliar. Sellers then uses the phrase to explain the museum's decline, since the same appeal let oddity shows succeed. “Rational amusement” was this museum’s instrument but also, by a curious irony, its eventual undoing.” p. 1

Zolberg tests the idea against the Centre Pompidou, whose audiences proved as narrow as any French museum's, and against American outreach programmes, and concludes that art education can be treated as a social right.

Siegel, Jonah (ed.) (2008). The Emergence of the Modern Museum: An Anthology of Nineteenth-Century Sources. New York: Oxford University Press.

A public museum is always a compromise among competing aims, such as protecting precious objects, enabling advanced study, and introducing unprepared visitors to culture, shaped by what objects were acquired, what buildings were available and what funding could be won. (Siegel 2008PDF p. 11)

How it is used The editor uses the idea to frame the whole anthology and to read the selections as records of these trade-offs rather than as one story of progress. He notes that parliamentary testimony moves from art history to the effect of weather on paintings to the pay of guards, so the sources cannot be sorted into neat categories. The idea lets him show the heterogeneity of the material without naming a single purpose as the museum's essence.

Silverman, Lois H. (2010). The Social Work of Museums. London: Routledge.

A systems-based model in which a museum experience is shaped by physical, personal and social factors, and in which the people a visitor encounters, real or implied, are part of the experience. How it is used Silverman uses meaning-making to explain how a museum visit yields benefits for self, pair, family and group: personal connections brought into the visit produce social consequences that are measurable at each level. Objects, things and materiality

Appadurai and Kopytoff on the social life and biography of things, Gell, Latour and actor-networks, material-culture theory, and the turn to the senses and affect. 64 concepts from 44 texts

Approaches in this theme treat the museum object as an active thing, not a neutral carrier of information. They ask what objects do once collected and displayed, how their meanings shift as they pass between contexts, and how bodies and senses take part in encounters with them. Our texts draw on Kopytoff and Appadurai on the social life of things (Hill 2012p. 174; Conn 1998p. 24), on Latour and Gell on agency and entanglement (Lu 2014p. 88; Hicks 2020), on Pearce's material-culture theory, built on Hegel, Miller and Barthes (Pearce 1992p. 135), and on Merleau-Ponty, Dewey and Tomkins in the turn to the senses and affect (Dudley 2010p. 5; Dudley 2010p. 41).

Dudley's volume on museum materialities (Dudley 2010p. 5) and Pearce's study of collections (Pearce 1992p. 135) stand at the centre of the theme. Siegel (Siegel 2020p. 19) tests the promise of an unmediated encounter with things, and Hicks (Hicks 2020) rejects the biography model outright.

Kopytoff's cultural biography of things

Kopytoff's account of things with significant ages, changes of status and new identities is the most widely used inspiration here. Wehner and Sear use it to plan the National Museum of Australia's Australian Journeys gallery, writing a biography for each key object and treating it "as in some way similar to persons" (Dudley 2010p. 146). Tythacott applies it to five Putuo Island figures at Liverpool Museum from 1867 to 1997, arguing that no display restored the temple's darkened setting (Hill 2012p. 174). Veldkamp treats replicas of a Paekche incense burner as things with a life of their own, not as failed copies (Veldkamp 2014p. 558). Alberti criticises the method for neglecting the afterlife of objects in the museum, and adds conservation, cataloguing and storage as the stage where their lives continued (Alberti 2009p. 5).

Exchange and removal from use

Several authors test the claim that a museum object, removed from use, gains meaning through that loss. Conn, drawing on Simmel and Appadurai, argues that clamshells and potsherds gained a didactic value in display, a value that depended on visitors (Conn 1998p. 24). Arnold grants that museums decontextualise objects but denies that the economic system around them is sealed off, so one object acquires several uses at once (Arnold 2006). Paver adapts Thompson and Pomian, who treat rubbish as a passage to the museum, by showing that Nazi-era objects were displayed in the containers they were stored in after 1945, so disuse explains what is shown (Paver 2018p. 175).

Latour, Gell and the actor-network

Latour's refusal of a gap between material and social is applied in several ways. Lu maps the networks of Royal Asiatic Society members, French Jesuits and British officials to argue that the Shanghai Museum could not have been founded or survived without them (Lu 2014p. 88). Siegel adopts the refusal but prefers "realism" to "network", since networks can flatten the individual responses Siegel studies (Siegel 2020p. 32). Cras and Debluë adapt Latour's argument on abstraction to Paris economics exhibitions of 1855 to 1900 and to the Swiss Social Museum (Guy 2024p. 205). Hicks criticises entanglement, the Gell and Thomas idea, for omitting the moments when relations are cut by killing and looting, and proposes necrography in its place (Hicks 2020).

Marx, Benjamin and fetishism

Commodity fetishism is the main critical frame, though authors use it differently. Jordanova adapts Marx and Freud, arguing that museums invite us to look and so draw us to reify objects as commodities (Vergo 1989p. 38). Clifford applies Marx to argue that the museum mystifies the labour and power of acquisition, and proposes returning objects to their lost status as fetishes (Stocking 1985p. 239). Ho and Li criticise the commodification thesis itself: Mao-era souvenirs such as the "Struggle the Landlord" cards re-present the past in ways that can undercut official narratives (Ho & Li 2016p. 25). Sherman adapts Quatremère's 1796 and 1815 texts, which describe the Louvre as turning a "monument of painting into a picture shop", placing them beside Marx and Benjamin to show that the critique predates both (Sherman & Rogoff 1994p. 131). McClellan accepts that works lose force out of context but argues that "the aura of the work in situ has not been destroyed so much as replaced with a new aura" (McClellan 1994p. 201).

Pearce and the structure of collections

Pearce takes objectification from Hegel, as developed by Miller, to argue that systematic collections keep subject and object in an ongoing relation, while souvenir and fetish collections fix one against the other (Pearce 1992p. 135). Applying Ellen's processes to Yoruba material, Pearce explains a collection's dual emotional and intellectual nature, using Barthes's signifier and signified (Pearce 1992p. 67). Asma treats specimens as ciphers whose meaning depends on the system they sit in, so Hunter's London arrangement says something other than earlier cabinets did (Asma 2001).

Phenomenology and the encounter with the thing

Siegel tests the promise of an unmediated encounter, in Heidegger's jug, Bennett's storm drain and Fried's objecthood, and finds that Heidegger's thingness and Bennett's epiphany both presuppose a divide between subject and object (Siegel 2020p. 18; Siegel 2020p. 19). Siegel also criticises the demystifying school, which explains art by its interests and leaves the pleasure of matter unexplained (Siegel 2020p. 15). Dudley draws on Merleau-Ponty and Dewey, arguing that the object becomes manifest through the viewer's interaction, and tests this on Celia Fiennes's surprise at how light a cane in the Ashmolean was (Dudley 2010p. 5; Dudley 2010p. 9). Wingfield's darsan, being seen by the image, explains why visitors pause before the Sultanganj Buddha (Dudley 2010p. 65).

Affect and the senses

Witcomb takes affect from Tomkins as a pre-rational response that can transform viewers. It explains why a hand-made model of Treblinka in Melbourne produced grief where professional Holocaust models produced numbness (Dudley 2010p. 41). Witcomb's sticky objects, drawn from Ahmed, gather feeling across the eight stories of Love and Sorrow, so that its emotions are built by design (Damousi 2020p. 175). Wehner and Sear coin object knowledge, the embodied understanding of form, weight and making, and insist that "Object knowledge is, we would argue, embodied knowledge" (Dudley 2010p. 151). Ting adapts Tilley's object as metaphor to ceramics, reading a Ding bowl through familiar sensations and conceding that the approach may distort formal qualities (Dudley 2010p. 189). Morse extends the approach to care, arguing that handling museum objects gives care in the museum a distinct materiality (Morse 2021p. 189).

Context, display and changing meaning

Barringer's point about removal and display underlies the editors' afterword, which follows a figurehead from HMS Seringapatam through a dockyard to the National Maritime Museum (Longair & McAleer 2012p. 8). Saumarez Smith applies the idea of meaning transformed within the museum to three V&A cases, arguing that artefacts keep changing meaning after acquisition (Vergo 1989p. 9). Aldrich assesses displays by whether they keep an object's pedigree, including its colonial route into the collection (Aldrich 2005p. 290).

Debates and limits

Several texts dispute the approach's central claims. Alberti doubts that objects are the main actors, arguing that people acting on them shaped disciplines and meanings (Alberti 2009p. 5). Hicks goes further, rejecting biography and entanglement together, and presents a looted object's museum history as one of loss rather than accumulation (Hicks 2020). Yanni sides with Secord that specimens beat motorised models, but treats Gould's absolute faith in authenticity as a wishful leap back (Yanni 1999p. 155). What the approach tends to leave out, according to these texts, is the violence of removal (Hicks 2020) and the afterlife of objects in the museum (Alberti 2009p. 5).

Carrying it over to a new case

  • Trace one object through successive accession entries, labels and displays in a regional museum, asking whose interests changed its identity at each stage, as Tythacott did for the Putuo figures (Hill 2012p. 174).
  • Write a biography of a Chinese ceramic or Southeast Asian ritual object, from making and use to acquisition and display, and mark where its context was lost or restored (MacKenzie 2009p. 11).
  • Compare the object knowledge of visitors who handle a ceramic in a study room with those who see it in a case, to find which qualities appear only through handling (Dudley 2010p. 151).
  • Ask which objects in a regional display recur across stories and which carry feeling rather than information, as Witcomb's sticky objects do (Damousi 2020p. 175).
  • Audit a gallery's labels for how much they say about each object's route into the collection, and compare that with what they say about the source society (Aldrich 2005p. 290).
  • Trace one museum object's status across the institutions that hold it, rather than explaining it by a single social or material base (Siegel 2020p. 32).
  • Test whether a non-Western object gains meaning through removal from use, or whether its community's uses survive in labels and visitors' practices (Arnold 2006).

Where to start reading

  • Pearce, Susan M. (1992). Museums, Objects, and Collections: A Cultural Study. Leicester: Leicester University Press. objectification, Ellen's processes and the limits of structuralism
  • Siegel, Jonah (2020). Material Inspirations: The Interests of the Art Object in the Nineteenth Century and After. Oxford: Oxford University Press. the unmediated encounter set against demystification and network theory
  • Hicks, Dan (2020). The Brutish Museums: The Benin Bronzes, Colonial Violence and Cultural Restitution. London: Pluto Press. the case against biography and entanglement, and the violence of removal
  • Alberti, Samuel J. M. M. (2009). Nature and Culture: Objects, Disciplines and the Manchester Museum. Manchester: Manchester University Press. object biography and the afterlife of objects in the museum
  • Hill, Kate (ed.) (2012). Museums and Biographies: Stories, Objects, Identities. Woodbridge: Boydell Press. Tythacott's Putuo figures as a sequence of classifications
All 64 concepts recorded under this theme, by text
Alberti, Samuel J. M. M. (2009). Nature and Culture: Objects, Disciplines and the Manchester Museum. Manchester: Manchester University Press.
object biography (social life of things)Alberticriticisesanalytic concept

Objects are treated as having a life or career, with significant ages, changes of status and relationships with people, and the questions asked of a person's biography can be asked of them. (Alberti 2009p. 5)

Draws on Igor Kopytoff; Arjun Appadurai

How it is used Alberti uses the approach to organise chapters 4 to 6, following objects from acquisition through practice to display. Alberti criticises it, however: objects were not the main actors, people acting on them shaped disciplines and meanings, and object biographers neglect the afterlife of objects in the museum. Alberti therefore adds the museum's own practices of conservation, cataloguing and storage as the stage where objects' lives continued.

“Material culture is thus afforded a metaphorical ‘life’ or ‘career’.” p. 5
sperm whale skeletonChurchill coin bequestLindow Man exhibitionKhnum-Nakht mummy

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could follow a single East Asian object from purchase to storage to display and ask which people, rather than which object, changed its status at each stage.

Aldrich, Robert (2005). Vestiges of the Colonial Empire in France: Monuments, Museums and Colonial Memories. Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan.
pedigree of objectsAldrichappliesmethod

Every object in a non-Western collection has a history of how it entered the collection, which is part of its colonial history. Display that removes this information erases part of the object's pedigree and the memory of the colonial context in which it was collected. (Aldrich 2005p. 268)

How it is used Aldrich assesses modern displays by whether they keep an object's pedigree. Aldrich praises the Musée Dapper's aesthetic presentation but notes its lack of colonial history, and he argues in chapter 6 that the Quai Branly and other modernised museums must trace each object's route into the collection as well as its source society. The concept lets him set aesthetic display against historical display.

“colonial patina means erasing memories of the phenomenon of colonialism” p. 290
Musée DapperMusée Guimet renovationQuai Branly project

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could audit the labels of an Asian gallery for how much information it gives on the route of each object into the collection, and compare the result with the labels' treatment of the source society.

Arnold, Ken (2006). Cabinets for the Curious: Looking Back at Early English Museums. Aldershot: Ashgate.
objects removed from use (Baudrillard and Pomian)Arnoldcriticisestheoretical framing

The claim that a museum object is by definition taken out of practical use and so gains meaning through that loss. Arnold draws on Baudrillard's distinction between using and possessing an object and on Pomian's description of museum objects as kept out of the economic circuit. (Arnold 2006)

Draws on Jean Baudrillard; Krystof Pomian

How it is used Arnold starts from this idea in chapter 8 and then criticises it. Arnold grants that museums decontextualise objects, but argues that the economic system around them is not sealed off: museums make meaning, educate, define taste and enter politics, so one object acquires several uses at once. This lets him move from whether objects have use to which uses museum objects have, which is the question his functional strategy then pursues in anthropology, medicine and decorative arts.

“Useful in flagging up an important aspect of how museums manage to de-contextualise objects”
anthropology museums and their tool displaysmedical museumsdecorative-arts collections

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask whether a non-Western object in a Western museum gains meaning through removal from use, or whether its community's uses survive in its labels and in visitors' practices.

Asma, Stephen T. (2001). Stuffed Animals and Pickled Heads: The Culture and Evolution of Natural History Museums. New York: Oxford University Press.
specimen as cipherAsmaappliesanalytic concept

A specimen has no fixed meaning in isolation. Its significance comes from the sentence or system in which it is placed, so the same bird's wing means something different in a curiosity cabinet and in a homology exhibit. (Asma 2001)

How it is used Asma uses this to set his method apart from humanities readings that let the interpreter's imagination supply the context. Asma tracks what each museum's context made of its specimens. Applied to Hunter's London arrangement, which grouped organs across species by function, the same specimens are shown to say something different from those in earlier cabinets.

“Specimens are a lot like words: They don’t mean anything unless they’re in the context of a sentence or a system, and their meanings are extremely promiscuous.”
Hunterian Museum, LondonGalerie d’anatomie comparée, Paris

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask how a Chinese or Indonesian specimen changes meaning when moved from a local collection into a European cabinet or a school display, and which system of labels and arrangement fixed that change.

Conn, Steven (1998). Museums and American Intellectual Life, 1876–1926. Chicago: University of Chicago Press.
value through exchangeConnadaptsanalytic concept

The idea, drawn from Simmel and Appadurai, that objects gain value through circulation and exchange. Museum objects are removed from circulation, so they gain an intellectual or didactic value instead, created by the systematics of display and by visitors' attention. (Conn 1998p. 23)

Draws on Georg Simmel; Arjun Appadurai; Jean Baudrillard

How it is used Conn uses the exchange theory to explain why clamshells and potsherds acquired a value in museum displays that they had lacked before. Conn adds Baudrillard's point that a removed object's meaning is up to the subject who removed it. Conn then argues that this intellectual value depended on visitors: if no one came, the objects became essentially worthless. The concept lets him describe the museum as a market for knowledge rather than for things.

“Appadurai see value as created through exchange” p. 24
natural history museums (clamshells, potsherds)Academy of Natural Sciences

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could compare the intellectual value that a display gives an object with its market price, asking how the valuation of an object changes once it leaves a museum.

Coombes, Annie E. (1994). Reinventing Africa: Museums, Material Culture and Popular Imagination in Late Victorian and Edwardian England. New Haven: Yale University Press.
hybridity as a post-colonial object conceptCoombescriticisescritique

Hybridity is the term museums now use to describe colonial objects as products of mixed cultures; the author argues that the term repeats the older discourses of racial purity and originary unity in another form. (Coombes 1994p. 217)

How it is used Coombes turns the celebration of hybridity against the museums that use it, arguing that it can disguise the unequal power that produced the objects. Coombes applies this to exhibitions of the 1980s and to the Benin bronzes on the British Museum staircase, and treats restitution demands as the place where that tension is most visible.

“racial purity, originary unity and progress have re-emerged in another form.” p. 217
Hidden Peoples of the Amazon (Museum of Mankind, 1985)The Spirit Sings (Calgary, 1988)Benin bronzes in the British Museum

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The critique could be turned on a Western museum's Asian galleries that present cultural mixture as a virtue, asking whose power the mixture disguises.

Cuno, James (ed.) (2009). Whose Culture? The Promise of Museums and the Debate over Antiquities. Princeton: Princeton University Press.
many contexts of an objectCunocriticisescritique

An antiquity has many successive contexts of making, use, reuse, collecting and display, not only the archaeological find-spot. On this view the archaeologists’ single context leaves out most of what an object is. (Cuno 2009p. 2)

How it is used Cuno uses the idea to answer the claim that unprovenanced objects are meaningless. Each later use and display counts as a context, so the Laocoön stays important though it was found by accident in 1506. The argument lets him say that museums can give objects meaning that excavation cannot.

“many contexts—and not even its original context—is not considered.” p. 3
LaocoönRosetta StoneArt Institute of Chicago objects

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could list the successive contexts of a Chinese bronze or Southeast Asian sculpture in a Western museum (temple use, dealer sale, collector’s cabinet, display label) and ask which of them the museum’s records preserve.

Damousi, Joy; Tout-Smith, Deborah; Ziino, Bart (eds.) (2020). Museums, History and the Intimate Experience of the Great War: Love and Sorrow. London: Routledge.
sticky objectsWitcombadaptsanalytic concept

Objects that accumulate layers of meaning and affect through repeated appearance in an exhibition, so that they leave a residue on those who come into contact with them. Witcomb takes the notion from Ahmed’s account of affect as what sticks and sustains connections between ideas, values and objects. (Damousi 2020p. 174)

Draws on Sarah Ahmed

How it is used Witcomb uses sticky objects to hold together the eight personal stories of Love and Sorrow. Objects such as Ruby Roberts’s returned bootie and the Kemp family’s panorama recur through the galleries and gather feeling that the faces and voices then carry to visitors. The concept lets her argue that the exhibition’s emotions are built by design rather than sentimentality.

“This residue is what Ahmed describes as affect.” p. 175
Ruby Roberts’s undelivered bootie, Roberts familyGlencorse Wood panorama, Kemp familyEliza Amery’s letter

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could trace which objects in a different museum’s display recur across stories and how their accumulated meanings change between sections, for example in a regional or colonial collection. The question is which objects in such a display hold feeling and which carry only information.

Dudley, Sandra H. (ed.) (2010). Museum Materialities: Objects, Engagements, Interpretations. London: Routledge.
object-subject engagementDudleyadaptstheoretical framing

The museum object is the meeting of a physical thing and a perceiving person, in which the object's material qualities and the viewer's sensory and emotional response together make the object real. Materiality is the sum of physical characteristics, sensory experience and meaning. (Dudley 2010p. 5)

Draws on Tilley; Pearce; Gosden; Gell; Merleau-Ponty; Dewey

How it is used Dudley uses this to challenge the object-information package model that she says museum studies assumes, and to justify the case for handling, touch and imagined sensory engagement as a building block of visitor experience. Dudley applies it to the V&A's Touch Me exhibition, handling collections and Celia Fiennes's surprise at how light a cane in the Ashmolean was, to show how visual display leads viewers to misjudge weight, texture and affective charge. The concept lets her argue that sight alone cannot give access to the material qualities of an object.

“through this interaction that the thing becomes properly manifest to the viewer” p. 5
V&A Touch Me exhibition (2005)museum handling collectionsAshmolean cane, described by Celia Fiennes in 1702

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could test the object-subject model on a Southeast Asian collection in a Western museum, asking which sensory qualities (weight, scent, surface) visitors can reach in the display and which only in handling sessions.

affect (pre-rational response)Witcombappliesanalytic concept

A pre-rational bodily response, drawn from Tomkins, that precedes meaning and is prompted by bodily movement and attention around an object. Witcomb treats it as capable of transforming viewers, not only of prompting recognition. (Dudley 2010p. 41)

Draws on Tomkins; Best; Deleuze; Baker

How it is used Witcomb uses affect to explain why a hand-made model of the Treblinka camp, shown in Melbourne, moved her to grief when professional Holocaust models left her numb. Witcomb reads the model's naive detail, colour, survivor-maker and status as a miniature as sources of its pull, and this lets her argue that such objects need interpretation that opens a gap for memory rather than closing it into a standard narrative. Affect also underwrites her critique of Stewart's account of miniatures.

“Affect is a pre-rational or pre-cognitive response to stimuli which can range from the pleasurable to the abject.” p. 41
Treblinka miniature model, Jewish Holocaust Museum and Research Centre, MelbourneProfessional Holocaust models at Auschwitz, the Imperial War Museum and the US Holocaust Memorial Museum (contrast)

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask which objects in a Chinese or Southeast Asian collection in a Western museum prompt bodily responses such as crouching, circling or peering, and whether the label opens or closes that response.

darsan (being seen by the image)Wingfieldappliesanalytic concept

A South Asian religious practice of presenting oneself before an image to be seen, in which looking is understood as a form of touching, so that the devotee is seen by and affected by the image. Wingfield uses it to explain the charisma of the Sultanganj Buddha. (Dudley 2010p. 65)

Draws on Eck

How it is used Wingfield attributes the Buddha's charisma to the skill of its makers in creating a face and eyes that seem to look, and he sets the visitors who touch the statue beside the South Asian understanding that the image sees and touches the devotee. The concept helps explain why visitors with no Buddhist commitment still pause, examine and reach out to the figure. It also lets him read the Buddha Day blessing and the Burmese monks' 'opening the eyes' ceremony as continuations of that encounter.

“The experience of darsan is not one of seeing a religious statue, but of being seen” p. 65
Sultanganj Buddha, Birmingham Museum & Art GalleryBuddha Day 2008 blessing in the Buddha Gallery

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask whether a museum's Asian religious objects draw visitors into a similar contact, and how a label or a ceremony changes it.

object biographyWehner and Searadaptsmethod

Each key object is traced through its making, use, circulation and meaning, treating the object as in some way similar to a person, so that its agency in human experience and historical change can be drawn out. The method was used to plan the National Museum of Australia's Australian Journeys gallery. (Dudley 2010p. 146)

Draws on Janet Hoskins; Kopytoff; Tilley; Gosden and Marshall

How it is used The authors use object biographies as the planning tool for Australian Journeys, writing a biography for each key object such as a gold-washing cradle, a snuff box given to Governor King in 1801 and a Latvian national dress. Colleagues judged the biographies too particular, and the authors responded by developing object knowledge as the exhibition-facing counterpart. The method lets them argue that the objects, rather than the text, should carry the meaning in the galleries.

“We conceptualized objects, to quote Janet Hoskins, ‘as in some way similar to persons’” p. 146
Australian Journeys gallery, National Museum of AustraliaGold-washing cradle from the Victorian goldfieldsSnuff box given to Governor King in 1801Latvian national dress made over twenty years

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could write object biographies for a Chinese ceramic or a Southeast Asian ritual object in a Western collection, tracing its acquisition and display alongside its making and use, to see how the museum's history shapes the object's agency.

object knowledgeWehner and Searcoinsanalytic concept

Embodied understanding of an object's form, texture, weight and construction, and of how it was made and used, which visitors gain through looking, handling and imagining. The authors call it a knowledge of being and the mechanism through which objects exert agency. (Dudley 2010p. 151)

Draws on MacDougall

How it is used Wehner and Sear coin the term to name the knowledge visitors build from the form, texture and making of objects, which they say text labels cannot give. They build exhibition devices on it: four-sided cases with the text outside, sensory stations such as an embroidered map to trace with a finger and the smell of dried sea cucumber beside Makassar trepang cauldrons, and objects to be viewed from both sides. The concept lets them argue that exhibitions should open an inter-subjective space in which visitors imagine another's experience while recognising their own.

“Object knowledge is, we would argue, embodied knowledge.” p. 151
Australian Journeys sensory stationsDàn tre bamboo instrument viewed from both sidesTrepang fishermen's cauldrons from MakassarConvict love tokens

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could compare the object knowledge of visitors who handle a Chinese ceramic in a study room with that of visitors who see it in a case, asking which qualities (weight, glaze, foot) appear only through handling.

metaphorical associationTingadaptsanalytic concept

An interpretive principle that links an object's formal qualities to visitors' personal experience and imagination, so that a Chinese ceramic can be approached through familiar sensations and emotions rather than only through typology. Ting extends Tilley's object as metaphor to ceramics. (Dudley 2010p. 189)

Draws on Tilley; Golding

How it is used Ting uses metaphorical association to frame the Creative Space project at Bristol City Museum, where students compared a biscuit to bisque, explored ceramics blindfolded and listened to music while looking at bowls and jars before writing labels. Ting treats the resulting labels, such as a black tea bowl imagined as a survivor of an explosion, as evidence that personal readings are as valid as official histories, while conceding that the approach may distort formal qualities and confirm misunderstanding. The concept lets her treat the Ding bowl, the Yuan wine jar and the Song celadon as sites of personal meaning.

“I devise an interpretive principle, metaphorical association” p. 189
Ding bowl from Dingzhou, Bristol City Museum Schiller GalleryYuan blue-and-white wine jarSong celadon bowl with peony spraySouthern Song black tea ware

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could apply the same principle to Southeast Asian textiles or instruments in a Western museum, to test whether metaphor opens meaning or displaces the object's own history.

Guy, Kate; Williams, Hajra; Wintle, Claire (eds.) (2024). Histories of Exhibition Design in the Museum: Makers, Process, and Practice. London: Routledge.
embodied and emotional labour of exhibition makingGuy, Williams, Wintlecombinesanalytic concept

The physical and emotional work of exhibition making, including affective responses that shape knowledge, carried out by makers as well as visitors. The introduction draws on Witcomb's account of affect as prerational and embodied, and on Minott's study of the emotional labour of museum workers. (Guy 2024p. 7)

Draws on Andrea Witcomb; Rachael Minott

How it is used The volume combines the two strands and applies them to exhibition makers over time, so that the emotional labour of, for example, Lacey's account of Towles or Williams's account of Poovaya-Smith becomes part of the history of design. The combination lets the editors claim that exhibitions have always been products of intellectual, emotional and embodied practice.

“between intellectual, emotional, and embodied design practices.” p. 7
American Museum of Natural History (Lacey)Cartwright Hall, Bradford (Williams)Crossroads of Continents (Charles)

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The concept could be used on mannequin makers and conservators in an East Asian museum, asking which physical and emotional work is recorded in their archives and which is lost.

re-materialisation of economic knowledgeCras, Debluëadaptsanalytic concept

The making of economic ideas visible and intelligible through objects, machines, bodily activity and playful statistics, which museums and fairs have used as the discipline grew more abstract. The authors take the abstraction of science from Latour and argue that display also re-materialises it. (Guy 2024p. 205)

Draws on Bruno Latour

How it is used Cras and Debluë adapt Latour's argument on abstraction to exhibitions, applying it to Paris economics exhibitions from 1855 to 1900 and to the Swiss Social Museum in Zurich, where a visitor-operated diorama turned social problems into matters of individual responsibility. The concept lets the authors show that the authority of economic discourse, not the type of institution, separates the displays.

“exhibitions of economics have staged the re-materialisation of” p. 205
Paris economics exhibitions, 1855-1900Swiss Social Museum, Zurich

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The concept could be used on economic or statistical displays in an East Asian museum, asking how figures and interactive devices make development or trade look like individual responsibility.

Hall, Patricia; Seemann, Charlie (eds.) (1987). Folklife and Museums: Selected Readings. Nashville: American Association for State and Local History.
performance-centered approachYoungadaptstheoretical framing

A folklore approach that studies the total performance and the events leading up to it, with a focus on process rather than on the frozen object or text. Young uses it to argue that an object should be shown with the context that produced it and with the interpretations of its makers and users. (Hall & Seemann 1987p. 102)

How it is used Young carries the approach from folklore into the anthropological museum. Young argues that an exhibit should show several interpretations of one event, including those of the people who made and used the objects, and should present the losses as well as the gains from acculturation. The approach lets her criticise pedestal displays of Kwakiutl masks, Navajo sandpaintings and Zuni pottery that present ceremonial or everyday objects as high art.

“focus on process rather than product.” p. 102
Pueblo of Zuni exhibitsKwakiutl masks on pedestalsNavajo sandpaintings and baskets

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could apply the approach to a display of an East or Southeast Asian ceremonial object and ask whose interpretation of the event the label leaves out.

Hicks, Dan (2020). The Brutish Museums: The Benin Bronzes, Colonial Violence and Cultural Restitution. London: Pluto Press.
object biographyHicksrejectscritique

The museum model in which each accession adds a layer to an object's life history, with new values and meanings as it moves between contexts, as in the 'cultural biography of objects' and 'the social life of things'. Hicks treats it as a dominant but misleading framing. (Hicks 2020)

Draws on Kopytoff

How it is used Hicks rejects the biography model rather than applying it. Hicks argues that it overstates the stability and coherence of things and that the British Museum uses it to relativise restitution claims, for example for the Parthenon marbles. Hicks sets it against Kopytoff's account of people turned into commodities, which he uses to argue that sacred royal objects were 'cargo' whose history is one of violent removal, not accumulation. The critique lets him present the museum's history of a looted object as a history of loss.

“overstating the stability and coherence of things as they move between contexts”
Parthenon (Elgin) marbles at the British MuseumPitt Rivers relational museum project

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The critique suggests testing any museum's object-history labels against the dates and circumstances of removal, to see whether a biography hides the act of taking. A researcher could ask who writes the accession narrative and what it leaves out.

entanglementHickscriticisescritique

The idea, developed by Gell and Thomas, that people and objects are mutually entangled, so that exchange between colonial and Indigenous agents is reciprocal and the categories of native and European blur. Hicks presents it as the second dominant idea that has held back discussion of colonial violence and restitution. (Hicks 2020)

Draws on Alfred Gell; Nick Thomas; Bruno Latour

How it is used Hicks criticises entanglement as a method of swapping analytical focus between the agency of people and things, which he says omits the moments when relations are cut by killing, bombardment and looting. Hicks applies this to Thomas's 'museum as method' and to the Pitt Rivers relational museum project, whose book invited readers on 'an anthropological adventure' without naming the violence. The critique lets him replace entanglement with necrography and argue that the museum should be acknowledged as a weapon.

“actively omits those moments where a relationship is constituted by separations not entanglements”
Pitt Rivers relational museum project (Knowing Things, 2007)Pacific material in Thomas's Entangled Objects

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could check any entanglement-based exhibition for the events it leaves out, such as a violent removal, a sale or a death. The question is which relations in a collection were separations rather than exchanges.

Hill, Kate (2016). Women and Museums, 1850–1914: Modernity and the Gendering of Knowledge. Manchester: Manchester University Press.
collective object biographyHilladaptsmethod

A version of object biography that follows the routes by which groups of similar objects, not single famous ones, reached the museum, so that the meanings objects carried from the home persist and can unsettle museum categories. (Hill 2016PDF p. 91)

Draws on Arjun Appadurai; Igor Kopytoff

How it is used Hill modifies the standard object biography, which depends on rich documentation, because most women's donations have a sentence or two of record. Working with groups of textiles, relics, souvenirs and 'old things' from nine museums' registers, she shows that domestic history carried into the museum and made the objects hard to classify.

“I attempt something more akin to a collective” PDF p. 91
textiles and clothing at Leicester, Norwich, Warrington and Bristolrelics and souvenirs'old things' such as bygones
