Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The method suits a thinly documented accession register, such as a colonial-era regional museum's receiving book, where single objects have little record but groups of similar gifts can show the routes by which they came in.

Hill, Kate (2005). Culture and Class in English Public Museums, 1850–1914. Aldershot: Ashgate.
objects as metonym and metaphorHilladaptstheoretical framing

A museum object is at once a real survival from its original context and a sign in the museum, so its meaning can be reinterpreted, yet its reality as a metonym gives it more power as a symbol than an obvious representation has. Hill takes the idea from Pearce and the structural anthropology of Lévi-Strauss. (Hill 2005p. 7)

Draws on Susan Pearce; Lévi-Strauss

How it is used Hill uses the idea to justify reading objects as evidence of meaning rather than as neutral specimens. It lets him argue that a trophy stands for the donor's mastery over nature while its meaning could be reinterpreted by curators. He applies it to Liverpool's trophy-like gifts and to Preston's casts, but notes that structuralism cannot address change, and so adds the historical sequence of donations to the analysis.

“The actual object, therefore, is always metonym and metaphor at the same time.” p. 7
Liverpool trophy-like giftsPreston casts and statues

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could take one object in a Western museum from Asia, such as a sword or a textile, and ask which part of its meaning is metonymic (its origin) and which metaphorical (the donor's status), and how the label changed the balance.

Hill, Kate (ed.) (2012). Museums and Biographies: Stories, Objects, Identities. Woodbridge: Boydell Press.
object biographyTythacottadaptsanalytic concept

The idea that an object has a series of lives and identities, so that its meaning depends on the sequence of contexts it passes through rather than on one moment. Tythacott applies it to the Putuo bronzes, whose identity changed with each curator and classification. (Hill 2012p. 173)

Draws on Igor Kopytoff

How it is used Tythacott follows the five Putuo Island figures from their seizure in the 1840s through Liverpool Museum’s classifications, and shows that each guardian’s interests changed what the bronzes meant. Tythacott uses the idea to argue that the original temple setting, with its darkened atmosphere and symbolic colours, was never reproduced by any of the museum’s displays. The method lets her treat museum classification itself as one of the lives of an object.

“particular moment or aspect of its lifecycle. Rather, it is accumulated experience that gives things” p. 174
Five Buddhist deity figures from Putuo Island at Liverpool Museum, 1867–1997

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could trace the successive classifications of a single Japanese or Southeast Asian object through the accession registers of a regional museum to see which curators’ interests shaped its identity. The question is what its label and category changed each time it moved.

Hill, Kate (ed.) (2021). Museums, Modernity and Conflict: Museums and Collections in and of War since the Nineteenth Century. London: Routledge.
circulations culturelles in times of strifeStammersadaptsanalytic concept

The movement of artworks between countries, which Stammers treats as a matter of wartime and revolutionary upheaval: as the chapter's sources show, political crisis pushed works out of Paris and into London sales. He applies the idea to a later period than the scholarship he cites, which he says has been developed mainly for the 1830s and 1840s. (Hill 2021p. 30)

How it is used Stammers uses the idea as a frame for the London sales after 1870. The flow of Paris art into London is set beside the Palais-Royal sales of 1792 and the Commune period, and the conclusion presents the 1870-71 pattern as a repeat of an earlier one. The Christie's consignment records let him name consigners and link wartime sales to individual collectors, so the concept is tested against documentary evidence rather than used as a loose label.

“There would be clear benefits of extending the existing work on” p. 30
Palais-Royal collections, 1792 and 1870-71Prince Napoleon's sale, London 1872Christie's sales of 1871

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could extend the idea to East Asian sales in the 1930s and 1940s, asking which wartime sales of Chinese or Japanese art passed through London or Paris and whether they followed the same pattern of consignment.

Ho, Denise Y.; Li, Jie (2016). “From Landlord Manor to Red Memorabilia: Reincarnations of a Chinese Museum Town”. Modern China.
object lessonHo, Liappliesanalytic concept

A way of teaching with tangible things that stimulates the senses as well as the mind. The Landlord Manor used it to define everyday goods in class terms, so that a grain peck became a measure of exploitation and the dragon bed was converted into days of labour. (Ho & Li 2016p. 9)

How it is used The authors read the museum as a schoolroom and show how its object lessons taught visitors to see ordinary things as evidence of class. The concept links an early twentieth-century pedagogy, the Mao-era bitterness meals and the 1964 children's book The Detestable Landlord within one argument about how material culture was made political.

“we argue that the museum was a schoolroom” p. 9
Landlord Manor Museum: oversized peck, dragon bed, winnowing machineThe Detestable Landlord (1964 children's book)

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could compare a museum's labels and object lists with the class or civic curriculum of its time, to see which everyday objects were taught as evidence of a political lesson.

commodity formHo, Licriticisescritique

The idea that Mao memorabilia sold as souvenirs and in museum shops is a commodity. The authors argue that the commodity form is more complex than the claim that commodification erases history, because marketing can offer alternative and even subversive readings of the recent past. (Ho & Li 2016p. 25)

Draws on Denton; Dutton

How it is used The authors argue against the commodification thesis by showing that Mao-era goods, such as the 'Struggle the Landlord' card game and the Jianchuan shop stock, re-present the Mao era in ways that can undercut official narratives. This makes the market one more site of contest over memory rather than its end.

“we argue that the commodity form is more complex.” p. 25
Anren souvenir shops and 'Struggle the Landlord' cardsJianchuan Museum Cluster souvenirs

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): One could test whether souvenir sales at a historical site broaden or narrow its interpretation, by comparing the objects sold with the objects on display.

Hudson, Kenneth (1975). A Social History of Museums: What the Visitors Thought. London: Macmillan.
participation and closing the intervalMcLuhancriticisestheoretical framing

Touch creates an interval between visitor and object, and the interval has to be closed, so that participation and rhythm arise from the visitor's activity. The idea is put forward by McLuhan in the 1967 seminar on museum communication, which Hudson reports. (Hudson 1975p. 91)

Draws on Marshall McLuhan; Harley W. Parker

How it is used Hudson reports the McLuhan and Parker position in a 'Catalogue of Notions' and then judges it: the ideas are fashionable and will soon seem dated, and open-air museums may not meet McLuhan's definition of participation. Hudson uses the idea as a test for the open-air museum rather than adopting it.

“the interval has to be closed” p. 91
1967 seminar on museum communicationopen-air museums and historic houses

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The idea of closing the interval could be applied to a single object-label or handling case, asking whether touch or talk changes what the visitor does.

Impey, Oliver; MacGregor, Arthur (eds.) (1985). The Origins of Museums: The Cabinet of Curiosities in Sixteenth- and Seventeenth-Century Europe. Oxford: Clarendon Press.
trade goods versus curious objectsImpeyappliesanalytic concept

A distinction between goods sold in trade and objects kept as curiosities, which Impey says must be made later, since in the early period of trade even ordinary goods could be treated as curious in Europe. (Impey & MacGregor 1985p. 365)

How it is used Impey uses the distinction to trace how Japanese goods moved from trade to collecting over the seventeenth century, rather than assuming collectors' pieces from the start. Impey sorts the lacquer into true trade goods made to European orders, special orders such as the van Diemen box, and chance pieces such as the Copenhagen picnic set, and notes that Japanese goods were at first not much sought after in Europe.

“be treated as such in Europe” p. 365
Dutch-ordered Namban and export lacquer coffers and cabinetsvan Diemen box (V&A)Copenhagen lacquer picnic setBurghley House porcelain

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could sort the Asian goods in a given European collection into trade, special-order and chance categories to see when each entered the household and when it became a collector's piece.

migration of objects between cabinet categoriesImpey, MacGregorappliesanalytic concept

The idea that an object's place in a collection changed with knowledge and with its availability: unicorn horn lost its status once identified as narwhal, and porcelain moved from the Kunstkammer into the household as it became common. (Impey & MacGregor 1985PDF p. 19)

How it is used The introduction uses these cases to show that the categories of the cabinet are not fixed in the objects, so that contemporary terms cannot be relied on to classify a collection. It also gives the reverse case, a majolica service that entered the inventories only later, once it was accepted as a work of art or an antique.

“migration of objects from one type of collection to another” PDF p. 19
unicorn horn identified as narwhalporcelain moving into the householdAlbrecht V's majolica service

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): An object's accession, relabelling and movement between inventories could be traced to show when its status changed, as a way of reading a collection's history.

Kavanagh, Gaynor (ed.) (1996). Making Histories in Museums. London: Leicester University Press.
interpretative flexibility of technology (SCOT)Fitzgeraldadaptstheoretical framing

Technologies do not have one inevitable form. Different social groups give them different meanings, so their form and function are shaped by whose interests count. Fitzgerald takes this from the social construction of technology as developed by Bijker and Pinch. (Kavanagh 1996p. 124)

Draws on Bijker; Pinch

How it is used Fitzgerald proposes a SCOT-based interpretative style in place of the internalist and celebratory styles, so that exhibitions show the failures and the costs of technology as well as its benefits. Fitzgerald illustrates the approach with a 1993 Manchester exhibition using a bicycle display, hairdryer cartoons and a kitchen with interactive disability barriers.

“Individual modern technologies mean very different things to different groups of people in society.” p. 125
1993 Manchester technology exhibition (bicycle, hairdryer cartoons, kitchen with disability barriers)a proposed civil aviation exhibition

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could apply the method to an industrial or transport technology in an Asian museum and ask which groups, such as workers, neighbours or the state, give it different meanings.

museum narrative as the present author's accountOwenappliesanalytic concept

Following Shanks and Tilley and contextual archaeology, museum narratives about the past reflect the present author's social and personal experience and cannot simply explain past realities. Objects carry symbolic meanings that the display must interpret. (Kavanagh 1996p. 203)

Draws on Hodder; Shanks; Tilley

How it is used Owen applies this to archaeological galleries, testing three principles (objects as expressions of social life, links to the present, and admitting interpretation) against the Museum of London, Colchester and Stoke-on-Trent. Owen finds the People Before London gallery closest to these principles because it admits the bias of the record.

“narratives in archaeology displays do not explain past realities, but discuss past material culture” p. 203
Museum of London, People Before London galleryColchester Castle MuseumStoke-on-Trent City Museum

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The question of whose present shapes an archaeological narrative could be asked of displays of Southeast Asian prehistory in Western museums.

Krech, Shepard, III; Hail, Barbara A. (eds.) (1999). Collecting Native America, 1870–1960. Washington: Smithsonian Institution Press.
recontextualization of sacred objectsLeeappliesanalytic concept

The process by which removing an object from a ritual setting and placing it in a collection detaches it from the practice it served, so that the object no longer speaks for the ceremony. (Krech & Hail 1999)

Draws on Nicholas Thomas

How it is used Lee applies Thomas's point that missionaries were attracted to sacred artifacts to Jackson's collection. Lee argues that appropriation both removed objects from circulation and changed their meaning, so that the mask in an exhibit repudiates the ceremony it once served. The idea gives the chapter its explanation of why missionaries valued sacred objects.

“Detaching an artifact from its ambient effectively neutralized the practice as well as the object”
Jackson's collection of sacred Tlingit masks and objects

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The question for a collection in an East or Southeast Asian temple or village context is which objects were removed from ritual use, by whom and when, and whether the collector's label kept the ritual meaning or replaced it.

Logan, William; Nic Craith, Máiréad; Kockel, Ullrich (eds.) (2016). A Companion to Heritage Studies. Chichester: Wiley Blackwell.
embodimentAkagawaadaptsanalytic concept

The idea that a cultural skill lives in a person, passed on from one body to another, so that the succession of a craft matters as much as its material form for authenticity and for intangible heritage. (Logan 2016)

Draws on Yanagi Soetsu; John Collins; Taylor

How it is used Akagawa uses embodiment to argue that Japanese conservation philosophy, from the Mingei movement and the 1950 Cultural Properties Law to the living national treasures, shaped the Nara Document and the UNESCO intangible heritage model. Akagawa then shows the term dropping out of UNESCO's wording, and so contests the model's claim to be neutral about materiality.

“Only when a skill that is embodied in a person is passed on and embodied in another is the succession born”
Mingei folk-craft movement, JapanCultural Properties Law (1950)Living National Treasures programmeNara Document on Authenticity (1994)

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The idea could be used to ask, for a museum collection of crafts in a Southeast Asian country, whether the collection preserves the objects or the practice of making them.

Longair, Sarah; McAleer, John (eds.) (2012). Curating Empire: Museums and the British Imperial Experience. Manchester: Manchester University Press.
meanings of objects inflected by display contextLongair, McAleerappliestheoretical framing

Objects change meaning with the context of their display, and moving them from a periphery to the imperial centre alters how they are understood, while keeping them near their origin also repurposes them. (Longair & McAleer 2012p. 8)

Draws on Tim Barringer

How it is used The editors take Barringer's point about removal and display and apply it in the afterword to two objects. A carved figurehead from HMS Seringapatam, probably made in India, is read as possibly showing Tipu riding a roc; its meaning shifts from warship to dockyard to the National Maritime Museum and then to a 2011 display on British relations with Asia. The Tiger's own chapter, in turn, follows its shift from trophy to masterpiece, so that repatriation would change its meaning again.

“the meanings of objects were inflected, and even reinvented, by the context in which they were displayed” p. 8
Tipu's Tiger (East India House, India Office, Imperial Institute, V&A)HMS Seringapatam figurehead (National Maritime Museum)

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could trace a single object's successive labels and displays to see how each setting changed what visitors were told it meant.

Lu, Tracey L-D (2014). Museums in China: Power, Politics and Identities. London: Routledge.
actor-network theoryLuappliesmethod

A method that studies humans and material items together, along with the social networks through which these actors function. (Lu 2014p. 88)

Draws on Latour; Byrne et al.

How it is used Lu applies it to the Shanghai Museum, mapping its network of Royal Asiatic Society members, French Jesuits, International Settlement council members and British officials, to argue that it could not have been founded or survived without these links. For the Nantong Museum she turns to the political and social network of Zhang Jian and other official-scholars instead, a contrast with the Shanghai case.

“The actor-network theory (Latour 2005) has been applied to museological” p. 88
Shanghai MuseumNantong Museum

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could draw the network of donors, curators and officials for a museum in another city, and see whether its survival depends on the same kind of links.

MacKenzie, John M. (2009). Museums and Empire: Natural History, Human Cultures and Colonial Identities. Manchester: Manchester University Press.
social life of things and object biographyMacKenzieadaptstheoretical framing

Things in museums change status from everyday items into representatives of culture, so they have a social life and their biographies can be written, but they are necessarily ripped from their natural or social contexts and can only regain one through captions or displays. (MacKenzie 2009p. 11)

Draws on Arjun Appadurai; Barringer and Flynn

How it is used MacKenzie accepts the framing and then qualifies it by treating specimens as emissaries whose messages are read differently by curators, white viewers and, later, indigenous visitors. MacKenzie argues that early cases failed to restore context and that film and sound might do so better. The concept lets him explain why the same object could carry different meanings for different viewers over time.

“have been ascribed a social life, acquired through their change of status” p. 11
Early cases in colonial museumsModern visual media used in displays

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): One could write the biography of a single Asian object in a Western museum, from its shipment and catalogue entry to its display, and mark each point where its context was lost or restored.

McClellan, Andrew (1994). Inventing the Louvre: Art, Politics, and the Origins of the Modern Museum in Eighteenth-Century Paris. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.
displacement and auraMcClellantestscritique

The argument that removing a work from its original setting lessens its affective power and historical resonance, which Quatremere and Deseine used against the Musee des monuments. McClellan adds that the museum creates a new aura, that of the museum masterpiece, while also producing new historical insight. (McClellan 1994p. 195)

Draws on Quatremère de Quincy; Louis-Pierre Deseine

How it is used McClellan tests the displacement argument against the Musee des monuments and the Vatican Pinacoteca. McClellan accepts that objects lose force out of context, especially baroque monuments, but argues against Quatremere's view that the museum has only destroyed meaning, citing Schlegel's new reading of the Grand Gallery. The test lets him separate losses that are real from the aesthetic pleasure the critique ignores.

“the aura of the work in situ has not been destroyed so much as replaced with a new aura” p. 201
Musee des monuments francaisVatican Pinacoteca after 1815Louvre Grand Gallery (Schlegel's reading)

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The argument invites a question about any displaced object: which of its meanings depended on its original setting, which were gained in the museum, and whether a display can restore some of the first while keeping the second.

Meyer, Andrea; Savoy, Bénédicte (eds.) (2014). The Museum Is Open: Towards a Transnational History of Museums 1750–1940. Berlin: De Gruyter.
canonization and decanonization of objectsBrusiuscriticisesanalytic concept

The process by which objects from the Near East gained, or failed to gain, a place in the European canon once they reached a museum, and by which the museum’s own attempts to build a canon could also unsettle it. Objects have no fixed meaning until they have been through a long transit. (Meyer & Savoy 2014p. 24)

Draws on Krzysztof Pomian

How it is used Brusius takes Pomian’s account of the museum object as a semiophore, which assumes a stable life before and after the museum, and argues that the Nineveh sculptures and the Cyrus Cylinder were unstable in transit. The finds fitted neither the Greek nor the Egyptian galleries, and they did not match biblical expectations, so the British Museum had to decide what they were for. The case shows that a museum’s canon was shaped by objects it could not classify.

“archaeological museum objects from the Orient undergo processes of canonization” p. 24
Layard’s Nineveh and Nimrud finds at the British MuseumCyrus Cylinder

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The idea suggests asking how an object from a colonial excavation was classified during the years it sat unlabelled in a store, and whether its meaning in the Asian museum it later reached was settled by the same process.

Morse, Nuala (2021). The Museum as a Space of Social Care. London: Routledge.
museumness of careMorseappliesanalytic concept

The distinctive way care in engagement sessions depends on museum materials, such as handling objects, replicas and creative materials, which connect people and create the relational, affective and material dimensions of the work. (Morse 2021p. 18)

Draws on Morse and Munro (2015)

How it is used Morse develops an earlier idea of hers to argue that objects are not incidental to care in the museum. Morse shows staff using handling boxes and objects to make connections on a dementia ward and in other sessions, and argues that the materiality of museum collections is what distinguishes museum care from social work or therapy.

“there is a distinctive materiality to the ‘museumness’ of care.” p. 189
handling boxes on the dementia wardobject handling in drug and alcohol and stroke sessionsmuseum collection objects used in engagement

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The question for a museum of Asian material culture is whether its objects can carry care work in the same way, and which objects, handling protocols and cultural sensitivities would be needed.

Muchitsch, Wolfgang (ed.) (2013). Does War Belong in Museums? The Representation of Violence in Exhibitions. Bielefeld: transcript.
technical auraRathsappliesanalytic concept

The fascination that the machines exert on visitors through their technical presence, which turns attention to engineering and hides the war and the people behind the tanks. Raths treats the aura as the main asset of a museum and the main obstacle to critical history. (Muchitsch 2013p. 85)

How it is used Raths uses the idea to explain why visitors resist critical history at the German Tank Museum in Munster and why the old concept kept war out of view. The technical aura sustains the myth of a clean Wehrmacht tank corps. The 2011 reorganisation of the Hall of Collections, with battle injuries and rank-and-file uniforms, is designed to counter it.

“technical aura of the objects in the tank museum is so dominating” p. 86
German Tank Museum, Munster

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could test whether aircraft or naval halls in other military museums show the same technical aura, and whether removing the machines' technical framing changes what visitors learn.

Outka, Elizabeth (2009). Consuming Traditions: Modernity, Modernism, and the Commodified Authentic. New York: Oxford University Press.
originary authenticOutkacoinsanalytic concept

The second form of the commodified authentic, which equates authenticity with the original, the one-of-a-kind or the prototype, sold as a genuine article that is also easily bought and reproduced. (Outka 2009p. 9)

How it is used Outka introduces the originary authentic alongside the nostalgic and aesthetic forms and links it to the shop window, where a single genuine commodity is displayed. In chapter 4 she reads the Selfridges buyers’ search for “the original makers” of goods as this form applied to products, with the Japanese craftsman as an example. The concept lets her show that modernist writers used the same appeal to the first and the new.

“Part of the originary’s allure was its evocation of the prototype.” p. 9
Goods sought by Selfridges buyersJapanese articles in the 1909 Times advertisementsShop window display

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask whether a museum shop or exhibition sells the one-of-a-kind or the prototype as a purchasable object, and how the promise of an original is kept alongside the promise of reproduction.

Paver, Chloe E. M. (2018). Exhibiting the Nazi Past: Museum Objects Between the Material and the Immaterial. Cham: Palgrave Macmillan.
object as signifier and the rhetorical figures of synecdoche, metonymy and metaphorPaveradaptsanalytic concept

Museum objects stand for wider aspects of the past through the rhetorical figures of synecdoche, metonymy and metaphor. Because every museum object is a part of a larger past and contiguous with many aspects of it, the figures only become useful when they ask which whole an object stands for and what kind of contiguity makes it worth displaying. (Paver 2018p. 27)

Draws on Korff and Roth; Pomian; Mieke Bal

How it is used Paver applies the figures to the 2012 Nuremberg crystal vase, which is read as a part of the pogrom and as contiguous with the violence that broke it, and to the Hohenems keys. Paver adapts them by adding her own questions, such as what kinds of contiguity make objects from this era worth collecting and which time a museum makes an object contiguous with, so that the figures become a way of comparing displays rather than a general description of museum objects.

“linguistic figures of synecdoche, metaphor and metonymy.” p. 27
Nuremberg Dokumentationszentrum crystal vase (2012)Jüdisches Museum Hohenems keysNordico Stadtmuseum Linz cradle and bomb

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could take a damaged or confiscated object in a regional or colonial-history museum and ask which whole it stands for and what contiguity justifies showing it, then compare the answers across institutions.

object as conduit for experience, emotions and mentalitiesPaverappliesanalytic concept

Objects are not only witnesses to or documents of experience but carry the experiences, emotions and mentalities of the people who acquired, used, lost or were persecuted through them. The model is drawn from scholarship on the history of emotions and sensibilities, which Paver connects to Confino. (Paver 2018p. 27)

Draws on Alon Confino; Lucien Febvre

How it is used Paver applies the model to the Jakob vase, reading the family's pleasure in its acquisition, their sense of threat from state power and their mourning through its fragments, and the perpetrators' mentality in the loss of inhibition shown by its smashing. The model lets the chapter tie an object to experience without reducing it to a document, and it sets up the chapter 3 readings of majority mentalities.

“than simply ‘witnesses’ to or ‘documents’ of) experience, emotions and” p. 28
Nuremberg Dokumentationszentrum crystal vase (2012)

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could take one personal object from a family donation and ask which experiences it carried for its owners and which mentalities it records in those who took it, comparing a German and an Austrian case.

object life cycle and the rubbish phasePaveradaptsanalytic concept

Objects pass through successive life phases of use, disuse and value, and a no-longer-valued object can survive as rubbish before it becomes durable or is disposed of. In Paver's use the museum is a further phase of the object's life, and the phases themselves carry meaning. (Paver 2018p. 53)

Draws on Michael Thompson; Krzysztof Pomian; Igor Kopytoff; Karin Dannehl; Charles Saumarez Smith

How it is used Paver uses the life cycle to read the vase's destruction as the moment it became rubbish, its preservation as a sign of lasting trauma and its display as a third phase. Paver adapts the model against Thompson and Pomian, who assume that rubbish is a passage towards the museum, by pointing out that many Nazi-era objects were kept in the containers they were stored in after 1945 and are displayed in that state, so disuse rather than disposal explains what is shown.

“Michael Thompson argues that society divides objects into the transient” p. 53
Nuremberg Dokumentationszentrum crystal vase (2012)Nazi badges kept in a chocolate box, Cologne

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could trace the storage containers of donated objects in another national museum to test whether post-war disuse, rather than disposal, accounts for what is displayed.

Pearce, Susan M. (1992). Museums, Objects, and Collections: A Cultural Study. Leicester: Leicester University Press.
objectificationPearceadaptsanalytic concept

A subject externalises itself in a creative act and then takes the external object back into further activity, so that subject and object are joined in an ongoing relationship. Pearce uses it to explain why systematic collections are formed by imposing ideas on material and returning to that material to test them. (Pearce 1992p. 110)

Draws on Hegel; Miller

How it is used Pearce adopts Miller's reading of Hegel to show why souvenir and fetish collections are static and sterile, since each subordinates either object or subject, while systematic collections keep the relationship in process. The concept lets her reject the dualism of person and thing without denying the collector's or curator's role in shaping what is kept.

“Hegel’s concept of ‘objectification’ as developed by Miller may help us” p. 135
systematic collections across the museum disciplinesPitt Rivers's typological collections

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The idea could be used on a collection of Chinese or Japanese material assembled by a Western collector, asking whether its arrangement externalised the classificatory ideas of the collector's own culture.

cognitive processes of collecting (Ellen)Pearceappliesanalytic concept

Ellen identifies four processes behind collection-making: recognising a concrete existence or concretising abstractions; a state of mind in which signifier and signified are conflated; attributing living qualities to objects; and an ambiguous relationship in which people control objects and objects control people. Pearce uses these to explain the emotional and intellectual dual nature of a collection. (Pearce 1992p. 67)

Draws on Ellen; Barthes

How it is used Pearce applies the model to the Yoruba material in Figure 3.2, showing how the collector's personality and situation shaped a collection that still has a real relationship to Yoruba society. Barthes's signifier and signified are used to explain why a collection carries both the emotional resonance of its real source and an intellectual, metaphorical meaning that can be reinterpreted.

“In his discussion on fetishism, to which we shall return, Ellen (1988)” p. 67
Yoruba material (Figure 3.2)a Seychelles fish specimen in a museum

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The model could be used on a collection of Southeast Asian objects bought by a Western traveller, asking how the collector's habit of treating objects as living things shaped what was kept and how it was labelled.

structure and binary opposition (Saussure, Barthes, Leach)Pearcetestsanalytic concept

Objects are communication systems that can be plotted as sets of binary oppositions, drawing on Saussure's distinction between levels of language and on Barthes's signifier and signified. Pearce applies this to clothing, a terraced house, a teapot and a cattle herd, and to museum displays. (Pearce 1992p. 51)

Draws on Saussure; Barthes; Leach; Miller

How it is used Pearce applies the method to the Abbey Barn display at Glastonbury, organised as paired themes around the life of a farm labourer, and then sets out objections: structuralist readings are subjective, strip objects of their particular value and cannot explain change. Pearce keeps structuralism as a useful analytical technique while judging it ahistorical.

“Saussure’s recognition that language operates at two distinct levels: that” p. 247
Abbey Barn display, Glastonburywillow-pattern plates in a 1990 seminar

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): Binary sets could compare how an Asian collection is displayed in a Western museum with how it was displayed in its source region, testing whether the oppositions belong to the museum or to the makers.

Pearson, Catherine (2017). Museums in the Second World War: Curators, Culture and Change. London: Routledge.
layers of meaning in the objectPearsonappliesanalytic concept

The idea that an object kept statically conserved still changes its meaning and history as it acquires multiple interpretations, shaped by political and cultural circumstances, so that its significance is not fixed by the collection. (Pearson 2017)

Draws on Pearce; Monti and Keene

How it is used Pearson applies the idea to ordinary objects brought out of store for wartime displays, which acquired new meanings tied to the experience of visitors. It supports her wider argument that the meanings of objects shifted during the war and that these shifts were not curators' decisions alone.

“continue to evolve as it acquires multiple interpretations and layers of meaning, influenced by political and”
objects in Tin through the Agesobjects drawn from store for topical displays

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The idea could guide a study of how the meaning of a stored object changes when it is brought out for a temporary display, using exhibition records as evidence.

Sherman, Daniel J.; Rogoff, Irit (eds.) (1994). Museum Culture: Histories, Discourses, Spectacles. Minneapolis: University of Minnesota Press.
the museum's loss of context and moral purposeShermanadaptscritique

Quatremere's objection that a museum removes works from their original context and so strips them of moral purpose, turning them into objects of price. Sherman reads it as a prehistory of Marx's commodity fetishism and Benjamin's aura. (Sherman & Rogoff 1994p. 130)

Draws on Quatremere de Quincy; Marx; Walter Benjamin

How it is used Sherman adapts Quatremere's 1796 and 1815 texts, placing them beside Marx, Adorno and Benjamin to show that the critique of the art museum began before them. Sherman reads the museum's removal of works as a loss of utility, and he ends with Broodthaers's 'museum fiction' as a modernist version of the same argument.

“monument of painting into a picture shop” p. 131
the Louvre at its creationthe art museum as a 'picture shop', in Quatremere's phrase

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The argument that removal from context turns objects into commodities could be tested on Asian objects in Western collections, asking what their moral or ritual use was before they were displayed as price.

Siegel, Jonah (2020). Material Inspirations: The Interests of the Art Object in the Nineteenth Century and After. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
demystificationSiegelcriticisescritique

Explaining an artwork by the economic or social interests behind it, so that its material qualities are traced back to contracts, costs and class. Siegel treats it as the dominant approach to matter in cultural theory since the 1970s. (Siegel 2020p. 11)

Draws on Baxandall; Bourdieu; Marx

How it is used Siegel takes Baxandall's reading of Ghirlandaio's contract, with its ultramarine clause, as the model of the approach. Setting Baxandall beside Bourdieu's Distinction, he argues that both reduce the object to the social interest behind it. He concludes that this offers a willfully limited approach even to the material, and leaves the pleasure of matter unexplained.

“Follow the money and you will know why that blue is there, Baxandall tells us.” p. 15
Ghirlandaio, Adoration of the Magi, Ospedale degli Innocenti, Florence (c. 1488)

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A museum label or catalogue entry that gives only the commission and price of an object could be tested against what its materials, such as pigments or lacquers, do to its display.

the experiential encounter with the thingSiegelteststheoretical framing

The school that seeks a sudden, unmediated encounter with the thing, as in Heidegger's jug, Bennett's storm drain and Fried's objecthood. Siegel groups these as an account of matter that begins from the perceiving subject. (Siegel 2020p. 18)

Draws on Heidegger; Jane Bennett; Michael Fried; Mitchell

How it is used Siegel tests the promise of an unmediated encounter against Hegel's account of the beautiful and Pater's depersonalised moments. Siegel finds that Heidegger's thingness and Bennett's storm-drain epiphany both presuppose a divide between subject and object. Fried's objecthood is then set beside Appadurai's commodity, which shows how ambiguous the category of the thing is.

“Thinging is the nearing of the world” p. 19
Heidegger's jugBennett's storm drainFried's Minimalist objects

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The experiential claim could be tested on a single display case in a regional museum, asking what the viewer's encounter adds beyond the label and the setting.

realism (against network)Siegeladaptstheoretical framing

Latour's refusal of a gap between the material and the social: material and social ties are made together in associations of humans and non-humans, so causality cannot be routed back to a material or a social base. (Siegel 2020p. 31)

Draws on Bruno Latour

How it is used Siegel adopts Latour's refusal of a gap between material and social, but prefers 'realism' to 'network' because networks can flatten the individual responses he wants to study. Siegel uses the model to read the institution, the perceiving subject and the art object together, and to ask how the experience of art was negotiated across the century. Latour's critique of sociological materialism thus supports his view that art was work toward binding society together.

“are only primitive ways of packaging the” p. 32
nineteenth-century art institutions and the experience of their objects (general argument)

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The model asks a researcher to trace how a single museum object's status shifts across the institutions that hold it, rather than explaining it by one social or material base.

Siegel, Jonah (ed.) (2008). The Emergence of the Modern Museum: An Anthology of Nineteenth-Century Sources. New York: Oxford University Press.
loss and fragmentation of the museum's objectsSiegeladaptstheoretical framing

Objects enter the museum after their original world has been disturbed or destroyed, so every museum rests on dislocation and cannot be the natural home of the material it displays. (Siegel 2008p. 5)

Draws on Heidegger; Walter Benjamin

How it is used The editor uses this to read Napoleonic plunder, the Orleans sale and the 1816 Elgin Marbles purchase as cases in which building a public collection depends on dispersal elsewhere. He ties the losses to displays of power, arguing that the trophies empires gather mark the disparity of power between centre and conquered areas. His footnote names Heidegger and Benjamin as the accounts of loss in exhibition that inform this view, and it lets him treat museum collections as hostages or refugees rather than as neutral stores.

“The museum creates wholes that speak of fragmentation;” p. 5
Napoleonic plunderElgin MarblesOrleans collection salethe Louvre collection

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could follow the same dislocation through the Asian objects in these sources, such as the Burmese figure of Gaudma in the 1836 British Museum or the Siamese gifts at South Kensington, and ask what context each lost on its way into the collection.

Silverman, Lois H. (2010). The Social Work of Museums. London: Routledge.
the meaning of thingsSilvermanappliesanalytic concept

Objects, whatever their origin, provoke responses that connect visitors to identity, relationships, the society they live in and the sacred, so that objects are the heart of museum communication. (Silverman 2010p. 16)

Draws on Pearce; Csikszentmihalyi; Rochberg-Halton

How it is used Silverman treats objects as the main medium of museum social work: she takes visitor talk about objects as evidence of meaning-making in action, and uses the Nachi Waterfall painting to show how a single object can create a spiritual encounter. This places the social benefit in the encounter with the object rather than in the institution.

“As many scholars agree, museum objects elicit a variety of responses that” p. 16
museum objects in generalNachi Waterfall painting, Nezu Institute of Fine Arts, Tokyo

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask which objects in a Southeast Asian museum visitors actually talk about, and whether that talk expresses the identity or relationship meanings Silverman describes.

Stewart, Susan (1984). On Longing: Narratives of the Miniature, the Gigantic, the Souvenir, the Collection. Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press.
the miniature as figure for the interior selfStewartappliesanalytic concept

The miniature is a closed, spatially enclosed world that arrests time, and in the text it stands for the interior space and private time of the bourgeois subject. Toys, dollhouses and miniature books are emblems of a stopped, possessed life. (Stewart 1984PDF p. 13)

How it is used Stewart applies the miniature to the toy, the dollhouse and miniature books, and then to the 1948 Museum of Art in Miniature, which reduced the Metropolitan Museum to stamps pasted into an album. The case shows how a museum can be re-experienced as a private, transcendent object, which Stewart sets against the historical and contextual reality of the museum itself.

“The miniature is considered in this essay as a metaphor for the” PDF p. 13
miniature booksdollhouseMuseum of Art in Miniature (1948)flea circus and miniature railways

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The same figure could be used to read a museum's scaled-down displays or dioramas of other cultures as private, closed worlds that arrest history.

Stocking, George W., Jr. (ed.) (1985). Objects and Others: Essays on Museums and Material Culture. Madison: University of Wisconsin Press.
museum as archive of material objects of 'others'Stockingappliestheoretical framing

The museum is an archive of three-dimensional material objects that come from the past and from other peoples, and that carry relations of power, wealth and aesthetic value as well as meaning. Stocking sets out these dimensions, which he counts as dimensions of the archive, in his introduction. (Stocking 1985p. 4)

How it is used Stocking uses this framing to put the historical essays in one context: each institutional story (Peabody, Pitt Rivers, the Trocadero, the American Museum) is read as a case of how object, time, power and aesthetic value were settled in one museum. The framing is not tested against a single case; it is the reason he gives for why institutional histories bear on the wider issues of the title.

“archives of what anthropologists have called "material culture.” p. 4
Peabody MuseumPitt Rivers collectionAmerican Museum of Natural HistoryTrocadero

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask which of these dimensions shaped a given regional collection, such as Southeast Asian material held by a European museum, and whether the aesthetic or the power dimension changed its accession and display.

object orientation of museum anthropologyStockingappliesanalytic concept

The tendency of museum-based anthropology to treat culture as collections of things and their makers as objects, which Stocking ties to evolutionary racialism and to the dominance of object-centred museum men. Its decline is part of the move from object-based to behaviour and culture-based work. (Stocking 1985p. 114)

How it is used Stocking uses the object orientation to explain why Rockefeller money, by financing fieldwork through universities rather than museums, could end the museum era. The argument is that the Foundation's shift to behaviour and culture was a change of conception as well as of funding. He uses the concept as the frame for the whole essay and weighs the Kirchhoff affair against it, finding the colonial charge secondary.

“conspired to sustain an object orientation in anthropological” p. 114
Rockefeller grants in Peking, Hawaii and AustraliaRadcliffe-Brown's chair at Sydney

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask whether museum collections of Southeast Asian objects made in the interwar years were arranged as things or as field-based cultural evidence, and whether funding decided the difference.

fetishism of collectionsCliffordappliesanalytic concept

The point where a collection's classification and display give way to private fixation on a single object. Clifford treats the line between collection and fetishism, drawn by Susan Stewart, as the mark of the good collector, and as the reverse of the proper relation with objects. (Stocking 1985p. 239)

Draws on Susan Stewart; Marx; Baudrillard

How it is used Clifford uses Stewart's line between collection and fetishism to read Fenton's poem and the Pitt Rivers Museum, and to argue, following Marx's account of commodity fetishism, that the museum mystifies the historical labour and power of acquisition as adequate representation. The concept is the basis of his first intervention, which is to return objects to their lost status as fetishes so that they fixate rather than only edify.

“boundary between collection and fetishism is mediated by classification and” p. 239
Pitt Rivers Museum (Fenton's poem)New York tribal-art exhibitions, 1984-85

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask whether an individual Japanese sword or Khmer head in a European museum was displayed as part of a classified series or as a singular object of fascination.

Tseng, Alice Y. (2008). The Imperial Museums of Meiji Japan: Architecture and the Art of the Nation. Seattle: University of Washington Press.
the icon-to-art-object shiftTsengtestsanalytic concept

Transferring religious sculpture and painting from temple altars to museum vitrines shifted them from the liturgical sphere to the aesthetic one, so that their legibility and value changed. Scholars attribute the change to modernisation or to the Western and Westernised Asian gaze; Tseng argues the change is not complete. (Tseng 2008p. 144)

Draws on John Rosenfield; Bernard Faure; Gregory Levine

How it is used Tseng tests Faure's explanation against the continuing practice of temple airings, the visitors who bow to a Buddha image in a museum, and Levine's account of multivalent devotion, connoisseurship and curiosity. Tseng concludes that the line between cult icon and art object is more porous than the scholarship assumes, and uses this to organise the chapter's argument that the Nara museum made icons visible as national art while keeping them close to their Nara origins through loans and compensation rules.

“Western and Westernized Asian gaze on said objects” p. 145
Imperial Nara MuseumHōryūji iconstemple airings at Nara

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could compare the status of Buddhist sculpture in a national museum with that of the same objects in active temples, asking which value the display gives them and which it withholds.

Veldkamp, Elmer (2014). “Keeping It Real: The Exhibition of Artifact Replicas in National Museums of Korea”. Acta Koreana, 17.2 (December 2014): 557-581.
singularization (cultural biography of things)Veldkampappliesanalytic concept

The story of how a thing is singled out from a class of similar things through classification and reclassification as its context changes. Veldkamp applies it to replicated artifacts, whose meaning shifts with their setting. (Veldkamp 2014p. 558)

Draws on Kopytoff

How it is used Veldkamp takes Kopytoff's cultural biography of things as the frame for the article and uses it to trace replicas across museums, souvenirs and logos, so that the same incense burner becomes a different object in each setting. It lets him treat a replica as a thing with a life of its own rather than as a failed copy.

“providing the story of various singularizations of replicated artifacts” p. 558
Paekche incense burner replica, National Museum of Korea and National Folk Museum timelineReplicas of the Kongju gold ornaments

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could follow one object's replicas through a set of museums and souvenir shops, noting how each setting changes what the replica is taken to be.

Vergo, Peter (ed.) (1989). The New Museology. London: Reaktion Books.
meaning transformed within the museumSaumarez Smithappliesanalytic concept

Artefacts removed from private use and placed in a museum acquire a new meaning presented as neutral, but that meaning keeps shifting through the object's later history inside the museum. (Vergo 1989p. 9)

How it is used Saumarez Smith applies the idea to three Victoria and Albert Museum cases that he chose as problematic rather than representative: the Saxon statue Thuner, the Mark Lane archway and the Clifford's Inn panelled room. Each shows an object's meaning changing inside the museum, which undermines the assumption that artefacts are static and safe. He uses this to argue for mixed display styles, awareness of artifice and more reflexive museum scholarship.

“The process whereby the meaning of artefacts can be transformed through their history within a museum” p. 9
Victoria and Albert Museum: Saxon statue ThunerMark Lane archwayClifford's Inn panelled room

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The idea could be used to trace one Asian object, such as a ceramic or lacquer piece, through its accession, reinstallation and label changes in a Western museum.

fetishJordanovaadaptsanalytic concept

A term from anthropology, Marxism and psychoanalysis for an object that seems to hold magical power or social relations as properties of its own. Jordanova uses it for the way exhibited objects seem to contain their meaning. (Vergo 1989p. 38)

Draws on Marx; Freud

How it is used Jordanova links museum looking to reification: because museums invite us to look at objects, they also draw us to treat them as commodities, and to treat the objects of other cultures as masterpieces. Jordanova adapts Marx's account of commodity fetishism and Freud's clinical account of fetishes to museum display, separating the fetish's power to freeze social relations from its psychic investment. The term lets her bring the material and the psychic into one account of museums.

“museums, when they invite us to look at objects, also draw us to reify them, to treat them as commodities” p. 38
African objects collected by Picasso in anthropological museumsCambridge University Museum of Archaeology and Anthropology catalogue (1984)

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The term could be used to ask whether a Japanese sword or Southeast Asian textile is shown in a Western museum as a masterpiece or as ethnographic evidence, and what that choice does to the object.

Yallop, Jacqueline (2011). Magpies, Squirrels and Thieves: How the Victorians Collected the World. London: Atlantic Books.
objects as cultural evidenceYallopappliesanalytic concept

Objects read as evidence of a country's history and culture rather than as decoration or curiosities. The text attributes this stance to Bushell, who treated his Peking purchases as cultural artefacts and historic markers. (Yallop 2011)

How it is used Yallop uses the idea to argue that Bushell's Chinese objects changed how London viewed China, because each was explained through markets, texts and the stories of its owners. The concept links his collecting to Franks's ethnographic policy, which Yallop presents as a wish that objects should speak for themselves. It lets the author claim a pioneering role for Bushell that a purely aesthetic reading of his purchases could not show.

“Bushell understood that they were cultural artefacts, historic markers which gave him an insight”
Bushell's Chinese consignments to South Kensington, 1874-1883Franks's ethnographic collection at the British Museum

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could check whether a given museum's catalogue entries for non-European objects describe them as evidence of a culture or as curiosities, and how that changed over time.

ethnographic objects as art or cultural curiosityYallopappliesanalytic concept

The question of whether non-European objects that did not fit the hierarchy of fine art were art at all, or cultural curiosities of social value. Museum staff of the 1860s to 1880s had to decide where to place them. (Yallop 2011)

How it is used Yallop frames the dilemma with the arrival of new objects at South Kensington and the British Museum, and uses Franks's readiness to collect even 'the commonest things of the country' as the answer that a museum could explain the world through ordinary objects. The idea lets the author set Franks's broad policy beside Bushell's practice of describing objects in their context. It gives the chapter its argument about how the museum changed what counted as worth showing.

“even ‘the commonest things of the country’, he maintained, had a place in explaining and understanding the world”
Franks's acquisitions at the British MuseumBushell's Peking shipments to South Kensington

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): One could ask which non-European objects in a given museum were reclassified from curiosity to art, and when, by comparing accession registers with display records.

Yanni, Carla (1999). Nature’s Museums: Victorian Science and the Architecture of Display. Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press.
Authenticity of specimens (aura)Yannitestscritique

The debate over whether real specimens still give museums their value. Gould has an absolute faith in authentic objects; Secord argues that dinosaur bones have no aura and that visitors should see the object the scientist studies, not a robot. (Yanni 1999p. 155)

Draws on Gould; Secord

How it is used Yanni uses the two positions to test what authentic objects still do for museums. Yanni sides with Secord that specimens beat motorised models because visitors see what the palaeontologist studies, but treats Gould’s faith as a wishful leap back to nineteenth-century naturalists. Yanni adds that Victorian museums first began to present science as tangible products.

“This absolute faith in authenticity rejects academic” p. 155
Natural History Museum, London dinosaur displaysField Museum, Chicago

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask, for a given gallery, whether the object on show is the one scientists study, or a cast or model, and what the visitor is shown about the process of study.

Collecting, curiosity and the order of knowledge

Pomian, Stewart, Foucault's epistemes and histories of classification: how collections are formed and how they order nature, art and the past. 63 concepts from 39 texts

Collecting approaches ask how objects came to be gathered, and what order a collection gives to nature, art and the past. The approach asks both who gathered an object and which classification then gave it a place in the world. For museums the question is less what a display shows than what it claims to contain, and by which routes its objects arrived (Krech & Hail 1999; Conn 1998p. 107). Several texts treat a collection as an argument it makes about the world. Our texts draw chiefly on Pomian, Stewart, Foucault, Benjamin and Popper. Yanni sets Pomian's Wunderkammer, an encyclopedic miniature of the universe, against Hooper-Greenhill's warning about origins (Yanni 1999p. 16), and Bennett adopts Pomian's semiophores (Bennett 1995p. 165). Stewart's miniature and containment are applied by Denton and Black (Denton 2014p. 91; Black 2000p. 60). Foucault's epistemes organise Hooper-Greenhill's history of the cabinet (Hooper-Greenhill 1992p. 12). Benjamin's practical memory is set against the museum's treatment of objects (Sherman & Rogoff 1994PDF p. 16). The texts at the centre are Hooper-Greenhill (Hooper-Greenhill 1992), Stewart (Stewart 1984), Findlen (Findlen 1994), Pearce (Pearce 1992) and Alberti (Alberti 2009).

Stewart's miniature and containment, with Kirshenblatt-Gimblett's excision

Stewart treats the collection as a finite, classified series that contains the world by control, so that the collection "is often about containment on the level of its content" (Stewart 1984p. 161). Denton applies the miniature to the old Shanghai models and the replica villages of Splendid China, arguing that it offers a simulated past that feeds a possessive gaze (Denton 2014p. 91; Denton 2014p. 253). Black adapts the idea twice: collapsed significance explains why the Rubaiyat is treated as a pocket gem (Black 2000p. 60), and "the domesticated exotic" describes FitzGerald's purchases and translation as one act of possession (Black 2000p. 50). Kirshenblatt-Gimblett starts from excision instead: "ethnographic objects are made, not found, despite claims to the contrary" (Kirshenblatt-Gimblett 1998p. 3).

Pomian's semiophores and the cabinet as microcosm

Pomian's semiophores are objects prized for the meaning they produce, which make an invisible order visible (Bennett 1995p. 165). Bennett uses them to distinguish galleries by the contract each sets between the visible and the invisible (Bennett 1995p. 165). Scheicher sets the Ambras contents on the scale of the universe as Fludd envisaged it (Impey & MacGregor 1985p. 41). Boström tests that model against the Hainhofer cabinets: Uppsala has naturalia, artificialia and the four elements and so fits, while the Pomeranian cabinet does not (Impey & MacGregor 1985p. 133). Hopkins reads Ole Worm's cabinet as the nearest precursor of the modern museum (Hopkins 2021).

Foucault's epistemes and the rationality of early collections

Hooper-Greenhill uses Foucault's epistemes to argue that a collection counts as knowledge in one period and as irrational in another. The Medici Palace is read through resemblance, the cabinet of the world through the Renaissance episteme, and the Royal Society Repository through the classical table of difference (Hooper-Greenhill 1992p. 12; Hooper-Greenhill 1992p. 102). Arnold uses the Renaissance episteme to fix the logic of signatures in medicinal chemistry, so that unicorn horn and formed stones are not turned into modern categories (Arnold 2006). Yanni answers Crimp by noting that Foucault did not claim master narratives stay fixed, so a cabinet with another classification could still be an origin (Yanni 1999p. 20).

Findlen's wonder, curiosity and saved appearances

Findlen takes wonder to be the response to the unexpected, which naturalists explained as a natural event rather than a sign: "natural events always qualified as wonders, but only sometimes as signs" (Findlen 1994p. 22). Curiosity led naturalists into the world, and Findlen argues against the Galileian and Cartesian view that it was disorderly (Findlen 1994p. 54; Findlen 1994p. 94). Collecting let naturalists "save appearances", fitting New World plants into Aristotelian categories rather than unsettling them (Findlen 1994p. 4). Yanni follows Findlen's case that Italian cabinets were early natural history museums (Yanni 1999p. 16).

Pearce's modes and the collector's motives

Pearce distinguishes souvenirs, which carry a life history; fetish collections, which express a possessive self; and systematic collections, which select examples to stand for a class (Pearce 1992p. 110; Pearce 1992p. 129). Hill applies these modes to donations in Preston and Liverpool, finding Preston's gifts mostly souvenir and fetishistic and Liverpool's more systematic (Hill 2005p. 69). Hill treats the trophy as a particular form of souvenir, collected to create prestige (Hill 2005p. 7). Asma tests Baudrillard's mastery against the Jonas Brothers' trophy catalogues, finding it fits the hunter's trophies but not museum specimens, and judges Freud's account too speculative (Asma 2001).

Object-based knowledge and the epistemology of the hunt

Conn describes an object-based epistemology in which objects carried meaning that careful arrangement would reveal, and in which displays could teach untrained viewers (Conn 1998p. 107). Conn adapts Jakobson's pair of synecdoche and metonymy to show gallery sequences as visual arguments, as at the 1904 Philippine exhibit (Conn 1998p. 141). Arnold's epistemology of the hunt works from the single example, and Arnold extends Ginsburg's examples back to Hippocratic medicine (Arnold 2006). Jordanova criticises the belief that visitors learn from looking: "it is an illusion to believe that museums can teach their visitors about abstract terms" (Vergo 1989p. 40).

Classification and disciplinary order

Alberti reads the Manchester Museum's layout as a map of disciplines with borders and contested frontiers (Alberti 2009p. 4). The 1912-13 and 1927 extensions fixed the separation of natural and cultural collections, so the galleries lagged behind academic change (Alberti 2009p. 3). Chapman tests the principle of continuity against Leiden's geographical arrangement, and finds that Pitt Rivers's rotunda kept typological continuity but privileged geography (Stocking 1985p. 33). Porter criticises the SHIC classification, which sets domestic work apart from production and so makes women's labour hard to see (Lumley 1988p. 109).

Colonial and imperial collecting

MacKenzie treats Anderson's classificatory grid as a test, granting its ideal of serial visibility but arguing that funding, staff and audiences kept colonial museums partial (MacKenzie 2009p. 8). Jasanoff treats the British empire as a collection pieced together over time, with Clive as the first imperial collector of British India (Jasanoff 2005p. 6; Jasanoff 2005p. 32). Greenhalgh's shopping lists, written instructions sent to travellers, shaped which sites were dug (Greenhalgh 2019PDF p. 13). Cvetkovski's Stockholm system registers objects by the collection they came into, which produced ethnic and geographic classes in the Russian Ethnographic Museum (Cvetkovski & Hofmeister 2014p. 240).

Art, artifact and the reproduced canon

Clifford divides non-Western objects into scientific artifacts and aesthetic works, so that in the art museum an object is primarily "beautiful and in the ethnographic museum it is interesting (Stocking 1985p. 242). Siegel shows that the classical canon was known mainly through copies, so that to know them was to know copies, whether in two dimensions or three" (Siegel 2020p. 148). Peters argues that photographic campaigns did not only reflect the art-historical canon but helped to form it (Meyer & Savoy 2014p. 57).

Debates and limits

Several texts push back on the approach. Bennett judges Foucault's opposition between museum and fair too starkly stated and insufficiently historical (Bennett 1995p. 3), and argues that the exhibitionary complex shows power through spectacle as well as surveillance (Bennett 1995p. 61). Hill tests Foucault and Habermas against English donation records and finds municipal museums neither as efficient nor as progressive as their rhetoric (Hill 2005p. 5; Hill 2005p. 10). MacKenzie calls Anderson's grid only partly grounded in reality (MacKenzie 2009p. 8). Pearce answers the post-structuralist denial of meaning with Popper's third world, so that some interpretations are better than others (Pearce 1992p. 369). Stewart sets aside the non-Western tradition of scale, treating Japanese netsuke and Persian, Indian and Chinese forms as outside the study (Stewart 1984PDF p. 14). The transnational volume holds that Pomian's account of the museum object, which assumes a stable life before and after the museum, does not explain how meaning forms in transit (Meyer & Savoy 2014p. 20).

Carrying it over to a new case

  • Ask which objects in a Southeast Asian collection in a Western museum were detached in the field, and whether any regained a context (Kirshenblatt-Gimblett 1998p. 2).
  • Compare the miniature city models in a new district's planning hall with Denton's old-Shanghai models, to see whether they offer the same possessive gaze on future property (Denton 2014p. 91).
  • Sort a regional museum's accessions by Pearce's three modes to see whether donors gave for memory, status or knowledge (Pearce 1992p. 110; Hill 2005p. 69).
  • Read a single collector's holdings in an East or Southeast Asian museum as a whole, and ask what the collector set out to assemble before counting gaps (Sleeper-Smith 2009p. 68).
  • Test whether a private Southeast Asian cabinet is a microcosm by checking whether its contents cover every category of the world it claims to represent (Impey & MacGregor 1985p. 41).
  • Compare the registration of Asian objects by donor or purchase with their later display by region (Cvetkovski & Hofmeister 2014p. 240).
  • Ask which regions an encyclopedic museum's display leaves out of its claim to represent the world (Gardner 2020; Cuno 2008PDF p. 25).

Where to start reading

  • Stewart, Susan (1984). On Longing: Narratives of the Miniature, the Gigantic, the Souvenir, the Collection. Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press. Stewart on the miniature, containment and the museum as a fiction of representation.
  • Denton, Kirk A. (2014). Exhibiting the Past: Historical Memory and the Politics of Museums in Postsocialist China. Honolulu: University of Hawai‘i Press. Denton on the miniature as a state-built past.
  • Black, Barbara J. (2000). On Exhibit: Victorians and Their Museums. Charlottesville: University Press of Virginia. Black on the domesticated exotic and collapsed significance.
  • Hooper-Greenhill, Eilean (1992). Museums and the Shaping of Knowledge. London: Routledge. Hooper-Greenhill on the episteme and the cabinet of the world.
  • Yanni, Carla (1999). Nature’s Museums: Victorian Science and the Architecture of Display. Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press. Yanni on Pomian, Crimp and Foucault in the debate over origins.
  • Pearce, Susan M. (1992). Museums, Objects, and Collections: A Cultural Study. Leicester: Leicester University Press. Pearce on the three modes of collecting and the third world of meaning.
  • Findlen, Paula (1994). Possessing Nature: Museums, Collecting, and Scientific Culture in Early Modern Italy. Berkeley: University of California Press. Findlen on wonder, curiosity and saved appearances.
  • Alberti, Samuel J. M. M. (2009). Nature and Culture: Objects, Disciplines and the Manchester Museum. Manchester: Manchester University Press. Alberti on the map of disciplines.
