Alberti, Samuel J. M. M. (2009). Nature and Culture: Objects, Disciplines and the Manchester Museum. Manchester: Manchester University Press.
disciplinary topography (cultural cartography)Albertiappliesanalytic concept

The layout of a museum's collections is read as a map of knowledge in which disciplines have territories, borders and border disputes, and curators draw those boundaries much as states draw frontiers. (Alberti 2009p. 4)

Draws on Ken Arnold; Thomas Gieryn

How it is used Alberti applies the cartographic metaphor to where different groups of artefacts and curators were located in the Manchester building, and asks whether display grammars were shared between disciplines. The first half of the book is therefore a study of the museum's spatial and administrative layout as well as its ideas. The map lets him show that disciplines had jagged borders and contested boundaries rather than fixed ones.

“What emerges in the first half of this book, then, is a map.” p. 4
Manchester Museum galleries, 1887-19901912-13 and 1927 extensions

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could map where each cultural and natural collection sat in another museum's plans and ask whether the same grammar of display governed East Asian, Pacific or European material.

disciplines built from objectsAlbertiappliestheoretical framing

Disciplines are not stable, coherent units of knowledge but fluid, contingent groupings, and they are also material, built from buildings, tools and objects that can both signal change and slow it. (Alberti 2009p. 3)

Draws on Simon Knell

How it is used Alberti takes Knell's point that natural scientists, archaeologists and art historians build subjects from material things and applies it to the museum's building programme. The extensions of 1912-13 and 1927 fixed the separation of natural and cultural collections, so the permanent galleries lagged behind academic change. This lets him explain why archaeology and ethnology stayed in one building after anthropology had moved on.

“they are fluid, contingent groupings” p. 3
1912-13 and 1927 buildingsEgyptology and archaeology galleries

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): One could ask whether a museum's building plan, such as a separate Asian wing or a fixed gallery sequence, held its disciplines in place in the same way, using floor plans and reinstallation dates.

fivefold typology of acquisitionAlbertiappliestypology

Objects reached the museum by five routes, gift, purchase, fieldwork, transfer or loan, and each route involved different donors, agents and relationships. (Alberti 2009p. 5)

How it is used Alberti applies exchange theory to the cases in chapter 4, so that the Lloyd Japanese gift, the Churchill coin bequest, the purchase of an elephant after Belle Vue Zoo and the Castlefield excavations each sit under a separate route. The typology lets him show how each route changed the donors involved and the meanings objects carried. It also sets museum acquisition alongside zoos and menageries.

“propose a fivefold typology of acquisition: by gift, purchase, fieldwork, transfer or” p. 5
Robert Wylie Lloyd's Japanese collectionChurchill coin bequestMaharajah elephantCastlefield excavations

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The five routes could be used to compare how a Western museum acquired East and Southeast Asian material, separating colonial purchase from donation and exchange.

federation of knowledge practicesAlbertiappliesanalytic concept

Knowledge practices within the museum formed a federation of semi-independent units rather than a single hierarchy, so that archaeology became a federal nation of collections under one roof rather than a set of city-states. (Alberti 2009p. 79)

Draws on John Pickstone

How it is used Alberti uses the metaphor to describe archaeology and classical collections after the planned Mediterranean gallery brought together collections that had operated separately. It sets this against the earlier city-state pattern and shows that disciplinary independence was reached in federal rather than unified form. The metaphor thus explains why the humanities were autonomous within the museum but still connected.

“archaeology was no longer a collection of city-states but a” p. 79
Mediterranean gallery plansLindow Man exhibitionEgyptology and archaeology collections

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The federation image could be tested on another museum to see whether its Asian, Pacific and European collections formed a federation or a single department.

Arnold, Ken (2006). Cabinets for the Curious: Looking Back at Early English Museums. Aldershot: Ashgate.
epistemology of the huntArnoldadaptsanalytic concept

A way of making knowledge that works from the single example and stays bound to particular instances rather than rising to general laws. Arnold takes it as the method of seventeenth-century museum-science, which he sets against the inductive, law-seeking science that Kuhn privileged. (Arnold 2006)

Draws on William Eamon; Ginsburg; Bruce Trigger; Walter Ong

How it is used Arnold applies the idea to the collectors and fact-gatherers of the Royal Society and the Ashmolean, arguing that historians of science have overlooked them because Kuhn's account admitted only the mathematical and experimental traditions. The concept lets him restore natural historians and collectors as producers of knowledge, and it links the book's three strategies to a shared root. He combines it with Trigger's idiographic and nomothetic distinction and extends Ginsburg's late nineteenth-century examples back to Hippocratic medicine and the Renaissance.

“Museum-science was instead characterised by the rhythm of passing from one particular to the next”
Royal Society and Ashmolean collectingMorelli, Freud and Sherlock Holmes as parallelsHippocratic medicine

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask whether a regional museum's accession practice shows the same case-by-case reasoning, which would test whether the idea survives outside the Royal Society milieu.

narrative, functional and taxonomic strategiesArnoldcoinsanalytic concept

Three ways of getting knowledge out of museum objects: describing them and telling stories about them (narrative), understanding their essence through use (functional), and arranging them by their relations to one another (taxonomic). Arnold argues that seventeenth-century collectors used all three and that later museums split them into separate disciplinary styles. (Arnold 2006)

How it is used Arnold uses the triad as the structure of the book, giving a part to each strategy and tracing it from the seventeenth century to the present: narrative in historical and biographical museums, functional in anthropology and medicine, taxonomic in natural history and the classification of art. In the conclusion he uses the camera to show the cost of the split: a design museum treats it by its look, a science museum by its mechanism and an art museum by its images, so no display shows how it worked.

“producing knowledge from things can be located at the intersection of three methodological co-ordinates”
Plot and Bargrave's narrative cataloguesPitt Rivers and anthropology museumsthe British Museum's 1759 plancamera displays in design, science and art museums

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A curator could take one collection and list which objects are described, which are used and which are ordered, to see which strategy the display neglects.

Renaissance epistemeArnoldappliestheoretical framing

Foucault's term for an earlier ordering of knowledge in which resemblances were read as signs. Arnold uses it for the doctrine of signatures in medicinal chemistry, whose logic he argues cannot be translated directly into modern meanings. (Arnold 2006)

Draws on Michel Foucault

How it is used Arnold uses Foucault to fix a historical caution: the sympathies and signatures that medicinal chemists read in unicorn horn, mummies and formed stones make sense only within the Renaissance episteme, so modern readers must not turn them into present categories. Foucault is used to fix the period's logic rather than to explain what the collectors did, and the chapter combines this with Ashmole's interest in hidden qualities.

“as Foucault so clearly argued, the reign of this magical system of thought during what he termed the “Renaissance episteme”
medicinal chemistry in the Ashmolean and apothecary collectionsunicorn horn, mummies and formed stones

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A curator could ask how a display of medicinal objects should explain the old signature logic, and what a visitor is expected to make of it.

Asma, Stephen T. (2001). Stuffed Animals and Pickled Heads: The Culture and Evolution of Natural History Museums. New York: Oxford University Press.
collecting as mastery (Freud and Baudrillard)Asmateststheoretical framing

Freud reads collecting as a sublimation of infantile pleasures, including the retention of faeces, and an attempt to re-create an original unity. Baudrillard reads collecting as a power game in which the collected object reflects the collector's mastery over a living creature turned into a manageable trophy. (Asma 2001)

Draws on Sigmund Freud; Jean Baudrillard; Rheims

How it is used Asma tests both accounts against the trophy and souvenir catalogues of the Jonas Brothers taxidermy firm. Baudrillard's idea of mastery fits the hunter's trophies closely, while Freud's account is judged too speculative and untestable. Asma then argues that trophy taxidermy is not what natural history museums do with specimens, so neither theory explains museum collecting without qualification.

“Page after page of animal trophies, which made no pretense to educate, began to drive Baudrillard’s point home to me.”
Jonas Brothers taxidermy catalogues (1965 'Game Trails')Field Museum, Chicago

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could read the trophy and souvenir catalogues of a hunting or taxidermy trade in a Southeast Asian or East Asian setting through Baudrillard's idea of mastery, asking whether the objects demonstrate control over animals, over people, or over a colonial order.

function over form in arrangementAsmaappliesanalytic concept

Hunter and Cuvier organised natural history by physiological function, what an organ does in an animal's life, rather than by outward form. Cuvier's 'conditions of existence' tie each structure to a survival function, and Hunter's cabinet shows a 'rational economy of functions' rather than a catalogue of forms. (Asma 2001)

Draws on Cuvier; Hunter

How it is used Asma uses the idea to explain the move from the curiosity cabinet to scientific display. Hunter's London arrangement went from full skeletons to dissected viscera and physiological systems, so that the collection showed how forms serve life's strategies. Asma sets Cuvier's embranchement classification beside it and reads both as the ground on which later questions of function, form and transformation were built.

“Both Cuvier and Hunter, working independently (though a case might be made for Hunter’s priority), reoriented natural history away from the structures and toward the functions of organisms.”
Hunterian Museum, LondonGalerie d’anatomie comparée, Paris

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask whether a museum of Japanese or Korean natural history or medicine was arranged by function or by form, and whether that arrangement encoded a physiological or a national order.

nonoverlapping magisteria (NOMA)Asmacriticisescritique

Gould's proposal that science and religion are separate domains of teaching authority, so that neither can conflict with the other. Asma reads it as a settlement that keeps evolution teaching uncompromised and that places morality outside the empirical world. (Asma 2001)

Draws on Stephen Jay Gould

How it is used Asma accepts the NOMA settlement as a way of keeping evolution uncompromised, but argues that facts and values cannot be cleanly separated, since Gould's own ontology and morality rest on experience rather than on the non-empirical domain he assigns them to. Asma sets the Field Museum's visitor letters and talk-back boards against the division, as visitors refuse to keep the two apart.

“Gould seems to resonate with the phenomenalist tradition that we saw emerge with John Hunter and Georges Cuvier.”
Field Museum 'Life over Time' exhibitPope John Paul II's statement on evolution

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could test whether a settlement of the NOMA kind is used in a Japanese, Korean or Southeast Asian museum on evolution, national history or religious heritage, and who draws the boundary between the domains.

culture-bound classificationAsmatestsanalytic concept

Most of the ways in which people carve up nature are arbitrary, though culture-bound, choices, unlike the life-and-death classifications that reality forces. Borges's invented Chinese encyclopedia and Foucault's reading of it show how one culture's categories can look absurd to another. (Asma 2001)

Draws on Jorge Luis Borges; Michel Foucault

How it is used Asma uses the Borges passage as a test of ordinary classification: some categories are fixed by reality, and the rest are conventions. Asma applies this to Linnaeus's varieties of mankind (americanus, europeaus, asiaticus, africanus) and to the looser 'varieties' Homo sapiens ferus and monstrosus, showing that a classificatory scheme can carry racial and cultural assumptions as well as biological ones.

“which we carve up nature involve rather arbitrary, though culture-bound, choices.”
Linnaeus, Systema naturae (tenth edition)

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask which categories in a Chinese, Japanese or Southeast Asian museum's labels are reality-forced and which are conventions, and how such conventions were introduced by European or national classificatory schemes.

Bennett, Tony (1995). The Birth of the Museum: History, Theory, Politics. London: Routledge.
semiophoresBennettadaptsanalytic concept

Objects prized for their capacity to produce meaning rather than for use, which take part in an exchange between visible and invisible worlds. Every collection makes an invisible order visible through its semiophores. (Bennett 1995p. 165)

Draws on Krzysztof Pomian

How it is used Bennett adopts Pomian's semiophore to show that all collecting institutions, including museums and temples, present an order the visitor cannot see directly. Bennett applies this to art galleries, where modernist display hides the order, and uses it to distinguish galleries by the kind of contract they set up between the visible and the invisible. That distinction underlies his argument about who can read them.

“Pomian defines such objects as semiophores - that” p. 165
Lenoir's Musee des monuments francaisthe chronological hang of the National Gallery in Londonlate nineteenth-century provincial art museums

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The idea could be used to compare a temple treasury with a national museum in an East Asian city, asking which invisible order each one claims to make visible.

Black, Barbara J. (2000). On Exhibit: Victorians and Their Museums. Charlottesville: University Press of Virginia.
exotic at home: the domesticated exoticBlackappliesanalytic concept

The Victorian taste for objects from distant places kept inside the house, where the exotic is tamed, familiarised and made to confirm the owner's superiority. FitzGerald's Khayyam translation is the case through which Black defines it. (Black 2000p. 50)

How it is used Black uses the phrase to link FitzGerald's home purchases, his letters on the Baker Street Bazaar and his translation of the Rubaiyat. Black argues that FitzGerald shaped Khayyam into the same exotic domesticity that he wanted in his house, so that the poem became a collectible in the drawing room. The concept lets Black show how the translation and the collection are one act of possession.

“the domesticated exotic” p. 50
FitzGerald's Little Grange and his purchases at Baker Street BazaarFitzGerald's translation of the Rubaiyat

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask which Asian objects were bought for British and European domestic interiors, and whether their function there was the same taming of the exotic that Black finds in FitzGerald.

collapsed significanceBlackappliesanalytic concept

Stewart's term for the way the miniature and the small collectible lose the scale of the things they represent and gain value through their possessable smallness. Black applies it to the Rubaiyat, which is treated as a gem that can be held in the hand. (Black 2000p. 60)

Draws on Susan Stewart

How it is used Black uses the concept to explain why the Rubaiyat is so often called a gem or pearl: its small dimensions and its miniature packaging make it an object of possession. Black shows how this supports the poem's role as an orientalised curiosity, sealed in its diminutive form. The concept links the poem's reception to the logic of the collection.

“delineate what Susan Stewart calls “collapsed significance.” p. 60
the Rubaiyat as a pocket gem in editions and critical reception

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask whether small collectibles of East or Southeast Asian material, such as miniature bronzes or netsuke, lost their original scale and meaning in the same way when they entered Western cabinets and albums.

Conn, Steven (1998). Museums and American Intellectual Life, 1876–1926. Chicago: University of Chicago Press.
object-based epistemologyConncoinsanalytic concept

The late-nineteenth-century assumption that objects carried meaning that careful arrangement and observation would reveal, so that systematically displayed specimens could teach untrained viewers. The book's organising concept, which Conn says had largely disappeared from mainstream American intellectual life by the 1920s. (Conn 1998p. 4)

How it is used Conn uses the concept to explain how natural history, anthropology and commercial museums were organised and why they lost authority. Conn applies it to the Academy of Natural Sciences, the Penn and Field museums, the Commercial Museum and Ford's history, and presents Boas's 1907 essay on museum administration as the point where anthropology declared its independence from it. It lets him argue that museums were serious knowledge institutions, against readings that see only power.

“from an object-based epistemology” p. 108
Academy of Natural Sciences, PhiladelphiaUniversity of Pennsylvania MuseumField Museum, ChicagoPhiladelphia Commercial MuseumHenry Ford Museum

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could test the idea on a non-university museum after 1920, asking whether its objects were still expected to carry their own meaning or were framed as illustrations of a text.

synecdoche and metonymy of objectsConnadaptsanalytic concept

Museum objects stood for wholes in two ways: as synecdoches, where a specimen or pot represented its whole category, and as metonyms, where it stood for a part of a wider body of knowledge such as natural history or anthropology. Conn takes the pair from a linguistic model of selection and combination. (Conn 1998p. 4)

Draws on Roman Jakobson; Terence Hawkes; Susan Stewart

How it is used Conn uses the pair to explain how gallery sequences formed a visual argument of progress from savage to civilised. Conn applies it to the 1904 Philippine exhibit, where people and products were displayed as a synecdoche for the islands, so that the Philippines were, in his words, conquered again, and to the Commercial Museum, where objects stood for world business. The terms let him show how display made claims that documents did not have to make.

“purported to function as a synecdoche” p. 141
Academy of Natural SciencesLouisiana Purchase Exposition, St. Louis, 1904 (Philippine exhibit)Philadelphia Commercial Museum

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The pair could be used to compare a world's-fair display of a colonised people with the same objects later catalogued in a museum, to see what each claimed its objects stood for.

Coombes, Annie E. (1994). Reinventing Africa: Museums, Material Culture and Popular Imagination in Late Victorian and Edwardian England. New Haven: Yale University Press.
racial typology of the ethnographic collectionCoombesappliestypology

Classification of peoples into fixed racial divisions with assumed moral and mental characteristics, used to order ethnographic material in museum galleries and to rank the civilisations represented. (Coombes 1994p. 141)

Draws on Keane

How it is used Coombes uses Keane's hierarchy, which the Liverpool curators followed, to show how museum galleries were arranged by race and how the arrangement implied moral hierarchy. The Liverpool reorganisation of 1901, with the Mongolian race on the top floor and the Caucasian in the main hall, is her main case of how classification was made into display.

“Keane assigned the Ethiopic negro to the lowest division of mankind” p. 141
Liverpool Mayer Museum (1896-1901)Horniman MuseumPitt Rivers Museum

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask how a Western museum's racial classification placed China, Japan or Southeast Asia within a scheme of civilisation, and how that order changed when the collection was reorganised.

Cuno, James (2008). Who Owns Antiquity? Museums and the Battle over Our Ancient Heritage. Princeton: Princeton University Press.
encyclopedic museumCunoappliestheoretical framing

A museum whose collections represent the artistic legacy of the world across cultures, which the text presents as the Enlightenment's universal project and as the opposite of the local focus of national museums. (Cuno 2008PDF p. 25)

How it is used Cuno defends the encyclopedic museum against charges of imperialism. Cuno argues that the British Museum and its successors arose from Enlightenment ambitions, that their collections were largely acquired legally on the terms of their time, and that they should be kept and extended through exchange rather than loans. It lets him present Chinese and Egyptian objects in Western collections as part of a shared heritage rather than as spoils.

“This is the promise of the encyclopedic museum: the museum as a repository of things and” PDF p. 25
the British Museumthe Art Institute of Chicagothe Harvard art museums and the Dunhuang Tang sculpture

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): One could ask what a Chinese or Southeast Asian object gains or loses in a Western encyclopedic display compared with its original site, as Cuno does with the Mogao sculpture in chapter four.

Cvetkovski, Roland; Hofmeister, Alexis (eds.) (2014). An Empire of Others: Creating Ethnographic Knowledge in Imperial Russia and the USSR. Budapest: Central European University Press.
ethnographic knowledge as cultural techniqueCvetkovskiadaptstheoretical framing

Ethnographic knowledge is treated as a practice with its own conditions of production, validation and circulation, not only as a body of results. The editors take the term from Köstlin and read it historically rather than as a separation of culture from politics. (Cvetkovski & Hofmeister 2014p. 1)

Draws on Konrad Köstlin

How it is used The introduction takes Köstlin's idea that ethnography is a cultural technique and turns it against his separation of ethnographic matters from state affairs. This lets the editors frame the volume's case studies (census categories, museum registers, expeditions, school folklore) as sites where knowledge was made under specific conditions. The idea supplies the volume's structure: paradigms, representations and peoples as three ways of looking at the same production process.

“identifying ethnographic knowledge as a genuine cultural technique,” p. 5
1897 census categoriesRussian Ethnographic MuseumImperial Russian Geographical Society

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The idea could be used to ask how a single museum's registers, labels or travelling collections were produced as knowledge, not only what they show. It invites a comparison with other national ethnographies or with colonial collecting in Southeast Asia.

Stockholm systemCvetkovskiappliestypology

A registration principle that records objects by the collection they came into, not by the territory they came from. The museum adopted it, with a parallel 'Copenhagen system' in the academy museum, and modified it to local needs. (Cvetkovski & Hofmeister 2014p. 240)

How it is used The chapter applies the Stockholm system to show that the museum's storage order created other classes of objects: ethnic (the imperial Inuit, Aleut and Tlingit collections), geographic (a Chinese collection, a Central Asian carpet collection), religious (a Buddhist collection) and material (a spoon collection). The author uses this to argue that the storage order was universal and could serve national, imperial or colonial museums alike, so that objects did not mirror one ideology.

“did not record the objects strictly by the territory where they” p. 240
Russian Ethnographic Museum storageAcademy museum (Kunstkamera) registration

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could apply the same check to an Asian collection in a Western museum: compare its registration by donor or purchase with its later display by region or nation.

Denton, Kirk A. (2014). Exhibiting the Past: Historical Memory and the Politics of Museums in Postsocialist China. Honolulu: University of Hawai‘i Press.
the miniatureDentonappliesanalytic concept

Miniature models and replica villages compress time and space into a whole that the visitor can take in at once, giving a sense of the nation or of the past as a totality. Denton uses Stewart's idea of the miniature to explain the feel of these displays. (Denton 2014p. 91)

Draws on Susan Stewart

How it is used Denton applies the miniature to the models of old Shanghai in the Shanghai Municipal History Museum, to the replica villages of Splendid China, and to the models of the planning halls. Denton argues that the miniature offers a simulated past that dispenses with historical authenticity, and that it feeds a possessive gaze that ties visitors to bourgeois fantasies.

“This miniaturized world recreates the past in realistic detail” p. 91
Shanghai Municipal History MuseumSplendid China theme park, ShenzhenChinese Nationalities Museumurban planning exhibition halls

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask whether miniature city models in a museum of a new district offer visitors the same possessive gaze on future property that Denton finds in old-Shanghai models.

Findlen, Paula (1994). Possessing Nature: Museums, Collecting, and Scientific Culture in Early Modern Italy. Berkeley: University of California Press.
wonder and signFindlenappliesanalytic concept

Wonder is the response to the unexpected, which naturalists tried to explain as a natural event rather than as a sign with religious or political meaning. Findlen states the distinction in Daston's terms: preternatural events always counted as wonders, but only sometimes as signs. (Findlen 1994p. 22)

Draws on Lorraine Daston

How it is used Findlen uses the wonder and sign distinction to explain how Aldrovandi handled the dragon: he chose a largely naturalistic explanation and called it a wonder, not a sign, which suited his cousin the pope and his own claim to expertise. Baroque collectors pushed the same category further, and Findlen uses that continuity to argue that the marvelous was a normal part of naturalist practice rather than a lapse from it.

“natural events always qualified as wonders, but only sometimes as signs.” p. 22
Aldrovandi's dragon of 1572Moscardo's Verona museumCospi's Bologna museum

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could apply the wonder and sign distinction to other portents shown in collections, such as a monstrous birth or an earthquake displayed in a colonial or East Asian cabinet, and ask who decided which reading was official.

curiosityFindlencriticisesanalytic concept

The drive to know that took naturalists out into the world and defined knowledge in terms of wonder and experience. Findlen treats curiosity as a positive force in the early modern museum rather than as the opposite of scientific method. (Findlen 1994p. 54)

Draws on Krzysztof Pomian

How it is used Findlen uses Pomian's description of Moscardo's Verona museum as a universe in which any question could legitimately be posed, but she argues against the Galileian and Cartesian judgment that curiosity was disorderly and unscientific. The instability of Baroque collections, on her account, reflects a science that had not yet set clear criteria for truth, so she can treat the Baroque museum as part of scientific culture rather than a prelude to it.

“Curiosity led naturalists out into the world.” p. 54
Moscardo's Verona museumCospi's Bologna museum (Legati's 1677 catalogue)Aldrovandi's museum

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could test whether collections in other regions, such as Dutch or Iberian cabinets, tolerated the same contradictions, and whether curiosity was valued there as a method or condemned as a vice.

saved appearancesFindlenappliesanalytic concept

The museum's capacity to fit new objects into the inherited Aristotelian and Plinian framework without overturning it. Findlen uses the phrase for the collecting of naturalists who wished to modify ancient authority rather than replace it. (Findlen 1994p. 4)

How it is used Findlen applies the idea to the new materials of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries: naturalists placed New World plants in Old World categories, and Jesuits built a Christian synthesis of all cultures and their artifacts. The idea lets her argue that collecting renewed ancient natural philosophy rather than breaking with it, and explains why the museum stood for Aristotelian natural history well into the 1600s.

“the museum "saved appearances" rather than unsettling ancient systems” p. 4
Aldrovandi's treatment of New World plantsKircher's Roman College museum

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask which East or Southeast Asian collection absorbed foreign objects into an inherited local order in this way, and what that order was.

book of natureFindlenadaptsanalytic concept

The metaphor of nature as a text to be read. Findlen shows the seventeenth-century naturalists using the collection to ground their claim to read this book, so that possessing nature mattered as much as the reading of texts. (Findlen 1994p. 57)

Draws on Hans Blumenberg; Michel Foucault

How it is used Findlen uses the metaphor to explain why collecting mattered to the new philosophy. Cesi urged the Lincean academy to read the universal book of the world, and Boccone still called nature a set of hieroglyphics, but for her the possession of nature, not reading alone, gave the metaphor its force. That is how the same objects that supported Aristotelian naturalists such as Aldrovandi, Kircher and Bonanni came to undermine them.

“it is necessary to read this great, truly named universal book of the world.” p. 57
the Accademia dei Lincei under CesiBoccone's museumthe museums of Kircher and Bonanni

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask which other collections, such as a Chinese cabinet, a Japanese herbal or a colonial botanic garden, were described as a readable text, and who was held able to read it.

Fromm, Annette B.; Golding, Viv; Rekdal, Per B. (eds.) (2014). Museums and Truth. Newcastle upon Tyne: Cambridge Scholars Publishing.
sacred objects and the museum tabooReinadaptsanalytic concept

Sacred objects stand outside economic exchange and are shielded by taboo. Museum accession, inventory and removal from the market resemble their treatment, so the museum's own rule becomes 'do not touch'. (Fromm 2014p. 129)

Draws on Kohl; Derlon

How it is used Rein draws on Kohl's comparison to argue that a collected object passes through steps resembling rites of passage. Rein uses this to explain why religious items cannot simply be shown as pure art, and why the context-party's relational approach must reckon with sacred knowledge that is restricted. The analogy is the basis of her opening case of the Montréal taxi driver, whose religious items in a public space raised the same questions of tolerance and secularity.

“is translated into the museum’s world: do not” p. 129
Religious items in a Montréal taxi (opening case)Museum collections in general

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could compare the handling rules in a museum store with the community's own taboos for the same object, to see where the two sets of rules differ.

Gardner, James (2020). The Louvre: The Many Lives of the World’s Most Famous Museum. New York: Atlantic Monthly Press.
encyclopedic museum and arbiter of collective visual cultureGardnerappliestypology

The Louvre as the first and greatest encyclopedic museum, bringing together the art of almost every age and region, with the ambition to judge the visual culture of all mankind, as against earlier cabinets that displayed whatever came their way. (Gardner 2020)

How it is used Gardner uses the type to explain the museum's scale and authority and to set it against earlier collections. Gardner dates the systematic display of the whole of art to the Bourbon Restoration, when non-Western and older cultures entered the galleries, and he reads the Napoleonic seizures against this ambition. The type gives him a standard by which the museum's acquisitions can be judged.

“The transcendent, almost arrogant ambition of the Louvre—to serve not only as repository but also as arbiter of the collective visual culture of mankind—must be appreciated in this light.”
Napoleonic seizures from Italy and Germanyearly British Museum and AshmoleanRestoration display of Egyptian and Assyrian art

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The type could be used to ask how an encyclopedic claim is built for a museum of a non-European state, and which regions it leaves out of its arbitration of visual culture.

Greenhalgh, Michael (2019). Plundered Empire: Acquiring Antiquities from Ottoman Lands. Leiden: Brill.
shopping listGreenhalghappliesanalytic concept

Written specifications for acquisitions, drawn up in the West from ancient authors, earlier travellers' reports and the wants lists of scholars, which travellers were sent to fill. The book's first section is devoted to these lists and the instructions that followed them. (Greenhalgh 2019PDF p. 13)

How it is used The idea links the scholarship of European capitals to the field: Colbert's commissions of 1675 and the instructions Robert Wood drew up for the Society of Dilettanti are read as orders, and the expeditions are judged by what they found and shipped. It shows how planning from home shaped which sites were dug.

“which were essentially shopping lists” PDF p. 13
Colbert's commissions to French travellers, 1675Society of Dilettanti expedition to Asia Minor, 1764-1766

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could reconstruct the wants lists behind a museum's Asian acquisitions and check how far the shipments matched them, to see whether a collection was planned or opportunistic.

Hall, Patricia; Seemann, Charlie (eds.) (1987). Folklife and Museums: Selected Readings. Nashville: American Association for State and Local History.
ethnographic modelKirshenblatt-Gimblettappliestypology

A way of presenting a culture through ordinary people in living communities, using categories internal to that community and treating context as the frame of meaning. It is set against the history model, which celebrates great men and prominent families, and the art model, which selects objects by an aesthetic criterion. (Hall & Seemann 1987p. 151)

How it is used Kirshenblatt-Gimblett uses the model as a standard against which to judge exhibitions of American Jewish life. Kirshenblatt-Gimblett calls the American Museum of Natural History's section on Jews and Judaism normative and outside time and place, and she questions the aesthetic of naivete on which the Museum of American Folk Art's selection rests. Kirshenblatt-Gimblett proposes project-based collecting and live presentation as ways to meet the model, since they let the community speak through its own categories.

“Third, most modern ethnographic approaches place a premium on categories, values, and understandings that are internal to” p. 152
Jews and Judaism section, American Museum of Natural History'The Jewish Heritage in American Folk Art', Museum of American Folk Artsalvage collecting at the Israel Museum

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could apply the model to a diaspora gallery in a Western museum and ask whether its categories are the community's own or the museum's.

Hill, Kate (2005). Culture and Class in English Public Museums, 1850–1914. Aldershot: Ashgate.
modes of collecting: souvenir, fetishistic, systematic, trophyHillappliestypology

Pearce's four rationales for forming collections: the souvenir tied to a life history, the fetishistic accumulation within a collector-defined category, the systematic set that illustrates principles, and the trophy from hunting that expresses mastery. Hill uses them to classify donations to municipal museums. (Hill 2005p. 69)

Draws on Susan Pearce

How it is used Hill applies the typology to donation lists in Preston and Liverpool and reads each gift for the rationale it expresses. Hill finds Preston's gifts mostly souvenir and fetishistic, expressing the personality of local elites, while Liverpool's were more systematic and educative. Trophies appear around 1900, when big game hunting results are given for display, and the Jacson and Foster collections show traces of all modes. The typology lets him argue that municipal collections kept much of the character of the older cabinet.

“distinguished by Pearce is the souvenir. This is an object collected primarily for its” p. 69
Preston Harris Museum donationsLiverpool Museum donationsJacson and Foster collections, Preston 1894Earl of Derby's natural history collection

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could sort the accessions of a colonial or regional museum by these four rationales to see whether donors gave for memory, status, knowledge or mastery over other peoples.

Hill, Kate (ed.) (2012). Museums and Biographies: Stories, Objects, Identities. Woodbridge: Boydell Press.
contaminated collectionsCarreauadaptsanalytic concept

Nick Stanley’s term for collections that are always shaped by the people who form them, so that amateur collections are judged by the contaminant. Carreau extends it so that the contaminants include the collector’s other roles and the biographies of the objects. (Hill 2012p. 203)

Draws on Nick Stanley

How it is used Carreau argues that Beasley’s collection is ‘even more contaminated than previously thought’, because he was also a museum founder, an experimental museologist, a Royal Anthropological Institute member and the author of a monograph. Each object carried its own biography, connecting it to other people and places. The extension lets her explain how the collection moved into and out of museums, rather than dismissing an amateur collection as unreliable.

“In fact, it is even more contaminated than previously thought.” p. 213
Harry Geoffrey Beasley’s collection and Cranmore Ethnographical Museum, Chislehurst

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The idea could be used on a private collection of Southeast Asian objects to ask which of the collector’s roles, dealers and objects’ earlier owners shaped what the museum now holds.

Hooper-Greenhill, Eilean (1992). Museums and the Shaping of Knowledge. London: Routledge.
epistemeHooper-Greenhillappliesperiodisation

The unconscious but productive set of relations within which knowledge is produced and rationality defined in a given period. The text distinguishes Renaissance, classical and modern epistemes, each with its own rules of resemblance, classification or representation. (Hooper-Greenhill 1992p. 12)

Draws on Foucault

How it is used The episteme explains why the same kind of collection counts as knowledge at one time and as irrational at another. Hooper-Greenhill reads the Medici Palace through magical correspondence and resemblance, the cabinet of the world through the Renaissance episteme, and the Repository through the classical table of difference. Normal histories that treat earlier collections as failed precursors are set against this frame.

“Foucault discovered and describes three major epistemes.” p. 12
Medici Palacecabinet of the worldRoyal Society RepositoryLouvremodern museum

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): One could ask which episteme organised a non-European museum’s collections in each period, and whether its classificatory system changed with the framework of its colonial or national sponsors.

cabinet of the worldHooper-Greenhillappliestypology

A Renaissance form of collection meant to represent the whole of creation through assembled material things, ordered by resemblance and by the art of memory. The author presents it as a rational structure within its own episteme, not as a disordered precursor of the modern museum. (Hooper-Greenhill 1992p. 102)

Draws on Foucault; Yates

How it is used Hooper-Greenhill uses the concept to argue that the Kunstkammern in Munich, Ambras and Prague were deliberate programmes of knowledge and imperial meaning. Small cabinets made by the merchant Hainhofer for princes are read as cabinets of the world in miniature, and palace-gardens are treated the same way. The category lets her criticise histories that judge these collections by the modern category of ‘art’ and call them ‘miscellaneous’ and ‘confused’.

“The ‘cabinet of the world’ was Camillo’s” p. 102
Kunstkammer of Albrecht V, MunichAmbras of Ferdinand IIKunstkammer of Rudolf II, PragueHainhofer cabinets for princes

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask whether a colonial or non-European collection assembled as a ‘world in miniature’ was organised by a comparable programme of representation, and whether it was later judged irrational for the same reasons.

Hopkins, Owen (2021). The Museum: From Its Origins to the 21st Century.
cabinet of curiosities as microcosmHopkinsappliestypology

A private collection of natural specimens, artificial objects and scientific instruments that encapsulates the known world in one room. The studiolo and the cabinet were places of private study and devotion, and the closest precursor to the modern museum. (Hopkins 2021)

How it is used Hopkins reads Rubens and Brueghel's The Sense of Sight (1617) as a picture of the cabinet as a microcosm of the world, and treats Ole Worm's cabinet in Copenhagen as the nearest precursor of the modern museum. The idea lets him trace how the museum inherited the aim of holding the world in one place, before the Enlightenment turned that aim towards classification.

“it stands as an encapsulation of the known world and a symbol that the boundaries of that world were fast expanding”
Ole Worm's cabinet, CopenhagenPiero de' Medici's studiolo, FlorenceTradescant's Ark, later the Ashmolean, Oxford

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could test this on a Southeast Asian private collection, asking whether its display was also a microcosm of a colonial or trading world, and what the arrangement of its objects shows about that world.

Impey, Oliver; MacGregor, Arthur (eds.) (1985). The Origins of Museums: The Cabinet of Curiosities in Sixteenth- and Seventeenth-Century Europe. Oxford: Clarendon Press.
Kunst- and Wunderkammer (terminology and typology)Impey, MacGregorcriticisestypology

The distinction between a Kunstkammer (artful things) and a Wunderkammer (wonders) that von Schlosser made, which the introduction treats as unstable: the terms shifted with geography, chronology, social standing and personality, so they cannot sort collections reliably. (Impey & MacGregor 1985PDF p. 19)

Draws on Julius von Schlosser

How it is used The introduction uses the instability of the terms to challenge the binary on which von Schlosser built his survey, and points out that an object could move between the two types as its status changed. Seelig applies a related distinction from Quiccheberg, between a promptuarium of miraculous things and a conclave of artful things, to read the Munich collection, while Schepelern rejects Schlosser's north-south split in mentality. The point lets the volume treat each collection on its own inventory terms.

“was affected by matters of geography,” PDF p. 20
Munich KunstkammerCopenhagen and Gottorp collectionsthe cabinets in general

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could check a museum's own terms for its collections, such as 'Indian' or 'curiosities' in an inventory, before reading its contents as a typology of its time.

universal programme (universal Kunstkammer)Impey, MacGregor, Scheicherappliestheoretical framing

The idea that the cabinet was an attempt to represent the whole of nature and human making in one place, with naturalia, artefacts, instruments, antiquities and mirabilia arranged on a universal scale. (Impey & MacGregor 1985PDF p. 17)

Draws on Francis Bacon

How it is used The introduction quotes Bacon's description of the learned gentleman's apparatus, including the 'goodly, huge cabinet', to argue that the miscellaneous contents of cabinets were the means of a programme aiming at universality rather than a sign of whim. Scheicher applies the universal Kunstkammer to Ambras, dividing its contents into naturalia, artefacts, instruments, mirabilia and coins, and Schepelern argues that princes aimed at totality while philosophers arranged objects by natural system.

“programme whose aim was nothing less than universality.” PDF p. 18
Ambras (Scheicher)Gottorp and Copenhagen collections (Schepelern)

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The same grid of categories could be used on a later museum's catalogue to ask whether its breadth was meant to represent a totality or a chosen selection.

microcosmScheicher, Boström, Fučíkovátestsanalytic concept

A collection modelled on the cosmos, in which the kingdoms of nature, the four elements and the arts appear as a world in miniature. The term is taken from the cosmology of Robert Fludd and from Rudolf II's self-image as master of the world. (Impey & MacGregor 1985p. 41)

Draws on Robert Fludd; Thomas DaCosta Kaufmann

How it is used Scheicher sets the Ambras content on a scale of the universe as Fludd envisaged it. Boström tests Fludd's model against the two Hainhofer cabinets: the Uppsala cabinet includes naturalia, artificialia and the four elements, so it fits the model, while the Pomeranian cabinet has no natural or artificial collections and so is not a microcosm. The test lets Boström separate a true microcosm from a cabinet that only shows art. Fučíková cites Kaufmann's reading of Rudolf's possession of the world in microcosm as a symbolic claim.

“unlike that in Uppsala, no microcosm” p. 133
Ambras (Scheicher)Uppsala Kunstschrank (Boström)Pomeranian cabinet (Boström)Prague (Fučíková)

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask of any cabinet whether its contents cover all categories of the world it claims to represent, as a test of whether it is a microcosm.

cabinet as working resourceFučíkováadaptsanalytic concept

The view that Rudolf II's Kunstkammer was a stock of raw materials, such as ores, stones, shells and horns, serving craft workshops and court artists, and not only a display, and that it was never meant for a wider public. (Impey & MacGregor 1985p. 68)

How it is used Fučíková uses this reading to set aside the idea of a cabinet as passive display: the same objects served production, and the collection was for the emperor's own use. Fučíková sets it beside the symbolic and diplomatic readings of Neumann and Kaufmann, adapting the cabinet concept to a working collection.

“it was a living organism and a fascinating resource” p. 68
Rudolf II's Kunstkammer, Prague

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask, for any early collection, which objects were kept for use in workshops or study and which for display, using the inventory to separate them.

Jasanoff, Maya (2005). Edge of Empire: Conquest and Collecting in the East, 1750–1850. London: Fourth Estate.
the British Empire as a collectionJasanoffcoinstheoretical framing

The British empire is treated as a collection itself: pieced together over time by accident, circumstance and intention, rather than as a single imperial project. Individual collectors stand for the wider process of acquiring territory and people. (Jasanoff 2005p. 6)

How it is used The framing lets Jasanoff avoid explaining collecting as a transparent expression of imperial power, which she rejects. Instead it organises the narrative around collectors such as Clive, whom she calls the first imperial collector of British India, so that territorial acquisition and object acquisition are told as one process. It also supports her argument that British rule was more contingent than the familiar imperial project suggests.

“pieced together and gaining definition over time” p. 6
Robert Clive in Bengalthe Company's conquest of MysoreHenry Salt and the Egyptian antiquities

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The framing could be turned on a national museum's Asian holdings, asking whether its growth followed the same piecemeal pattern as the empire it served. A researcher could trace how the collection and the territory it came from were acquired in the same years.

Karp, Ivan; Lavine, Steven D. (eds.) (1991). Exhibiting Cultures: The Poetics and Politics of Museum Display. Washington: Smithsonian Institution Press.
ethnographic object: excision, in situ and in contextKirshenblatt-Gimblettappliestypology

An ethnographic object is made so by excision and detachment, so exhibitions present fragments. In situ displays such as period rooms, habitat groups and recreated villages place objects in a recreated whole, while in context displays explain objects through labels, classifications and programmes. (Karp & Lavine 1991)

How it is used Kirshenblatt-Gimblett uses the pair to analyse the history of display from cabinets of curiosities and Peale's Museum through Goode's object lessons to the Egyptian Hall, where living Bushmen and Laplanders were shown as rarities. Kirshenblatt-Gimblett applies it to festivals, folkloric troupes and homeland exhibitions for immigrants, and to the Festival of American Folklife and the Festival of India's mela, where performers are staged as authentic while being shaped by tourism and nationalism. The pair lets her ask what a display includes and where its meaning is located.

“The artfulness of the ethnographic object is an art of excision, of detachment, an art of the excerpt.”
Peale's MuseumEgyptian HallNathan Dunn's Chinese collectionFestival of American FolklifeFestival of India mela

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The distinction could be used to classify any new display of an object from another culture by asking whether it places the object in a recreated whole or explains it through labels.

Kirshenblatt-Gimblett, Barbara (1998). Destination Culture: Tourism, Museums, and Heritage. Berkeley: University of California Press.
the ethnographic object as fragment (detachment)Kirshenblatt-Gimblettappliesanalytic concept

Objects become ethnographic through the act of detaching them from their setting and carrying them away, so they are fragments made by the disciplines that define them rather than found. Their meaning comes from juxtaposition in a new context, not from their origin. (Kirshenblatt-Gimblett 1998p. 2)

How it is used The author uses the idea to recast Peale's museum, the British Museum's Ethnographical Gallery and Goode's label-centred Smithsonian displays as machines of detachment. Applied to Dunn's Chinese figures, it lets her ask how a collection of portraits of individuals is turned into a picture of a whole culture. The fragment is the basis for her claim that all display is interested.

“ethnographic objects are made, not found, despite claims to the contrary.” p. 3
Peale's museum, PhiladelphiaBritish Museum Ethnographical GallerySmithsonian (Goode's exhibits)Nathan Dunn's Chinese collection

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask which objects from a Southeast Asian collection in a Western museum were detached in the field, by whom, and whether they ever regained a context in the place they came from.

Krech, Shepard, III; Hail, Barbara A. (eds.) (1999). Collecting Native America, 1870–1960. Washington: Smithsonian Institution Press.
professionalizing anthropological museum and erasure of alternative acquisitionJacknisappliesanalytic concept

The shift, as anthropology professionalized, to collections defined by trained scholars and documented systematically, which in Jacknis's account pushed out the exchanges, personal collections and oppositional modes by which many objects had been acquired. (Krech & Hail 1999)

Draws on Henry May

How it is used Jacknis applies the idea to Hearst's Southwest holdings. Jacknis uses May's three competing ideologies of the Wheeler era to place the museum between democratic culture and specialized research, and argues that the scholarly definition of what should be collected erased the less systematic routes by which the collections were formed. The argument lets him explain the Southwest holdings as a university museum's aims more than a patron's taste.

“What was erased, however, were the alternate and even oppositional modes of acquisition.”
Phoebe Hearst's Southwest collectionsMesa Verde potteryMcLeod baskets

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask which acquisition routes were lost when a university or national museum in East or Southeast Asia professionalized its collections, using exchange records and donor files to recover them.

educational collecting as cultural productionParezo and Hoerigappliesanalytic concept

A form of collecting in which the collector first forms an image or idea and then gathers objects to validate it, so that the collection creates knowledge as well as consuming it. (Krech & Hail 1999)

Draws on Margery Akin; Pierre Bourdieu; Belk et al.

How it is used Parezo and Hoerig apply the idea to Seton and Wheelwright to explain why both collections were organized around teaching rather than the objects themselves. Seton's artifacts modelled costumes for youth groups; Wheelwright's documented a single culture through sandpaintings and chants. The authors conclude that knowledge, not the objects, was the critical part of both collections.

“Educational collecting often involves first constructing an idea or an image and then, secondarily, amassing things.”
Seton Village museumMuseum of Navajo Ceremonial Art

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The idea could help study a collector who builds a picture of a national or ethnic culture, such as a museum of a region's minority peoples, by asking which image the collection was assembled to prove.

Lumley, Robert (ed.) (1988). The Museum Time-Machine: Putting Cultures on Display. London: Routledge.
SHIC classificationPortercriticisestypology

The hierarchical system of object classification for social and local history, which divides life into spheres such as community, domestic and family, personal and working life, so that domestic work is set apart from production. (Lumley 1988p. 109)

How it is used Porter applies the classification to the organisation of social history collections, where the domestic sphere is set in antithesis to working activity. Porter shows how this places housework outside the working sphere and makes women's labour hard to see, and she sets the classification against the York Castle Museum and Science Museum appliance displays. Porter’s argument is that shared classifications carry shared prejudices into collecting and display, so the bias is built into the catalogue as well as into individual decisions.

“Both are hierarchical systems organized around spheres of use” p. 109
York Castle Museum appliance display (1985)Science Museum domestic appliance gallery

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The idea suggests a question for any collection: which categories put a group of activities outside the main sphere, and which objects therefore never reach display.

Macdonald, Sharon; Fyfe, Gordon (eds.) (1996). Theorizing Museums: Representing Identity and Diversity in a Changing World. Oxford: Blackwell.
cosmological ordering of museum spacePröslerappliestheoretical framing

The early museum as a cosmological model of order, in which collections and cabinets give every object of knowledge a place, as in Camillo's memory theatre, where a cosmological scheme classified textual knowledge and rendered it spatial. The model is argued to descend into modern national museums. (Macdonald & Fyfe 1996PDF p. 34)

Draws on Cicero; Yates; Foucault

How it is used Prösler traces museum origins from Camillo's theatre and the Medici studiolo to the Royal Society's repository and then to nineteenth-century national museums. Prösler applies the model to the National Museum in Colombo, where the Sanni masks are read as remnants of a traditional past and where the display's hierarchical ordering of knowledge and peoples is reinterpreted in global categories of nation. Prösler concludes that local visitors read such displays in their own ways.

“was provided by a cosmological scheme which classified all” PDF p. 34
Camillo's memory theatreMedici studioloRoyal Society repositoryNational Museum, Colombo

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The model could be applied to the early collections of a Southeast Asian national museum, such as colonial cabinets in Batavia or Bangkok, to ask which ordering of the world those collections expressed.

MacKenzie, John M. (2009). Museums and Empire: Natural History, Human Cultures and Colonial Identities. Manchester: Manchester University Press.
imperial archiveMacKenzietestsanalytic concept

The colonial museum as a key imperial archive, a source of specimens, objects and records that constantly updated the natural and anthropological markers of colonial rule, and aimed at a totalising classificatory order in which everything had a serial number. (MacKenzie 2009p. 8)

Draws on Benedict Anderson; Thomas Richards

How it is used MacKenzie takes Anderson's account of the colonial state's classificatory grid as a test rather than a premise. MacKenzie grants the ideal of serial visibility but argues that funding, staff and expertise, trustees and audiences kept museums well short of it, so the archive was partial in practice. The idea lets him set the ordering ambition of the colonial museum against the evidence of its settler-colony histories.

“It was also a key ‘imperial archive’, both” p. 8
Colonial museums in the settler territoriesMuseums in the Malay states

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask whether a Southeast Asian colonial museum's accession registers show a serial, totalising order or a partial one shaped by thin funding. The contrast would test Anderson's grid against a specific collection.

McClellan, Andrew (1994). Inventing the Louvre: Art, Politics, and the Origins of the Modern Museum in Eighteenth-Century Paris. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.
comparative viewingMcClellanappliesmethod

A mode of looking at pictures by setting them against one another so that each is judged by its performance in the parts of painting (drawing, colour, expression), in contrast to chronological or national ordering. The Luxembourg Gallery deliberately encouraged it. (McClellan 1994p. 3)

Draws on André Félibien; Roger de Piles

How it is used McClellan reconstructs the eighteenth-century viewing habits from Félibien and de Piles and reads the Luxembourg's juxtapositions through them, so that an arrangement that looks unsystematic to a modern eye appears as a pedagogic design. The method lets the author argue that the Luxembourg was not a conventional princely cabinet and that the later school-and-chronology hang replaced a real alternative.

“encouraged a comparative mode of viewing that revealed the strengths and weaknesses of chosen artists and the schools to which they belonged” p. 3
Luxembourg Gallery, 1750-79Revolutionary Louvre hang of 1793

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could apply the same test to a hang of Asian ceramics or paintings in a Western museum, asking whether juxtaposition was designed to teach comparison of techniques or to display a collector's taste.

Meyer, Andrea; Savoy, Bénédicte (eds.) (2014). The Museum Is Open: Towards a Transnational History of Museums 1750–1940. Berlin: De Gruyter.
photographic connoisseurshipPetersappliesanalytic concept

A form of connoisseurship that works from photographic reproductions of museum works rather than from the originals, made possible by the wide availability of photographs of museum collections from the 1850s. (Meyer & Savoy 2014p. 57)

Draws on Hubert Locher

How it is used Peters uses the term to argue that the photographic campaigns did more than record the art historical canon: they helped form it. Peters tests this against Prince Albert’s Raphael project, the commercial work of Fenton and Thompson, and Braun’s refusal at the Louvre, which pushed him toward drawings and carbon prints. The argument gives her a way to describe the move from connoisseurship of originals to connoisseurship of images.

“not only reflected the art historical canon – they also helped to form it.” p. 57
Raphael drawings and paintings project, WindsorBritish Museum and South Kensington Museum photographsLouvre paintingsBerlin Gemaldegalerie

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The concept asks whether reproductions of Asian collections in European publications or archives shaped which objects scholars treated as canonical, and whether that was true in the other direction too.

Miller, Edward (1973). That Noble Cabinet: A History of the British Museum. London: André Deutsch.
classical taste of the TrusteesMillerappliesanalytic concept

The Trustees, raised on classical taste, valued classical statuary and coins and resisted non-classical antiquities for decades, so that Egyptian, Oriental and ethnographical objects came in only with difficulty. (Miller 1973p. 210)

How it is used Miller uses the idea to explain why the Department of Antiquities was dominated by classical acquisitions and why Keepers such as Hawkins had to work around the Board. The case material is Asian: the 1836 refusal of a collection of oriental antiquities, the Burmese figure of 1825 kept as a curiosity, and Masson's complaint about the China and Japan cases. Asian material thus appears as an unwanted residue, which is the point of the chapter.

“To spend good money on anything” p. 221
the Department of Antiquities 1820-1860oriental antiquities offered in 1836the Gaudma figure of 1825

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A question for another national museum: which non-European objects were refused, and whether the refusals followed the same preference for classical statuary.

Pearce, Susan M. (1992). Museums, Objects, and Collections: A Cultural Study. Leicester: Leicester University Press.
souvenir, fetishistic and systematic collectingPearceappliestypology

Collecting falls into three modes: souvenirs, which carry personal pasts and stay private; fetish collections, built from samples that express a possessive self and are seldom displayed; and systematic collections, which select examples to stand for a class and invite public argument. Real collections move between these poles, and one object can be a souvenir for one person and a fetish for another. (Pearce 1992p. 110)

Draws on Stewart; Ellen; Marx

How it is used Pearce uses the typology to organise chapters 3 and 4 and to read cases: Freud's antiquities as a fetish collection, Joseph Mayer's Liverpool collection as another, and Pitt Rivers's typological arrangements as the classic systematic collection. Because a collection's meaning depends on who holds it and what happens to it, the typology lets her argue that the museum's systematic mode is the one that most readily opens a public argument.

“The detachment of fetish collections explains why” p. 129
Freud's collection in Vienna and LondonJoseph Mayer's Liverpool collectionPitt Rivers's typological collections

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could sort a collector's holdings in an Asian or Western museum into these modes, asking which objects were kept as personal souvenirs and which were arranged to stand for a class.

third world of objective knowledge (Popper)Pearceadaptstheoretical framing

Popper's third world is the realm of objective contents of thought, such as journals, books and libraries. Pearce extends it to museum collections and exhibitions, which can be judged as arguments independent of the subjects who made or viewed them. (Pearce 1992p. 374)

Draws on Popper; Collingwood; Kuhn; Gombrich

How it is used Pearce uses the third world to escape both the claim of objective authority and post-structuralist relativism. Museum meanings are judged by critical argument, so some interpretations are better than others, as Gombrich's Night Watch example is used to show. Collingwood's coherence and correspondence and Kuhn's consensus of informed communities supply the test, and the curator becomes a persuasive interpreter within a participating community.

“The third world contains journals, books and libraries and, Popper might” p. 374
exhibitions as third-world argumentsThe West as America (1991)Still Life at Manchester Museum (1992)

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask whether an exhibition in a Chinese or Japanese museum can be judged as an objective argument by specialists from outside the museum, as opposed to a statement of the institution's authority.

Sellers, Charles Coleman (1980). Mr. Peale’s Museum: Charles Willson Peale and the First Popular Museum of Natural Science and Art. New York: W. W. Norton.
chain of natureSellersrejectstheoretical framing

The eighteenth-century view that species form a continuous, ordered sequence with fixed dependencies between them, which Peale's gallery arranged under the heading 'Homo sapiens in the Chain of Nature'. Sellers reports that younger scientists dismissed it in favour of the possibility of extinction. (Sellers 1980p. 30)

How it is used Sellers uses the phrase to mark a change in natural history: a gallery arranged as a chain of nature gives way to the view that some species had vanished. Sellers quotes Barton's denial of the chain and notes that Rembrandt Peale eventually convinced his father that some species had dropped out of it. The idea is shown as overtaken by new understanding rather than refuted by a single experiment.

“There is no such thing as a chain of nature,” p. 103
the gallery's arrangement of Homo sapiensBarton's objection

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask when a museum's gallery sequence encoded a chain of being, and when an Asian or colonial collection was rearranged under evolutionary or taxonomic order instead.

Sherman, Daniel J.; Rogoff, Irit (eds.) (1994). Museum Culture: Histories, Discourses, Spectacles. Minneapolis: University of Minnesota Press.
the four structuring concepts of object, context, public and receptionSherman and Rogoffcoinsanalytic concept

The editors' four linked notions on which every museum rests: objects and their classification, the context (nation, community, period or style) they are held to signify, the public the museum claims to serve, and the way that public receives the display. They are the framework for reading all the essays. (Sherman & Rogoff 1994PDF p. 15)

How it is used The editors use the four terms as the common basis of the whole volume, though each essay focuses on one or another. In the introduction they show how a classification sets the context, which in turn selects a public, so that the museum constructs 'a self, the viewer, or in collective terms a public'. The framework lets the essays on Koven, Zolberg, Hoffmann and Wallis be read as studies of the same chain.

“The four structuring concepts of object, context, public, and reception” PDF p. 15
the art museum in generalthe Whitechapel picture exhibitionsnational festival exhibitions

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The four terms could be used to compare how a regional museum in one Asian country classifies an object as national, local or colonial, and whom the displays assume their viewers to be.

collecting as an act that defies use and capitalSherman and Rogoffappliescritique

Adorno and Benjamin describe collecting as the removal of objects from their original function, so that they enter a new historical system and become a 'practical memory'. The museum, by contrast, treats its objects independently of the material conditions of its own period. (Sherman & Rogoff 1994PDF p. 15)

Draws on Adorno; Walter Benjamin

How it is used The editors quote Benjamin's Passagenwerk on collecting, then use Adorno's critique of the museum as culturally conservative to set the museum's treatment of objects against Benjamin's politically re-collected objects. The contrast becomes the basis for the case of artists who expose the museum's ideology.

“Collecting is a form of practical memory” PDF p. 16
the museum's treatment of collected objects generally

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): Benjamin's distinction could test whether the private collections of Asian objects that entered Western museums became 'practical memory' for their collectors, or simply stock in a system of value.

Siegel, Jonah (2020). Material Inspirations: The Interests of the Art Object in the Nineteenth Century and After. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
the classical canon as images on paperSiegelappliesanalytic concept

The idea that for the nineteenth century classical sculpture was known mainly through copies, prints and compendia, so that a canon of images stood in for a set of material objects. (Siegel 2020p. 145)

Draws on Spence; Tooke; Winckelmann; Caylus; Lessing

How it is used Siegel applies the concept to Blake's engravings for Rees's Cyclopaedia and to the Townley collection, the Elgin Marbles and the British Museum. Siegel shows that the Laocoön and Apollo Belvedere were known largely through reproduction and textual compendia. This lets him argue that the search for an ideal antiquity was an anxious response to a past reachable only through reproduction.

“To know them was to know copies, whether in two dimensions or three” p. 148
Blake's plates for Rees's CyclopaediaTownley collectionElgin MarblesBritish MuseumLaocoön at the Vatican

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A museum's plaster casts or prints could be read as the working canon of its visitors, asking which copies a regional collection actually displayed.

Sleeper-Smith, Susan (ed.) (2009). Contesting Knowledge: Museums and Indigenous Perspectives. Lincoln: University of Nebraska Press.
collections as complete outcomes of colonial practiceMcMullenappliesanalytic concept

Following Gosden and Knowles, a collection is read not as a partial record of a culture but as the complete result of one collector's colonial practices, so that the whole the collector intended is the first object of study. (Sleeper-Smith 2009p. 68)

Draws on Chris Gosden; Chantal Knowles; Brian Durrans

How it is used McMullen applies the idea to Heye, whose systematic early-object collection the NMAI has described as the work of an obsessive 'boxcar' collector. McMullen argues that his collection has to be read for what he intended, and that the museum's own purposes must also be unpacked. The idea lets her recover Heye's career from the archive rather than from anecdote.

“complete, although particular, outcomes” p. 68
George Gustav Heye's collectionNational Museum of the American Indian

Stewart, Susan (1984). On Longing: Narratives of the Miniature, the Gigantic, the Souvenir, the Collection. Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press.
the collection as containment of experienceStewartappliesanalytic concept

The collection is a finite, classified series that contains the world by control and confinement, and it turns history into order and possession. Its knowledge is eclectic and ahistorical, so that it is particularistic and random. (Stewart 1984p. 161)

Draws on Bunn

How it is used Stewart applies the concept to Pepys's library, hoarded coins and Tiffany postal scales, and borrows Bunn's idea that a surplus of significance can overwhelm the collector. The collection becomes a model of how private possession stands in for knowledge and for the self.

“The collection is often about containment on the level of its content” p. 161
Samuel Pepys's arrangement of his libraryhoarded coinsthe collector's cabinet of Mario Praz

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The notion of containment could be used to ask what a regional or foreign collection in a Western museum is made to contain, and what it leaves out of its frame.

the museum as the central metaphor of the collectionStewartappliesanalytic concept

The museum, more than the library, is the central model of the collection, because it claims to be representative and to close all space and time within its context. Its representational authority rests on the displacement of part for whole and on a classification scheme that accounts for the world. (Stewart 1984p. 161)

Draws on Eugenio Donato

How it is used Stewart takes Donato's account of the museum's representational fiction and applies it to the natural history museum and the zoo, arguing that the Linnaean system articulates plant identities in the museum rather than the other way around. The concept lets the author treat museum tableaux as forms of simultaneity and reconciliation.

Stocking, George W., Jr. (ed.) (1985). Objects and Others: Essays on Museums and Material Culture. Madison: University of Wisconsin Press.
principle of continuity and typological arrangementChapmantestsanalytic concept

Pitt Rivers's rule that artifacts change by small gradations of form, so that a series of objects can be arranged by typological continuity and read as an evolutionary sequence. Chapman says Pitt Rivers elaborated the rule with ideas from Herbert Spencer, and that it could lead to degeneration as well as progress. (Stocking 1985p. 33)

Draws on Herbert Spencer

How it is used Chapman sets the principle against the geographical system of Leiden, against the schemes of Jomard and Klemm, and against Christy's collection, and shows that it was tested in practice. When Pitt Rivers planned his concentric anthropological rotunda, the principle of typological continuity was preserved but the effect was to privilege geographical over evolutionary connection. The concept lets Chapman explain why museum arrangements moved toward geography in the end.

“Unified by the principle of continuity, or modification by small gradations” p. 33
Pitt Rivers collection at Farnham and OxfordLeiden geographical arrangementChristy collection

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could test whether a regional museum's series of Southeast Asian weapons or ceramics was arranged by gradation of form or by place of origin, and what visitors were shown by each.

art and artifact as two classifications of non-Western objectsCliffordappliestypology

Since about 1900, non-Western objects have been sorted into scientific cultural artifacts, displayed with their group and their function, and aesthetic works of art, identified with a named creator. Objects migrate between the two, and in the ethnographic museum the object is 'interesting' where in the art museum it is 'beautiful' or 'original'. (Stocking 1985p. 242)

How it is used Clifford uses the division to read Williams's account of Ars Americana moving between the Louvre, the Bibliotheque Nationale, the Musee Guimet and the Trocadero, and then the 1984-85 New York exhibitions that set tribal objects beside modernist works. The typology lets him argue that the modernist revolution blurred the division and changed an object's status without any change in the object. He sets the volume's nineteenth-century cases against the present in this way.

“in the art museum it is primarily "beautiful” p. 242
Trocadero (Ars Americana)Museum of Modern Art, New York, 1984-85Metropolitan Museum of Art, 1984-85

Vergo, Peter (ed.) (1989). The New Museology. London: Reaktion Books.
knowing through lookingJordanovacriticisescritique

The belief that visitors gain knowledge directly from displayed objects. Jordanova argues it is an illusion produced by architecture, arrangement and labels, and that museums cannot teach abstract ideas such as childhood or nature. (Vergo 1989p. 40)

Draws on Donna Haraway; James Clifford

How it is used Jordanova tests the assumption against museums of childhood and science, and against Haraway's analysis of the American Museum of Natural History's primate hall. Jordanova argues that no object can embody an abstraction. Jordanova’s treatment of anthropological objects shows that the claim to restore objects to their social context depends on realist representation, which keeps the other in the position of an object. Jordanova concludes that the illusion needs historical scrutiny.
