Yanni, Carla (1999). Nature’s Museums: Victorian Science and the Architecture of Display. Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press.
Cabinet of curiosities as precursor of the museumYannitestsanalytic concept

The question whether the seventeenth-century Wunderkammer, which Pomian defines as an encyclopedic miniature of the universe, was an origin of the nineteenth-century museum. Yanni answers it in a limited sense: cabinets made displays of nature a means of learning, although their classification differed. (Yanni 1999p. 16)

Draws on Pomian; Hooper-Greenhill; Crimp; Findlen

How it is used Yanni sets Pomian’s definition against Hooper-Greenhill’s warning about searching for origins and Crimp’s rejection of the link. Yanni answers Crimp by noting that Crimp was concerned with the art museum and that Foucault did not claim master narratives stay fixed, so a cabinet could have another classification and still be an origin. Yanni then follows Findlen’s case that Italian cabinets were early natural history museums and uses it to show that nineteenth-century museums extended learning beyond the elite.

“curiosities is the necessary precursor to nineteenth-century museums.” p. 20

Meanings of nature (creation, natural resource, secular science)Yannicoinstypology

A typology of the meanings Victorians gave nature: God’s second book or creation, nature as resource for commerce and empire, and secular science. Yanni argues that each building expressed a different one, and that the meaning was local and contextual. (Yanni 1999p. 13)

How it is used The typology organises the case studies: Oxford expresses nature as creation, Edinburgh and the Museum of Practical Geology nature as resource, and the Natural History Museum a range from creation to secular science. It lets Yanni argue that nature held different meanings for different audiences, so the buildings are evidence of conflicting definitions rather than of one scientific worldview.

Memory, heritage and difficult pasts

Nora, Halbwachs, Lowenthal and the critics of the heritage industry; commemoration, nostalgia, authenticity, trauma and war. 61 concepts from 38 texts

Memory and heritage approaches treat a museum as a place where a community's past is selected, fixed and performed in the present, rather than as a neutral store of evidence. They ask what a museum remembers, for whom, and what it leaves out. Behind most of the work in our texts stand Pierre Nora and Maurice Halbwachs, whose distinction between memory and history and whose account of collective memory recur across the records (Denton 2014p. 11; Muchitsch 2013p. 166; Aldrich 2005p. 6). Other inspirations include Aleida and Jan Assmann, Marianne Hirsch, Ruskin, Benjamin and Kirshenblatt-Gimblett's account of heritage as production (Hill 2012p. 299; Damousi 2020p. 100; Siegel 2020p. 234; Kirshenblatt-Gimblett 1998p. 149). The texts at the centre of the approach are Kirshenblatt-Gimblett (Kirshenblatt-Gimblett 1998), Denton (Denton 2014), Askew (Askew 2007), Aldrich (Aldrich 2005), Outka (Outka 2009) and Paver (Paver 2018). Several of them examine colonial, wartime or post-conflict museums, where what is remembered is most contested.

Nora and Halbwachs: memory against history

Nora's distinction, as our records give it, sets memory as emotional, selective and bound to groups against history as a critical activity with a universal claim (Muchitsch 2013p. 166). Bounia and Stylianou-Lambert apply it to photographs in five Cypriot war museums, where selection and framing sustain one community's story and silence another, and mandatory school visits keep that memory uncontested (Muchitsch 2013p. 167). Denton uses Nora's lieux de mémoire to argue that Chinese museums both restore and reify the past, deritualising local memory in favour of a national story (Denton 2014p. 11; Denton 2014p. 22). Denton also adapts Gillis's distinction between official and vernacular memory, arguing that the two overlap in China, with Halbwachs explaining why visitors accept official narratives without noticing (Denton 2014p. 13; Denton 2014p. 14). Aldrich applies sites of memory to colonial statues and museum rooms in France, so that such collections count as more directly colonial sites than their artworks suggest (Aldrich 2005p. 6; Aldrich 2005p. 245). Kavanagh, drawing on Halbwachs, sets memory and history as two constructions that meet visitors' recollections, and argues that museums should show that collision rather than settle it (Kavanagh 1996p. 5; Kavanagh 1996p. 8).

Heritage as production, and nostalgia

Kirshenblatt-Gimblett coins the view that heritage is "a new mode of cultural production in the present that has recourse to the past" (Kirshenblatt-Gimblett 1998p. 149). The author applies it to Ellis Island, Plimoth Plantation and Colonial Williamsburg, to show that these sites produce a version of the past rather than recover it (Kirshenblatt-Gimblett 1998p. 7). Hoyau criticises the effective nostalgia of the French Heritage Year of 1980, reading ecomuseums and inventories as one policy that makes the past a tool of community mobilisation (Lumley 1988p. 30; Lumley 1988p. 32). Bennett applies the countryside of the mind to Beamish, where the country house organises town, countryside and class as one harmonious order, so that an open-air museum can show industry without showing conflict (Lumley 1988p. 68; Lumley 1988p. 69). Denton reads Shanghai's history museum and Xintiandi as commercial nostalgia that serves the state's image of a global economic centre, drawing on Boym and Dai Jinhua (Denton 2014p. 88; Denton 2014p. 89). Askew frames nostalgia as the emotional work the Hearn museums perform, while Sorensen argues that theme parks deny the passage of time, so that the past looks like the present (Askew 2007p. 140; Vergo 1989p. 65). Stewart treats nostalgia as the characteristic emotion of narrative: "Nostalgia is a sadness without an object" (Stewart 1984p. 23).

Authenticity: pastness, relation and regimes

Veldkamp uses Holtorf's pastness to judge a replica of a Paekche incense burner and a reconstructed tomb at Kongju, arguing that replicas can give general visitors an authentic experience (Veldkamp 2014p. 574). Arnold describes the appeal of historical and biographical museums as a pay-off between belief and trust in the real object, and argues that this matters more once digital reproduction is available (Arnold 2006). Scarborough adapts authenticity as a relation to the audience, so that the staged documents of the Getty's Evidence of Movement require visitors to act as detectives (Dudley 2010p. 260; Dudley 2010p. 263). Bilsel introduces regimes of the authentic for the bureaucratic practices that make some objects count as originals, and rejects reception history, which treats later appropriation as an abuse of an original (Bilsel 2012PDF p. 31; Bilsel 2012PDF p. 33). Silina, following Shaposhnikov, locates authenticity in an isolated unique present chosen by the curator, not in preserved objects (Silina 2026p. 39; Silina 2026p. 41).

Ruin, relic and cenotaph

Siegel adopts Benjamin's allegory, a time-bound signification projected onto material traces, against the symbol, and sets Warburg's reading of Raphael's herm beside it (Siegel 2020p. 233; Siegel 2020p. 234). Using Ruskin's ruined cathedral, Siegel holds the modern public responsible for the destruction of old monuments, a boundless and always-failing responsibility (Siegel 2020p. 251). Yallop takes Ruskin's stay what is fleeting as the test of whether collectors' gifts kept their collections whole, and finds that they did not (Yallop 2011). Black applies the concept of the museum as cenotaph to Morris and Wells, where the museum becomes a memorial to a lost past rather than a working institution (Black 2000p. 169).

Testimony, postmemory and cultural memory

De Jong applies Aleida and Jan Assmann's distinction between communicative and cultural memory to witness accounts, which become cultural memory when paired with objects such as gloves at Bergen-Belsen (Hill 2012p. 299; Hill 2012p. 301). Witcomb adapts Holocaust testimony theory to a war-centenary exhibition, where descendants' screen testimony makes visitors witnesses (Damousi 2020p. 176). Thomson applies Hirsch's postmemory to family war stories, in which letters reassured and veterans spared their children, and uses repatriation files as a corrective (Damousi 2020p. 100; Damousi 2020p. 101). Paver tests the punctum of time, taken from Hirsch and Spitzer, against a home-made object from the deportations, and finds that it only partly fits (Paver 2018p. 117). Paver also applies Aleida Assmann's passive cultural forgetting to show the boxes in which objects were stored after 1945 (Paver 2018p. 175).

Selective forgetting and the contested colonial past

Aldrich uses Renan's remark that forgetting is essential to nation-building, and Debray's contrast between Haiti and France, to read gaps such as the long silence over the Algerian War as one pattern (Aldrich 2005p. 7). Aldrich's ambivalence is a key for reading monuments such as the Fréjus memorial, which is neither simply celebratory nor simply critical (Aldrich 2005p. 8). Hicks coins necrography to count looted Benin objects back through the events and sales that took them, and argues that display extends the violence (Hicks 2020). Gillman criticises the UNESCO idea of a common heritage of humanity by asking whose heritage the Bamiyan Buddhas are, and calls their destruction a "crime against the common heritage of humanity" (Cuno 2009p. 166). Lee reads the National Museum of Korea as "the museum has become a palimpsest" of colonial and postcolonial history (Knell et al. 2011p. 373). Yoshida applies victimizer consciousness to Japan's acceptance of war responsibility, and the history wars to four museums whose captions changed under pressure (Yoshida 2014PDF p. 17; Yoshida 2014p. 162; Yoshida 2014p. 176). Ho and Li use the museum as courtroom to explain the post-Mao dispute over Liu Wencai, where exhibits act as evidence and rival tours as counter-testimony (Ho & Li 2016p. 20).

Contagion, souvenir and performance

Hall adapts Frazer's contagious magic to explain why visitors feel closer to objects touched by famous people, even when the objects are not interpreted at all (Hall & Seemann 1987p. 84). Stewart describes the souvenir as a partial sample: "The souvenir therefore contracts the world in order to" expand the personal, carrying a narrative rather than its original context (Stewart 1984PDF p. 13). Urry adapts Connerton's distinction between incorporating and inscribing practices, arguing that museums are inscriptions that visitors re-read in performance (Macdonald & Fyfe 1996PDF p. 55; Macdonald & Fyfe 1996PDF p. 60). Seemann criticises easy choices of live presenters, such as revivalists, and insists that performance keep the community's context (Hall & Seemann 1987p. 61). Rattue finds oral-assumptive symbolic behaviour in a regimental museum's objects and General Gordon relics (Kavanagh 1996p. 219). Pearson adapts Kavanagh's dream space, in which visitors' private memories meet the museum's order, and sets wartime recollections against the official reports (Pearson 2017).

Debates and limits

The texts disagree most sharply over whether museums impose memory or are read against their makers. Denton's overlap model rejects a reading in which the audience is either passive or dissident, since visitors can accept official narratives and also shape them (Denton 2014p. 14). Kirshenblatt-Gimblett rejects the heritage industry's discourse of reclamation, arguing that heritage produces rather than recovers the past (Kirshenblatt-Gimblett 1998p. 149). Daly and Chan test the trade-off claim against Tuol Sleng and Yasukuni, and question how far officials involved in the events shape the narrative (Logan 2016). Silina places authenticity in the structure of time rather than in preserved objects, and notes that later critics who measured authenticity by originals dismissed the museum (Silina 2026p. 39; Silina 2026p. 41). Bilsel rejects reception history, which treats later appropriation as an abuse of an original (Bilsel 2012PDF p. 33). Outka treats the commodified authentic as a sustained contradiction rather than a fraud, which sets Outka against critics who unmask it (Outka 2009p. 4).

Carrying it over to a new case

  • Ask who adds value to a way of life that is no longer viable in a historic quarter of a Southeast Asian city, and who produces that value. This follows Kirshenblatt-Gimblett's model of heritage as production (Kirshenblatt-Gimblett 1998p. 149).
  • Compare the official and vernacular overlap model with a memorial where the state is absent, to see whether local memory echoes official vocabulary (Denton 2014p. 13).
  • Read a contested exhibit as a court record: who testifies, what counts as evidence and what verdict the museum is expected to give (Ho & Li 2016p. 20).
  • Trace which objects in a donor or gift collection still survive as a unit after fifty years, using inventories and deaccession records. Yallop's test of stay what is fleeting models this question (Yallop 2011).
  • Assess a replica or reconstructed site against Veldkamp's three criteria, material clues, fit with visitor expectations and a plausible narrative, and ask which one visitors respond to (Veldkamp 2014p. 574).
  • Ask whether captions on donated objects in a regional museum use delay words such as erst and bis, and whether the containers they arrived in are on display. This follows Paver's passive forgetting (Paver 2018p. 175).
  • Trace each object from a punitive campaign to the event or sale that took it, starting with the dealers and officers named in the accession files. This follows Hicks's necrography (Hicks 2020).

Where to start reading

  • Kirshenblatt-Gimblett, Barbara (1998). Destination Culture: Tourism, Museums, and Heritage. Berkeley: University of California Press. Heritage as production and how a restored site sells its own pastness.
  • Denton, Kirk A. (2014). Exhibiting the Past: Historical Memory and the Politics of Museums in Postsocialist China. Honolulu: University of Hawai‘i Press. The lieux de mémoire, official and vernacular memory, and nostalgia applied to a national museum.
  • Aldrich, Robert (2005). Vestiges of the Colonial Empire in France: Monuments, Museums and Colonial Memories. Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan. Sites of memory and ambivalence applied to colonial monuments.
  • Muchitsch, Wolfgang (ed.) (2013). Does War Belong in Museums? The Representation of Violence in Exhibitions. Bielefeld: transcript. Memory against history in photographs in war museums.
  • Veldkamp, Elmer (2014). “Keeping It Real: The Exhibition of Artifact Replicas in National Museums of Korea”. Acta Koreana, 17.2 (December 2014): 557-581. Pastness and the replica as an authentic experience.
  • Damousi, Joy; Tout-Smith, Deborah; Ziino, Bart (eds.) (2020). Museums, History and the Intimate Experience of the Great War: Love and Sorrow. London: Routledge. Testimony and postmemory in a war-centenary exhibition.
  • Hicks, Dan (2020). The Brutish Museums: The Benin Bronzes, Colonial Violence and Cultural Restitution. London: Pluto Press. Necrography, the method of tracing loot to its events.

Aldrich, Robert (2005). Vestiges of the Colonial Empire in France: Monuments, Museums and Colonial Memories. Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan.
colonial lieux de mémoire (sites of memory)Aldrichadaptstheoretical framing

Monuments, museums and other markers are places where memory is built, displayed, forgotten or recalled. Aldrich applies this to colonial traces in metropolitan France, so that a statue, plaque, street name or museum room becomes evidence of how the nation has or has not come to terms with empire. (Aldrich 2005p. 6)

Draws on Halbwachs; Nora

How it is used Aldrich takes Nora's idea of sites of memory, with Halbwachs's account of collective memory as its basis, and applies it to colonial monuments and museums across France, from the Fréjus Indochina memorial to the Musée Guimet and the non-Western collections in national museums. The idea lets him argue that such collections are more directly colonial sites than they are usually taken to be, which a study of artworks alone would not show.

“are more directly colonial lieux de mémoire” p. 245
Fréjus Indochina memorialMusée Guimetnon-Western collections in French museumsParis streets and statues

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The same framing could be used to ask which colonial sites in a city such as Lisbon or Antwerp are commemorated, which are absent, and how their silences differ. It would need the local inventory that Aldrich says he did not compile.

selective memory and forgettingAldrichappliesanalytic concept

Forgetting is as significant as remembering. The French did not erase their colonial past entirely; they recalled some episodes, such as the abolition of slavery, and passed over others, such as slavery itself, so the record shows selective recollection. (Aldrich 2005p. 7)

Draws on Renan; Marc Augé; Régis Debray

How it is used Aldrich uses Renan's remark that forgetting is essential to nation-building, and Debray's comment that Haiti suffers from too much memory and France from too little, as a frame for his three phases and for the gaps in the record, such as the long silence over the Algerian War. The concept lets him read the absence of Indochinese War monuments and the praise of abolition as parts of one pattern of selective memory rather than as separate failures.

“The French celebrated the emancipation of slaves, while” p. 7
abolition commemorationsIndochinese and Algerian war monumentsNantes and the slave tradeSaint-Domingue anniversary

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could compare which episodes of an imperial past a national museum chooses to show and which it leaves out, and test whether that selection follows the same pattern across former empires.

ambivalenceAldrichappliesanalytic concept

Attitudes to the colonies combine nostalgia, residual pride, doubts about the worth of the effort, shame and occasional outrage. Aldrich uses the word as a general description of French attitudes rather than as a single verdict on any monument. (Aldrich 2005p. 8)

How it is used Ambivalence is Aldrich's key for reading individual sites. The Fréjus memorial's bas-relief, which shows a Frenchman and an Indochinese as allies, and its dates, which join 1939 to 1956, are read as mixed messages; the book closes by saying the presentation of empire remains open because each group holds conflicting memories. The concept allows him to judge a monument neither as simply celebratory nor as simply critical.

Bilsel, Can (2012). Antiquity on Display: Regimes of the Authentic in Berlin’s Pergamon Museum. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
regimes of the authenticBilselcoinsanalytic concept

The modern disciplinary and bureaucratic practices of archaeology, museology and historic preservation, which separate monuments and sites from everyday use and make some objects count as authentic while copies do not. (Bilsel 2012PDF p. 31)

How it is used Bilsel introduces the term to answer his question of how and when the authentic came to matter. In the epilogue he connects the Berlin displays with the classical authority of Millin and Quatremère, Viollet-le-Duc's restoration, Riegl's cult of age value, the 1931 Athens Conference and Balanos's work on the Acropolis, arguing that the Pergamon reconstructions were authenticated by the museum and the photograph rather than discovered in the monument. He uses the destruction of the Victoria and Albert Museum's Indian architectural displays in 1955 as evidence that the regime changed over the century.

The German tradition that studies the later interpretations of an ancient monument, which assumes an original independent of its modern uses. (Bilsel 2012PDF p. 33)

The museum in decline as a memorial to a past that has already been lost, which invites the reader to ponder the imbalance between cultural gain and loss that the museum signals. (Black 2000p. 169)

How it is used Black applies the concept to Morris's News from Nowhere and Wells's The Time Machine, in which the museum is moribund and becomes a memorial rather than a working institution. The concept lets him argue that these fictions place the museum at the centre of a crisis about inheritance and cultural loss. It links the late-Victorian stories to the coda's reading of Freud's study as a memorial to loss.

“becomes a cenotaph” p. 169
Morris's News from NowhereWells's The Time Machine

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask whether museums in East or Southeast Asia that were built for a lost imperial or royal past, or that were closed and reopened as memorials, take on the same cenotaph role and what they commemorate.

Cuno, James (ed.) (2009). Whose Culture? The Promise of Museums and the Debate over Antiquities. Princeton: Princeton University Press.
common heritage of humanityGillmancriticisescritique

The phrase, used by UNESCO, that treats monuments as the property of all humanity. Gillman asks whose heritage a monument is when the people who live beside it do not regard it as theirs. (Cuno 2009p. 166)

Draws on UNESCO

How it is used Gillman applies the phrase to the Bamiyan Buddhas, which the Taliban did not regard as theirs though Tibetan and Japanese Buddhists might. Gillman also weighs group property rights against legal title for the Parthenon sculptures. Gillman concludes that such claims are noble but conflict with export controls and carry a cost for the encyclopedic museum.

“crime against the common heritage of humanity.” p. 166
Bamiyan BuddhasParthenon sculptures, British MuseumLansdowne portrait of Washington

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask to whom a Buddhist sculpture in a European museum belongs, and whether the claim is made by a state, a community or a religious institution.

Damousi, Joy; Tout-Smith, Deborah; Ziino, Bart (eds.) (2020). Museums, History and the Intimate Experience of the Great War: Love and Sorrow. London: Routledge.
testimony and witnessWitcombadaptsanalytic concept

Testimony is a speech act that reanimates the dead, reconstitutes the survivor as a person and makes a demand on the listener. Witcomb adapts Holocaust testimony theory so that visitors and the descendants who speak in the exhibition become witnesses to the earlier love and sorrow. (Damousi 2020p. 176)

Draws on Nanette Auerhahn; Dori Laub; Roger Simon

How it is used Witcomb transfers the testimony framework from Holocaust collection to a war-centenary exhibition whose stakes are lower. Descendants on screen give a second testimony in the present, which makes visitors witnesses and binds the pain across generations. The concept lets her claim that the exhibition makes a demand on its audience.

“In the case of Love and Sorrow, this gift is enacted through” p. 176
Descendant of Eliza Amery giving testimony on screenDescendants of the eight protagonists generally

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The question for another museum is whether it can make visitors into witnesses without a living descendant, and what a descendant’s testimony adds that an archival voice does not. The framework could also be set against colonial collections whose subjects did not give testimony.

postmemoryThomsonappliestheoretical framing

Memory of a traumatic past passed to the generation that did not live through it, which in family histories of war replaces veterans’ testimony once no veterans are alive. Thomson takes the term from Hirsch’s work on Holocaust memory. (Damousi 2020p. 100)

Draws on Marianne Hirsch

How it is used Thomson applies postmemory to explain why family war stories are especially vulnerable to mythology: letters reassured, photographs showed happy times, and veterans spared their children. Thomson then uses the repatriation files as a corrective, so that the family myth of Hector Thomson’s wartime life gives way to the evidence of mental illness.

“In our era of “postmemory” – to use the term coined by” p. 100
Hector Thomson’s Repatriation filesAnzac Memories and its revised edition

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask how postmemory shapes the family donations that stock a regional museum’s war collection, and whether donated letters are curated to reassure. The question is what the archive lets the next generation find that the family tellings left out.

Denton, Kirk A. (2014). Exhibiting the Past: Historical Memory and the Politics of Museums in Postsocialist China. Honolulu: University of Hawai‘i Press.
lieux de memoireDentonappliesanalytic concept

Sites where memory is embodied because living everyday memory has been broken. Museums are such sites, and they impose a collective national memory in place of personal and local forms of the past. (Denton 2014p. 11)

Draws on Pierre Nora

How it is used Denton uses Nora to place museums within the memory crisis that followed the French Revolution, and to argue that they both restore and reify the past. Denton applies the idea to China by showing how museums deritualize local memory and put a national story in its place, in the national museum and in the local culture museums that follow.

“what Pierre Nora calls lieux de mémoire (realms, or sites, of memory)” p. 11
National Museum of Chinalocal culture museums

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask whether a municipal museum that replaces a demolished neighbourhood acts as a lieu de memoire for a community that no longer lives there.

official and vernacular memoryDentonadaptsanalytic concept

A distinction between memory promoted by the state and memory held by ordinary people. Denton argues that in China the two overlap, because individual recollections are shaped by state narratives and can also shape them. (Denton 2014p. 13)

Draws on Gillis; Susan Crane; Maurice Halbwachs

How it is used Denton takes Gillis's distinction from the literature and tests it against the Chinese case, drawing on Hershatter's study of women activists' memories. Denton adapts it into a model of overlap, and uses Halbwachs on influences that go unperceived to explain why visitors may accept official narratives. This lets her avoid treating the audience as either passive or dissident.

“the two are actually intertwined in much more complex ways than this” p. 14
state history museums and their visitorswomen activists' recollections (Hershatter)

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could use the overlap model on memorial sites where the state is absent, to see whether vernacular memory there echoes official vocabulary.

nostalgic exhibitionary modeDentonappliesanalytic concept

A way of representing the past through everyday life, models and atmosphere that drops revolution and class and produces longing for an idealized Republican-era city. Denton treats it as a product of market reform. (Denton 2014p. 88)

Draws on Svetlana Boym; Dai Jinhua; Ban Wang; Jordan Sand

How it is used Denton uses the mode to read the Shanghai Municipal History Museum, Xintiandi and the First CCP Congress site, and Lu Village, as commercial nostalgia. Denton argues that this nostalgia serves the state's view of Shanghai as a global economic centre. Denton draws on Boym and Dai Jinhua to link it to postsocialist consumer culture, and compares the Shanghai museum with Sand's reading of the Edo-Tokyo Museum.

“nostalgic exhibitionary mode, which is a product of the market economy the party” p. 88
Shanghai Municipal History MuseumXintiandi and the First CCP Congress Meeting HallNanjing Presidential PalaceLu Village theme park

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could test the mode on a rapidly rebuilt city museum elsewhere in Asia to see whether a pre-revolutionary commercial past is used to justify present development.

Dudley, Sandra H. (ed.) (2010). Museum Materialities: Objects, Engagements, Interpretations. London: Routledge.
authenticity as a relation to the audienceScarboroughadaptsanalytic concept

The authenticity of a performance document lies in its relationship to its audience rather than in a lost original event, so each viewing is shaped by the exhibition space and by conversation with others. Scarborough applies this to photographs, scores and relics of performance art. (Dudley 2010p. 260)

Draws on Auslander; Jones

How it is used Scarborough uses the idea to explain why the Getty's Evidence of Movement, which grouped staged photographs, scores, videos and relics without narrative, required visitors to act as detectives. Scarborough cites the faked Schwarzkogler photographs, Tate Liverpool's Art, Lies and Videotape and Klein's Leap into the Void to show that documents were often staged and promoted by artists. The concept lets her argue that viewers perform the meaning-making alongside the artists, rather than recovering a truth about an absent event.

“important questions about the place of authenticity in relationships between objects and their audiences” p. 260
Evidence of Movement, Getty Research Institute (2007)Schwarzkogler photographsArt, Lies and Videotape, Tate Liverpool (2003)Yves Klein, Leap into the Void

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could apply the audience-relational test to an exhibition of colonial-era photographs or staged ritual performances from Southeast Asia, asking which documents were made for later audiences and how the display frames the event.

Duncan, Carol (1995). Civilizing Rituals: Inside Public Art Museums. London: Routledge.
donor memorialDuncancoinstypology

A collection kept intact under one donor's name, often in a replica of an aristocratic residence or a mausoleum, which casts visitors as guests admiring an absent owner rather than citizens sharing a common culture. (Duncan 1995p. 61–62)

How it is used Duncan uses the type to explain the private and restricted rooms inside public museums and reads the National Gallery in Washington as a memorial with the state standing in for the donor. The concept shows donors' memorial ambitions working against the civic programme of the public museum, and treats the Met's restricted wings as evidence that donors still seek something eternal.

Wallace CollectionFrick CollectionHuntingtonGetty at MalibuDulwich Picture Gallery

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask whether a bequest of Asian objects kept in a single named wing of a Western museum works as a donor memorial in this sense, and what it does to the museum's civic programme.

Fromm, Annette B.; Golding, Viv; Rekdal, Per B. (eds.) (2014). Museums and Truth. Newcastle upon Tyne: Cambridge Scholars Publishing.
intangible reparationsMcKinnonappliesanalytic concept

Reparations for a community that go beyond money and land to include the recovery of lost cultural, religious and political practices, delivered in part through a museum of memory dedicated to that community's history. (Fromm 2014p. 64)

How it is used McKinnon uses the concept to make the proposed Maya Achí museum of memory part of the reparations process, rather than only a record of the Río Negro massacres. The museum is meant to combine historical memory with the recovery of Achí cultural practices, and her argument is that the 2010 accord calling for the museum depends on political will. The concept is the bridge between the campaign's demands and her own proposal.

“proposal for intangible reparations, focusing on the establishment of a” p. 64
Maya Achí museum of memory proposal, GuatemalaRío Negro massacres (1980-1982)

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask whether a claim for the return or compensation of an object can be met partly by a community-run display of lost practices, as the Achí proposal does.

Hall, Patricia; Seemann, Charlie (eds.) (1987). Folklife and Museums: Selected Readings. Nashville: American Association for State and Local History.
authenticity and context of live presentersSeemanncriticisescritique

The concern that a live folk artist presented in a museum is an actual bearer of the tradition and that the performance keeps the community's context rather than a smoothed-over 'good show'. Seemann names authenticity and context as his two main concerns. (Hall & Seemann 1987p. 61)

How it is used Seemann uses the concern to criticise easy choices of performers, such as revivalists who learned quilting in a community college class, and institutional pressure that overstructures a tradition. Seemann turns it into practical advice, such as finding artists through state folklorists and university programmes and using a presenter to bridge cultural gaps, so that live performance carries context that an object label cannot.

“authentic bearers of folk traditions in the museum as it is to exhibit only” p. 61
quilting demonstrations by revivalistsBlack Heritage Month presentationscalendar festivals such as Christmas, Passover and Thanksgiving

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could check whether the performers in a museum's programme for a diaspora community are bearers of the tradition, and record how the presenter explains its context.

contagious magicHalladaptstheoretical framing

The belief that supernatural power passes through contact between a magical object and a person. Hall uses it to explain why visitors feel closer to an object that someone famous made, used or slept in. (Hall & Seemann 1987p. 84)

Draws on Sir James G. Frazer

How it is used Hall adapts Frazer's idea, which she takes from superstition and belief studies, to explain the appeal of artifacts that are not interpreted at all. Hall links it to the shrine-like draw of famous-personality museums and 'so-and-so slept here' sites, and then to a marketing argument for history museums. The concept lets her treat a visitor's emotional response to an artifact as a folkloristic phenomenon.

“First presented years ago by Sir James G. Frazer in” p. 84
famous-personality museums'so-and-so slept here' historic sitesGraceland, Elvis Presley's Memphis home

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask whether an Asian object in a Western museum gains a shrine-like appeal from its associated donor or user, and how a label mediates that proximity.

Hicks, Dan (2020). The Brutish Museums: The Benin Bronzes, Colonial Violence and Cultural Restitution. London: Pluto Press.
necrographyHickscoinsmethod

A forensic writing of death and loss, proposed as an alternative to the life-history accounts of objects; necrology names the knowledge made through death and loss in the anthropology museum. The method treats each looted object as a record of the event that took it. (Hicks 2020)

Draws on Achille Mbembe; Foucault

How it is used Hicks applies the method to the Benin loot by counting objects back through the events that took them, and by tracing the sales, gifts and dealers, such as William Downing Webster, that dispersed them. Chapter 13 applies it to seventeen British officers and officials, and he uses it to argue that a museum's display of loot extends the violence rather than representing the past. He draws on Foucault's account of the autopsy and Mbembe's necropolitics, and the method carries into a call for curators to make necrological research their principal task.

“forensic death-writing that the colonial museum, not yet dead, requires of us”
Benin 1897 loot in the Pitt Rivers Museumsales and gifts of seventeen British officers and officialsBenin plaques and ivories across collections worldwide

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The method could be applied to any museum holding material from a punitive campaign, starting with the dealers and officers named in its accession files. A researcher could ask which objects in such a museum can be traced to a death or a sale, rather than only to a donor.

Hill, Kate (2016). Women and Museums, 1850–1914: Modernity and the Gendering of Knowledge. Manchester: Manchester University Press.
authenticity and the domestic objectHilladaptsanalytic concept

The value of old, domestic and family-kept objects as authentic, grounded in continuity through time and in the identity of the person who owned them, which Hill traces to Ruskinian and Morrisian ideas about craft and preservation. (Hill 2016PDF p. 97)

Draws on John Ruskin; William Morris; Chris Miele

How it is used Hill argues that women's family gifts develop the Ruskinian concept further by tying authenticity to family continuity and to the feminine person who holds the object in the present. This let museums accept baby bonnets, christening gowns and other domestic things that did not fit scientific categories, and it gave women a leading part in the revaluation of manufactured things around 1900.

“Women’s donations often foregrounded a sense of truthfulness” PDF p. 108
baby bonnets, caps and christening gowns given as family objectsrelics and souvenirs at Warrington and Bristol

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The same idea could be applied to heirloom textiles or household objects given to a museum in a former colony, asking whether family continuity, rather than ethnographic rarity, gave them their public value.

Hill, Kate (ed.) (2012). Museums and Biographies: Stories, Objects, Identities. Woodbridge: Boydell Press.
communicative and cultural memoryde Jongappliesanalytic concept

The Assmanns’ distinction between memory carried in everyday oral recollection within a living group and memory fixed in durable forms such as institutions and objects. De Jong applies it to how witnesses’ accounts become museum material. (Hill 2012p. 299)

Draws on Aleida Assmann; Jan Assmann; Maurice Halbwachs

How it is used De Jong uses the distinction to argue that curators turn witnesses’ stories into carriers of cultural memory. Clips are paired with objects, such as a pair of gloves at Bergen-Belsen, so that each authenticates the other. The concept shows why the individual life-story becomes a sample standing for a time, a community or an event, chosen by curators who did not witness it.

“Assmann have defned two modes for collectively remembering the past” p. 299
Bergen-Belsen memorialNeuengamme memorialMuseum of Europe’s ‘It’s our history!’ exhibitionImperial War Museum Sound Archive

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A museum of a Japanese or Chinese diaspora community could ask which witness recordings it exhibits and whether they become cultural memory once paired with objects.

Hill, Kate (ed.) (2021). Museums, Modernity and Conflict: Museums and Collections in and of War since the Nineteenth Century. London: Routledge.
indexicality of memorial landscapesPastorappliesanalytic concept

Violi's idea that the significance of memorial landscapes lies in their indexicality: the trauma is contained in the spatiality of the site, but it becomes visible only once the traces are preserved and given meaning. Conservation of such 'traumatic landscapes' moves between obsessive preservation and a downplay of authenticity. (Hill 2021p. 182)

Draws on Violi

How it is used Pastor applies the idea to the Ravensbrück memorial. Because the trauma is held in the site, she argues that the GDR's 1945-style landscape, rebuilt from an RAF aerial photograph and cleared of Soviet army buildings, and the present visitor landscape are both curatorial decisions rather than authentic evidence. The concept lets her show that the bleak landscape visitors see is a choice of two different memorial narratives.

“Violi pointed out that the significance of memorial landscapes lies in” p. 182
Ravensbrück memorial landscapeUckermark camp siteformer Siemens factory area

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could use the same question on another camp or site of violence: which traces were kept, which were cleared, and which are missing from the official visitor map.

private and public memoryPagnottatestsanalytic concept

The contrast between official war art, commissioned for public display, and small personal objects made or kept by soldiers and their families, such as trench art. The chapter treats the two as different forms of memorialisation that a museum can show together. (Hill 2021p. 244)

Draws on Caroline Winter

How it is used Pagnotta tests the contrast against the Canadian War Museum's official art collection and the trench art of Private Arthur Frederick Lee. The service file and medical record date the making of his objects, and the chapter follows how his watch fob and identity bracelet changed meaning across generations as family mementos. The argument is that the official and private forms belong together, so the museum should exhibit them side by side.

“between private and public memory in Canadian First World War” p. 244
Canadian War Museum Art and Memorials CollectionPrivate Arthur Frederick Lee's trench art

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could pair the official war art of another country with privately made objects from the same families, asking which generation's memory each display serves and whether the two can be dated from service records.

Ho, Denise Y.; Li, Jie (2016). “From Landlord Manor to Red Memorabilia: Reincarnations of a Chinese Museum Town”. Modern China.
museum as courtroomHo, Licoinsanalytic concept

The museum as a place where historical cases are judged and contested. Its exhibits serve as material evidence, and after the Mao era rival testimonies, from the old cadres and from Liu Xiaofei, are offered inside it. (Ho & Li 2016p. 20)

How it is used The authors use the courtroom to explain the post-Mao dispute over Liu Wencai: the exhibits act as evidence, and Liu Xiaofei's tours act as counter-testimony. It lets them argue that the manor is still a witness and that the Party's legitimacy is at stake in the verdict.

“the model work now a case to be judged.” p. 20
Landlord Manor Museum after 1978Liu Xiaofei's tours and family gatheringsXiaoshu's books

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could read a contested exhibit as a court record: who testifies, what counts as evidence, and what verdict the museum is expected to give.

Kavanagh, Gaynor (ed.) (1996). Making Histories in Museums. London: Leicester University Press.
memory as construction, set against historyKavanaghappliesanalytic concept

History is a self-conscious, contextual account, while memory is instinctual and personal, and both are constructions that shift with circumstance and audience. Exhibitions meet visitors' memories, which may contradict the official story. (Kavanagh 1996p. 5)

Draws on Halbwachs

How it is used Kavanagh sets the clash between two former prisoners' memories of The Great Escape against the film's account, and the 1994 veterans' rejection of a family-day D-Day commemoration, to argue that museums should show the collision of history and memory rather than settle it.

“Memories, like histories, are constructions and therefore can be both” p. 8
The Great Escape camp memories (documentary)1994 fiftieth-anniversary D-Day family day, Hyde Park

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could set the recollections of veterans, workers or migrants against the official display of a war or colonial collection and ask where the two diverge.

a montage of memoriesBelladaptsanalytic concept

Thompson's phrase for a collective recollection that is not simply false but an averaged blend of many memories. Bell uses it for the nostalgic models of rural life that curators and visitors carry into rural museums. (Kavanagh 1996p. 32)

Draws on E.P. Thompson

How it is used Bell uses the phrase to show that visitors' loss of older rural skills is real but partial, and that curators must deal with these models rather than either endorse or dismiss them. Bell combines it with documents, oral history and reconstruction, such as the eighteenth-century plough at the Ulster Folk and Transport Museum, to test the models.

“rather it is a montage of memories, an average” p. 32
Ulster Folk and Transport MuseumScandinavian and British folk museums

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A curator of a farm or folk display in East Asia could test visitors' recollections of village life against documents before presenting them as a model of the past.

folklore as oral-assumptive symbolic behaviourRattueappliesanalytic concept

Folklore is behaviour that is not necessarily oral but assumes a system of everyday speech and action, and refers to things indirectly, through representation. This definition is broad enough to find folklore in objects such as flames on grenades or relic cults. (Kavanagh 1996p. 219)

How it is used Rattue uses the definition to show that folklore can be found in his own military museum's objects and in the cult of General Gordon, and then proposes three approaches to displaying it: role-play, local customs as identity, and oral surveys that recognise recording alters what is recorded.

“Folklore, then, is 'oral-assumptive symbolic behaviour'” p. 219
grenade flames and wartime stories in a regimental museumGeneral Gordon relicsBishop's House, Sheffield

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could look for the folklore that surrounds a Chinese or Japanese object in a Western collection, such as its legends and the stories told by donors, rather than only its material history.

Kirshenblatt-Gimblett, Barbara (1998). Destination Culture: Tourism, Museums, and Heritage. Berkeley: University of California Press.
heritage as new production in the presentKirshenblatt-Gimblettcoinstheoretical framing

Heritage is not something lost and found, but a mode of cultural production in the present that has recourse to the past. It gives buildings and ways of life that are no longer viable a second life as exhibits of themselves, and adds value through pastness, exhibition, difference and indigeneity. (Kirshenblatt-Gimblett 1998p. 7)

How it is used This is the book's central claim, and the author applies it to Ellis Island, Plimoth Plantation, Colonial Williamsburg and Maori performance to show that these sites produce a version of the past rather than recover it. It lets her treat restoration, tourism and the 'value added' of a place as one process, and argue that the production itself must be analysed alongside the history it claims to show.

“Heritage is a new mode of cultural production in the present that has recourse to the past.” p. 149
Ellis IslandPlimoth PlantationColonial WilliamsburgCairns, QueenslandMaori village at Rotorua

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask how a historic quarter in a Southeast Asian city adds value to a way of life that is no longer viable, and who produces that value.

Knell, Simon J.; Aronsson, Peter; Amundsen, Arne Bugge; et al. (eds.) (2011). National Museums: New Studies from Around the World. London: Routledge.
palimpsest of colonial and postcolonial historyLeeappliesanalytic concept

The museum building and its exhibitions as layered writing of colonial and postcolonial history, in which a past that was built over survives in the structure, so that the new museum keeps the old building's politics visible. (Knell et al. 2011p. 373)

How it is used Lee reads the National Museum of Korea as a palimpsest. The colonial Governor-General's building, designed in part by the Japanese architect Ichiro Nomura, who also designed the Governor-General's building in Taiwan, was demolished in 1995 as a renationalisation campaign. Lee sets the state-run contemporary art museum's Amity exhibitions against the independent Insa Art Space, which he finds revealed national complexity better than the large institution.

“the museum has become a palimpsest” p. 373
National Museum of Korea, SeoulGovernor-General's building, SeoulInsa Art Space

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A building that replaced a colonial structure could be read as a palimpsest, asking which layers the new architecture keeps visible and which it removes.

Krech, Shepard, III; Hail, Barbara A. (eds.) (1999). Collecting Native America, 1870–1960. Washington: Smithsonian Institution Press.
salvage and the vanishing IndianMcCaffreycriticisescritique

The belief, shared by collectors of the period, that Native peoples were disappearing and that their artifacts preserved a romantic past; McCaffrey treats the belief itself as a historical object that shaped the display of objects. (Krech & Hail 1999)

How it is used McCaffrey criticises McCord's displays for decontextualizing objects and for projecting an idealized, timeless image of aboriginal people. The critique links the collector's view of a vanishing people to the stereotype produced by his galleries, and it sets that view against the present-day survival and self-representation of the communities.

“to perpetuate an idealized image of aboriginal people that situated them in a timeless past”
McCord National Museum's Indian rooms (1921)

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The same critique could be applied to a museum of Southeast Asian or East Asian minority peoples, asking whether displays of a vanishing or traditional people fixed them in a timeless past and how the community now presents itself.

Logan, William; Nic Craith, Máiréad; Kockel, Ullrich (eds.) (2016). A Companion to Heritage Studies. Chichester: Wiley Blackwell.
memory ecologyConnorcombinesanalytic concept

A relational account in which memory lies in associative networks of people, practices and places rather than in objects, so that a reconstructed monument carries memory only when practices gather around it. (Logan 2016)

Draws on Latour; Ingold; Meskell; Morton

How it is used Connor combines relational theories of agency with an argument against the overvaluing of material authenticity. Applied to the reconstructed Stari Most at Mostar, it shows that the bridge's meaning as a shared urban life depends on practices such as the annual Ikari diving tradition, which reconnects the city across its ethnic divide. She sets this against heritage readings that treat the reconstruction as a sufficient symbol of reconciliation.

“a memory ecology is not only or even primarily”
Stari Most, MostarIkari diving tradition, Mostar

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The idea could guide a study of a rebuilt museum or memorial to ask which practices and people sustain its memory work, rather than judging it by the object alone.

stability, justice and reconciliation trade-off in post-conflict heritageDaly and Chantestscritique

The claim that in post-conflict settings heritage usually serves at most two of stability, justice and reconciliation, because pragmatic settlements shield perpetrators who keep their influence and so deny victims justice and healing. (Logan 2016)

Draws on Ciorciari; Bloomfield, Barnes and Huyse

How it is used Daly and Chan test the claim against Cambodia and Japan. At Tuol Sleng in Phnom Penh, photographs of Khmer Rouge cadres sit among images of their victims, and guides describe perpetrators as young, poor and brainwashed; the authors question how far officials who were themselves involved shape the narrative. For Japan they show that the Yasukuni and Yushukan narrative of victimhood was partly shaped by American occupation priorities, and they trace the Chinese and US objections to the Hiroshima nomination.

“combination of stability, justice, and reconciliation, but usually never all three at the same time”
Tuol Sleng Genocide Museum, Phnom PenhYasukuni shrine and Yushukan MuseumHiroshima Peace Memorial (Genbaku Dome)Nagasaki Atomic Bomb Museum

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The trade-off could be used to ask, for a memorial in another post-conflict state, which guilty parties its narrative leaves out and whose stability it serves.

Lumley, Robert (ed.) (1988). The Museum Time-Machine: Putting Cultures on Display. London: Routledge.
effective nostalgiaHoyaucriticisescritique

The landscape produced by French heritage policy, in which the past is made pleasant, plural and unchanging, so that nostalgia serves present political goals rather than historical understanding. (Lumley 1988p. 30)

How it is used Hoyau applies the idea to the French Heritage Year of 1980, reading its projects (ecomuseums in Brittany, inventories of cinemas and industrial sites, school events, cultural tourism) as one policy. Hoyau sets nostalgia against neutral preservation and argues that the soft socialism and decentralisation behind the programme make the past a tool of community mobilisation. The concept lets him show that the policy's effect is political even where its content looks harmless.

“the landscape of effective nostalgia” p. 32
French Heritage Year 1980Breton ecomuseumsindustrial heritage inventories

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask whether a local heritage scheme in another country makes its nostalgic content work for a political programme, by setting its policy documents beside its displays.

countryside of the mindBennettappliesanalytic concept

A rural, harmonious vision of English life, imagined as the opposite of industrial society, which makes industrial change look like a continuation of an older order and naturalises the power of the bourgeoisie. (Lumley 1988p. 68)

Draws on Martin Wiener

How it is used Bennett applies the idea to Beamish, where the country house of Beamish Hall, with its controlling gaze, organises town and countryside, industry and agriculture, and the classes that live in separate zones, as one harmonious order. Bennett relates this to the Skansen and Greenfield Village traditions and compares the same ideal in Ironbridge, where West finds an organic ruralism. The concept explains why an open-air museum can show industry without showing conflict.

“seeming to materialize the countryside of the mind” p. 69
BeamishIronbridge Gorge MuseumSkansenGreenfield Village

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could test whether a rural or village reconstruction in another region tells industrial change as a continuation of an older order, using its guidebooks and its building arrangement.

Macdonald, Sharon; Fyfe, Gordon (eds.) (1996). Theorizing Museums: Representing Identity and Diversity in a Changing World. Oxford: Blackwell.
incorporating and inscribing practicesUrryadaptsanalytic concept

Connerton's distinction between practices that transmit memory through bodily activity, which works only when bodies are co-present (incorporating), and devices such as print, photographs and indexes that store information after the human has stopped informing (inscribing). (Macdonald & Fyfe 1996PDF p. 55)

Draws on Connerton; Bergson; Mead

Urry uses this to argue that museums are inscriptions that visitors re-read in performance: reminiscence at heritage sites, including Macdonald's study of visitors reading a Science Museum exhibition against its designers' intent.

Nation, identity and imagined community

Anderson, Hobsbawm and Ranger, and concepts for how museums narrate nations, make citizens and stage state identity. 29 concepts from 20 texts

This family of approaches treats museums as producers of national belonging rather than neutral records of a national past. Its question is how a museum makes a nation look old, singular and self-evident: which origin story it tells, which people it presents as citizens, and which pasts it leaves out. Benedict Anderson's imagined community stands behind the strands that treat the nation as narrated and performed (Sherman & Rogoff 1994p. 272; Knell et al. 2011p. 4). Hobsbawm and Ranger supply invented tradition (Denton 2014p. 27), and Gellner and Hobsbawm, through Cuno, the dating of nationalism as a recent elite project (Cuno 2008PDF p. 115). Bennett's nationing of history draws on Poulantzas (Bennett 1995p. 141). The texts at the centre are Denton on postsocialist China (Denton 2014p. 27), Yoshida on war and peace museums (Yoshida 2014p. 234), Cuno on antiquity and cosmopolitanism (Cuno 2008PDF p. 144), and Naquin on the Beijing Palace Museum's foreign shows (Naquin 2004p. 372). Other authors take up the same ideas in Japan, Israel, Turkey, Russia and the United States, so that the approach is tested across very different national settings.

Anderson's imagined community, and rival memories

Anderson's idea is that a nation is an imagined community. Wallis takes the nation as an empty and elastic container into which any art can be placed, and uses it to read the Festival of Indonesia, which presented a three-thousand-year history for a republic founded in 1945 (Sherman & Rogoff 1994p. 272). Knell takes the imagined community into the museum itself: the museum performs the nation through scripted objects and settings, more believably than theatre because the objects look real (Knell et al. 2011p. 4; Knell et al. 2011p. 26). Bennett combines Poulantzas's account of the state's historicising work with Anderson's account of the nation's time, to show that Australian museums extended the national past back to 1788 (Bennett 1995p. 141). Scheidhauer sets Halbwachs's split between individual and collective memory against the Kaesŏng Koryŏ Museum, which holds a shared cultural nation beside the state nation (Knell et al. 2011p. 357; Knell et al. 2011p. 361).

Invented tradition and the dating of nationalism

Hobsbawm and Ranger's invented tradition is a modern act that severs from the past and reconnects with it, most likely when rapid change weakens older patterns. Denton applies it to the origin stories of the Chinese nation: the Museum of Chinese History and the 2011 Ancient China hall claim continuity, while local museums claim plural origins (Denton 2014p. 27; Denton 2014p. 29). Cuno uses the historians' dating of nationalism against the modern national claim on ancient remains. Italy has been a republic only since 1946, and Italian and Chinese cultural property laws assume an unbroken national culture that the history does not support (Cuno 2008PDF p. 116). Denton uses the idea to explain state narrative; Cuno uses the dating as a critique of law.

Cosmopolitanism and plural identity

Cuno takes cosmopolitanism from Diogenes, Hume, Nussbaum and Said as the ethical basis of encyclopedic collecting, because culture has never known political boundaries and is always hybrid (Cuno 2008PDF p. 144). He applies this to Chang'an, with its Buddhist, Central Asian and foreign communities (Cuno 2008PDF p. 107). His plural identity draws on Said's "flowing currents and Maalouf's mixed identity. Cuno uses it to argue that national attribution of antiquities rests on a false assumption, and that the Poly Museum chairman cannot speak for all Chinese people, including the Uighurs (Cuno 2008PDF p. 110; Cuno 2008PDF p. 104). Against purity and primacy, he sets the Buddhist and Central Asian influences on Dunhuang: our ignorance of the very hybridity of culture" (Cuno 2008PDF p. 133; Cuno 2008PDF p. 107).

Cultural patrimony and World Heritage as a state claim

Appiah separates two senses of cultural patrimony: the products of a people, and a people's transhistorical identity (Cuno 2009p. 73). He tests the doctrine at Nok sculptures whose makers' descendants are unknown, and at Asante objects looted from the Kumasi palace in 1874, and accepts repatriation mainly where objects were stolen from known owners (Cuno 2009p. 73; Cuno 2009p. 79). Yan applies World Heritage as a tool of nation-building to the dossiers of the Great Wall, the Potala Palace and Fujian Tulou. Listings claim temporal continuity and spatial unity, drawing on Duara's critique of linear national narrative, and historians' accounts are set against them (Logan 2016).

Constructed identity and ethnogenesis

Naquin treats ethnicity as a situational and constructed part of identity, a view she says reached Qing scholarship by the late 1980s, drawing on Rawski (Naquin 2004p. 381). She uses it to judge the catalogues: the 1988-89 Melbourne catalogue still worked with difference and absorption, while the 1996 Paris catalogue gave the Manchu names of the emperors (Naquin 2004p. 381). MacKenzie layers imperial, colonial, provincial and national identities, so each museum must be read in its own period (MacKenzie 2009p. 6; MacKenzie 2009p. 270). Abashin tests the "Marrist conception of ethnogenesis" against the History of the Peoples of Uzbekistan, and shows that Tolstov's compound origin won through institutional struggle (Cvetkovski & Hofmeister 2014p. 168; Cvetkovski & Hofmeister 2014p. 162).

Foundation myth and the military-nation

Kern takes the foundation myth from Langewiesche, in which a nation locates its origin in a war. She applies it to the Independence War of 1919 to 1923, the founding event of the Turkish Republic, and shows that the Istanbul panoramas re-interpret it: the Miniatürk panorama moves the myth to a populist, religious and economic nation, while the 1453 panorama moves it back to the Ottoman conquest of Constantinople (Muchitsch 2013p. 206; Muchitsch 2013p. 212). Using Altınay, she reads the military-nation against the Ankara portrait galleries, and argues that conservative interests adapt the myth while still repeating national ideology (Muchitsch 2013p. 209; Muchitsch 2013p. 217).

Indigenous sovereignty and community space

McMullen uses cultural sovereignty, drawing on Cobb and Lyons, to judge the National Museum of the American Indian. The museum cannot serve Native sovereignty until it understands George Gustav Heye's intent and restores the documentation his practices left out (Sleeper-Smith 2009p. 81; Sleeper-Smith 2009p. 83). Child's Indigenous space names tribal museums rooted in a Western model yet reflecting Native values and languages: "Indigenous spaces that both reflect Native values and knowledge systems" (Sleeper-Smith 2009p. 253). She reads the Osage Tribal Museum and the Mashantucket Pequot Museum as centres of community life, not only as preservation or correction of history (Sleeper-Smith 2009p. 253).

Critique of nationalist display

Several authors test the national museum against evidence and find it constructed. Azoulay's first procedure, fabricated objects shown among authentic ones, makes an invented past look like evidence at the Tower of David Museum, Bezalel and Yad Vashem: "is actually a powerful ideological device" (Sherman & Rogoff 1994p. 87; Sherman & Rogoff 1994p. 86). Pyun applies "one nation and one people" to the Osaka Museum of History and the National Folk Museum's wedding diorama, and tests it against foreign residents and migrant workers (Guy 2024p. 170; Guy 2024p. 183). Askew calls the dichotomy of Old and New Japan in the Hearn museums overly simplified (Askew 2007p. 137). Yoshida tests patriotism against human rights, judging Yushukan and the Chiran kamikaze museum less favourably than the Kyoto museum (Yoshida 2014p. 234; Yoshida 2014p. 235), and criticises the us-and-them framing of Chinese and South Korean museums (Yoshida 2014p. 236).

National collections and transnational circulation

Miller traces the British Museum's national claim from Sloane's bequest, accepted by Parliament in 1753, to Hill's 1930s fund-raising (Miller 1973p. 45; Miller 1973p. 332). March treats the Museu d'Art de Catalunya as a nation-building museum whose unfinished national catalogue made the 1936 rescue of works urgent (Hill 2021p. 86). Gardner reads the Mona Lisa's tours and the Louvre Abu Dhabi as the government's export of French culture (Gardner 2020). The Pushkin Museum's borrowed European models, with its Russian stairs and Hall of Fame, show national affirmation through transnational means (Meyer & Savoy 2014p. 87).

Debates and limits

The texts disagree most sharply over whether a museum's national story can be corrected from within. Yoshida accepts that peace museums need not show Japanese atrocities, but rejects those that glorify aggression, and he reports Japanese critics who call atrocity displays self-flagellation (Yoshida 2014p. 233). Denton qualifies the state-control reading: exhibits are negotiated among curators, officials and historians, and visitors' experience varies (Denton 2014p. 13). Appiah and Cuno reach different limits on repatriation: Appiah accepts it mainly for objects stolen from known owners (Cuno 2009p. 79), while Cuno argues against national retention laws altogether (Cuno 2008PDF p. 133). The approach tends to leave out the ordinary people, minorities and migrants whom the national story does not display, as Askew shows for Kumamoto (Askew 2007p. 133).

Carrying it over to a new case

  • Ask which origin story a new national museum tells and which past it sets aside, as Denton does for the Ancient China hall, and compare it with a museum in another postsocialist state (Denton 2014p. 27).
  • Trace the national performance beyond the galleries, into the streets around the museum, as Knell does for the Edo-Tokyo Museum (Knell et al. 2011p. 26).
  • Compare the date a state gives its nationalism with the dates of its museums and cultural property laws, as Cuno does for Italy and China (Cuno 2008PDF p. 116).
  • Read the claims of a heritage dossier against the historians' record, as Yan does for Kashgar (Logan 2016).
  • Check whether ethnic or national labels in a museum's catalogue were revised in later editions, as Naquin does for Melbourne and Paris (Naquin 2004p. 381).
  • Test the military-nation on a museum for another post-imperial army, asking whether its myth was adapted or abandoned after political change (Muchitsch 2013p. 217).
  • Ask what a minority collection held far from its community would need in order to serve cultural sovereignty, as McMullen does for the NMAI (Sleeper-Smith 2009p. 83).

Where to start reading

  • Bennett, Tony (1995). The Birth of the Museum: History, Theory, Politics. London: Routledge. Bennett, for how the national past is anchored in deep time and annexes other histories.
  • Knell, Simon J.; Aronsson, Peter; Amundsen, Arne Bugge; et al. (eds.) (2011). National Museums: New Studies from Around the World. London: Routledge. Knell, for the performance model and Anderson's imagined community in the museum.
  • Cuno, James (2008). Who Owns Antiquity? Museums and the Battle over Our Ancient Heritage. Princeton: Princeton University Press. Cuno, for cosmopolitanism, plural identity and the critique of national cultural property laws.
  • Sherman, Daniel J.; Rogoff, Irit (eds.) (1994). Museum Culture: Histories, Discourses, Spectacles. Minneapolis: University of Minnesota Press. Sherman and Rogoff, for Azoulay's fabricated exhibits and Wallis's national allegory.
  • Denton, Kirk A. (2014). Exhibiting the Past: Historical Memory and the Politics of Museums in Postsocialist China. Honolulu: University of Hawai‘i Press. Denton, for invented tradition applied to the origin stories of the Chinese state.
  • Yoshida, Takashi (2014). From Cultures of War to Cultures of Peace: War and Peace Museums in Japan, China, and South Korea. Portland, ME: MerwinAsia. Yoshida, for patriotism as a test and the us-and-them framing of museums.
  • Sleeper-Smith, Susan (ed.) (2009). Contesting Knowledge: Museums and Indigenous Perspectives. Lincoln: University of Nebraska Press. Sleeper-Smith, for cultural sovereignty and Indigenous space.

Askew shows that it works in each museum, from the Matsue samurai street to the Kumamoto house, and argues that it is an overly simplified view that ignores the fluid nature of 'Old Japan' and that Hearn's letters contradict. It lets her explain why the common people of Kumamoto, whom Hearn disliked, are missing from the displays.

Bennett, Tony (1995). The Birth of the Museum: History, Theory, Politics. London: Routledge.
nationing historyBennettcombinestheoretical framing

The process by which the state turns the past into a single national history, territorialising history and historicising territory by annexing or eliminating other histories. Bennett takes the formulation from Poulantzas and sets it beside Anderson's account of the nation's sense of time. (Bennett 1995p. 141)

Draws on Poulantzas; Benedict Anderson

How it is used Bennett combines Poulantzas's account of the state's historicising work with Anderson's contrast between the nation and older realms. Bennett uses the two to argue that Australian museums and sites extended the national past back to 1788 by anchoring it in deep time, and to explain why the histories of other groups could be included in that past while the penal past was softened.

Cuno, James (2008). Who Owns Antiquity? Museums and the Battle over Our Ancient Heritage. Princeton: Princeton University Press.
cosmopolitanismCunoappliestheoretical framing

The view that people belong to a world community and that cultures are hybrid and interconnected. Cuno sets it against nationalism and offers it as the justification for encyclopedic museums and their education. (Cuno 2008PDF p. 144)

Draws on Diogenes; Hume; Nussbaum; Said

How it is used Cuno uses cosmopolitanism as the ethical basis for encyclopedic collecting. Cuno answers the charge that it is a Western imposition by citing postcolonial critics who propose a new cosmopolitanism, and he argues that objects show cultural in-betweenness. Cuno applies the idea to China by pointing to the Buddhist, Central Asian and foreign communities of Chang'an, arguing that Chinese culture was always formed by exchange.

“museums aspire to the condition of cosmopolitanism as articulated by Diogenes” PDF p. 144
Chang'an and Dunhuangthe British Museumthe Art Institute of Chicago

plural identity (identity as flowing currents)Cunoappliesanalytic concept

The idea that a person has many overlapping identities, of which nationality is only one, and that the state forces people to choose. Cuno uses it to question the assumption that an antiquity belongs to a nation because it came from its territory. (Cuno 2008PDF p. 110)

Draws on Edward Said; Amin Maalouf; Amartya Sen

How it is used Cuno takes Said's image of identity as flowing currents and Maalouf's account of a mixed identity to argue that national attribution of antiquities rests on a false assumption. Sen's childhood in Dhaka shows how a state or community forces a single choice. Cuno applies the same point to the Uighurs and Han Chinese, arguing that the Poly Museum chairman's claim to speak for all Chinese people cannot be true.

“a set of currents, flowing currents, rather than a fixed place or a stable set of objects.” PDF p. 110

nationalism as a recent elite constructionCunoappliestheoretical framing

The claim that nationalism is a recent political doctrine, dating from the Enlightenment and the revolutions or from industrialisation, and built by elites for political legitimacy. (Cuno 2008PDF p. 115)

Draws on Eric Hobsbawm; Ernest Gellner; Benedict Anderson

How it is used Cuno uses the historians' dating of nationalism to argue that the modern national claim on ancient remains is anachronistic. Cuno notes that Italy has been a republic only since 1946 and argues that Italy's and China's laws assume an unbroken national culture that the history does not support. The argument is used against cultural property laws rather than to explain them.

cultural purity and hybridityCunocriticisescritique

The belief that a national culture is pure and self-generated, set against the view that culture develops through contact across several centres. Cuno uses it to criticise nationalist heritage policy. (Cuno 2008PDF p. 107)

How it is used Cuno applies the critique to China, where he sees cultural purity, longevity and primacy as the basis of the state's self-image and of the Xia-Shang-Zhou Chronology Project. Against this he sets the Buddhist and Central Asian influences on Dunhuang and the cosmopolitan Chang'an. He generalises it in the conclusion, where the ignorance of cultural hybridity is blamed for nationalist and sectarian violence.
