Empire, race and the display of others

Said's Orientalism, Clifford and Pratt's contact zone, Fabian, postcolonial and indigenous critique: how museums collected and represented other peoples. 55 concepts from 36 texts

This family of approaches asks how museums gathered and displayed other peoples under empire, and what the display told visitors about the people shown and about those who showed them (Sleeper-Smith 2009p. 9; Çelik 2016p. 157). Its theorists, as our texts use them, are Edward Said on Orientalism, Johannes Fabian on the denial of coevalness, Mary Louise Pratt and James Clifford on the contact zone, and Homi Bhabha on the third space (Knell et al. 2011p. 298; Fromm 2014p. 183; Arnold 2006).

The texts at its centre are Çelik on Ottoman and American excavation museums (Çelik 2016p. 4), Jasanoff on collecting as imperial rule in India and Egypt (Jasanoff 2005p. 64), Hicks on the British sacking of Benin and its afterlife in museums (Hicks 2020), Silverman's essays in the Sleeper-Smith volume on Indigenous display (Sleeper-Smith 2009p. 9), and Greenhalgh on antiquities removed from the Ottoman lands (Greenhalgh 2019PDF p. 16). Their concern is acquisition, labelling and the display of other peoples as evidence of a relation of power. The approach asks how that relation was made to look like knowledge.

Said's Orientalism and its critics

Said's account of Orientalism is the most widely used idea in these texts, and the authors use it in opposite ways. Çelik reads excavation reports as "shaped by imperialism, colonialism, and Orientalism at their peaks" (Çelik 2016p. 157). Through the stock images of Orientalism she shows the same framing in Layard, Peters, Hilprecht, Osman Hamdi and Osgan Efendi, so that class and education, not the East–West divide, become the sharper lines (Çelik 2016p. 157). Wallis applies Said to a Turkish festival, arguing that the nation adopted a self-Orientalising mode to present itself to Americans (Sherman & Rogoff 1994p. 271). Black reads FitzGerald's cuts to the Khayyam quatrains as a form of possession (Black 2000p. 54).

Other authors test or reject it. Tseng finds that Japan was never part of Said's Orient, so the Ueno facade becomes an unstable sign of a generalised East (Tseng 2008p. 71). Aldrich tests Said against French Orientalist painting and separates it from direct colonial propaganda (Aldrich 2005p. 208). Greenhalgh sets Orientalism aside and keeps the explanation on funding, permits and shipping (Greenhalgh 2019p. 18). Jasanoff adapts Said by showing the East India Company "collecting an empire" (Jasanoff 2005p. 64), and criticises the oppositional picture of Europe's expansion in favour of collaboration (Jasanoff 2005p. 7).

Contact zone and the third space

Clifford's contact zone describes the museum as "a power-charged set of exchanges" (Arnold 2006). Arnold applies it to present-day ethnography museums, where native perspectives challenge functional display. He does not adopt it wholesale: he keeps functional analysis beside it and argues that the friction between them may be the source of creativity (Arnold 2006). Liffman uses Pratt and Clifford for the Our Peoples Huichol exhibition at the NMAI, to show Indigenous agency inside a national institution (Sleeper-Smith 2009p. 194). Barrett asks whether such engagement shares authority or only repeats old relations (Barrett 2011p. 110). Choi takes Bhabha's third space as an alternative both to the aesthetic displays of the National Museum of Korea and to forum models, so that visitors' contradictory identities become objects of enquiry (Knell et al. 2011p. 297).

Denial of coevalness

Grinell applies Fabian's critique of anthropological observation to ethnographic museums. He asks whether community work can invite non-coeval people into the modern museum's time without being absorbed by its classical narrative (Fromm 2014p. 183). Magubane uses the term for the London showcases, where the claim that Africans had no notion of time was repeatedly undercut, because the exhibition needed the performers' testimony and skill and so had to treat them as coevals (Sleeper-Smith 2009p. 56). Hicks combines Fabian with Mbembe, Fanon and Césaire, and reads the Benin material in the Pitt Rivers typological display as a lost world. He argues that the museum, not only the army, made Benin a lost world (Hicks 2020).

Culture of imperialism and colonial display

Aldrich treats empire as a culture as well as a set of policies, so that monuments and museums become sites where a colonial culture was made in France (Aldrich 2005p. 8). He applies this to the 1931 Exposition coloniale and to non-Western collections produced by culture contact (Aldrich 2005p. 8). Lu adapts Anderson's account of heritage as regalia for a secular colonial state. China was a semi-colony with concessions, so the Western museums served both Chinese modernisation and Western power (Lu 2014p. 59). Denton extends Hirsch's Soviet model of ethnographic museums to China in the 1950s (Denton 2014p. 200). Conn's "epistemology of imperialism" describes the Philadelphia Commercial Museum, where objects substituted for colonial experience and commerce absorbed colonial acquisition (Conn 1998p. 117).

Loot, trophies and the scramble

Hicks applies "corporate-militarist colonialism", combining Weber's booty capitalism with Luxemburg's militarism. He treats the Benin attack as one episode in a continuous series of Royal Niger Company campaigns, and argues that companies, markets and museums worked together (Hicks 2020). He also reads the attackers' violence as attributed to the victims in "white projection (Hicks 2020). Greenhalgh calls antiquities trophies, and reads acquisition as a contest in which the West won the victory of civilisation over Turkish" barbarism (Greenhalgh 2019PDF p. 16). Yallop reads objects from intransigent states as a way of announcing supremacy (Yallop 2011). Jasanoff pairs the 1860 sacking of the Summer Palace with Tipu's collections, where a demonised enemy's possessions passed to European hands (Jasanoff 2005p. 183).

Ethnographic classification and race

Silverman argues that ethnography's scientific justification of conquest persisted into museum display (Sleeper-Smith 2009p. 9). Coombes shows the press and officers' memoirs building the image of Benin as degraded (Coombes 1994p. 11). Hill shows that Liverpool classed all human artefacts by their maker's race, with Melanian and Caucasian displays differentiated by technique, so that its ethnography naturalised a hierarchy (Hill 2005p. 114). Mogilner finds the "mixed physical type" scientifically plausible but politically problematic (Cvetkovski & Hofmeister 2014p. 94). Cvetkovski argues that the Russian ethnographic museum presented the empire's peoples as objects seen as other, not as the imperial self (Cvetkovski & Hofmeister 2014p. 251). Ayers tests the inventory rubric 'Indian', which labelled Chinese, Japanese and Southeast Asian goods alike, against the objects (Impey & MacGregor 1985p. 355).

Labels, translation and universal claims

Golding uses cultural translation against both relativism and an intolerance-engendering interpretation, and argues that curators must examine their own position within global hierarchies (Fromm 2014p. 11). Zhang and Francis adapt Geertz's thick description as "thick design", carried out through the designer's long collaboration with a source community (Guy 2024p. 138). Kirshenblatt-Gimblett calls 'multicultural' and 'international' euphemisms that pluralise the Other while leaving the 'we' as one (Kirshenblatt-Gimblett 1998p. 243). Dewdney, Dibosa and Walsh apply Fanon's epidermalization to Tate Britain's policies (Sandell & Nightingale 2012). O'Neill applies Steiner's argument that the West can no longer assume its own centrality to museums of religion (Kavanagh 1996p. 193).

Debates and limits

The sharpest disagreements concern Said. Greenhalgh rejects Orientalism as an explanation of travellers' collecting, which he says Lewis has disposed of (Greenhalgh 2019p. 18). Bilsel criticises the post-Orientalist critique as a framework, arguing that the link between display and hegemony was neither determined nor stable, and that excavator and excavated were constituted together (Bilsel 2012PDF p. 31). Cvetkovski and Mogilner test the categories from inside the imperial material: Cvetkovski rejects the assumption that objects carried imperial knowledge by themselves (Cvetkovski & Hofmeister 2014p. 213), and Mogilner shows that the category failed in practical policy (Cvetkovski & Hofmeister 2014p. 94). Conn's own account shows what the commercial frame leaves out: the 1899 congress treats the Philippines only briefly, so that commerce remained the bearer of peace (Conn 1998p. 117).

Carrying it over to a new case

  • Compare the expedition compound and the neighbouring village at a foreign dig in Southeast Asia, to see whether the pair repeats the colonial template of control and display that Çelik reads at Palmyra, Sardis and Nippur (Çelik 2016p. 9).
  • Trace the Asian shipments to a given museum against political events in the source country, to test whether acquisition followed a scramble or diverged from it (MacKenzie 2009p. 9).
  • Compare the labels and catalogue entries of a museum's Asian galleries across several decades, to see when a framing such as the 1872 "effeminate race" language changed (Yallop 2011).
  • Read a museum's Asian galleries against the labels 'international' and 'multicultural', asking which groups are called which and who is left as the unmarked national (Kirshenblatt-Gimblett 1998p. 243).
  • Ask which explanation the documents support for a given East or Southeast Asian collection, whether funding, export permits, shipping or attitudes, rather than starting from the category of Orientalism (Greenhalgh 2019p. 18).
  • Read a minority or Indigenous gallery in a national museum as a contact zone, asking who appropriates the space and for what ends (Sleeper-Smith 2009p. 194).
  • Ask whether an Asian collection was grouped under 'Oriental' or 'Indian' for administrative reasons, and test each inventory entry against its object (Impey & MacGregor 1985p. 355).

Where to start reading

  • Çelik, Zeynep (2016). About Antiquities: Politics of Archaeology in the Ottoman Empire. Austin: University of Texas Press. Çelik's chapters on the Istanbul and New York museums: the clearest case of the world-system premise and of Orientalist stock images in excavation reports.
  • Arnold, Ken (2006). Cabinets for the Curious: Looking Back at Early English Museums. Aldershot: Ashgate. Arnold's contact-zone passage: how a functional museum and a contact zone sit side by side, and where the friction lies.
  • Sleeper-Smith, Susan (ed.) (2009). Contesting Knowledge: Museums and Indigenous Perspectives. Lincoln: University of Nebraska Press. Silverman, Liffman and Magubane in one volume: ethnography's persistence and how Indigenous curators contest display.
  • Jasanoff, Maya (2005). Edge of Empire: Conquest and Collecting in the East, 1750–1850. London: Fourth Estate. Jasanoff: collecting as imperial rule, and the collaborative alternative to Said's frame.
  • Hicks, Dan (2020). The Brutish Museums: The Benin Bronzes, Colonial Violence and Cultural Restitution. London: Pluto Press. Hicks: how loot, white projection and chronopolitics combine in one museum case.
  • Fromm, Annette B.; Golding, Viv; Rekdal, Per B. (eds.) (2014). Museums and Truth. Newcastle upon Tyne: Cambridge Scholars Publishing. Golding: cultural translation as the alternative to relativism.

Conn, Steven (1998). Museums and American Intellectual Life, 1876–1926. Chicago: University of Chicago Press.
epistemology of imperialismConncoinsanalytic concept

Conn's term for the Philadelphia Commercial Museum's effort to build knowledge of foreign markets into its displays, so that American firms could gain what European colonies gave their merchants without colonial rule. Objects were made to substitute for colonial experience and to represent the world's business. (Conn 1998p. 117)

How it is used Conn uses the term to argue that scientific commerce could absorb colonial acquisition. Conn traces the museum's regional arrangement, its Bureau of Information and its trade guides, and reads its Madagascar exhibit, which set indigenous textiles beside European cloth, as a market process with the cultural disruption left out. Conn shows the 1899 congress treating the Philippines only briefly, so that commerce remained the bearer of peace. The term lets him make the Commercial Museum a central institution of American imperialism while keeping its contradictions visible; he refers to the wider interdependence of American and European colonialism through Amy Kaplan.

“To create an epistemology of imperialism the Commercial Museum” p. 117
Philadelphia Commercial Museum1897 and 1899 International Commercial CongressesSt. Louis Philippine exhibit, 1904

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The idea could be applied to another trade museum in an imperial setting, such as a Japanese commercial museum of the 1910s, asking how it substituted displayed commodities for on-site knowledge that a colonial administration would otherwise have supplied.

Coombes, Annie E. (1994). Reinventing Africa: Museums, Material Culture and Popular Imagination in Late Victorian and Edwardian England. New Haven: Yale University Press.
degeneracy of a 'degraded' raceCoombesappliesanalytic concept

The representation of a people, here the Benin, as degraded and savage despite evidence of an ancient and developed society, used to undermine that evidence and to justify colonial action. (Coombes 1994p. 11)

How it is used Coombes shows the press and the officers' memoirs building the degeneracy image through juxtaposition of text and illustration, and treats it as a convenient means of undermining the bronzes as evidence of civilisation. Coombes links it to the 'Orient' as a concept already familiar in Britain, and then shows that West African writers used the same vocabulary to answer it.

“The emphasis on Benin as a ‘degraded’ race is an important feature of the representation” p. 11
Benin expedition (1897) press and memoirsBenin bronzes at the Liverpool, Horniman and Pitt Rivers collections

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The concept could be used to ask whether Asian objects in Western museums were described as the products of decline, and whether that framing was applied to some regions and not others.

Cvetkovski, Roland; Hofmeister, Alexis (eds.) (2014). An Empire of Others: Creating Ethnographic Knowledge in Imperial Russia and the USSR. Budapest: Central European University Press.
representation of the OtherCvetkovskirejectsanalytic concept

The chapter's term for what the museum actually did: it presented the peoples of the empire as objects that visitors saw as other, rather than reflecting the imperial self back to them. It is set against the idea that the museum mirrored imperial identity. (Cvetkovski & Hofmeister 2014p. 213)

How it is used The author rejects the assumption of the museum's founders that objects would carry imperial knowledge by themselves. Using the 1910 reviewer's criticism of fragmentary scenes and faceless mannequins, the chapter argues that the objects produced a kind of equality among peoples and a physical manifestation of imperial variety, not an imperial self-image. The argument lets the author separate presentation from representation.

“imperial self; more likely it was in itself the representation of the Other.” p. 251
1910 trial exhibition, Russian Ethnographic MuseumBogdanov's review of the exhibition

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The same test could be run on a national museum of an Asian state: does its display of minorities or foreign peoples represent the state's self-image, or the visitor's own position as a viewer of others?

mixed physical typeMogilnertestsanalytic concept

The most common result of anthropometric measurement in the Moscow research programme, which described populations of the empire as regional mixed types rather than as hierarchical races. In the chapter it names the liberal anthropologists' term for empire-wide classification. (Cvetkovski & Hofmeister 2014p. 94)

How it is used Mogilner tests the concept against imperial politics and finds that it was scientifically plausible but politically problematic. Liberal anthropologists treated the empire as a supranational polity with a common scientific frame, while the empire's actual modernisation marginalised mixed and complex identities. The author uses the term to show the gap between an academic classification and the categories of practical policy.

“highly problematic political concept that had no equivalent in the current” p. 94
Moscow Imperial Society of Lovers of Natural Sciences, Anthropology and EthnographyRussian anthropometric surveys by district and province

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask whether a similar 'mixed' category was used in Asian colonial or post-colonial censuses, and what its political uses were.

philosophical geographyGlebovappliestheoretical framing

A vision of the world shaped by an increasingly global and comparative map of civilisation, in which peoples were placed along a scale. The chapter uses it for the European and Russian mapping of Siberia and the peoples of Northeast Asia. (Cvetkovski & Hofmeister 2014p. 289)

Draws on Larry Wolff

How it is used Glebov applies the idea to show that the mapping of Siberia produced discourses that made its peoples strange, as in the comparisons drawn by Ledyard and Witsen's taxonomy of the peoples of Northeast Asia. The use lets the chapter set the ethnography of the frontier within the wider geography of civilisation, rather than treating Siberia as a self-contained colony.

“a vision of the world informed” p. 289
SiberiaNortheast AsiaWitsen's Tartarije

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The same frame could be used to ask how European travel writing on China, Japan or Mongolia placed those peoples on a civilisational map, and how Russian sources changed that map.

Denton, Kirk A. (2014). Exhibiting the Past: Historical Memory and the Politics of Museums in Postsocialist China. Honolulu: University of Hawai‘i Press.
empire of nationsDentonappliestheoretical framing

Hirsch's account of ethnographic museums as tools for building a multinational Soviet empire. Denton shows that the model was exported to China in the 1950s, where minority groups were displayed as parts of one nation. (Denton 2014p. 200)

Draws on Francine Hirsch

How it is used Denton uses Hirsch to set the Soviet ethnographic model beside the PRC's minority museums. Denton argues that minority cultures are shown as evidence of unity under a shared ideology and as a backward other that Han-led modernization must uplift, and she applies this to the Yunnan Museum of Nationalities, the Beijing Nationalities Culture Palace and the Chinese Nationalities Museum.

“eventually making its way to China in the 1950s” p. 200
Yunnan Museum of NationalitiesBeijing Nationalities Culture PalaceChinese Nationalities Museum

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could compare minority displays in China with those in other post-imperial states to see which groups are shown as unifying evidence and which as the backward other.

Duncan, Carol (1995). Civilizing Rituals: Inside Public Art Museums. London: Routledge.
art/artifact distinctionDuncanrejectscritique

The division between art, admitted to aesthetic contemplation in museums, and artifacts, studied as ethnographic or scientific specimens. Duncan argues that the division ranks western and non-western societies on a hierarchy. (Duncan 1995p. 5–6)

Draws on Raymond Williams

How it is used Duncan does not choose between the two terms but collapses the distinction, treating art-museum art as a species of ritual artifact. This lets her argue that the aesthetic museum and the educational museum are both ritual spaces and generate ideology in their own ways, and that the hierarchy between art and artifact is itself produced by museum display.

primitive art wings added to art museumsseparate museums of non-western art

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could follow an East Asian object from an ethnographic collection into an American art museum and ask what changes in its status and display when it is moved from artifact to art.

Fromm, Annette B.; Golding, Viv; Rekdal, Per B. (eds.) (2014). Museums and Truth. Newcastle upon Tyne: Cambridge Scholars Publishing.
cultural translationGoldingadaptsanalytic concept

Understanding another culture is not the swapping of terms between languages but grasping the sense of practices within a form of life, which means engaging the senses and shared activity and recognising the power relations that shape what can be understood. (Fromm 2014p. 11)

Draws on Talal Asad; Wittgenstein; Winch

How it is used Golding uses the idea against both relativism (what she calls 'charitable' translation) and an intolerance-engendering interpretation that Asad warns about. Golding adds that understanding happens within global hierarchies of wealth and control, so curators must examine their own position and that of their audiences. Golding applies this to hard cases such as the EDL and Islam4UK, asking what points of contact might exist between them and less extreme positions.

“It moves beyond the notion of one mind approaching” p. 12
English Defence League and Islam4UK, as questions for museum dialogue

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask whether a museum's labels explain a religious or political practice from inside its 'form of life', or only translate its terms into the museum's own vocabulary.

denial of coevalnessGrinellappliesanalytic concept

The exclusion of some people from public life by placing them in another time: the observer takes a position uphill on a temporal slope, so the other is presented as belonging to an earlier stage and not as a contemporary subject. (Fromm 2014p. 183)

Draws on Johannes Fabian

How it is used Grinell applies Fabian's critique of anthropological observation to ethnographic museums and asks whether it is confined to them. Grinell argues that community work in museums can be read as inviting non-coeval communities into the time and space of the modern museum, and asks how this can be shown without absorption into the classical museum narrative. The concept gives him the argument that a museum's chronology can exclude people as surely as its gates.

“denial of coevalness (Fabian 1983).” p. 183
Ethnographic collections and community work in museums, in general

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could examine whether a museum's timeline places non-Western collections in a sequence of progress, and whether the community objects are labelled as contemporary.

Greenhalgh, Michael (2019). Plundered Empire: Acquiring Antiquities from Ottoman Lands. Leiden: Brill.
OrientalismGreenhalghrejectscritique

A framework that Greenhalgh names and sets aside. He does not take Orientalism as an explanation of the travellers' collecting, and says that Bernard Lewis disposed of it decades ago. Other national accounts of archaeology are said to have imperial, colonial or orientalist axes to grind. (Greenhalgh 2019PDF p. 12)

Draws on Bernard Lewis

How it is used By setting Orientalism aside, Greenhalgh keeps the explanation on acquisition, funding, permits and shipping, which the documents can establish, rather than on the attitudes of travellers. He presents his own book as a complement to national histories of archaeology, not a competitor, which is how he marks his distance from them.

“satisfactorily disposed of (in my view) by Bernard” p. 18
travellers' accounts of the Ottoman lands in general

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher on East or Southeast Asian collecting could ask which explanation the documents support (funding, export permits, shipping or attitudes) rather than starting from the category of Orientalism.

trophyGreenhalghappliesanalytic concept

Antiquities that travellers carried home and called trophies, a word the book takes from the Greek memorial of victory set up on a battlefield. Greenhalgh contrasts it with Roman trophies, which were decorated with spoils in Rome rather than set up on the field. (Greenhalgh 2019PDF p. 15)

Draws on Encyclopaedia Britannica 1911, s.v. trophy

How it is used The word lets Greenhalgh read acquisitions as contests in which the West won a victory of civilisation over Turkish barbarism, and then turns the term back on Europeans, who could be called barbarians too. It links the collecting to war, as in the Venetian fortresses marked with the Lion of St Mark.

“the victory of civilisation over Turkish” PDF p. 16
Venetian fortresses marked with the Lion of St Marktravellers' acquisitions in the Ottoman lands

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask how a museum's own language of acquisition framed objects as trophies of a contest, and compare it with the terms used in later returns or loans.

Guy, Kate; Williams, Hajra; Wintle, Claire (eds.) (2024). Histories of Exhibition Design in the Museum: Makers, Process, and Practice. London: Routledge.
ethnographic perspective and thick designZhang, Francisadaptsanalytic concept

A way of designing exhibitions in which the designer, through long collaboration with a source community, takes on the ethnographer's practice of 'deep hanging out'. Its product is 'thick design', the designer's equivalent of Geertz's thick description, which carries the context of making into the exhibition. (Guy 2024p. 138)

Draws on Clifford Geertz; Renato Rosaldo; Hal Foster

How it is used The authors adapt Geertz's distinction between thin and thick description and apply it to the Dali Project and Tradition@Present, arguing that the designer's fieldwork and the exhibition design parallel the anthropologist's fieldnotes and monograph. They set this against the Chinese ethnographic museum's inward focus and the European tradition of displaying non-Europeans, and they modify Feest's question about whether ethnographic museums need ethnography into which ethnography is needed, and where.

“If the result of all this ethnographic labour is thick” p. 139
Dali Project, GuizhouTradition@Present (2013), Chinese National Museum of Ethnology

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask whether an ethnographic museum in another Asian country, such as a Southeast Asian national or minority museum, could commission designers to undertake fieldwork with the communities whose objects it displays.

Hicks, Dan (2020). The Brutish Museums: The Benin Bronzes, Colonial Violence and Cultural Restitution. London: Pluto Press.
chronopoliticsHickscombinesanalytic concept

The use of time by museums as a weapon: the museum turns people and objects into statues, mummies and fetishes, denies coevalness, and makes conquered cultures appear to belong to a lost past. Hicks argues that the museum extends the violence of 1897 across time. (Hicks 2020)

Draws on Achille Mbembe; Johannes Fabian; Frantz Fanon; Aimé Césaire; Edward Burnett Tylor

How it is used Hicks applies the idea to the Pitt Rivers typological display, which began as a collection of arms, and to Tylor's 'object lessons', which Ralph Moor invoked to justify punishing Benin. Hicks combines Mbembe's account of mummification, Fabian's denial of coevalness, and Fanon's 'immobile world of statues' with Césaire's 'chosification' to argue that the Benin material was displayed as a coherent archaeological body and so as a lost world. The combination lets him argue that the museum, not only the army, made Benin a lost world.

“museums became a key regime of practice through which Africans were dehumanised”
Pitt Rivers typological museum, OxfordBenin 'Court Art' vitrineTervuren human zoo

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The idea suggests asking how a museum's typological or chronological arrangement of a collection makes its source cultures appear to belong to an earlier time. A researcher could compare the object-lesson labelling of two museums of the same period.

white projectionHickscoinsanalytic concept

The attribution of the attackers' own violence to their victims, so that the sacking of Benin City appears as retaliation for a massacre and African rulers appear as the aggressors, head-hunters or practitioners of human sacrifice. Hicks presents it as a belief system for white supremacy, repeated by the press and by museum curators. (Hicks 2020)

How it is used Hicks applies the concept to the press coverage of the Phillips mission and to the British accounts of human sacrifice, and to the curators who repeated them, including William Fagg at the British Museum. Hicks uses it to read the 1897 'retaliation' as an inversion in which the attackers claimed the trophies had already been looted by Africans, and to link the Victorian ethnological museum's exhibitionary complex to the defence of colonial violence. The concept lets him break the frame of a timeless colonial past, which is the aim of the necrographic method.

“By the 1890s, the ideology of projection had moved much further, becoming more than just propaganda – a belief system for a new kind of white supremacy.”
Benin 1897 in the press and museum interpretationthe Phillips mission accounts, 1896-97

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The concept could be used to test any museum's interpretation panel of a punitive campaign, to see whether the attackers' violence is reversed onto the victims. It also suggests comparing the press framing of two campaigns in the same period.

corporate-militarist colonialismHicksappliestheoretical framing

The form of British colonialism in West Africa in which chartered companies, above all the Royal Niger Company, and a militarist state ran trade, treaties and punitive expeditions together, with loot and violence as central instruments of extraction. Hicks treats the Benin attack as one part of this continuous operation. (Hicks 2020)

Draws on Max Weber; Rosa Luxemburg

How it is used Hicks applies the frame to the Brohemie expedition of 1894 and the Brass expedition of 1895, and to the Royal Niger Company's campaigns, presenting the Benin attack as one episode of a continuous series rather than a single retaliation. Weber's 'booty capitalism' and Luxemburg's point about militarism are used to show that loot was a principal means of domination and not a by-product. The frame lets him argue that the nation state is the wrong target of critique and that companies, markets and museums worked together.

“that of corporate colonialism, extractive militarism”
Royal Niger Company campaignsBrohemie expedition, 1894 (Nana Olomu)Brass expedition, 1895 (Nembe)Benin, 1897

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could test the frame on another company-led or protectorate campaign, such as the British North Borneo Company, chartered in 1881 and listed in the text, to ask whether looting followed the same pattern. The question is whether loot was a planned instrument there as well.

Hill, Kate (2005). Culture and Class in English Public Museums, 1850–1914. Aldershot: Ashgate.
racial ordering of man-made objects (Melanian, Mongolian, Caucasian)Hillappliesanalytic concept

The classification of all human artefacts by the race of their maker into three categories, adopted at Liverpool after its director Forbes arrived, with display techniques differentiated so that each category carried a message about racial characteristics. Hill draws on Coombes for the central role of the African body in ethnography after 1890. (Hill 2005p. 114)

Draws on Annie Coombes

How it is used Hill uses Coombes's account to show how Liverpool's displays made the classification scientific. Melanian and Caucasian displays were differentiated by technique: African groups appeared as casts, photographs and maps in an evolutionary sequence, while Caucasian objects were admired rather than interpreted. This lets Hill argue that Liverpool's ethnography, like its natural history, naturalised a hierarchy, whereas the Preston statues carried a more subjective and aesthetic message.

“So now all the man-made objects could be used to carry a message about racial” p. 114
Liverpool Museum ethnography and African HallLiverpool Races of Mankind series

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask how a regional museum classified its Asian ethnography by race, nation or civilisation, and whether any category for East or Southeast Asian peoples was given evolutionary or racial meaning.

Hopkins, Owen (2021). The Museum: From Its Origins to the 21st Century.
post-national museumHopkinsadaptstypology

A museum that seeks to transcend national stories and give equal prominence to several histories and narratives, including ones that contradict each other. It starts from the claim that cultures are hybrid and that the nation state is itself an invention of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. (Hopkins 2021)

Draws on Edward Said

How it is used Hopkins adopts Said's claim that cultures are hybrid and tests the category on Dakar's Museum of Black Civilizations and on other museums that extend global networks. Hopkins notes that Chinese money in the Dakar museum can be read as a sign of alliances outside Western control, which lets him use the category to read China's role in African and global museum projects.

“all cultures are involved in one another; none is single and pure.”
Musée des Civilisations Noires, DakarNational Museum of African American History and Culture, WashingtonBenin Dialogue Group

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The category could be used to ask whether a national museum in Southeast Asia that presents several communities' histories side by side is post-national in Hopkins's sense, or still organised around one national story.

Impey, Oliver; MacGregor, Arthur (eds.) (1985). The Origins of Museums: The Cabinet of Curiosities in Sixteenth- and Seventeenth-Century Europe. Oxford: Clarendon Press.
'Indian' as a catch-all label for Asian and other goodsAyers, Seeligtestsanalytic concept

The inventory rubric 'Indian' (and 'Turkish') used for goods from many regions, including Chinese, Japanese and Southeast Asian objects, so that the label gives no reliable evidence of origin. (Impey & MacGregor 1985p. 355)

How it is used Ayers uses the problem as a warning and then tests the labels against the objects: he reattributes some Ambras lacquer to factories in the Ryukyu Islands and separates Chinese porcelain from other Asian goods in Venice, Florence and Innsbruck. Seelig records the same rubrics at Munich and treats them as a sign of how the court itself classified the non-European goods.

“labelled alike as ‘Indian’” p. 355
Ambras lacquer (Ryukyu attribution)Munich inventory of 1598Venetian and Florentine porcelain

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could list every 'Indian' or 'Oriental' entry in an inventory and test each against the object to measure how far the rubric hides the real origin of goods.

Jasanoff, Maya (2005). Edge of Empire: Conquest and Collecting in the East, 1750–1850. London: Fourth Estate.
Orientalism as the collecting of knowledgeJasanoffadaptsanalytic concept

Gathering knowledge about Asia (manuscripts, languages, legal codes, histories) was a prerequisite for, and sometimes a substitute for, imperial authority. The author uses the term in both the contemporary and the postcolonial senses, so Orientalism covers both amateur scholarship and rule. (Jasanoff 2005p. 64)

Draws on Edward Said

How it is used Jasanoff applies Said's account of Orientalism to Warren Hastings, whose manuscript collecting and patronage of Halhed's Code of Gentoo Laws served the Company's government as well as scholarship. Jasanoff adapts it by keeping the scholarly enthusiasm of the amateur Orientalists and showing it as part of imperial rule rather than a separate pastime. The idea lets her argue that the East India Company was in effect collecting an empire through its archives and books.

“the East India Company really was collecting an empire” p. 64
Warren Hastings's manuscripts and patronageHalhed's Code of Gentoo LawsAsiatic Society of Bengal

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The idea could be applied to a museum of Southeast Asian or Chinese material, asking how a collecting scheme served a colonial administration's legal or political needs rather than only scholarship. It suggests comparing Dutch or French collections in the same region.

crossing and mixing (collaborative empire)Jasanoffcriticisescritique

Cultural encounter under empire is understood as crossing and mixing as well as division. Imperial power depended on continental Europeans and on Indian subjects, so British rule was partly collaborative and hybrid rather than a one-sided imposition. (Jasanoff 2005p. 7)

Draws on Edward Said; Subaltern Studies

How it is used Jasanoff criticises the postcolonial habit of portraying Europe's expansion as an oppositional affair and uses the collaborative picture instead. Jasanoff applies it to Lucknow, where East and West mixed more than in almost any Asian city, and to the Indian sepoys sent to Egypt. The argument lets her show Indian and European agents shaping the empire, not only being acted upon by it.

“fundamentally oppositional, one-sided affair” p. 7
Lucknow court cultureIndian sepoys in the Egyptian campaignMughal and Ottoman domains

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The idea could be used to read a museum built on a colonial city's mixed elite, such as a Southeast Asian port, asking which local collectors shaped the holdings. It suggests testing whether collaboration appears in the object records as well as in the narrative.

demonized enemyJasanoffappliesanalytic concept

An imperial enemy is denounced for cruelty while its possessions are eagerly collected by Europeans for their beauty and novelty. The author links the two as a repeated pattern of rivalry and looting. (Jasanoff 2005p. 183)

How it is used Jasanoff sets the 1860 sacking of the Summer Palace beside the Seringapatam collecting, arguing that in both cases a demonised enemy's possessions passed into European civilians' hands. The pairing lets her treat the Summer Palace as a parallel that extends her account of Tipu's collections beyond India. The China case is a single paragraph and is not developed further.

“while the emperor’s possessions were eagerly collected by European” p. 183
the Summer Palace, Beijing, 1860Tipu Sultan's collections at Seringapatam

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The pattern could be tested on other Chinese objects in Western museums acquired during the Opium Wars, asking whether the denunciation of the enemy shaped how the objects were acquired and labelled. A researcher could compare these cases with the Seringapatam material.

Kavanagh, Gaynor (ed.) (1996). Making Histories in Museums. London: Leicester University Press.
the loss of the West as the centre of civilisationO'Neillappliestheoretical framing

Steiner's argument that Western culture can no longer assume that its own legacy is the best that has been thought, nor that progress will spread from the West to all people. O'Neill uses it to argue that museums cannot take their humanist values for granted. (Kavanagh 1996p. 193)

Draws on George Steiner

How it is used O'Neill uses Steiner to criticise museums that preserve their institutions and their Western framing without reflection, and to argue that museums of religion must show the human costs of history. O'Neill then compares Marburg, St Mungo's and the Ulster reconstructed churches against this standard.

“We can, Steiner argues, no longer assume that the West is the locale of high civilization:” p. 193
Marburg Religionskundliche SammlungSt Mungo Museum of Religious Life and Art, GlasgowUlster Folk and Transport Museum reconstructed churches

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The argument could be used to ask how a Western museum of religion presents Asian traditions of belief, whether as exotic, as art or as values that can be compared with its own.

the 'Other' and 'One of Us'Merriman and Poovaya-Smithcriticisescritique

Notions of who counts as the 'Other' and who as 'One of Us' are blurring. The authors argue against separatist displays that set minority histories apart from the mainstream, and in favour of showing points of interaction between cultures. (Kavanagh 1996p. 182)

How it is used The authors weigh separate community museums against mainstream projects and conclude that Bradford's Asian communities would have felt downgraded by a separate museum alone. They therefore favour combining community museums with mainstream presence, and display Bradford's Asian heritage on the same floor as the European collections.

“notions of what constitutes the 'Other' or 'One of Us' are beginning to blur” p. 185
Bradford's proposed Sikh community museumGeffrye Museum 'Chinese Homes' exhibition, 1992Bradford display of the Asian presence in Britain

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The argument could be applied to a Southeast Asian community in a British or American city, asking whether its history should be shown in a separate museum or within the main displays.

Kirshenblatt-Gimblett, Barbara (1998). Destination Culture: Tourism, Museums, and Heritage. Berkeley: University of California Press.
'multicultural' and 'international' as euphemismsKirshenblatt-Gimblettcriticisescritique

Labels such as 'multicultural' and 'international' pluralise the Other while leaving the 'we' as one, so that an immigrant performer is 'multicultural' and a visiting Japanese group is 'international'. They are euphemisms for not white and not American, and they hide the asymmetries of power they seem to challenge. (Kirshenblatt-Gimblett 1998p. 243)

How it is used The author reads the festival's publicity and its reviewers' vocabulary to show that the Cambodian musician Chim Reap is called multicultural while a Japanese Bon Odori group is called international. She argues that the ethnographic survives as the hidden term of the festival's equation, so that difference is banalised by being turned into art.

“the Cambodian musician Chim Reap, an immigrant, is "multicultural" (a euphemism for not white)” p. 243
1990 Los Angeles FestivalChim Reap (Cambodian musician)Gujo Hachiman Bon Odori

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The labels could be tested on a museum's Southeast Asian galleries: which groups are called 'international' and which are 'multicultural', and who is left as the unmarked national.

Knell, Simon J.; Aronsson, Peter; Amundsen, Arne Bugge; et al. (eds.) (2011). National Museums: New Studies from Around the World. London: Routledge.
Orientalism in the display of Chinese artBarnesappliescritique

Said's argument that Western representations of the East assert an absolute difference between Orient and Occident. Barnes uses it to read Victorian displays that grouped Chinese, Japanese, Indian, Korean and Persian art as one oriental tradition, set apart from Western art. (Knell et al. 2011p. 397)

Draws on Said

How it is used Barnes reads the South Kensington Museum's separation of Chinese art from Western art through Said. Barnes argues that displaying the objects together made them one homogeneous oriental tradition, and she adds the curator John Ayers's view that 'oriental' has no real origin. Barnes then reads looted objects such as the Qianlong throne as reclaimed by their new owners, which shows how the displays made Britain, not China, the subject.

“asserted the absolute difference between the Orient” p. 397
South Kensington Museum Asian galleriesQianlong lacquered throne, Victoria and Albert MuseumChina Court, Great Exhibition 1851

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The idea could be used to read a present-day Asian gallery: whether objects from different East Asian cultures are displayed as one tradition, and what that grouping says about the museum's self-image.

third spaceChoiadaptstheoretical framing

Bhabha's self-contradictory space where the roles of colonizer and colonized blur. Choi uses it as a space where visitors can tell their own stories, with Pratt's contact zone as the safe place where the marginalised can speak. (Knell et al. 2011p. 297)

Draws on Bhabha; Pratt; Spivak; Hooper-Greenhill

How it is used Choi takes the third space as an alternative both to the aesthetic, context-free displays of the National Museum of Korea and to forum-style models that offer only cultural diversity. Choi argues that visitors' contradictory identities, including her own, should become objects of enquiry, so that Koreans can define themselves without accepting the terms of colonial power, the terms in which Yanagi's aesthetic of sorrow framed Korean art.

“Bhabha first conceptualized the third space as a self-contradictory” p. 298
National Museum of Korea, Seoul

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A museum in a post-colonial city could test whether a visitor forum or a third-space gallery lets visitors with colonial family memories tell their own stories.

Krech, Shepard, III; Hail, Barbara A. (eds.) (1999). Collecting Native America, 1870–1960. Washington: Smithsonian Institution Press.
missionary discourseLeeappliesanalytic concept

A missionary's use of Native artifacts as the contrast against which a Christian civilization is shown as progress, so that the objects stand for the old religion being displaced. (Krech & Hail 1999)

Draws on Nicholas Thomas

How it is used Lee uses the idea to explain Jackson's collecting as a means to conversion rather than a purely scientific or curio-trade activity. The Sitka museum, the Princeton cabinet and his lectures on Tlingit dances all serve this discourse. The concept lets Lee show the contradiction in collecting artifacts while destroying the institutions that produced them.

“a missionary discourse in which he called on Native artifacts to provide the contrastive unit against which to construct the enlightened Christian path to eternal salvation.”
Sheldon Jackson's Princeton cabinetSitka Industrial and Training SchoolSheldon Jackson Museum

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The concept could be used to ask how collections of Christian missions or colonial schools in East or Southeast Asia contrasted local objects with the converts' new faith, and what those displays asked visitors to conclude.

Logan, William; Nic Craith, Máiréad; Kockel, Ullrich (eds.) (2016). A Companion to Heritage Studies. Chichester: Wiley Blackwell.
exoticlandiaSilverman and Hallettcoinscritique

A generic tourism imaginary in which national governments market the exotic clichés of costumed natives, curious customs and dramatic landscapes, so that very different countries become interchangeable. (Logan 2016)

Draws on Said; Salazar

How it is used Silverman and Hallett use the term to read the 2009-2011 Incredible India and the 2012 Perú campaigns through critical discourse analysis. They show that both videos downplay monuments such as the Taj Mahal and Machu Picchu in favour of embodied encounters, and that their scripts are strikingly alike. They set this against Said's Orientalism and argue that here the nation-state, not Europeans, is doing the exoticising.

“a generic tourism imaginary”
Incredible India 2009-2011 (India)Perú 2012 (Peru)

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The term could be tested on other national tourism campaigns to ask whether the same scripts appear when a state markets a heritage site to foreign visitors.

Longair, Sarah; McAleer, John (eds.) (2012). Curating Empire: Museums and the British Imperial Experience. Manchester: Manchester University Press.
recolonisationMcCarthyadaptsanalytic concept

Belich's term for the phase, after the 1880s, in which settler societies such as New Zealand remade themselves as loyal offshoots of Britain, a 'Better Britain of the South Pacific', and reshaped their relations with indigenous people. (Longair & McAleer 2012p. 61)

Draws on James Belich

How it is used McCarthy uses the idea to reread Maori participation in museums and exhibitions. Maori were not only displayed but also took part, as in the visits recorded in the Colonial Museum's visitors' books after a carved meeting house was installed, in Makereti's troupe at the 1911 Festival of Empire, and in the protest against the Maori display at Wembley. He treats their presence as part of a struggle for a more equitable place in New Zealand society, and so adapts Belich's account from the settler perspective to the indigenous one.

“in which they remade themselves through a process” p. 61
Colonial Museum, WellingtonFestival of Empire 1911 (Makereti's Te Arawa troupe)New Zealand contribution to Wembley, 1924-25

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The concept could be used to ask how other settler museums, such as those in Canada or South Africa, recorded indigenous visitors and performers as participants.

automata and the OrientQureshiappliesanalytic concept

Mechanical intelligence was linked to the Orient, so automata that seemed to reason were read as the products of alien cunning, and their concealed human operators as sign of a tyrannical ruler. (Longair & McAleer 2012p. 215)

Draws on Simon Schaffer

How it is used Qureshi uses Schaffer's argument to explain how the Tiger, a crude mechanism with one moving part, was read at East India House as an immediate symbol of Tipu's tyranny. Tipu as an alien is shown as mindlessly obsessed with conquest, lacking the rational reason of the British, and the Tiger is called a 'toy'. The concept adds a political layer to the barbarity reading of the display and links the Tiger to wider Western myths of Chinese, Japanese and Turkish cunning.

“aliens are automata, mindless subjects of tyranny” p. 216
Tipu's Tiger at East India HouseLater Victorian descriptions of the mechanism

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The concept could be tested on other automata or mechanical curiosities in British collections to see whether their displays carried similar claims about the cunning of their makers.

Lu, Tracey L-D (2014). Museums in China: Power, Politics and Identities. London: Routledge.
heritage museumised as regalia for a colonial stateLuadaptstheoretical framing

Colonial governments presented indigenous heritage sites in museums and gardens with explanatory labels, to show that local people could not keep their own past and to legitimate colonial rule by making the sites into regalia of the state. (Lu 2014p. 59)

Draws on Anderson B.

How it is used Lu takes Anderson’s account of Dutch and French heritage management in Vietnam, Burma and Indonesia as a model for the early museums in Shandong and Shanghai, then qualifies it: China was a semi-colony with concessions rather than a colony, and Chinese intellectuals wanted to learn from the West. The Western museums therefore served both Chinese modernisation and Western power.

“regalia for a secular colonial state’ (Anderson B. 2006: 181–2, italic original)” p. 59
Shandong missionary museumsShanghai MuseumZikawei Museum

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could test whether heritage museums in another concession port were set up to show local people a state’s order, using labels, gardens and dating tables as evidence.

dichotomised discourse of advanced West and antique ChinaLucoinsanalytic concept

A discourse, built by foreign and Chinese museums, that sets Western science and technology against the antiquity, and so obsolescence, of Chinese heritage; within China it sets the advanced urban and Han against the backward rural and the minorities. (Lu 2014p. 215)

How it is used Lu uses it in the conclusion to link the early missionary and elite museums, which first set Western knowledge against Chinese tradition, with later museums that repeat the contrast inside China through historic ethnocentrism and urban-rural divides. It connects the 1930s museums to the textbook history heard from students in 2013 and to the ethnic discrimination the ecomuseums are said to reinforce.

“dichotomized discourse on the advanced” p. 215
Zikawei MuseumShanghai MuseumMuseums in mainland China today

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could check whether a museum’s own labels set one civilisation against another, or one region against another, and count the terms used.

Macdonald, Sharon; Fyfe, Gordon (eds.) (1996). Theorizing Museums: Representing Identity and Diversity in a Changing World. Oxford: Blackwell.
vernacular historiographyGablecriticisescritique

The informal historical understanding that frontline guides use to tell a museum's story. At Colonial Williamsburg it took the form of a 'just the facts' approach that treated missing documents as grounds for silence and kept racial categories fixed. (Macdonald & Fyfe 1996PDF p. 180)

Draws on new social history

How it is used Gable uses the concept to explain why the new social history of race did not change what guides said. White guides avoided miscegenation by insisting on facts that the documents did not supply, while black guides on the AAIP Other Half Tour told the Wythe House story; so the vernacular historiography reinforced the dichotomising thinking about race that the topic should have questioned. He sets the composite Wythe of 'Christmas at the Wythe House' against the openly fictional 'Affairs of the Heart' to show what each framing allows.

“reverting to a historiography of ‘just the facts’” PDF p. 182
Colonial WilliamsburgWythe HouseAAIP Other Half Tour

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The concept could guide a study of how frontline guides at a Chinese or Japanese heritage site talk about colonial or wartime contact, and whether documentary gaps are treated as reasons for silence.

MacKenzie, John M. (2009). Museums and Empire: Natural History, Human Cultures and Colonial Identities. Manchester: Manchester University Press.
scramble and otheringMacKenzieappliesanalytic concept

A worldwide scramble for ethnographic artefacts and human remains, carried out by museum agents, administrators, soldiers and missionaries, which made museum objects emblems of othering in both past and present contexts. (MacKenzie 2009p. 9)

How it is used MacKenzie applies the scramble to the Canadian museums, where rival collectors competed with American museums, and to the Chinese purchases of the Royal Ontario Museum, which he treats as part of a wider scramble for antiquities in the period. The concept lets him read collecting as an act of imperial power rather than only as a matter of taste or science.

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could date the Asian shipments to a given museum against the political events in the source country, to test whether acquisition followed the scramble pattern or diverged from it.

Meyer, Andrea; Savoy, Bénédicte (eds.) (2014). The Museum Is Open: Towards a Transnational History of Museums 1750–1940. Berlin: De Gruyter.
contact sphere of artKüsterappliesanalytic concept

The space in which art from Europe and from colonised places meets within a colonial museum. The author takes it to carry political significance, since the universal art a colonial museum claims can hide nationalism and the exclusion of local histories. (Meyer & Savoy 2014p. 247)

How it is used Küster applies the idea to the Musée Léon Dierx on La Réunion, where French art and history displaced the immigrant and enslaved histories of the island, and to the National Museum of Fine Arts in Algiers, which concentrated on Orientalist painting after its 1930 centenary. The concept lets her argue that the colonial museum’s universalism was a national claim, and that the transnational museum must be rethought in light of restitution demands.

“the contact sphere of art always has political significance.” p. 247
Musée Léon Dierx, La RéunionNational Museum of Fine Arts, Algiers

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The idea could be used on a colonial collection of Asian objects in a European museum, asking who was left out of its universal framing and what claims were later made on it.

Miller, Edward (1973). That Noble Cabinet: A History of the British Museum. London: André Deutsch.
ethnography as the plaything of administrative convenienceMillercriticisescritique

The ethnographical collections were moved between departments for administrative reasons rather than scholarly or public purposes, so after 1933 they sat in an uneasy partnership with Oriental Antiquities. (Miller 1973p. 326)

How it is used Miller uses the idea to explain the long neglect of the ethnographical collections, from Franks's 1866 case for an independent department through the 1927-29 Royal Commission to the 1933 reorganisation. Miller sets the collections of Asia, Africa, America and Oceania against Kenyon's evidence that they formed a large curiosity shop, and he criticises the government's decision not to create a separate ethnographical museum.

“The plaything of administrative convenience for” p. 330
the ethnographical collections 1866-1933the Department of Oriental Antiquities and Ethnography, 1933the Royal Commission of 1927-29

Sandell, Richard; Nightingale, Eithne (eds.) (2012). Museums, Equality and Social Justice. London: Routledge.
epidermalizationDewdney, Dibosa, Walshcriticisescritique

Fanon's term for reading identity through skin colour. The authors use it to show how diversity policy confuses difference with visible racial markers, so that questions of power are hidden. (Sandell & Nightingale 2012)

Draws on Frantz Fanon; Kobena Mercer

How it is used The authors argue that Tate Britain's policies counted BAME audiences, staff and artworks, treating difference as skin colour and leaving the networks that keep cultural flow moving in one direction unexamined. Combined with Mercer's notion of multicultural normalisation, the concept lets them argue that targeting and market segmentation produced separated segments rather than a shared public. It is a critique of policy, not of individual visitors.

“the work of difference becomes confused with variegation of skin colour”
Tate Britain (Tate Encounters research)Lubaina Himid's The Thin Black Line (1985), as the earlier politics of visibility

Sellers, Charles Coleman (1980). Mr. Peale’s Museum: Charles Willson Peale and the First Popular Museum of Natural Science and Art. New York: W. W. Norton.
the races of mankind (wax group)Sellersappliestypology

The group of wax figures completed in August 1797 that placed a Carib, a native of Kamchatka, a Chinese laborer, a Chinese mandarin and others together as contrasting races of mankind. Sellers notes that the faces were cast from people who were present in Philadelphia, and that Federalist critics ridiculed the show. (Sellers 1980p. 92)

How it is used Sellers treats the wax group as the museum's most contested application of its classificatory method to human beings, placed beside its birds and mammals. Sellers notes that the figures were partly cast from sailors and visiting servants, which shows how the display of others depended on the travellers and traders present in the city. Sellers mentions the anthropological significance ('the prehistory of anthropology') but does not develop it.

“Eight other wax figures were added to make a group of contrasting races of mankind, completed in August 1797” p. 92
Peale's wax figures of the racesthe Salem East India Marine Society's wax figures (compared)

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could compare which Asian peoples appeared in such wax groups in Western museums, and whose faces, costumes or poses came from travellers, servants or sailors rather than from anthropological study.

Sherman, Daniel J.; Rogoff, Irit (eds.) (1994). Museum Culture: Histories, Discourses, Spectacles. Minneapolis: University of Minnesota Press.
self-Orientalizing in national displayWallisappliescritique

Orientalism, in Said's sense, is a mythic and political image of the East built from Western projections. Wallis describes a case where a nation that had been Orientalised by Western colonialists adopts the same stereotypes itself in order to present its identity to Americans. (Sherman & Rogoff 1994p. 271)

Draws on Edward Said

How it is used Wallis applies Said's idea to the Turkish festival, arguing that the nation was 'forced to adopt' a self-Orientalizing mode because it had to dramatise conventional national images to establish its place in the international community. The concept lets him explain the elite court culture chosen for the show.

“Orientalism is a political fiction, a mythic idea” p. 271
Turkey: The Continuing MagnificenceThe Age of Sultan Suleyman the Magnificent

Sleeper-Smith, Susan (ed.) (2009). Contesting Knowledge: Museums and Indigenous Perspectives. Lincoln: University of Nebraska Press.
contact zoneLiffmanappliesanalytic concept

Mary Louise Pratt's and James Clifford's term for a place where different peoples meet, which Liffman applies to museums as sites of storytelling, Indigenous history and tribal politics. (Sleeper-Smith 2009p. 194)

Draws on Mary Louise Pratt; James Clifford

How it is used Liffman applies the term to the Our Peoples Huichol exhibition at the NMAI, where Huichol curators sought to display a land map and a consecrating ritual, and to the Huichol use of museum space for nonpublic ritual and art sales. It lets him show Indigenous agency inside a national institution rather than only its subordination.

“constitutes a kind of contact zone” p. 194
Our Peoples exhibition, NMAIMuseo Nacional de Antropología, Mexico City

denial of coevalnessMagubaneappliesanalytic concept

Johannes Fabian's term for the difficulty that arises when anthropologists rely on evidence from native informants while placing those people in a different temporal zone. Magubane uses it for the exhibited Africans, who had to be presented as coevals. (Sleeper-Smith 2009p. 56)

Draws on Johannes Fabian

How it is used Magubane shows that the showcases' claim that Africans had no notion of time was continually interrupted, because the exhibition needed the performers' testimony and skill and so had to recognize them as coevals. Magubane uses the tension to show that the performers' statements and bodies contested the scientific frame of the display.

“the seamlessness of this narrative was continually interrupted” p. 56
London ethnographic showcases (Egyptian Hall, St George's Gallery)

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could check a human display in an East or Southeast Asian context for the same contradiction between the exhibitors' claim of distance and their need for the performers' knowledge.

ethnography as scientific justificationSilvermanappliescritique

Silverman's account of ethnography as the 'scientific' justification for colonial conquest in the Americas and Africa, a mode of representation that has persisted into museum display. (Sleeper-Smith 2009p. 9)

How it is used Silverman applies the idea across the four essays: Langfur on Brazilian accounts of the Botocudo and the first national museums, Magubane on African human exhibits, McMullen on Heye, and Rassool on the District Six Museum. Silverman uses it to argue that the habits of ethnography persist in museums and that an object-centred national museum cannot speak for hundreds of nations.

“ethnography has influenced European modes of representing the” p. 9
Botocudo and Brazilian national museumsAfrican human exhibits in Europe and the United StatesNational Museum of the American IndianDistrict Six Museum

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could trace the same ethnographic framing in the first national museums of a Southeast Asian state, asking which accounts of local peoples supplied its displays.

Tseng, Alice Y. (2008). The Imperial Museums of Meiji Japan: Architecture and the Art of the Nation. Seattle: University of Washington Press.
the Saidian framework applied to Conder's Saracenic styleTsengtestscritique

Said's account of the Orient as the diametrical opposite of the European self, essentialised and fixed as the complement of a progressive West. Tseng applies it to Josiah Conder's description of the Ueno facade as Saracenic, then qualifies it because Japan was never part of Said's Orient. (Tseng 2008p. 71)

Draws on Said

How it is used Tseng reads Conder's Saracenic facade, and his separation of wooden and masonry construction as the boundary between Japan and the West, as an orientalist vision. Tseng then argues the framework needs adjusting: Japan was not colonised and did not share Europe's history of contention with the Orient, though the same essentialising strategies later appeared in Okakura's writings on Japanese uniqueness. The qualification lets her treat the Ueno facade as an unstable sign of a generalised East rather than as an Asian style.

“Here the Saidian framework appears” p. 71
Museum in Ueno Park facadeConder's pseudo-Saracenic style

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The qualification could be used to ask whether the Saidian frame fits the style choices made for museums built by colonial architects in Southeast Asia, where colonial control did apply.

Yallop, Jacqueline (2011). Magpies, Squirrels and Thieves: How the Victorians Collected the World. London: Atlantic Books.
the 'Chinese character' in museum displayYallopcriticisescritique

The 1872 South Kensington catalogue's description of the Chinese as a degenerate, effeminate race, through which the museum framed its Chinese objects for middle-class visitors. Yallop uses the phrase to show how display confirmed prejudice. (Yallop 2011)

How it is used Yallop quotes the catalogue to show how a museum could use objects to confirm the visitor's view of another people, and sets Bushell and Franks against that frame. The critique lets the author argue that Bushell's knowledge of Chinese history and Franks's wish for objects to speak for themselves worked against the museum's own writing. It is the basis of the claim that Bushell changed attitudes in a museum that remained contemptuous.

“It would hardly be supposed that an effeminate race like the Chinese should have a taste for working in metal”
the Chinese galleries at South Kensingtonthe 1872 Catalogue of Chinese Objects

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could compare the descriptive labels and catalogue entries for Chinese galleries across several decades to see when such language changed.

objects from intransigent states as spoilsYallopappliesanalytic concept

Objects taken from states that resisted British power, which made British victories visible in the museum. Yallop applies it to Afghan trophies and to Far Eastern acquisitions. (Yallop 2011)

How it is used Yallop uses the idea to link war and diplomacy to museum acquisitions: an Afghan gateway panel and arms from the Afghan wars reached South Kensington, and collecting from Japan and China acted to assert territorial and symbolic claims in a contest with other powers. This lets the author explain acquisitions as political acts, not only as matters of taste. It sets the imperial reading against the more scholarly aims of Franks and Bushell.

“objects from intransigent states was one way, at least, of announcing supremacy.”
the Afghan panel from the gateway of Ghuzni at South KensingtonSir Harry Parkes's Japanese sword and Queen Victoria's Japanese gifts

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): One could ask, for a given museum, which acquisitions followed a military or diplomatic event, and whether the dates line up with the event.

Ownership, restitution and the universal museum

Cultural property, looting, antiquities law, repatriation and the arguments for and against the encyclopaedic museum. 21 concepts from 13 texts

These approaches ask who may own museum objects, how they came to be held, and whether holdings can be defended against claims for return. They treat collections as property and test the museum's claim to serve everyone against the history of taking. Our texts place them in the lineage of Macpherson, through Clifford's possessive self (Stocking 1985p. 237; Stocking 1985p. 238); of Mauss, whose gift theory Hicks sets against the museum's objects (Hicks 2020); and of Marx and Luxemburg, read by Hicks (Hicks 2020). Merryman's object-oriented policy and Cuno's triad supply a standard for unprovenanced antiquities (Cuno 2009p. 183; Cuno 2008PDF p. 39).

Central to the theme are Greenhalgh on Ottoman antiquities (Greenhalgh 2019p. 7), Hicks on the Benin holdings (Hicks 2020), Çelik on Ottoman archaeology (Çelik 2016p. 215), and Cuno's Who Owns Antiquity? and the edited Whose Culture? (Cuno 2008PDF p. 14; Cuno 2009p. 17).

Possessive self and bounded possession

Clifford extends Macpherson's possessive self to collecting: "collecting has long been a strategy for the deployment of a possessive self," (Stocking 1985p. 238). Clifford applies this to Handler's study of Quebec's patrimoine, where nationalists claim a culture as a possession as the collector claims a self (Stocking 1985p. 237; Stocking 1985p. 238). Handler, by contrast, builds a typology of claims from what a group possesses and what relation it claims, applied to the Place Royale in Quebec City (Stocking 1985p. 211; Stocking 1985p. 212). Clifford uses the idea to explain the collector; Handler to classify claims.

Taking, plunder and looting

Hicks argues that anthropology has offered no theory of looting, so that objects held as duress carry unfulfilled obligations as well as life histories (Hicks 2020). Greenhalgh uses plunder as one term for local destruction, Ottoman gifts and European removals, treating them as one process (Greenhalgh 2019p. 7). Yallop applies the same logic to the Summer Palace: "There was widespread and chaotic looting," and the dispersed relics created the market for Chinese objects in Britain (Yallop 2011). Stewart criticises acquisition as a removal of context (Stewart 1984p. 162).

Encyclopaedic against nationalistic museums

Çelik quotes the directors' division of encyclopaedic and nationalistic museums, then shows that Western museums were built on imperial and national politics from the start (Çelik 2016p. 215; Çelik 2016p. 216). Cuno uses nationalist retentionist laws to judge source-nation requests, arguing they should be opposed rather than tightened (Cuno 2008PDF p. 25; Cuno 2008PDF p. 108). Merryman tests object-oriented against nation-oriented policy on single cases, finding return justified mainly where a living culture still uses the object in ritual (Cuno 2009p. 183; Cuno 2009p. 191). MacGregor uses trusteeship for all humanity to justify wide lending, and Appiah applies it to Nigeria's Nok sculptures (Cuno 2009p. 43; Cuno 2009p. 75).

Partage and the triad

Greenhalgh tests partage against Myrina near Smyrna, where the French managed the division to their advantage: "partage was a flawed system" (Greenhalgh 2019p. 547). Cuno adapts partage as a precedent that built several US university collections, and proposes its return against nationalist claims (Cuno 2008PDF p. 26; Cuno 2008PDF p. 132). Cuno also adopts Merryman's triad of preservation, knowledge and access to move the question from ownership to what an object and its context offer (Cuno 2008PDF p. 39; Cuno 2008PDF p. 132).

Legal title: lex situs and the pedigree rule

Palmer applies the lex situs rule: "This is known as the lex situs rule." Title is decided by the law where the object lay at sale, so a foreign sale can cut off the owner's title; Winkworth and the Stowlangtoft panels show that museums cannot rely on the law to protect national heritage (Vergo 1989p. 190). Boardman argues against pedigree rules, such as a cut-off before 1970, which penalise scholars and museums rather than looters (Cuno 2009p. 117; Cuno 2009p. 116).

Restitution and wartime protection

Gardner treats restitution as a process with its own politics: after 1815 the Bourbons had to settle the claims of several states, and the Louvre kept few major pieces (Gardner 2020). March uses the Spanish Civil War as a test bench for protection, measuring the Catalan move of works to Olot against the International Museums Office's remote-site criteria: "Spain was also a test bench for heritage protection." (Hill 2021p. 95; Hill 2021p. 88). Gardner writes a history of claims; March a history of practice.

Rescue, decolonisation and the record

Greenhalgh calls the rescue defence an old argument that recent defenders repeat, and tests it against the Elgin Marbles, the Getty Kouros and Iraq after 2003 (Greenhalgh 2019p. 557; Greenhalgh 2019p. 560). Hopkins reads the V&A director's position: "to decolonize is to decontextualise," so the task is interpretation, not return (Hopkins 2021). Hopkins criticises both the continuity argument and the view that all colonial objects were stolen (Hopkins 2021).

Inalienable possessions and intangible heritage

Kirshenblatt-Gimblett tests inalienable possessions: "Heritage tests the alienability of inalienable possessions." (Kirshenblatt-Gimblett 1998p. 149). Taonga at the Manawatu Museum show that a museum cannot animate what it has taken out of circulation, since vitality lies in transmission and performance (Kirshenblatt-Gimblett 1998p. 149; Kirshenblatt-Gimblett 1998p. 166). Brown moves the question to intangible heritage, which Indigenous groups claim as cultural property, and concludes that community curation cannot settle questions of representation (Cuno 2009p. 145; Cuno 2009p. 152).

Debates and limits

The sharpest disagreement concerns the encyclopaedic museum. Cuno defends it against archaeologists, the Chinese state and the Italian government, who present source-nation laws as protecting sites or expressing identity (Cuno 2008PDF p. 14; Cuno 2008PDF p. 109; Cuno 2008PDF p. 113). Hicks targets Cuno's universal museum defence (Hicks 2020). Çelik rejects the view that Western museums have histories cleansed of politics (Çelik 2016p. 216), and Greenhalgh calls the rescue defence tired (Greenhalgh 2019p. 560). Hopkins rejects both the continuity defence and the view that all colonial objects were stolen (Hopkins 2021). The gap the texts leave is the act of taking itself: Hicks notes that no anthropological theory of looting has been written (Hicks 2020).

Carrying it over to a new case

  • Ask, for any museum with Asian holdings acquired under colonial or war conditions, whether its encyclopaedic claim survives the question of how each object was obtained (Çelik 2016p. 215; Çelik 2016p. 216).
  • Trace each object's title through the law of the place where it lay at sale, as Palmer does for English sale rooms (Vergo 1989p. 190).
  • Compare partage agreements with an excavation's export records to see which share was sent and what was never declared (Greenhalgh 2019p. 547).
  • Check the rescue claim for a museum's Asian holdings against acquisition dates, the state of the site, and whether loss followed the purchase (Greenhalgh 2019p. 560).
  • Apply Merryman's Buddha-head test to a Southeast Asian sculpture in a European collection, asking whether the answer changes when a source community still uses the object in ritual (Cuno 2009p. 183; Cuno 2009p. 191).
  • Ask which intangible practices came into Western collections with Southeast Asian objects, following Brown's move from objects to knowledge (Cuno 2009p. 152).
  • Count death histories beside life histories in a catalogue, asking which objects were gifts, purchases or seizures (Hicks 2020).
  • Compare the 1970 cut-off in pedigree rules with the dates of Southeast Asian export laws, asking how many objects in Western collections would fall under it (Cuno 2009p. 117).

Where to start reading

  • Stocking, George W., Jr. (ed.) (1985). Objects and Others: Essays on Museums and Material Culture. Madison: University of Wisconsin Press. Clifford on the possessive self and Handler's typology of claims, for how ownership frames identity.
  • Greenhalgh, Michael (2019). Plundered Empire: Acquiring Antiquities from Ottoman Lands. Leiden: Brill. Greenhalgh on plunder, partage and the rescue defence, against the excavation evidence.
  • Hicks, Dan (2020). The Brutish Museums: The Benin Bronzes, Colonial Violence and Cultural Restitution. London: Pluto Press. Hicks on the theory of taking and the Benin holdings.
  • Cuno, James (2008). Who Owns Antiquity? Museums and the Battle over Our Ancient Heritage. Princeton: Princeton University Press. Cuno on nationalist laws, partage and Merryman's triad.
  • Cuno, James (ed.) (2009). Whose Culture? The Promise of Museums and the Debate over Antiquities. Princeton: Princeton University Press. Merryman on object-oriented policy, MacGregor on trusteeship, Boardman on the pedigree rule.
  • Çelik, Zeynep (2016). About Antiquities: Politics of Archaeology in the Ottoman Empire. Austin: University of Texas Press. Çelik on the encyclopaedic and nationalistic division.
  • Vergo, Peter (ed.) (1989). The New Museology. London: Reaktion Books. Palmer on lex situs and English title.
  • Kirshenblatt-Gimblett, Barbara (1998). Destination Culture: Tourism, Museums, and Heritage. Berkeley: University of California Press. Kirshenblatt-Gimblett on inalienable possessions.
