Çelik, Zeynep (2016). About Antiquities: Politics of Archaeology in the Ottoman Empire. Austin: University of Texas Press.
encyclopedic versus nationalistic museumsÇelikcriticisescritique

The division of museums into ‘encyclopedic’ or ‘humanistic’ institutions, which serve ‘all of us’ and whose collections are shared across the world, and ‘nationalistic’ museums, which tell a nation’s story and keep antiquities within its borders; Western directors use it to argue against repatriation. (Çelik 2016p. 215)

Draws on James Cuno; James F. Goode; Robin F. Rhodes; Dennis Doordan

How it is used Çelik quotes the directors’ division and then shows that the Western museums were themselves built on imperial and national politics from the start, so the present bickering over good and bad uses of antiquities conceals the question of objects illegally obtained by Western museums. The author applies the critique to Turkey’s claims against the Getty, Cleveland, the Metropolitan and Boston.

“the practical question of returning the objects illegally obtained by Western museums” p. 216
Getty MuseumCleveland Museum of ArtMetropolitan Museum of Art (Schimmel collection)Museum of Fine Arts, Boston (Weary Herakles)British Museum

Cuno, James (2008). Who Owns Antiquity? Museums and the Battle over Our Ancient Heritage. Princeton: Princeton University Press.
nationalist retentionist cultural property lawsCunocriticisescritique

Laws that declare antiquities and other cultural objects national property and restrict their export, sale and movement. The text reads them as intended to keep objects within the nation to affirm national identity, not as laws to protect archaeological sites. (Cuno 2008PDF p. 25)

How it is used Cuno uses the category to judge the political purpose of source-nation laws. Cuno applies it to Italy's requests to the United States and to China's 2005 request, arguing that the United States decides such requests on foreign-policy grounds, and to Greek, Egyptian and Chinese export laws. The category lets him argue that these laws have failed to stop looting and should be opposed rather than tightened.

“Nationalist retentionist cultural property laws are contrary to the generative principles of” PDF p. 108
Italy's request for US import restrictionsChina's 2005 request to the United StatesGreek, Egyptian and Chinese export laws

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could test Cuno's test on another request, such as Cambodia's, which appears in the list of granted US requests (line 1854), by comparing the stated archaeological grounds with the diplomatic context.

Merryman's triad of preservation, knowledge and accessCunoadaptsmethod

A set of principles for regulating unprovenanced antiquities: preservation of the object and its context, the pursuit of knowledge about the past, and access for scholars and the public. The text offers it as a replacement for ownership as the basis of policy. (Cuno 2008PDF p. 38)

Draws on John Henry Merryman

How it is used Cuno adopts the triad to shift the question from who owns an object to what it and its context can offer. Cuno returns to it in the epilogue, where he places it beside partage as a better principle than nationalist ones. It gives him a standard for judging acquisition and circulation without tying the outcome to a modern state's claim.

“Merryman’s triad shifts our attention from the “ownership” of antiquities to their” PDF p. 39
unprovenanced antiquities in generalthe epilogue's proposal for shared stewardship

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The triad could be used as a checklist for a single collection, asking for each object what preservation, knowledge and access it currently allows, and whether a loan or exchange would improve the score.

partageCunoadaptsmethod

The historical arrangement by which foreign-led excavations shared finds with the host country's archaeological museums. Cuno presents it as a lost alternative to national ownership of antiquities. (Cuno 2008PDF p. 26)

How it is used Cuno uses partage as a historical precedent. Cuno credits it with building the archaeological collections of several US university museums and of the British and Metropolitan museums, and in the epilogue he proposes its return as the practical answer to nationalist claims. The concept lets him argue that national laws, not the museums, ended a practice that once served both source countries and foreign museums.

“It is called partage.” PDF p. 26
archaeological museums at Chicago, Pennsylvania, Harvard and YaleBritish Museum and Metropolitan Museum collectionsEgypt, Iraq, Afghanistan and Turkey

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A study could trace which finds from one pre-1950s excavation were divided under partage, and then check how many of them are now in that excavation's host-country museums and how many in foreign ones.

Cuno, James (ed.) (2009). Whose Culture? The Promise of Museums and the Debate over Antiquities. Princeton: Princeton University Press.
object-oriented policy against nation-oriented policyMerrymancoinstheoretical framing

Cultural property policy should rank preservation, truth and access to the object above the claim of the nation where it was found. Merryman sets this against nation-oriented policies that treat objects as the property of their source state. (Cuno 2009p. 183)

How it is used Merryman tests the two approaches on single cases: a Cleveland Poussin bought without a French export permit, a looted Maya stela, a Kom sculpture, and a headless Buddha in Xi’an. Merryman finds that the approaches diverge in some cases and agree in others, and that return is justified mainly where a living culture still uses the object in ritual.

“would be improved by placing less emphasis on the nation and more on” p. 183
Cleveland PoussinMaya stelaKom sculptureheadless Buddha, Xi’an (hypothetical)Van Gogh smuggled from France (hypothetical)

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could apply the Buddha-head test to a Southeast Asian sculpture in a European collection and ask whether the object-oriented answer changes when a source community still uses the object.

trusteeship of objects for humanityMacGregoradaptstheoretical framing

The museum holds objects in trust for all humanity, present and future, rather than for the nation or a donor. MacGregor presents trusteeship as central to the British Museum’s founding, and Appiah uses the same idea in a narrower form. (Cuno 2009p. 43)

How it is used MacGregor uses trusteeship to justify lending the collection widely, from the Sudanese lyre shown during the Darfur debate to the Hazina exhibition chosen in Nairobi. Appiah applies it to Nigeria: its government may act as trustee of the Nok sculptures, which belong to all human beings.

“And the notion of trustees and trusteeship was, I think, central to it. It is” p. 43
British Museum loans (Darfur debate)Hazina exhibition, NairobiNok sculptures

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask whether a regional museum in East or Southeast Asia that lends or receives loans acts as trustee in MacGregor’s sense, and who appoints the trustee.

pedigree ruleBoardmancriticisescritique

Rules that treat an antiquity without a documented ownership history as tainted, especially with a cut-off such as a pedigree before 1970. Boardman argues such rules penalise scholars and museums rather than looters. (Cuno 2009p. 117)

How it is used Boardman argues against collecting legislation: a 1970 cut-off covers Egyptian statues and Victorian stamps alike, pushes finders to melt objects down, and keeps unprovenanced material from scholars. Boardman illustrates with a clay snake vase bought for Oxford and the Gundestrup cauldron, whose Danish bog find tells little about its date.

“What can be made of a law that regards objects with no apparent” p. 117
clay snake vase bought for OxfordChios building rubbleGundestrup cauldronEuphronios krater

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could compare the 1970 cut-off with the dates of Southeast Asian export or heritage laws and ask how many objects in Western collections would fall under such a rule.

intangible heritageBrownadaptsanalytic concept

Heritage made of songs, language, religious knowledge and ways of life rather than objects, which Indigenous groups now claim under the notion of cultural property. (Cuno 2009p. 145)

How it is used Brown moves the argument from objects to knowledge. Brown traces how NAGPRA encouraged such claims, criticises the Musée du quai Branly for separating indigenous and European art, and questions the shallow content of the National Museum of the American Indian. Brown concludes that community curation cannot settle questions of representation.

“intangible expressions of their cultures be subject to similar protection” p. 152
Musée du quai BranlyNational Museum of the American IndianMashantucket Pequot Museum

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask which intangible practices, such as ritual knowledge held by a community, came into Western collections with Southeast Asian objects, and whether consultation with the community there goes beyond consultation.

Gardner, James (2020). The Louvre: The Many Lives of the World’s Most Famous Museum. New York: Atlantic Monthly Press.
restitutionGardnerappliesanalytic concept

The return of works seized in war to their former owners under the terms of the peace, which the Bourbons had to settle first at the Louvre after 1815. (Gardner 2020)

How it is used Gardner treats restitution as a process with its own politics. Prussian generals, German princes, Spain, the Netherlands and Austria made claims, and the Italian works were resolved by treaty and by the Pope's agent Canova, so that the Louvre kept a few major pieces. The process explains why the museum had to fill its galleries with works bought from Borghese and why the Venus de Milo replaced the Medici Venus, which was sent back to Tuscany.

“If restitution was the first issue that the Bourbons had to address at the Louvre”
Italian works seized in 1797 to 1801Laocoön and Apollo BelvedereMedici Venus returned to Tuscany

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could chart the same sequence of claims for a later museum, asking which states made claims, by what treaty, and what was kept in exchange.

Greenhalgh, Michael (2019). Plundered Empire: Acquiring Antiquities from Ottoman Lands. Leiden: Brill.
plunderGreenhalghcoinsanalytic concept

Greenhalgh's broad term for the violent or dishonest acquisition of antiquities, covering inhabitants who destroyed or stripped sites, Ottoman officials who gave antiquities away, and European travellers who bought or removed them. Natural agents such as drought, malaria and piracy are treated as ravages that softened the land for plunder. (Greenhalgh 2019p. 7)

How it is used Using one term for local and foreign removal lets Greenhalgh treat Ottoman gifts to Britain, Germany and France, local lime-burning and European export as parts of one process, which the book follows from the field to the harbour. It also lets the book reject the idea that Westerners arrived to rescue a ruined Empire, since the plunder began with its inhabitants.

“Plundering applies both to inhabitants of the Empire who lay waste antique” p. 7
Ottoman gifts of antiquities to Britain, Germany and Francesites stripped by inhabitants before the West took an interesttravellers' removals from Egypt and Greece

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could use the broad definition to ask which removals from a museum's holdings were local, state-authorised or foreign, rather than assuming a single agent. It also invites comparing gifts by officials with purchases by travellers.

the rescue defenceGreenhalghcriticisescritique

The argument that museums acquire looted antiquities in order to rescue them from destruction or from public view. Greenhalgh treats it as an old and tired argument, which recent defenders of Western museums still repeat as a continuing alibi for the West. (Greenhalgh 2019p. 557)

Draws on Jenkins

How it is used Greenhalgh sets the rescue argument against the record: the Elgin Marbles, the Getty Kouros, and the looting after the 2003 invasion of Iraq, quoting Fisk and Stein on what was lost while Western authorities stood by. The argument is thus tested by what happened to the objects and sites rather than by its own logic.

“rescuing material that would otherwise be destroyed or lost from public” p. 560
Elgin MarblesGetty Kouroslooting in Iraq after 2003

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could test the rescue claim for a museum's Asian holdings against acquisition dates, the state of the site at the time, and whether loss or damage followed the purchase.

partageGreenhalghteststypology

The system under which excavators shared finds with the host state. Greenhalgh asks who made the division, whether it was equitable, and how many objects were carried off unseen, so that partage was a flawed system from the Empire's point of view. (Greenhalgh 2019p. 547)

Draws on Anderson 2017

How it is used Greenhalgh tests the system against the evidence of Myrina near Smyrna, where in 1880-1882 the French managed the partage to their advantage. The test turns on who controlled the division and whether anyone could know what was found, which shows that regulated excavation did not stop export.

“partage was a flawed system” p. 547
Myrina near Smyrna, 1880-1882

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could compare partage agreements with the export records of a museum's excavations to see which share was actually sent and what was never declared.

Hicks, Dan (2020). The Brutish Museums: The Benin Bronzes, Colonial Violence and Cultural Restitution. London: Pluto Press.
theory of takingHickscoinstheoretical framing

A proposed theory of how objects were taken rather than given, as opposed to anthropology's theory of gifts and reciprocity. Hicks argues that anthropology has never written a theory of looting, and that objects in museums held as 'duress' carry unfulfilled obligations and death histories as well as life histories. (Hicks 2020)

Draws on Marcel Mauss; Karl Marx; Rosa Luxemburg; Ann Laura Stoler

How it is used Hicks sets Mauss's gift theory against the objects of the museum, and Marx's primitive accumulation against Luxemburg's point that capitalism needed non-capitalist pasts, which he says Africa was cast into as 'pre-capitalist'. Hicks uses the idea to argue that the world culture museum is a temporal device whose cases hold unfulfilled obligations, and that restitution has to begin from the act of taking. It is applied to Benin holdings in the Pitt Rivers and British Museum and to African collections from Nigeria, Egypt and Ethiopia.

“Anthropology has offered no theory of the ‘permanent’ exhibition in museums of inalienable culture – things that could never be given”
Benin objects in the Pitt Rivers MuseumBritish Museum Benin holdingsAfrican collections from Nigeria, Egypt and Ethiopia

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask, for any museum with colonial-era holdings, whether its accession records describe the act of taking at all, and which of its objects were gifts, purchases or seizures. The idea also suggests counting death histories beside life histories in a catalogue.

Hill, Kate (ed.) (2021). Museums, Modernity and Conflict: Museums and Collections in and of War since the Nineteenth Century. London: Routledge.
wartime heritage protection as a test benchMarchappliesanalytic concept

The idea that the Spanish Civil War served as a trial of methods for protecting heritage in war, including evacuation, shelters and remote depots, and that the International Museums Office's 1939 advice to evacuate works from museums drew on that experience. (Hill 2021p. 95)

Draws on International Museums Office, La Protection des Monuments et Oeuvres d'Art en Temps de Guerre (1939)

How it is used March applies the idea to the Catalan rescue of 1936. The move of the main works to Olot, a town near the Pyrenees, is measured against the IMO's criteria for remote sites, and the 1939 guidance is read as a response to what Catalonia had tried. The comparison with the Prado's evacuation and the League of Nations transfer to Switzerland lets her show that protection was practised before it was codified.

“Spain was also a test bench for heritage protection.” p. 95
Museu d'Art de CatalunyaOlot depot, 1936Prado evacuationLeague of Nations transfer of Spanish works to Switzerland, 1939

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could check whether other civil wars, such as the Chinese civil war of the late 1940s, produced comparable evacuation records that might be read the same way as a rehearsal for later doctrine.

Hopkins, Owen (2021). The Museum: From Its Origins to the 21st Century.
decolonize is to decontextualiseHopkinscriticisescritique

Hopkins's gloss on the V&A director's position: for a museum like the V&A, decolonisation means reinterpreting the history of empire embedded in its objects, not removing them. Empire is part of the meaning of the collection, so the task is to interpret it, not to return the object. (Hopkins 2021)

How it is used Hopkins quotes Tristram Hunt's cautious approach to colonial objects and calls it an argument for continuity, then sets it against the activism of #MuseumsAreNotNeutral and against the view that all colonial objects were stolen. Hopkins argues that each object needs its own assessment of origin and provenance, which means the critique is directed at both the defenders and the critics of the museum.

“For a museum like the V&A, to decolonize is to decontextualise: the history of empire is embedded in its meaning and collections, and the question is how that is interpreted.”
V&A (Hunt's position)Benin BronzesSarr and Savoy report on restitution

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could apply the same test to a museum of Chinese or Japanese objects in a Western collection, asking what its interpretation says about empire, and whether reinterpretation is a substitute for return.

Kirshenblatt-Gimblett, Barbara (1998). Destination Culture: Tourism, Museums, and Heritage. Berkeley: University of California Press.
alienability of inalienable possessionsKirshenblatt-Gimblettappliesanalytic concept

Heritage tests whether objects and practices held as inalienable (taonga, or resources described as free, inherent and natural) can be exhibited or circulated without losing their value. Objects removed from their communities become severed links, while a living tradition survives in performance rather than in display. (Kirshenblatt-Gimblett 1998p. 149)

How it is used The author applies the idea to taonga at the Manawatu Museum, where the relationship of the objects to their communities is displayed, and to Maori marae that become tourist venues. She uses the basket-making anecdote to argue that vitality lies in transmission and performance, so that a museum cannot animate what it has taken out of circulation.

“Heritage tests the alienability of inalienable possessions.” p. 149
Manawatu Museum taonga, Palmerston NorthMaori marae as tourist venues

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The idea could be used to ask what happens when objects that a community holds as inalienable are exhibited by a state museum in Southeast Asia, and who decides on their circulation.

Stewart, Susan (1984). On Longing: Narratives of the Miniature, the Gigantic, the Souvenir, the Collection. Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press.
decontextualization in museum acquisitionsStewartcriticisescritique

Acquisition removes an object from its context of origin, so that the treasures of one culture come to be stored and displayed in the museums of another. The author treats this as a blithe gesture that suppresses the context of origin. (Stewart 1984p. 162)

How it is used Stewart criticises the usual acquisition practice as part of the museum's fiction of total representation. Stewart uses it as an example of the collection's wider movement from labour and origin into exchange and property, rather than discussing any particular museum or claim.

“the treasures of one culture being stored” p. 162
treasures of one culture held in the museums of anothernatural history museum

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The critique could frame a study of how foreign objects in a Western museum were acquired, asking what context was removed at the point of acquisition and who decided that it was not needed.

Stocking, George W., Jr. (ed.) (1985). Objects and Others: Essays on Museums and Material Culture. Madison: University of Wisconsin Press.
possessive individualism and the possessive selfCliffordappliestheoretical framing

Macpherson's account of the seventeenth-century self as owner, which Clifford extends to collecting: identity, cultural or personal, presupposes gathering up possessions, so that Western collecting builds a possessive self, culture and authenticity. He contrasts Melanesian accumulation, which is for giving away rather than holding. (Stocking 1985p. 237)

Draws on C. B. Macpherson

How it is used Clifford uses Macpherson to link Handler's study of Quebec's patrimoine to the act of collecting: nationalists claim a culture as a possession, and the Western collector claims a self in the same way. The Melanesian contrast is used to show that the possessive self is historical rather than universal. The frame lets him argue that the good collector is a possessive subject whose tastes are rule-governed.

“collecting has long been a strategy for the deployment of a possessive self,” p. 238
Quebec patrimoine (Handler)Western collections of non-Western objects

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask whether private collections of Asian ceramics or Japanese arms in European homes reproduced this possessive self, and how their later public display changed it.

cultural property and the typology of ownership claimsHandlercriticisestypology

A proposed typology of disputes over cultural property, built from whether a group possesses an object and what relation it claims to it. Handler's point is that disputants on every side treat culture as a bounded possession that can be owned, claimed or contested. (Stocking 1985p. 211)

How it is used Handler applies the typology to Quebec, using the Place Royale restoration in Quebec City as the main case: rebuilt French-Regime buildings were criticised as an artificial museum that destroyed a living district. Handler shows that nationalists and their critics both treat culture as a bounded possession, so the typology classifies the claims of both sides. Handler ends by noting that objects have become the symbol of culture itself.

“We might imagine a typology of cultural property claims, constructed from” p. 211
Place Royale, Quebec CityQuebec heritage legislation, 1922-1972

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could apply the same two-part test to a repatriation claim made by a source community against a Southeast Asian museum, asking what possession the museum holds and what relation the claimant asserts.

Vergo, Peter (ed.) (1989). The New Museology. London: Reaktion Books.
lex situs rulePalmerappliesanalytic concept

The rule that title to a movable object is decided by the law of the country where the object lay when the sale took place, so that a foreign sale can cut off the original owner's title. (Vergo 1989p. 190)

How it is used Palmer applies the rule to show that English law on title is haphazard. In Winkworth, Japanese works stolen from an English house and sold in Italy passed to a buyer with good title, and Slade J dismissed the owner's claim; the Stowlangtoft panels and the Ortiz Maori door make the same point. He uses these cases to argue that museums cannot rely on the law to protect national heritage, and that a good-faith purchase can still be conversion.

“This is known as the lex situs rule.” p. 190
Winkworth v Christie Manson & Woods (Japanese works of art)Stowlangtoft panelsOrtiz (Maori door)

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The rule could be used to trace how Asian objects reached Western sale rooms through foreign sales, and which country's law then governed the title.

Yallop, Jacqueline (2011). Magpies, Squirrels and Thieves: How the Victorians Collected the World. London: Atlantic Books.
looted relics in circulationYallopappliesanalytic concept

Relics removed in the 1860 sacking of the Summer Palace, which were then sold, given and dispersed through many museums and private collections. The text estimates that they reached more than 2,000 museums in forty-seven countries. (Yallop 2011)

How it is used Yallop uses the Summer Palace to show how war-time looting created the market for Chinese objects in Britain and beyond. The idea explains why Bushell's study of the palace buildings was incomplete, since the objects that would have explained them had gone elsewhere. The author links this looting to the international trade that Bushell later served for Walters and Bishop, and presents Franks's negotiated purchases as part of the same traffic.

“There was widespread and chaotic looting.”
the Summer Palace, Peking, 1860Franks's purchase of vases and roof tiles taken by a French officer

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could trace the provenance of a museum's Chinese ceramics back to 1860 to test how many arrived through soldiers' sales and donations.

Display, spectacle and the gaze

Benjamin, Debord, Baudrillard, Bal and others on representation; the poetics of exhibiting, design, architecture, performance and the visitor's body. 89 concepts from 54 texts

These approaches ask how display produces meaning: how the case, setting, route, lighting, label and performance shape what a visitor sees and feels, sometimes more than the object does. Our texts draw most often on Walter Benjamin, Tony Bennett, Michel Foucault and Jean Baudrillard, and add practical tools such as Kirshenblatt-Gimblett's pair of in situ and in context displays (Kirshenblatt-Gimblett 1998p. 3) and Alpers's museum vision, which Yanni takes as the starting point for his own argument (Yanni 1999p. 19). Benjamin supplies aura (Veldkamp 2014p. 563); Bennett the exhibitionary complex (Bennett 1995p. 60); Foucault the heterotopia, as Hopkins and Black use it (Hopkins 2021; Black 2000p. 26); and Baudrillard the simulacrum (Black 2000p. 37).

The texts at the centre of the theme are Kirshenblatt-Gimblett (Kirshenblatt-Gimblett 1998), whose chapters sort exhibits by mode of display; Yanni (Yanni 1999), who reads museum architecture as a claim about knowledge; Leahy (Rees Leahy 2012), who treats the museum as a site of learned bodily practice; and Bilsel (Bilsel 2012), who reads the Pergamon Museum as a frame that became the exhibit (Bilsel 2012PDF p. 30; Rees Leahy 2012p. 2).

Benjamin's aura

Aura is Benjamin's term for the unique presence of an original that mechanical reproduction erodes, and our texts use it in three ways. Veldkamp shows that glass cases and lighting keep even a replica at a distance that produces aura, so aura is made by display practice as well as by the object (Veldkamp 2014p. 563). Conn applies it to the art museum, where paintings already carried aura through their ritual context, while the Pennsylvania Museum tried to bestow aura on a few reproductions (Conn 1998p. 194p. 217). Bilsel locates aura in the sacral setting that made the Pergamon reconstructions seem original monuments, so critics who called the exhibits fakes were answering a claim the museum itself made (Bilsel 2012PDF p. 156).

Bennett's exhibitionary complex and the backteller

Bennett groups art and natural history museums, panoramas, fairs, arcades and department stores into one nineteenth-century complex that moved objects and bodies into public view, and sets it against Foucault's prison (Bennett 1995p. 60). Yanni accepts that space and vision matter but denies the reciprocity Bennett describes: it is absent from the art museums of Durand, Schinkel and Smirke (Yanni 1999p. 9). Hill argues that realistic display exercised power at an imaginative level, more than Bennett's account of backwalking allows (Hill 2005p. 107). Bennett's backteller, a term taken from Huxley, leads the visitor backwards from remains towards an evolutionary present that must be walked as a route (Bennett 1995p. 178).

Foucault's heterotopia

Hopkins calls the museum "the archetypal example" of Foucault's heterotopia and reads the Acropolis Museum as the place where its objects are made sacred (Hopkins 2021). Black applies the concept to the nineteenth-century museum and library, which gather all times and forms into one immobile place outside time (Black 2000p. 26). Hetherington combines heterotopia with Marin's utopies, so that Stonehenge becomes a museum without walls where competing utopias meet (Macdonald & Fyfe 1996PDF p. 160). Yanni calls Foucault's claim that society is one of surveillance rather than spectacle misleading, because the two regimes of power coincide (Yanni 1999p. 94).

Baudrillard's simulacrum and museumification

Black accepts Baudrillard's term museumification but dates it to the Victorian museum, not to the period after production (Black 2000p. 37). Lumley uses Eco's hyperreality and Baudrillard's simulation to judge Ironbridge, Beamish and the Museum of the Moving Image, and asks museums to show how they construct realities rather than pursue reality (Lumley 1988p. 11). Yamaguchi uses the simulacrum in a positive sense for mitate, in which an ordinary object is linked to a classical image and the invisible is made visible (Karp & Lavine 1991).

In situ and in context, and the display interface

Kirshenblatt-Gimblett separates in situ displays, which evoke a missing whole through dioramas, period rooms and live performers, from in context displays, which arrange objects by a conceptual frame (Kirshenblatt-Gimblett 1998p. 3). She applies the pair to the Balinese performances at the Paris Colonial Exposition and argues that the performers become signs of themselves (Kirshenblatt-Gimblett 1998p. 3). Her idea of display as interface compares Colonial Williamsburg, where staging is hidden, with the Bomas of Kenya, where it is foregrounded: "Display is an interface that mediates and thereby transforms what is shown into heritage" (Kirshenblatt-Gimblett 1998p. 7). She places authenticity in reception, and argues that the 1990 Los Angeles Festival undid the ethnographic label while depending on it (Kirshenblatt-Gimblett 1998p. 11p. 204).

Performance and the museum's script

MacKenzie treats colonial and national museums as stages on which identities are performed, and Chinese, Indian and Malay visitors in Singapore used them as an extension of their festivals (MacKenzie 2009p. 276). Ho and Li show, through the Rent Collection Courtyard, that designers mapped routes, eyelines and emotional sequence so that visitors were part of the performance (Ho & Li 2016p. 15). Leahy applies Butler's performatives to the museum's script, which makes the body "legible and manageable" (Rees Leahy 2012p. 100), and draws on Kirshenblatt-Gimblett for a performing museology (Rees Leahy 2012p. 2). Outka adapts performance studies to commercial display, where performing authenticity is both subversive and normative (Outka 2009p. 16).

Gaze, glance and museum vision

Yanni agrees with Alpers that the setting dictates vision, and extends the point to each museum's architecture (Yanni 1999p. 19). Karp takes Alpers's museum effect and turns it into a question of power, asking whether it exists at all in Japanese and Indian display (Karp & Lavine 1991). Leahy uses Bryson's gaze and glance to argue that the curators' model of attentive looking leaves out much actual looking, and uses Baxandall's period eye to test whether re-created shows reveal present habits of viewing (Rees Leahy 2012p. 47; Hill 2012p. 150). Tseng tests Hooper-Greenhill's limited visibility on the Buddhist icons of the Imperial Nara Museum, where the bars of the case cut across the statue (Tseng 2008p. 167).

Resonance and wonder

Greenblatt defines resonance as the power of the object to reach beyond its formal boundaries, and wonder as the power to hold attention on its uniqueness (Karp & Lavine 1991). He takes Prague's State Jewish Museum as pure resonance and the Museum of Modern Art as wonder, and argues that the best exhibitions combine the two (Karp & Lavine 1991). Arnold adapts the distinction, keeping the momentary response but treating it as the start of inquiry (Arnold 2006). Varutti draws on Greenblatt's wonder displays to argue that beauty-led display works as a belief enhancer, placing Shang bronzes beside Qing calligraphy (Knell et al. 2011p. 304).

Contextual and aesthetic display

Vergo rejects the aesthetic view of exhibitions, in which the object speaks with little adjunct material, citing a Scandinavian painting show at the Hayward Gallery with no captions or map (Vergo 1989p. 48). Jacknis tests Boas's view that artifacts make sense only in their cultural setting against the limits of trustees, storage and lighting, with the Northwest Coast Hall arranged by tribe after 1901 as his main case (Stocking 1985p. 77).

Debates and limits

The texts disagree most over whether display can be trusted to show what it claims. Hail criticises Sears for presenting re-created Lakota shields as authentic, without labels that disclose their making (Krech & Hail 1999). Veldkamp, by contrast, finds that replicas can carry aura for a general public (Veldkamp 2014p. 578). Ho and Li reject the museal view of Chinese museums as mausoleums, arguing from the Anren evidence that they are living spaces (Ho & Li 2016p. 4). Yanni criticises Bennett's conflation of museums with arcades and department stores (Yanni 1999p. 9), and Black criticises Baudrillard's dating of museumification (Black 2000p. 37). Winter rejects the thrill-seeking Historial de la Grande Guerre, whose pseudo-realism simulates the experience of combat (Muchitsch 2013p. 36). Vergo notes that hanging and captions can make an argument, so the typology alone does not settle the question (Vergo 1989p. 48).

Carrying it over to a new case

  • Compare the case, lighting and viewing distance of an original and a replica, to test whether aura belongs to the object or to its arrangement, as Veldkamp does at Kongju (Veldkamp 2014p. 578).
  • Trace the route through a regional museum's Asian galleries as a backteller, asking whether visitors are led towards a present they are meant to affirm, as Bennett does for Pitt Rivers (Bennett 1995p. 178).
  • Ask whether a national museum of a new identity works as a heterotopia that holds all eras at once, or whether its ritual is closer to civic performance (Hopkins 2021; Black 2000p. 26).
  • Test the period eye on a re-hung gallery of Chinese ceramics, asking whether it reveals earlier habits of viewing (Hill 2012p. 150).
  • Read the vitrine of a Buddhist or Shinto object in a Korean or Southeast Asian museum, and ask what the case removes from its devotional use, after Tseng (Tseng 2008p. 167).
  • Apply the performing museology test to a gallery's route and staff scripts, asking what the visit makes visible about the institution itself (Rees Leahy 2012p. 2).

Where to start reading

  • Kirshenblatt-Gimblett, Barbara (1998). Destination Culture: Tourism, Museums, and Heritage. Berkeley: University of California Press. the in situ and in context pair and the display interface, the clearest statement of how display does its work
  • Rees Leahy, Helen (2012). Museum Bodies: The Politics and Practices of Visiting and Viewing. Farnham: Ashgate. how the visiting body is scripted through performatives, glance and fatigue
  • Bennett, Tony (1995). The Birth of the Museum: History, Theory, Politics. London: Routledge. the exhibitionary complex and the backteller, for the museum as a machine that programmes behaviour
  • Yanni, Carla (1999). Nature’s Museums: Victorian Science and the Architecture of Display. Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press. the architecture of natural history museums as a claim about knowledge, with its critiques of Bennett and Foucault
  • Bilsel, Can (2012). Antiquity on Display: Regimes of the Authentic in Berlin’s Pergamon Museum. Oxford: Oxford University Press. the Pergamon frame, for a setting that became the exhibit
  • Karp, Ivan; Lavine, Steven D. (eds.) (1991). Exhibiting Cultures: The Poetics and Politics of Museum Display. Washington: Smithsonian Institution Press. Karp and Lavine on the museum effect and the politics of display
  • Black, Barbara J. (2000). On Exhibit: Victorians and Their Museums. Charlottesville: University Press of Virginia. Black on the Victorian museum, heterotopia and the simulacrum

Alberti, Samuel J. M. M. (2009). Nature and Culture: Objects, Disciplines and the Manchester Museum. Manchester: Manchester University Press.
exhibitionary practicesAlbertiappliesanalytic concept

Processes enacted on objects inside the museum fall into three clusters, physical, textual and exhibitionary, covering conservation and cataloguing as well as exhibition and its design. (Alberti 2009p. 5)

How it is used Alberti reorganises chapter 5 thematically around these three clusters, so that the work of technicians, conservators and designers counts as part of an object's history. Storage and display are read as shaping how objects were understood, and the chapter gives attention to the large part of the collection that was never displayed. The term moves the analysis from the gallery to the staff who maintained the collection.

“I have identified three clusters of processes – physical, textual” p. 5
sperm whale skeletonaccession ledgers and card cataloguesFrank Goodyear's conservation department

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The three clusters give a checklist for asking how a regional museum's storage and labelling, rather than its galleries, shaped the meaning of its Asian holdings.

Arnold, Ken (2006). Cabinets for the Curious: Looking Back at Early English Museums. Aldershot: Ashgate.
wonderArnoldadaptsanalytic concept

The response an object produces: an experience that cannot be fully told or described, which makes people talk and investigate and then exhausts their words. Arnold separates it from the Romantic sublime, ties it to disciplined curiosity, and sees it as the concept that united the three strategies of seventeenth-century museums. (Arnold 2006)

Draws on Stephen Greenblatt; Marina Warner; P. Fisher

How it is used Arnold uses wonder to recast the three strategies as one pursuit and to answer the present debate about how objects can still communicate. Arnold adapts Greenblatt's distinction between resonance and wonder by keeping the momentary, bedazzled response but treating it as the start of inquiry rather than its end. Arnold applies the idea to the Neuchâtel ethnographic museum, the one-picture gallery at Penza and the San Diego Zoo's Hippo Beach, and argues that digital reproduction makes the experience of the real object more valuable.

“It is the gesture rather than the word”
Neuchâtel ethnographic museumone-picture gallery at PenzaSan Diego Zoo's Hippo Beach

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask which objects in a given display produce the silence Arnold describes, and whether the labels invite visitors to talk about them afterwards.

Askew, Rie Kido (2007). “The Politics of Nostalgia: Museum Representations of Lafcadio Hearn in Japan”. museum and society, 5.3 (November 2007): 131-147.
exhibit, curator and visitor as text, author and readerAskewappliesmethod

Porter's framework as Askew uses it: the exhibit, with its objects, building, labels and video, is read as a text, the curator as its author and the visitor as its reader, so the museum's intentions can be questioned. (Askew 2007p. 132)

Draws on Porter

How it is used Askew reads the three museums as texts, using pamphlets, labels, the house and the video corner, and tests the curators' stated aims against what the displays show. This is the basis of her method of identifying what is commemorated and what is left out, and it lets her treat the displays as political statements rather than as biography.

“I have followed Porter’s analytical framework in identifying” p. 132
Matsue museumKumamoto museumYaizu museum

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The same reading could be applied to a museum in another country, using visitor responses as well as pamphlets to test whether readers take the curators' intended message.

Asma, Stephen T. (2001). Stuffed Animals and Pickled Heads: The Culture and Evolution of Natural History Museums. New York: Oxford University Press.
presentation frameAsmacoinstheoretical framing

The arrangement, setting and staging around a specimen, which carries meaning without being noticed. Asma wants the frame to be read, since the art of display should be invisible and yet communicates the museum's ideas about nature. (Asma 2001)

How it is used Asma makes the frame the object of analysis. Asma reads the floors of the Paris Grande Galerie, where biodiversity and the 'Life: An Amazing Spectacle' floors take up more space than the evolution floor, as a presentation choice that shapes the message. Asma uses the frame to explain why visitors take away facts but miss the arguments a display makes.

“they frequently fail to notice the presentation frame itself.”
Grande Galerie de l’évolution, ParisHunterian Museum, London

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could compare the presentation frame of a Japanese or Southeast Asian natural history or ethnographic hall, such as the order of its floors and the placement of labels, with that of a European museum, asking which messages visitors are meant to absorb without noticing.

intuition pumpsAsmaadaptsanalytic concept

A vivid image, metaphor or scene that structures thinking even though it is not a sound argument. Asma borrows Dennett's term for museum exhibits that lodge a memorable image in visitors' minds. (Asma 2001)

Draws on Daniel Dennett; Plato; Descartes; Hobbes

How it is used Asma transfers the term from philosophy to museums, so that the roulette wheels of 'Life over Time', dioramas and cladogram walking paths become the images visitors keep. Asma uses it to explain why display developers judge success by one or two lasting images, and links it to associationist learning in Locke and Hume, where vivid combinations of perceptions shape later recall.

“They are what I call “intuition pumps”—lovely thought experiments.”
Field Museum 'Life over Time' roulette wheelsFranklin Institute Science Museum gravity display

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask which single image a visitor to a regional museum (for example an Indonesian or Vietnamese history gallery) is most likely to retain, and whether that image is designed as an intuition pump or left to chance.

Bennett, Tony (1995). The Birth of the Museum: History, Theory, Politics. London: Routledge.
exhibitionary complexBennettcoinsanalytic concept

The nineteenth-century ensemble of art museums, history and natural history museums, panoramas, international exhibitions, arcades and department stores, which moved objects and bodies from private into public view. Bennett treats it as a distinct arrangement of power that runs parallel to, and differently from, Foucault's carceral system. (Bennett 1995p. 60)

How it is used Bennett uses the term to bring together institutions usually studied separately and to ask what they shared. Setting the complex against the prison lets him argue that these institutions did not withdraw bodies from view as prisons did but exposed them, producing a self-policing public. He then follows the complex through the Great Exhibition, the South Kensington Museum and the Chicago Midway.

“translated these into exhibitionary forms which, in simultaneously ordering” p. 61
the Great Exhibition of 1851the South Kensington Museumthe British Museum's fear of the crowdthe Chicago Midway

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The term could be tested on a colonial exhibition in Southeast Asia, such as the Dutch East Indies displays, by asking which institutions were grouped with the museum there and whether the carceral comparison holds.

backtellerBennettadaptsanalytic concept

A narrative machine that arranges objects into sequences of the past and makes the visitor reconstruct history by moving through them, working backwards from traces as detective fiction and palaeontology do. Bennett takes the word from Huxley and applies it to museum layouts. (Bennett 1995p. 178)

Draws on Huxley

How it is used Bennett takes Huxley's neologism and applies it to nineteenth-century museum layouts, arguing that the visitor was led backwards from remains toward an evolutionary present that had to be walked as a route. This lets him treat the museum as a performance that programmes behaviour, not only as a text, and he links it to Pitt Rivers's typological displays.

“The museum was another ' backteller ', a narrative machinery” p. 178
Pitt Rivers's anthropological rotundathe typological displays at Bethnal Greennatural history and ethnology galleries

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could read the route through a palace or temple museum in another country as a backteller, asking whether visitors were led to walk toward a present they were meant to affirm.

Bilsel, Can (2012). Antiquity on Display: Regimes of the Authentic in Berlin’s Pergamon Museum. Oxford: Oxford University Press.

The museum's architecture and decor are a frame that gives the works their meaning, and in the Pergamon case the frame, not the object, is the subject of study. The reconstructed altar and the architectural setting change places. (Bilsel 2012PDF p. 30)

How it is used Bilsel reads the Pergamon Museum's successive designs as alternative frames for one imagined architecture, the Great Altar, and argues that the Pergamon Room reverses the usual relation so that the setting, the universal history of art and architecture, becomes the object. The framing lets him follow changes in the building's design through the changing claims to authenticity of the displays, rather than writing a history of each object.

“I am most interested in the discourse of the museum conceived as the” PDF p. 30
Pergamon Museum, BerlinGreat Altar of Pergamon roomMiletus Market Gate

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask the same question of another reconstructed interior, such as a period room or a reconstructed palace hall in a non-European museum: which setting has been made to stand for the authentic work?

style room (Stilraum)Bilselappliesanalytic concept

Bode's technique of museum display, a period room that furnishes works in a historical interior, through which the curator negotiated between the monumental imperial museum and the taste of the private bourgeois viewer. (Bilsel 2012PDF p. 114)

How it is used Bilsel uses the style room to show that Bode's rooms set the architecture against the works it housed, the reverse of Wiegand's reconstructed facades. Bilsel contrasts the Stilraum with the epochal room (Epochenraum) in a note, to explain why Bode's displays did not claim to be ancient monuments. The concept lets him argue that Messel's scheme mapped a geography of cultures rather than a linear history.

“Stilraum (style room) must be seen as a technique of museum display through which the curator” PDF p. 114
Kaiser Friedrich Museum, BerlinMessel's planned style rooms on the Museum IslandBode's German Museum

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A period room in a museum of Asian art could be read as a Stilraum, asking for which bourgeois viewer its interior was made and how far it claimed to be authentic.

auraBilselappliesanalytic concept

The unique, sacral presence that a setting gives to an object, here the sense that the Pergamon Museum's reconstructions were original monuments of antiquity. (Bilsel 2012PDF p. 156)

Draws on Walter Benjamin

How it is used Bilsel uses Benjamin's term to describe how the Pergamon Museum sacralised its reconstructions by restoring an aura around supposedly original monuments, and he quotes a speech that called the museum a sacred island. The term explains why critics who dismissed the exhibits as fakes were answering a claim to authenticity the museum itself made.

“made this aura particularly clear, by calling the Pergamon Museum what it” PDF p. 156

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask which re-set or reconstructed objects in another museum are given a sacral setting, and whether visitors take the setting for the original.

Hildebrand's criteria of high artBilseltestsanalytic concept

Hildebrand's theory of relief, which holds that high sculpture keeps a strict boundary between the picture plane and real space, so that painterly relief counts as low art. (Bilsel 2012PDF p. 85)

Draws on Adolf Hildebrand

How it is used Bilsel tests the Pergamon frieze against Hildebrand's criteria. The Gigantomachy's painterly forms and its later display as a realist panorama cross the boundary between pictorial and architectural space, so the altar fails the criteria on all three counts. The test lets him show that the successive frames of the altar, from the 1886 Panorama to Wolff's 1901 museum, dissolved that boundary and turned the altar into a realist double.

“Hildebrand seeks to restore a strict boundary between the picture plane and” PDF p. 85
Pergamon friezePergamon Panorama of 1886Wolff's first Pergamon Museum of 1901

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The test could be applied to a reconstructed relief in a museum of Southeast Asian or East Asian sculpture, asking where the visitor stops seeing it as sculpture and starts seeing a picture.

Black, Barbara J. (2000). On Exhibit: Victorians and Their Museums. Charlottesville: University Press of Virginia.
heterotopiaBlackappliestheoretical framing

A real place that juxtaposes incompatible spaces and, in the nineteenth-century museum and library, gathers all times, epochs and forms into one immobile place outside time. Black takes it as the first way to see the museum before its utopian and dystopian readings. (Black 2000p. 26)

Draws on Michel Foucault

How it is used Black uses the concept to frame London's spectacles of the 1850s and 1860s, such as James Wyld's globe, as versions of the museum that build a whole world from fragments and place the viewer at its centre. The museum's accumulation of all times is then read as a modern and specifically western project. The concept gives the chapter its link between the museum and the city, where the museum is 'inconceivable without its modern-city setting'.

“The museum and the library are heterotopias” p. 26
James Wyld's globe, Leicester SquareSouth Kensington Museum

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask whether a non-European museum, or a regional museum in East or Southeast Asia, works as a heterotopia that holds all eras and cultures at once, and whether its display of several incompatible traditions has the same effect.

museumificationBlackcriticisescritique

Baudrillard's term for a condition in which life itself becomes catalogued, analysed and artificially revived as though real. Black accepts the term but dates it to the nineteenth century, not after it. (Black 2000p. 37)

Draws on Jean Baudrillard

How it is used Black tests Baudrillard's claim that the simulacrum comes after production and finds his timing wrong: the Victorian era was 'the first age of museumification'. Black uses Baudrillard's account of the need for a visible past and of 'cultural death' without collecting to explain Victorian museum narratives of labels, pediments and progression. The correction lets Black place the origin of the hyperreal in the Victorian museum itself.

“only mistake is arguing that the museum is a dimension of the” p. 38
Victorian London museums, read through their labels, pediments and tours

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could test whether museumification began earlier in a given Asian city, for example in colonial exhibitions or in the first national museums, and whether the dating of the simulacrum changes there.

museum poemBlackcoinstypology

A poem that places art among other objects in a crowded, commercial and political setting, rather than responding to a single painting or sculpture as ut pictura poesis and pictorialism did. The museum poem explores the commodification, ownership and transmission of art. (Black 2000p. 129)

Draws on ut pictura poesis

How it is used Black defines the museum poem against the pictorial tradition and uses it to read Keats's sonnets on the Elgin Marbles, Hardy's poems in the British Museum and Rossetti's The Burden of Nineveh. The category lets him argue that these poems engage with empire and cultural power rather than with the ideal of cultural unity. It also explains the chapter's claim that the museum changed what poetry could do with art.

“museum poems erect a new phenomenological construct” p. 129
Keats's Elgin Marbles sonnetsRossetti's The Burden of Nineveh

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask whether poems or literary responses to the display of Asian sculpture in Western museums, such as Japanese or Chinese objects in the British Museum, form the same kind of museum poem.

Conn, Steven (1998). Museums and American Intellectual Life, 1876–1926. Chicago: University of Chicago Press.
aura and ritual in the art museumConnappliestheoretical framing

Walter Benjamin's idea, used by Conn, that art objects keep an aura through their ritual context, so that art museums retained authority and authenticity for their objects. Conn also uses it to describe how aura could be bestowed on a few mechanically produced objects selected for display. (Conn 1998p. 194)

Draws on Walter Benjamin

How it is used Conn applies Benjamin to explain why art museums won the cultural hierarchy: paintings and sculpture already carried aura, while the Pennsylvania Museum, which had filled its galleries with objects deprived of aura by industrial origin, moved those objects to the basement and tried to bestow aura on a few reproductions. Conn reads the Pennsylvania Museum's curators as having anticipated Benjamin's 1936 essay by a generation, and the aura argument becomes the chapter's main explanation of the museum's move toward fine art.

“can be seen as places of ritual, in Walter Benjamin's” p. 194
Metropolitan Museum of ArtPennsylvania Museum (Philadelphia Museum of Art)Wilstach Collection

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask whether a regional or ethnographic museum that bestowed aura on photographic or reproduced objects did so for the same reasons, by testing which objects were kept on display and which went to storage.

spectatorial lustCoombesappliesanalytic concept

Hobson's term for the appetite for spectacle that made exhibitions effective as components of imperial discourse; the text treats it as the mechanism by which the events drew a public. (Coombes 1994p. 63)

Draws on John Atkinson Hobson

How it is used Coombes takes Hobson's account of the lust for spectacle as the starting point for her analysis of the exhibitions, and she argues that its effectivity lay in the way it made imperial narratives seem neutral entertainment and science at once. It supports her reading of the Stanley and African Exhibition as a place where the visitor was cast as explorer and philanthropist.

“The ‘spectatorial lust’ that John Atkinson Hobson defined as an indispensable corollary of” p. 63
Stanley and African Exhibition (1890)Barnum and Bailey's Great ShowEarl's Court exhibitions

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A study of a Western museum's Asian galleries could ask whether the same spectatorial appetite shaped which Asian objects were put on show and how visitors were positioned in front of them.

discourse of authenticityCoombesappliesanalytic concept

The claim, made in publicity, guides and reviews, that the scenes and performers of the exhibitions were a true and verifiable reproduction of colonial life, which was used to validate what was shown. (Coombes 1994p. 85)

How it is used Coombes shows the authenticity claim being made in the Stanley exhibition's catalogue and the press, and then in the performers' shows, where it borrowed from colonial romance and ethnographic writing. Coombes uses it to explain why spectators accepted racial spectacle as objective, and why the Zulu performers' own resistance threatened the claim.

“The discourse of authenticity took several forms between 1890 and 1913, and had a” p. 85
Stanley and African Exhibition (1890)Savage South Africa and the Zulu Kraal (1899)French Exhibition at Earl's Court

Damousi, Joy; Tout-Smith, Deborah; Ziino, Bart (eds.) (2020). Museums, History and the Intimate Experience of the Great War: Love and Sorrow. London: Routledge.
mimetic communicationWitcombappliesanalytic concept

Communication through bodily imitation of faces, voices and postures, which spreads emotion from one person to another rather than conveying information. Witcomb draws the idea from Gibbs’s essay and from Tomkins’s account of affect as facial and public. (Damousi 2020p. 175)

Draws on Anna Gibbs; Tomkins

How it is used Witcomb applies mimetic communication to the exhibition’s faces and voices, arguing that the photographs of people looking directly at the visitor transfer the families’ love and sorrow to the visitor. This lets her explain how visitors come to feel what the families felt, which she treats as the basis of the exhibition’s critical effect.

“We are encouraged to feel the same emotions they did via this process of” p. 175
Photographs of the eight families in Love and SorrowHearth and fireplace at the exhibition centre

Dudley, Sandra H. (ed.) (2010). Museum Materialities: Objects, Engagements, Interpretations. London: Routledge.
agent of changeDorsettteststheoretical framing

The idea that an artist invited to work with a museum's reserve collection can change how the museum sees its objects, set against curators' selection and interpretation. Dorsett argues that artists and curators work in incompatible semiotic frames, so the tension between them is productive. (Dudley 2010p. 242)

Draws on Moyle; Hooper-Greenhill

How it is used Dorsett tests the idea against Warhol's Raid the Icebox 1, where Warhol displayed storage shoes and the director came to see the collection differently, and against his own Cheltenham commission, which put barely visible storage objects and a rumour about a tram linked to Brian Jones into display cases. Dorsett concedes that the idea sounded too instrumental for his own understanding of artistic work and reads Warhol's enthusiasm for stuff as a density of presence that curators do not count. The concept lets him argue that artist and curator are not merely doing different things but are working within incompatible signification.

“I detect an artist’s enthusiasm for ‘stuff’.” p. 244
Raid the Icebox 1, Rhode Island School of Design (1969)Cheltenham Art Gallery and Museum centenary commission (1999)

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could invite an artist to work with an Asian export or ethnographic reserve collection and record where the artist's and curator's selections differ, to show how each frame gives the same storage objects a different meaning.

Duncan, Carol (1995). Civilizing Rituals: Inside Public Art Museums. London: Routledge.
advertising as parallel ritual of the consumer selfDuncancombinesanalytic concept

Advertising and the modern art museum both show an isolated self seeking personal gratification, and both suppress the moral-political self and the public good. (Duncan 1995p. 130–131)

Draws on Raymond Williams

How it is used Duncan sets the modern museum beside advertising to argue that its liminal space presents the individual apart from the social world, which advertising also teaches. This fit lets her explain modern art's freedom from politics as tied to consumer culture rather than to the autonomy of art alone, and she notes that Abstract Expressionism's rejection of history fits the Cold War liberal culture of the period.

Museum of Modern Art, New YorkPenthouse advertisement photographed on a bus shelterAbstract Expressionism

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could compare a heritage or art museum in a shopping district of an East or Southeast Asian city and ask whether its contemplative display sits alongside commodity display in the same way.

Findlen, Paula (1994). Possessing Nature: Museums, Collecting, and Scientific Culture in Early Modern Italy. Berkeley: University of California Press.
theater of nature (teatro di natura)Findlenappliesanalytic concept

The museum as a staged setting in which nature was shown, debated and used in public life. Findlen takes the term from Aldrovandi's own usage and from the wider literature that calls the museum a cabinet of curiosity, wonder room or theater of nature. (Findlen 1994p. 22)

How it is used Findlen reads Aldrovandi's dissection of the 1572 Bolognese dragon through this term: the museum became the place where a papal portent was given a natural rather than a sign-based reading, so the collection played a part in the politics of the new pope's court. The phrase lets her tie collecting to civic and papal life rather than treat the museum as a store of objects. The same term is used for the Bolognese and Neapolitan collections of the later sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, which allows a comparison of how the stage was set in each.

“The arrival of the monstrous dragon neatly illustrates the significance of Aldrovandi's "theater of nature" (teatro di natura) to the political and civic life of sixteenth-century Italy.” p. 23
Aldrovandi's Bologna museum and the 1572 dragonImperato's Naples museumCospi's Bologna museum

Fromm, Annette B.; Golding, Viv; Rekdal, Per B. (eds.) (2014). Museums and Truth. Newcastle upon Tyne: Cambridge Scholars Publishing.

Two ways of displaying religious objects. The art-party presents them as aesthetic works isolated from their context; the context-party tells the stories of their makers through relational dialogue with source communities. (Fromm 2014p. 131)

Glaubenssache at the Stapferhaus in Lenzburg made visitors declare themselves believers or non-believers, while Religious Energy at the Deutsches Hygiene-Museum in Dresden was more academic and descriptive. Glaubenssache, Stapferhaus LenzburgReligious Energy, Deutsches Hygiene-Museum Dresden

Gardner, James (2020). The Louvre: The Many Lives of the World’s Most Famous Museum. New York: Atlantic Monthly Press.
the Louvre as a work of artGardneradaptstheoretical framing

The claim that the Louvre's architecture, staircases and interiors, and not only the paintings and sculptures it holds, are art in their own right, to be judged as a totalising whole. (Gardner 2020)

Gardner argues that the Aile Lescot, the Colonnade, the Escalier Daru and the interior of the Grande Galerie deserve the attention given to the paintings, and that the ceilings of Romanelli and Le Brun are overlooked only because they do not sit in a frame. It lets him treat the Second Empire palace as a work to be judged rather than a backdrop.

“I will argue that the Louvre is as great a work of art as anything it”
Aile Lescot and the ColonnadeEscalier DaruGrande Galerie interior

The 1797 parade of seized works through Paris, staged on the model of Roman triumphs, in which the art was a public spectacle of conquest and not only an addition to a collection. (Gardner 2020)

Guy, Kate; Williams, Hajra; Wintle, Claire (eds.) (2024). Histories of Exhibition Design in the Museum: Makers, Process, and Practice. London: Routledge.

Bode's 1883 Old Master paintings exhibition, Berlin (Kriebel)

A deliberate graphic addition (text, image or other visual element) placed on a historic display so that it reframes the exhibit while keeping the original visible and making later reinterpretation legible. Piehl proposes an initial typology of such interventions. (Guy 2024p. 237)

American Museum of Natural History (Bones Hall)Field Museum, ChicagoSmithsonian National Museum of Natural History

Hall, Patricia; Seemann, Charlie (eds.) (1987). Folklife and Museums: Selected Readings. Nashville: American Association for State and Local History.
interpretation as metaphorMooreappliesanalytic concept

Interpretation is a metaphoric activity in which the interpreter asks 'What else is it like?' so that a visitor grasps an object through an analogy to his or her own experience. The analogy rests on a shared characteristic and should reveal a new connection. (Hall & Seemann 1987p. 52)

How it is used Moore uses the idea to recast folklife museums as interpretive programmes rather than buildings and artifacts. Moore pairs traditional quilting bees and celebratory ethnic meals with a community's social rules, so that visitors can grasp inclusiveness and reciprocity through familiar experience. Moore tests the idea on his own cases, such as the play party at Conner Prairie, where a teacher drew children away from their hand-clapping games toward the interpreters' presentation.

“Interpretation is essentially a metaphoric activity.” p. 52
Conner Prairie Pioneer SettlementMinneapolis Museum of Art quilting demonstrationsa New York immigrant museum's display of what East European newcomers wore
