Naturalistic displays of stuffed animals in habitat settings present both scientific truth and beauty, so they work on the imagination and produce an emotional response as well as information. Hill takes the idea from Haraway. (Hill 2005p. 107)

Draws on Donna Haraway

How it is used Hill argues that realistic display was the most significant innovation in municipal museums, because it combined truth and beauty and so exercised power at an imaginative level, more than Bennett's account of backwalking allows. Hill shows such displays returning from about 1870 as a popular strategy, redefined as scientific, and at Liverpool used to naturalise an evolutionary sequence and to present the trophy of big game as imperial power.

“according to Haraway, experienced as a magical revelation” p. 107
Liverpool natural history casesLiverpool Wild Animals galleryPreston

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask whether a colonial museum's habitat groups and taxidermy of animals from other regions produced the same sense of revelation, and whether that effect was used to stage imperial hunting.

Hill, Kate (ed.) (2012). Museums and Biographies: Stories, Objects, Identities. Woodbridge: Boydell Press.
period eyeLeahyappliestheoretical framing

Baxandall’s argument that the skills needed to see art are historically acquired, so each period has its own viewing norms. Leahy extends the idea to exhibitions, asking whether re-created shows can make present viewing habits visible. (Hill 2012p. 150)

Draws on Baxandall; Gide; Carrier

How it is used Leahy applies the period eye, together with Carrier’s point that modern gallery display is recent, to ask why some re-staged exhibitions make viewers aware of how they look and others do not. Leahy adds Gide’s mise en abyme as a reflexive device. The concepts are tested against the Courtauld’s Art on the Line, Tate Britain’s William Blake 1809 and Tate Modern’s 2009 reinstallation of Robert Morris, which she says lost its radical edge under modern safety rules.

“Baxandall’s notion of the ‘period eye’ as a way of historicising the experience of the exhibition” p. 150
Art on the Line, Courtauld Gallery (2001)William Blake 1809, Tate BritainRobert Morris reinstallation, Tate Modern (2009)

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The same test could be used on a re-hung Asian gallery to see whether the reinstallation reveals earlier habits of viewing Chinese ceramics or bronzes, such as the grey and pale backgrounds of the 1930s.

empathy as historical experienceStaraappliesanalytic concept

Lenoir’s use of monumental sculpture to make visitors identify with the personalities of the French past, so that history is felt as the lives of individuals rather than as rational progress. Stara reads visitors’ accounts as evidence for this. (Hill 2012p. 275)

How it is used Stara argues that Lenoir’s Museum of French Monuments offered empathy and emotion rather than rational progress, and uses Jules Michelet’s and Ann Plumptre’s accounts of reading the statues’ faces as evidence that the visitor identified with the figures. The concept lets her explain how the museum’s catalogue anecdotes made the nation’s personalities into the nation itself.

“the communication of history occurred on the level of empathy of one personality for another.” p. 275
Museum of French Monuments, Petits-Augustins, Paris (1795–1816)

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The idea could be tested on a museum of Asian art that uses dramatic personal stories for its galleries, asking whether visitors identify with the figures or with the nation.

Hill, Kate (ed.) (2021). Museums, Modernity and Conflict: Museums and Collections in and of War since the Nineteenth Century. London: Routledge.
peoplingTomasiewiczappliesanalytic concept

The representation of people in war galleries through mannequins, wax figures, testimony and invented narratives, to give visitors a sense of historical or lived experience. The chapter sets it against large objects as the two ways the Imperial War Museum shows war. (Hill 2021p. 213)

How it is used Tomasiewicz uses peopling and large objects as two components of the IWM's displays and argues that treating them as opposites, as the phrase 'a social history, not a military history museum' does, limits what the museum can show. Tomasiewicz applies the concept to the early mannequins and wax figures, the Blitz Experience (1989) and the Holocaust Galleries (2000), which relied on invented narratives and edited testimony, and concludes that the two approaches should be combined.

“Put simply, ‘peopling’ is the engendering of a sense of historical or” p. 213
Imperial War Museum, LondonBlitz Experience (1989)Holocaust Galleries (2000)D-Day Museum landing-craft projection

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could test the peopling-versus-objects split on a museum of another conflict, asking whether the tension between people and large objects in its galleries follows the same lines.

celebratory, sanitised and realistic displayTomasiewiczappliestypology

Scott's three ways of displaying objects in military museums: the celebratory approach creates a largely positive view of war by extolling military achievement; the sanitised and realistic modes are the other two named in the chapter. (Hill 2021p. 218)

Draws on Scott

How it is used Tomasiewicz applies Scott's typology to the two 15-inch naval guns placed in the IWM forecourt in 1968. The guns are read as celebratory objects, and the protests they provoked, including an arson attack on the dome, show how much the display mode mattered to visitors. The chapter combines the typology with Kjeldbæk's generations to explain the large-object side of the museum.

“military museums are also often displayed in three different ways” p. 219
Imperial War Museum forecourt naval guns (1968)

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could code the large objects in another war museum by Scott's three modes, to see whether celebration or realism dominates a given gallery.

Ho, Denise Y.; Li, Jie (2016). “From Landlord Manor to Red Memorabilia: Reincarnations of a Chinese Museum Town”. Modern China.
museal (museums as mausoleums)Ho, Lirejectscritique

The view that museums are static, past-facing spaces like mausoleums, cut off from the living. The authors cite it as the common reading of museums in China, and use 'museal' as Adorno's term for it. (Ho & Li 2016p. 4)

Draws on Theodore Adorno; Joseph Levenson; Mayfair Yang

How it is used The authors set the museal view against the Anren evidence and reject it: the Landlord Manor and its successors were living spaces that were made and remade by politics and the market, not museumified relics. The contrast is the frame of the introduction and lets them claim that museums in China have been dynamic public spaces that define and redefine the past.

“far from being museumified or museal—museums in China have been” p. 4
Landlord Manor Museum, AnrenJianchuan Museum Cluster

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could test whether another museum behaves as a living space by tracking how its exhibits change with political campaigns and market demand, treating the museal reading as the null hypothesis.

model theatrical work (museum as stage)Ho, Liappliesanalytic concept

The Rent Collection Courtyard as a work of theatre: its designers mapped the visitors' route, eyelines and emotional sequence, and wrote a script in which the audience was part of the performance. (Ho & Li 2016p. 15)

Draws on Clark

How it is used The authors use the model-work idea to show that sculptors, models and visitors were all performers, and to explain the camera work in the 1966 documentary and the 1967 musical adapted from the sculptures. It makes the audience active rather than a passive viewer of statues.

“Museum became stage.” p. 15
Rent Collection Courtyard, 1965 onwardShanghai replica1967 musical staged by Beijing rebel factions

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): One could use the stage idea to study the routes, lighting and sound of other exhibitions, asking how the path through the space is meant to produce a particular feeling.

guerilla exhibitsHo, Licoinsanalytic concept

Temporary or semi-permanent displays of sensitive, unapproved material, such as interrogation records, wanted circulars, documents from a film actor's suicide and Great Leap posters, shown inside a private museum under official surveillance. They offer a fragmentary counter-narrative. (Ho & Li 2016p. 29)

How it is used The authors use the term to describe how Fan Jianchuan tests the censors, placing sensitive documents among the collection and changing displays to avoid pressure. It places the cluster on the edge between official and unofficial history, while the authors note that these exhibits are fragmentary and often impermanent.

“what we call Fan Jianchuan’s “guerilla exhibits” of sensitive,” p. 29
Red Age Daily Necessities museumMuseum of Sent-Down Youthoutdoor Great Leap Forward display, 2009

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could record which materials a private museum shows, moves or removes over time, to see how commercial and censorship pressure shapes a collection.

Hooper-Greenhill, Eilean (1992). Museums and the Shaping of Knowledge. London: Routledge.
experience and pleasure as controlHooper-Greenhillcriticisescritique

The modern museum’s stress on experience, activity and pleasure, treated as a new form of discipline and control that softens conflict and disguises inequality, so that visitors may be silenced rather than enabled. (Hooper-Greenhill 1992p. 214)

Draws on Foucault

How it is used Hooper-Greenhill uses the idea to read living history at Oakwell Hall, total immersion events, interactive exhibits and the museum as a ‘total destination’ combining shops, restaurants and hotels. Hooper-Greenhill accepts that many perspectives are a gain but argues that pleasurable technologies can soothe, silence and close minds. The argument leads her to ask whether the modern age, and the modern museum with it, is coming to an end.

“technologies of discipline and control have evolved to soften the” p. 214
Oakwell Hall, BatleyGeffrye Museum, ‘Putting on the Style’ (1990)Science Museum, LaunchpadIronbridge Gorge Museum

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could test this on a visitor-experience programme in a museum, asking which histories are staged as pleasure, which visitors are addressed, and which questions the programme leaves closed.

Hopkins, Owen (2021). The Museum: From Its Origins to the 21st Century.
heterotopiaHopkinsappliestheoretical framing

A space that is both real and unreal and mirrors the world in microcosm. The museum creates this by bringing together objects from different times and places and presenting them with a reverence that borders on the sacred. (Hopkins 2021)

Draws on Michel Foucault

How it is used Hopkins calls the museum the archetypal example of Foucault's heterotopia, in the introduction, and then uses it to explain why entering a museum is a ritualistic, almost spiritual act, with its own rules of time and space. Hopkins applies this to the Parthenon and the Acropolis Museum, so that the architecture of the museum is read as the place where its objects are made sacred.

“the archetypal example of what the French philosopher Michel Foucault termed a ‘heterotopia’”
museums in generalthe Parthenon and the Acropolis Museum, Athens

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The concept could ask whether a museum of a newly built national identity, such as those in Chinese provinces, works as a heterotopia in the same way, or whether its ritual is closer to a civic performance.

building transcends the collectionHopkinsappliesanalytic concept

The museum building as a symbol that comes to outweigh its contents. Hopkins notes that such accusations were made against the Altes Museum and, earlier, the Guggenheim and Pompidou, and treats it as the defining feature of the global museum from the 1990s. (Hopkins 2021)

How it is used Hopkins uses the idea to link Japan's 1980s-90s building boom and China's 2000s-2010s building to Bilbao and the Gulf. The Japanese case is read as one driven by economic conditions, and the Chinese as a more dramatic case of the same phenomenon, which lets him argue that these buildings express the global form at regional and national scale.

“began to transcend the museum’s collection”
Edo-Tokyo Museum (1993)Benesse House, Naoshima (1992)Ordos MuseumGuggenheim Bilbao

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask whether a new museum building in a Chinese or Japanese city can be judged by how much its architecture outweighs its collection, using visitor figures and display areas as evidence.

Janes, Robert R. (2009). Museums in a Troubled World: Renewal, Irrelevance or Collapse?. London: Routledge.
linear exhibition as a bookJanesadaptscritique

Janes calls the traditional exhibition a linear construction of glass and wood with much two-dimensional text and objects that can only be looked at, which he treats as essentially a book without the book's advantages of portability and way-finding. (Janes 2009p. 79)

Draws on Kathleen McLean

How it is used Janes uses McLean's diagnosis of a 'stultifying sameness' in exhibitions and her discouraged visits as evidence that the linear form has lost its appeal, especially for young visitors. Janes links the form to the cost of exhibitions and the reluctance to renew them, so that the critique of display becomes a critique of the budget.

“constructions of glass and wood, incorporating massive amounts of two-dimensional” p. 79
a Canadian museum's CA$12 million permanent exhibitionthe long-lived permanent displays that are rarely renewed

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The critique could be used to compare the long-lived permanent galleries of a national museum in Southeast Asia with its temporary and programmed displays, asking which form engages young visitors.

Jasanoff, Maya (2005). Edge of Empire: Conquest and Collecting in the East, 1750–1850. London: Fourth Estate.
trophy of warJasanoffappliesanalytic concept

An object taken in war is displayed as proof of victory and as propaganda for the victors. Jasanoff treats the trophy as a deliberately constructed front that presented the Company's image rather than a simple cultural statement about the enemy. (Jasanoff 2005p. 180)

How it is used Jasanoff applies the idea to Tipu's Tiger, shown at India House from 1808, arguing that reading it only as chauvinistic cultural messaging accepts a constructed front at face value. Jasanoff extends it to the Townley Gallery's Egyptian pieces, which were trophies of war against France in the East. The argument lets her show that Richard Wellesley set a precedent for display of spoils that the Company followed for decades.

“war in the East, against France, at that” p. 225
Tipu's Tiger at India HouseTipu's throne and possessions at Government House, CalcuttaTownley Gallery, British Museum

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The trophy idea could be applied to a national museum object taken in an Asian war, asking how its label and display reshaped the enemy's image. A researcher could compare the display history of a Chinese or Burmese trophy with that of the Tiger.

Karp, Ivan; Lavine, Steven D. (eds.) (1991). Exhibiting Cultures: The Poetics and Politics of Museum Display. Washington: Smithsonian Institution Press.
museum effectKarpadaptsanalytic concept

The effect that the setting and installation of a museum gives to objects, independent of what the objects themselves are. Alpers coined the term for the way museums make objects into things to be looked at, and Karp treats it as a force whose messages have no fixed content. (Karp & Lavine 1991)

Draws on Svetlana Alpers

How it is used Karp takes Alpers's term from the defence of aesthetic looking and turns it into a question of power: because the museum effect can aid or impede understanding of what objects mean, it can serve interests other than those of artists and connoisseurs. Karp applies it to the Musée d'Orsay, Renaissance cabinets and the art gallery, and then asks whether the museum effect exists at all in Japanese and Indian display, where objects are not seen primarily for their crafted form. The term lets him move from aesthetic argument to the politics of national identity without leaving the exhibition.

“The consequences of putting objects into even the Spartan context of the art gallery makes the museum effect into an apparatus of power.”
Musée d'OrsayRenaissance cabinets of curiositiesDutch landscape installationJapanese and Indian display, as a contrast

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The term can be used to test any display for what its setting adds, for example a reconstructed shop or a period room, by asking what a visitor would conclude if the same objects were shown without that setting.

resonance and wonderGreenblattappliesanalytic concept

Two modes of experiencing a displayed object: resonance is the power of the object to evoke the cultural forces that produced it, and wonder is the power to stop the viewer and hold attention on the object's uniqueness. (Karp & Lavine 1991)

Draws on Thomas Greene; Louis Montrose; new historicism

How it is used Greenblatt sets the two modes against each other and tests them. The State Jewish Museum in Prague, with its confiscated synagogue objects and the names of the dead, is his case of pure resonance; the Museum of Modern Art, where looking is enchanted, is his case of wonder. He links resonance to the new historicism and to the vulnerability of artifacts, which he reads through Greene and Montrose, and he uses a Coca-Cola stand at the Mayan site of Coba to show how an everyday object can resonate more than an archaeological one. He then argues that the best exhibitions combine the two.

“By resonance I mean the power of the displayed object to reach out beyond its formal boundaries to a larger world”
State Jewish Museum, PragueMuseum of Modern ArtMusee d'OrsayCoba, Yucatanboutique lighting in commercial display

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The two terms give a way to rate a single museum, by asking whether it evokes the forces behind its objects or only stops the visitor in front of them.

mitateYamaguchiadaptsanalytic concept

A Japanese technique of citation in which an ordinary object is linked to a classical or mythological image, so that the object stands for another time, place or meaning and is shown as a simulacrum of a primordial thing. (Karp & Lavine 1991)

Draws on Masakatsu Gunji; Jean Baudrillard; Claude Levi-Strauss; Frances Yates

How it is used Yamaguchi uses mitate as the key to Japanese exhibition, from the Pillow-Book episode of the snow-covered mound to the tokonoma alcove, the osira-sama figurines and kabuki costume, where the clothing is what performs. Yamaguchi sets it against the Paris Exposition of 1867, where everyday commodities were made into art, and the Western museum, which excluded the sounds and smells of daily life. Yamaguchi also reads the nineteenth-century Japanese adoption of Western technology as an act of mitate, in which Western things were transplanted into Japan. Baudrillard's simulacrum is used in a positive sense to describe this rhetoric of turning the invisible into the visible.

“Mitate, in its original sense, was an exposition presented to the gods.”
tokonoma alcoveosira-sama figurineskabuki costumeMatara cake offering at Motsu templeParis Exposition of 1867

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The term could be used to ask whether a museum shop window or a cafe display is a mitate, a link between the ordinary object and a larger image the visitor is expected to supply.

rasaGoswamyadaptsanalytic concept

The Indian theory of aesthetic delight, in which an emotion (bhava) in the viewer becomes a state of heightened delight (rasa), so that art is judged by the experience it produces rather than by its chronology or artist. (Karp & Lavine 1991)

Draws on Bharata Muni (Natyasastra)

How it is used Goswamy organises two exhibitions, Rasa in Paris and Essence of Indian Art in San Francisco, by the nine rasas rather than by chronology, type or artist. Goswamy explains the theory with care and then weighs its limits, because genre painting and Mughal or Deccani work sit awkwardly within it. The design follows the theme, with sculpture and miniatures mixed within each section, rooms painted in the colour of each rasa, and nine-sided tables that let viewers see a miniature series in turn. He accepts that the result is a personal view and that visitors gained a sense of the Indian mind rather than a full account of Indian art.

“Rasa is a key to Indian art, and deserves to be better understood.”
Rasa, Grand Palais, Paris, 1986Essence of Indian Art, Asian Art Museum, San Francisco, 1986

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The approach asks what a viewer should feel when entering a room, which could be applied to a display of any culture whose art is organised around an emotional or ethical category.

Kavanagh, Gaynor (ed.) (1996). Making Histories in Museums. London: Leicester University Press.
symbolic spaces: cognitive, social and dream spacesKavanaghappliesanalytic concept

Museums are described, following Annis, as three kinds of symbolic space: the cognitive space of exhibitions, the social space of shared visits and conversation, and the dream space in which visitors respond to images and textures in personal ways. The exhibition is only one of the three. (Kavanagh 1996p. 3)

Draws on Sheldon Annis

How it is used Kavanagh uses the three spaces at the start of the introduction to argue that the visit, and not only the exhibition, produces memories and meanings. This lets her treat the exhibition's history as one element in a larger experience that curators have not yet taken seriously.

“museums essentially embody three forms of symbolic space” p. 3
history museum visits in general

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask which of the three spaces a Southeast Asian or East Asian gallery in a Western museum offers its visitors, and which it leaves out.

Kirshenblatt-Gimblett, Barbara (1998). Destination Culture: Tourism, Museums, and Heritage. Berkeley: University of California Press.
in situ and in context displayKirshenblatt-Gimblettappliestypology

In situ displays (dioramas, period rooms, reconstructed settings and live performers) evoke a missing whole through metonymy and mimesis. In context displays arrange objects by a conceptual frame such as taxonomy, sequence or development, and use labels and lectures to treat them as documents. (Kirshenblatt-Gimblett 1998p. 3)

How it is used The pair organises the chapter. The author sorts label-centred exhibits from the living Chinese figures and the Balinese performances, and uses the live case to argue that performers become signs of themselves, so that even self-representation remains representation. It shows why the in situ mode, which the author links to the visitor's wish for experience, tends to essentialise the people it presents.

“In situ displays are immersive and environmental.” p. 3
Nathan Dunn's Chinese figuresBalinese performances at the Paris Colonial ExpositionPlimoth PlantationPeale's museum

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The pair could be used to ask whether a museum in a Southeast Asian city presents its objects as documents or re-creates settings, and who is shown as a sign of whom.

display as interfaceKirshenblatt-Gimblettappliesanalytic concept

The display interface (costumed animators, the style of restoration, the handling of historical time, the staging of performance) mediates and transforms what is shown. The interface also carries meanings of its own, so that heritage can be made to convey messages of modernity. (Kirshenblatt-Gimblett 1998p. 7)

How it is used The author compares Colonial Williamsburg, where the interface is hidden to produce a 'tourist realism', with the Bomas of Kenya amphitheatre, where it is foregrounded to show national modernity, and Splendid China. This lets her argue that a heritage site means as much through its staging as through its content.

“Display is an interface that mediates and thereby transforms what is shown into heritage.” p. 7
Colonial WilliamsburgBomas of KenyaSplendid China

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The question of the interface could be asked of a state-run heritage park in East or Southeast Asia: what modernity does its staging convey beside the heritage on display?

heritage that forecloses what it showsKirshenblatt-Gimblettadaptsanalytic concept

Documentation and exhibition make what they show disappear. Heritage shows just enough to close the subject, as with a model village that replaces the people it displays or a drug laboratory whose details are withheld. (Kirshenblatt-Gimblett 1998p. 149)

Draws on Steven Mullaney

How it is used The author applies the idea to Splendid China, the planned relocation of Padaung women to a model village near Rangoon, a Sydney drug exhibit and a Maori model village, reading each as a case where showing displaces what is shown. Her reading of Mullaney's rehearsals of culture, which she takes as erasure rather than re-creation, lets her link Florida and Burma with the wider history of ethnographic display.

“Documentation and exhibition are implicated in the disappearance of what they show” p. 162
Splendid ChinaPadaung model village near RangoonJustice and Police Museum, SydneyMaori model village

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could compare the Burmese model village with other state-sponsored minority villages in the region, asking what each one withholds from its visitors.

authenticity located in reception (undoing the ethnographic)Kirshenblatt-Gimblettcriticisescritique

Authenticity is located in the moment of reception, when audiences confront what they do not understand, rather than in the performances themselves. Staging performances as avant-garde art 'undoes' the ethnographic label, while depending on it. (Kirshenblatt-Gimblett 1998p. 11)

Draws on Bertolt Brecht; Antonin Artaud

How it is used The author uses the idea to explain the 1990 Los Angeles Festival's programme of Javanese court dance, Korean shamans and Chinese Kun opera, and to argue that avant-garde reception depends on the ethnographic it claims to undo. It lets her show that the event presented Los Angeles as a civilised, multicultural city.

“located authenticity in a moment of reception, rather than in the performances themselves.” p. 11
1990 Los Angeles FestivalJavanese court danceKorean shamans from Chindo IslandChinese Kun opera

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask whether an avant-garde festival of Southeast Asian performance in a Western city gains its authenticity from the audience's confusion in the same way.

Knell, Simon J.; Aronsson, Peter; Amundsen, Arne Bugge; et al. (eds.) (2011). National Museums: New Studies from Around the World. London: Routledge.
aesthetics as belief enhancerVaruttiappliesanalytic concept

The idea that beauty-led display works as a belief enhancer, seducing the viewer and pleasing the senses, so that an abstract national identity is believed rather than argued. Varutti says aesthetics presents objects as wonders detached from their histories. (Knell et al. 2011p. 304)

Draws on Greenblatt; Preziosi; Shanks and Tilley

How it is used Varutti applies the idea to the Shanghai Museum, the Sanxingdui Museum and Beijing's National History Museum, where Shang bronzes sit beside Qing calligraphy under dramatic lighting. Varutti uses Preziosi's claim that museums manufacture belief and Greenblatt's wonder displays to argue that aesthetics presents a nation defined by longevity and refinement while avoiding questions of national unity.

“work as a ‘belief enhancer’ by seducing the viewer” p. 311
Shanghai MuseumSanxingdui MuseumNational History Museum, Beijing

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The model could be used to compare a national museum in another country, asking which beliefs the lighting and choice of masterpieces are meant to produce.

Krech, Shepard, III; Hail, Barbara A. (eds.) (1999). Collecting Native America, 1870–1960. Washington: Smithsonian Institution Press.
authenticity of re-created objectsHailcriticisescritique

The gap between a museum's avowed interest in authenticity and the re-created or invented objects it displays without labelling them as such. (Krech & Hail 1999)

How it is used Hail criticises Sears for presenting re-created Lakota shields and a copied Ojibwa petroglyph floor as authentic, noting that the shields were covers never carried into battle and that the labels said nothing of their making. The critique sets the museum's spiritual message against the documented circumstances of production, and it reads the shields as a source of income for their makers.

“Sears gave no indication in Fruitlands Indian Museum labels that the hanging shields were re-creations.”
Fruitlands American Indian Museum, Harvard, Massachusetts

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The question could be asked of any display of re-made ritual or craft objects, such as a museum of an East or Southeast Asian people that shows replicas, whether the labels disclose how they were made.

the typological exhibitKrechcriticisescritique

An arrangement of objects by category and region, rather than by life or history, which in Krech's reading reduced the people who made the objects to their artifacts and placed them in an archaeological past. (Krech & Hail 1999)

How it is used Krech criticises the King Philip Museum's cases for reducing American Indians to their artifacts and relegating them to an archaeological and ethnographic past. Krech links the display to other small regional museums without life groups, and so treats the arrangement as a feature of the period's museums rather than a quirk of one collector.

“These typological exhibits reduced American Indians to their artifacts, relegating them to an archaeological and ethnographic past”
King Philip Museum, Bristol, Rhode Island

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The typological approach could be tested on an East or Southeast Asian ethnographic gallery, asking whether arranging objects by category removed the people who made them from the displayed account.

Logan, William; Nic Craith, Máiréad; Kockel, Ullrich (eds.) (2016). A Companion to Heritage Studies. Chichester: Wiley Blackwell.
heritagescapingWintercoinsanalytic concept

A popular aesthetic of solitude, comfort and refuge, expressed in coffee-table books, restored houses and tropical modern design, which in Asia's small historic towns displaces the community-focused goals of conservation. (Logan 2016)

How it is used Winter applies the term to Galle Fort in Sri Lanka, linking restored houses to architectural books on tropical modernism and to Geoffrey Bawa, and uses it to explain gentrification after the post-2009 property boom. In the section on Asia he extends the pattern to District 798 in Beijing, Moganshan Road in Shanghai, Pingyao, Melaka and Luang Prabang, which frame his reading of Galle.

“Galle has seen the emergence of a form of heritagescaping characterized by certain architectural discourses and comfort aesthetics”
Galle Fort, Sri LankaDistrict 798, BeijingMoganshan Road, ShanghaiPingyao, ChinaMelaka, Malaysia

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask whether the same aesthetic is reshaping historic quarters in other World Heritage towns in Southeast Asia, and who is displaced when a restored house becomes a second home.

Lumley, Robert (ed.) (1988). The Museum Time-Machine: Putting Cultures on Display. London: Routledge.
realism and the real thingLumleyappliesanalytic concept

The pursuit of 'realism' in museum reconstructions, role-play, working exhibits and experience, which claims to show 'the real thing' but is in fact a construction that depends on the visitor's cooperation. (Lumley 1988p. 11)

Draws on Umberto Eco; Jean Baudrillard

How it is used Lumley uses Eco's hyperreality and Baudrillard's simulation to judge the open-air museums of Ironbridge and Beamish and the new Museum of the Moving Image. Lumley reports West's candle-making episode as evidence that the real thing is reached only by fabricating the absolute fake, and argues that museums should show how they construct realities rather than pursue reality. The concept gives the introduction one of its three recurring themes, beside commercialisation and the media.

“to paraphrase Eco, is that the only way to attain the” p. 12
Ironbridge Gorge MuseumBeamishMuseum of the Moving Image, London

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The idea suggests a question for any reconstruction: where its realism stops and the visitor's acceptance of an invented period begins, and whether the museum says so.

Macdonald, Sharon; Fyfe, Gordon (eds.) (1996). Theorizing Museums: Representing Identity and Diversity in a Changing World. Oxford: Blackwell.
heterotopia and utopiesHetheringtoncombinesanalytic concept

Heterotopias are sites of alternate order defined by incongruous spatial relations to other sites in a society; utopies, after Marin, are a spatial play between no-place and good-place. Together they describe a museum without walls as a space of competing orderings rather than a single order. (Macdonald & Fyfe 1996PDF p. 160)

Draws on Foucault; Marin; Malraux

How it is used Hetherington uses the two concepts to read Stonehenge as a museum without walls, where prehistoric, druidic, touristic and free-festival utopias meet, and where English Heritage and the National Trust stage an authenticity through a tunnel of English history. Hetherington uses the pairing also to argue that the classical museum has always been a site of utopian social ordering, so that multivocality is not a postmodern novelty.

“I would suggest that heterotopia be defined as sites of” PDF p. 160
Stonehengeclassical museum

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could read a war memorial or heritage park in an Asian city as a heterotopic site where competing groups' utopias meet, and ask which visitors become would-be curators of it.

dialogic ironyRiegeltestsanalytic concept

Irony understood, after Babcock, as a double play between social criticism and comedy. Irony in an exhibition either reinforces the distance between viewer and displayed culture or, when turned back on the museum's own mode of representation, opens a shared space. (Macdonald & Fyfe 1996PDF p. 87)

Draws on Babcock; Hutcheon; Kathleen Stewart

How it is used Riegel compares two Canadian exhibitions. Into the Heart of Africa used verbal irony that many visitors did not read as critique, so it reproduced the colonial relation it sought to undermine. Fluffs and Feathers placed visitors before a mirror in native costume and so turned irony on the museum's own voice. Riegel uses the contrast to argue that irony is a risky trope, which works only when it is aimed at the museum's mode of representation and not at the represented culture.

“The strategic use of irony makes the exhibition relational and” PDF p. 102
Into the Heart of Africa, Royal Ontario MuseumFluffs and Feathers, Royal Ontario Museum

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could test a display of Chinese or Southeast Asian material for whether visitors are invited into a double position, as in the mirror and costume device, or simply shown more objects.

MacKenzie, John M. (2009). Museums and Empire: Natural History, Human Cultures and Colonial Identities. Manchester: Manchester University Press.
museum as theatre of identityMacKenzieappliesanalytic concept

The museum as a stage on which identities are continually performed, through the interweaving of past, present and future, and whose performance changes with each generation of visitors. (MacKenzie 2009p. 276)

How it is used MacKenzie uses the metaphor to join the colonial museum's staging of identity in the settler colonies to the Southeast Asian case, where Chinese, Indian and Malay visitors used museums as an extension of their festivals. MacKenzie presents the modern national museum as the same stage turned to national purposes, and the metaphor carries his claim that colonial museums became nationalist institutions.

“museums have indeed become theatres, stages with” p. 276
South-East Asian museumsSingapore museums

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask which identities a Southeast Asian museum's galleries perform for different groups of visitors, and whether those performances differ by festival or by day of the week.

McClellan, Andrew (1994). Inventing the Louvre: Art, Politics, and the Origins of the Modern Museum in Eighteenth-Century Paris. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.
transparencyMcClellanappliesanalytic concept

The eighteenth-century wish for direct, unmediated contact with the material world, which the book links to conservation and lighting. Museums isolated works from one another and from their original contexts so that they could be seen as if freshly made. (McClellan 1994p. 6)

Draws on Michel Foucault; Barbara Stafford

How it is used McClellan uses the idea to explain why museum hangs, frames and restoration aimed to erase the life of a picture between the studio and the gallery. It lets the author treat conservation practice as an ideological choice rather than a neutral technical matter, and links eighteenth-century Salon viewing to later museum conventions.

“immediate and unmediated contact with the material world” p. 6
Late-eighteenth-century picture galleriesLuxembourg Gallery restoration

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask whether a non-European collection moved into a Western museum was likewise isolated from its own setting, and whether conservation records show the same drive for transparent viewing.

Meyer, Andrea; Savoy, Bénédicte (eds.) (2014). The Museum Is Open: Towards a Transnational History of Museums 1750–1940. Berlin: De Gruyter.

Vachon’s contrast between a museum of industrial arts that shows technical series, replicas and documents for working people, and the historical period display of the Musée de Cluny, which he judged a dead way of showing objects. (Meyer & Savoy 2014p. 141)

How it is used Tibbe uses the typology to explain Vachon’s reports on European museums, his praise for the Orientalisches Museum in Vienna, and his plan for a working museum at Saint-Étienne. Tibbe then tests the model against later history: the Musée des arts décoratifs in the Louvre, opened in 1905, turned to period rooms and aesthetic display, which Vachon had denounced. The test shows why his systematic model lost ground after 1900.

“Vachon deemed this an outdated “Cluny-esque” form” p. 145
Musée de ClunyOrientalisches Museum, ViennaMusée des arts décoratifs, ParisSaint-Étienne industrial art museum

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The typology invites a comparison of how a regional museum of applied arts in Asia was organised, as series and replicas or as period rooms, and what its curators thought the museum was for.

Muchitsch, Wolfgang (ed.) (2013). Does War Belong in Museums? The Representation of Violence in Exhibitions. Bielefeld: transcript.
pseudo-realismWintercriticisescritique

The false claim of those who write about war or design war museums that they can bring the visitor close to the experience of combat. Winter treats experience as a set of changing memories held from a subject-position, not a fixed bodily essence. (Muchitsch 2013p. 36)

Draws on Joan Scott

How it is used Winter uses the term to reject the thrill-seeking Historial de la Grande Guerre at Peronne, whose critic he says believes that nearness to weaponry brings the thrill of battle. Winter sets against it the idea of experience as dynamic, which he takes from Scott. The term lets him argue that a war museum should interrogate whether war can be represented at all rather than simulate it.

“what might be termed pseudo-realism” p. 36
Historial de la Grande Guerre, Peronne

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could test whether the diorama and panorama displays in the Vienna, Dresden or Turkish museums in this volume fall under the same charge of simulated experience.

documentation, mise en scene and ensembleHagemannappliestypology

Three ways of presenting the undetonated bomb in city museums. Documentation is plain labelling with the object on a plinth; mise en scene stages it among ruins, sirens or shelters to produce emotion and an impression of authenticity; ensemble combines it with other objects in an open or fragmented arrangement that both dramatises and alienates. (Muchitsch 2013p. 132)

Draws on Gottfried Korff; Martin Roth

How it is used Hagemann sorts the German city exhibitions she documented into these three forms and shows that mise en scene and ensemble both create an impression of authenticity. From this she concludes that the bomb becomes either a sacred relic of German civilian suffering or evidence against the Allies, depending on the text and setting, so curators must take a clear position.

“These are documentation, mise en scène and ensemble.” p. 132
RostockHamburgHalleWeimarSiegburg

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could apply the same three-part typology to how a bomb, shell or wreck is shown in a regional museum outside Germany.

Naquin, Susan (2004). “The Forbidden City Goes Abroad: Qing History and the Foreign Exhibitions of the Palace Museum, 1974–2004”. T’oung Pao, 90 (2004).
the Forbidden City as an absent presenceNaquinappliesanalytic concept

The palace itself, which could not travel, as the idea that holds the exhibitions together. The objects stand for a site the viewer cannot see, and the catalogue's photographs and maps are used to evoke it. (Naquin 2004p. 368)

How it is used Naquin argues that the catalogue photographs of courtyards and halls, the staged palace rooms and the maps of Beijing invoke the off-stage Forbidden City, and that this, rather than the objects' own categories, made each show cohere. It lets her explain why shows arranged by medium still read as one palace. The 2000-01 Bowers catalogue is her example of the same device at its fullest.

“not and could not be present.” p. 368
1981 Hong Kong 'Treasures from the Imperial Palace'2000-02 Bowers 'Secret World of the Forbidden City'exhibition catalogues in general

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask whether a provincial or foreign museum's overseas shows use an equivalent absent site, such as a house, a city or a monument, as their unifying frame, and what a visitor could know of that site from the catalogue alone.

the formulaic Forbidden City exhibitNaquinappliestypology

The recurring package of a show built around a throne set, imperial robes, armour, clocks, chime-stones, court paintings and portraits, which Naquin traces to the 1981 Hong Kong exhibition. (Naquin 2004p. 346)

How it is used Naquin uses the formula as a yardstick. Naquin traces its emergence in 1981 and its repetition in the 1982-83 Tokyo, 1984-85 Orlando and 2000-02 Bowers shows, so that each exhibition reads as a variation on one template. This lets her separate the repeated core from the material added later, such as Tibetan Buddhist objects and Western court artists.

“what would become the formulaic Forbidden City exhibit.” p. 346
1981 Hong Kong1982-83 Tokyo1984-85 Orlando2000-02 Bowers

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The same typology could be tested on another museum's export shows, to see whether a fixed package was used for export only or also at home.

Outka, Elizabeth (2009). Consuming Traditions: Modernity, Modernism, and the Commodified Authentic. New York: Oxford University Press.
performing authenticityOutkaadaptsanalytic concept

Authenticity understood as something staged and acted out. Consumers, writers and marketers move through images of authenticity while knowing them to be constructions, so that the contradiction is performed and kept alive rather than resolved. (Outka 2009p. 16)

Draws on Jon McKenzie; Richard Schechner

How it is used Outka adapts performance studies, which she says has stressed transgressive performance and neglected normative performance, and its attention to commerce as performance in Schechner. Outka’s cases show performance as both subversive, as when a shopper plays a class position not their own, and normative, as when it reinforces a hierarchy. In the relic room of Night and Day, Katharine Hilbery’s “calculated performance” is read through this lens.

“The contradiction implicit in performing authenticity is the very contradiction” p. 16
Hilbery relic room in Night and DaySelfridges Old-time Industry demonstrationsClass performance in Selfridges’ departments

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask how visitors to a historic house or heritage site perform a class or national identity through what they are shown, and whether the performance is subversive, normative or both.

window gazing (window shopping as performance)Outkaadaptsanalytic concept

The shop window as a site of identity formation: the viewer gazes at a constructed image of authenticity and refinement that hides its prices and sells a mood, and the act of looking is a performance the viewer knows to be constructed. (Outka 2009p. 137)

Draws on Bowlby; Anne Friedberg; Walter Benjamin

How it is used Outka uses Bowlby and Friedberg to set the store window against the mirror, and Benjamin’s flâneur against the female gazer. Outka then argues that Ralph Denham in Night and Day is Baudelaire’s flâneur reimagined by a female novelist, and that his gazing stands for a wartime wish for stability. The window’s aura is read as close to the tableau of the authentic dead but out of reach.

“Ralph is Baudelaire’s flâneur reimagined by a female novelist.” p. 137
Woolf’s Night and DaySelfridges window designsWartime London shop windows

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could read a museum or heritage site’s windows and vitrines as stages where visitors perform authenticity, and ask whose gaze the display anticipates.

Pearson, Catherine (2017). Museums in the Second World War: Curators, Culture and Change. London: Routledge.
museum of ideasPearsonappliesanalytic concept

Markham's concept of a museum that presents topical ideas, as opposed to a static collection, realised in wartime through temporary exhibitions that used objects to illustrate concepts. (Pearson 2017)

Draws on Markham

How it is used Pearson uses the idea to explain the topical exhibitions of wartime, such as Tin through the Ages and the disease display, which put ordinary objects from store to new use. It helps her show that the wartime museum was a place for ideas and debate rather than a channel for government messages.

“Markham’s concept of a ‘museum of ideas’ was evident in the many topical exhibitions that were developed”
Tin through the Ages, National Museum of WalesManchester Museum's war and disease exhibitionTown Planning and Town Fauna

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask whether a present-day topical exhibition on a current crisis follows Markham's model, and whether its objects are chosen to illustrate ideas or to represent a collection.

Rees Leahy, Helen (2012). Museum Bodies: The Politics and Practices of Visiting and Viewing. Farnham: Ashgate.
performing museologyLeahyappliestheoretical framing

A shift from an informing to a performing museology, in which the museum is treated less as a collection of objects than as a technology of skills, techniques and methods, and as a site of social and corporeal practice that makes the institution itself visible to its visitors. (Rees Leahy 2012p. 2)

Draws on Barbara Kirshenblatt-Gimblett

How it is used Leahy takes the idea as the frame for Sehgal's This Progress, in which performers disturb visitors' habits of walking and talking so that the institution is experienced as a site of proprioception and sociality. From this the book's subject follows: the visiting body rather than the collection. The concept lets her treat the museum's rules and displays as a performance rather than as neutral presentation.

“A performing museology makes the museum perform itself by” p. 3
Guggenheim Museum: Sehgal's This Progress (2010)

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask whether a museum's floor plan, staff scripts or public events make its own operations visible to visitors, and compare how museums with different public missions do this.

performatives and the museum's scriptLeahyadaptsanalytic concept

Judith Butler's authoritative speech acts, such as 'silence please', which perform an action and exercise binding power. The museum's script is a set of performatives that make visitors' bodies both legible and manageable, and it is also encoded in the rhythm of displays and the hang of pictures. (Rees Leahy 2012p. 100)

Draws on Judith Butler; Barbara Kirshenblatt-Gimblett

How it is used Leahy applies Butler to the museum's rules and displays and then to the visitors who comply with, ignore or resist them. Leahy’s argument is that a visitor's performance may conform to, ignore or resist the institutional performative, so the script never fully determines conduct. Recalcitrant bodies, from Duchamp's and Morris's exhibitions to Tate Modern's Turbine Hall, show the limits of the script.

“The museum’s script enunciates what Judith Butler terms a series of ‘performatives’ that make the body both legible and manageable.” p. 100
British MuseumRobert Morris retrospective, Tate (1971)Tate Modern Turbine Hall commissions

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could read the labels, rules and guard instructions of one museum as a set of performatives and compare which visitors act against them.

gaze and glanceLeahycombinesanalytic concept

The prolonged, attentive gaze that artists seek to attract and curators to manage, set against the distracted, sideways glance. Museum looking oscillates between the two, and a viewer can occupy both modes at once within a single scopic regime. (Rees Leahy 2012p. 47)

Draws on Norman Bryson; De Bolla

How it is used Leahy uses the pair to explain the Great Room at Somerset House, where the glance surveyed the exhibition en masse, and the 1857 Manchester exhibition, where visitors were overwhelmed. Taking the distracted glance seriously lets her argue that the curators' model of attentive looking leaves out much actual museum looking, including Rogoff's account of a Pollock visit at the Tate.

“Bryson describes the duality of looking that is implied in the distinction between the ‘gaze’ and the ‘glance’” p. 47
Royal Academy, Somerset HouseManchester Art Treasures Exhibition (1857)Tate Gallery Pollock exhibition

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): One could ask whether a crowded case of Asian ceramics or bronzes invites glancing or gazing, and whether labelling or lighting changes which.

museum fatigueLeahycriticisesanalytic concept

A condition of physical tiredness in which visitors lose the capacity to look properly. Gilman and his co-workers treated attention as a resource to be managed through layout, seating and gallery design. (Rees Leahy 2012p. 60)

Draws on Benjamin Ives Gilman; Edward S. Robinson; Arthur W. Melton

How it is used Leahy traces the concept from the early twentieth-century studies to later museum practice, including Gilman's proposal for stools rather than cushioned ottomans. Leahy sets Gilman's notion of 'good seeing' against the normative assumptions it carries, and treats fatigue as a product of how museums organise bodies and attention rather than a fixed state of visitors.

“Gilman’s taken-for-granted notion of ‘good seeing’ warrants” p. 61
US museums studied by Gilman, Robinson and Meltongallery seating history

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could check whether fatigue in a given museum appears in visitor books or interviews, and compare galleries with and without seating.

constructed situationSehgal, quoted by Leahyappliesanalytic concept

An unexpected encounter that stimulates visitors' critical awareness of themselves in material, social and institutional space, by overturning what they expect to do and feel on a museum visit. (Rees Leahy 2012p. 2)

How it is used Leahy takes Sehgal's term as the way into the book: This Progress makes visitors aware of their own circulation in the Guggenheim rotunda and so exposes the taken-for-granted habits of museum visiting that the rest of the book historicises. The term bridges contemporary art practice and the eighteenth-century history that follows.

“Sehgal describes This Progress as a ‘constructed situation’” p. 2
Guggenheim Museum: This Progress (2010)

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could stage or observe a comparable situation in a museum in the region and ask what visitors notice about their own movement.

Sellers, Charles Coleman (1980). Mr. Peale’s Museum: Charles Willson Peale and the First Popular Museum of Natural Science and Art. New York: W. W. Norton.
the total conceptSellersappliesanalytic concept

The principle that each natural form should be shown in all its variations, in its natural environment, and with related species in a comparable view, so that a display gives a complete picture of a kind rather than a set of specimens. Sellers treats it as the museum's distinctive scientific contribution. (Sellers 1980p. 2)

How it is used Sellers sets the total concept against the specialist collections that emerged during the museum's middle years, when each scientist isolated a specialty in a private collection. Sellers uses it to argue that Peale's museum mattered to American science despite being popular, and to name the standard by which the institution should be judged.

“Peale’s Museum stayed with the total concept: each natural form should be shown in all variations, in its natural environment, and with related species in a comparable view.” p. 2
Peale's bird and mammal displayshabitat groups

Siegel, Jonah (2020). Material Inspirations: The Interests of the Art Object in the Nineteenth Century and After. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
the museum as symbol and causeSiegelappliesanalytic concept

The museum as both a sign of the modern experience of art and a cause of it, so that arguments for cultural continuity and for cultural rupture depend on the juxtapositions that museums make possible. (Siegel 2020p. 280)

Ruskin's anxiety about juxtaposition in the Stanza della Segnatura and Pater's reading of the Townley Discobolus are both read as responses to the growth of British museums. He argues that for Pater the museum is a condition that critics must understand and work within, not a loss of meaning.

“the institution is at once a symbol and a cause of the modern situation” p. 280
British MuseumNational GalleryStanza della Segnatura, VaticanTownley Discobolus

Siegel, Jonah (ed.) (2008). The Emergence of the Modern Museum: An Anthology of Nineteenth-Century Sources. New York: Oxford University Press.

Objects shown in a museum carry no fixed message; viewers draw meanings the collectors did not intend, so the lessons of a display are always more or less than its planners hoped. (Siegel 2008p. 7)

He uses it to present the growth of the British Museum, the Assyrian finds and the Elgin Marbles as a sequence of revised hierarchies of meaning rather than a settled policy. The claim lets the anthology treat the question of what a museum should teach as open.

“not generally speak for themselves, and even when they appear to do so they do” p. 8
British MuseumElgin MarblesAssyrian sculptures

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask what a Siamese chair or a Japanese idol taught a Victorian visitor who saw it beside a Greek marble, and whether the labels or the surrounding displays steered that reading.

Silina, Maria (2026). Soviet Museums Between the Two World Wars: Art History on Display. London: Routledge.
ostranenie (estrangement of objects)Silinaadaptsanalytic concept

Viktor Shklovsky's term for the technique of making objects strange so that they escape automatic perception. Silina presents it as the basis of the formalist analytic apparatus, which Shaposhnikov drew on while diverging from it: for him an aesthetically valuable object keeps a distance from reality. Draws on Viktor Shklovsky

How it is used Silina uses the term to contrast formalist modernist display, which treats space as a neutral container for abstract qualities such as form and colour, with Shaposhnikov's view that space is itself historical. The concept gives her a shared starting point and a clear point of divergence between the two museum models.

“an aesthetically valuable object is one that maintains a certain distance from reality.” p. 40
Museum of Everyday-Life of the 1840s, Moscowmodernist art museum display

gaze-appeal (nagliadnost')Silinaappliesanalytic concept

The principle, which Serguei Oushakine named, that a display should work through convincing visual models rather than abstract language, so that visitors are drawn into the story of class struggle. The motto 'gaze-appeal is acceleration' expressed the early-1930s demand for visual immediacy in ideological display. (Silina 2026p. 100)

Draws on Serguei Oushakine

How it is used Silina applies the term to explain why Soviet curators preferred relations between objects, panels and installations to single showpieces, and why quick-response anti-religious and anti-imperialist exhibitions were built as spectacle. It links the Congress programme of 1930 with the Kauchuk Factory Club show and with Nikolai Simon's Constructivist installations.

“Gaze-appeal is acceleration” p. 101
Kauchuk Factory Club exhibitionNikolai Simon's installations for the Oriental museum project, 1931

Sleeper-Smith, Susan (ed.) (2009). Contesting Knowledge: Museums and Indigenous Perspectives. Lincoln: University of Nebraska Press.
aesthetic of controlled heterogeneityShannonadaptsanalytic concept

Annelise Riles's phrase for a layout in which varied text and graphics look heterogeneous at a glance but reveal replication on closer viewing. Shannon uses it for the community exhibits in the Our Lives gallery. (Sleeper-Smith 2009p. 229)

How it is used Shannon applies the idea to the Chicago, Igloolik and Kahnawake exhibits, which were distinct in content but grouped under one thematic structure and shared text panels, video screens and photographs. “Native voice is also embedded within a particular style of exhibit design” p. 229
Our Lives gallery, NMAI: Chicago, Igloolik and Kahnawake exhibits

Stewart, Susan (1984). On Longing: Narratives of the Miniature, the Gigantic, the Souvenir, the Collection. Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press.
the freak as a freak of cultureStewartadaptsanalytic concept

The freak is produced by the spectacle itself, which distances the viewer and marks the performer as an aberration; the viewer is thereby normalised. The body is made an object, silent and still, in a frame supplied by the pitchman. (Stewart 1984p. 109)

How it is used Stewart takes Fiedler's history of freaks as a source of evidence and adds an analysis of the spectacle's silence, which she reads as the structure that separates the freak from the viewer. “is a freak of culture. His or her anomalous status is” p. 109
freak shows and side showsSiamese twins Chang and Engdwarfs and giants exhibited in eighteenth-century handbills

Stocking, George W., Jr. (ed.) (1985). Objects and Others: Essays on Museums and Material Culture. Madison: University of Wisconsin Press.
contextual display (objects in their cultural setting)Jacknistestscritique

Boas's view that human artifacts make sense only in their cultural setting, so that a form's multiple functions and inner meaning should be kept and objects grouped by tribe rather than sorted by an invented evolutionary type. Jacknis calls Boas's position a nominalist and historical viewpoint, citing Stocking (1974). (Stocking 1985p. 77)

How it is used Jacknis uses the idea to measure Boas's exhibits against the constraints of trustees, storage, lighting and competing visitor needs. The Northwest Coast Hall arranged by tribe after 1901 is his main case, and the life groups and the labelling dispute show where contextual display met the limits of realistic display. The concept lets him argue that Boas's museum method was limited in principle, not only in practice, and that the break of 1905 ended the museum era in American anthropology.

“Against Mason's typological evolutionary scheme, Boas posed his own” p. 77

Tseng, Alice Y. (2008). The Imperial Museums of Meiji Japan: Architecture and the Art of the Nation. Seattle: University of Washington Press.
visibility and limited visibility in museum displayTsengtestsanalytic concept

Museum display is built on visibility: objects are laid out to be seen, and their use, history and motion are hard to show. Tseng takes Hooper-Greenhill's view that the visible is often only a limited visibility and tests it on the icons of the Imperial Nara Museum. (Tseng 2008p. 167)

Draws on Eilean Hooper-Greenhill

How it is used Tseng asks why the Buddhist statue is not in clear view in the Imperial Nara Museum and shows that the dialectic of visibility appears in the museum's experience: the bars of the case cut across the statue and the object is denied its devotional function and the other senses. The idea allows her to argue that the museum made Buddhist icons visible as art by removing them from the ritual uses that gave them meaning.

“of visibility emerge in the experience of the Imperial Nara Museum” p. 169
Imperial Nara MuseumBuddhist icons in glass casesSugimoto's paintings of the galleries

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could read the vitrine display of a Buddhist or Shinto object in a Southeast Asian or Korean museum and ask what the case removes from its devotional use.

contextual and classificatory modes of displayTsengcoinstypology

Two ways of relating objects to their setting. The contextual mode arranges objects in period interiors so they keep their original context, as in the Hōōden national pavilion at Chicago in 1893; the classificatory mode groups objects by function, medium and type and dislocates them from their context, as in the Imperial Kyoto Museum. (Tseng 2008p. 127)

How it is used Tseng uses the pair to explain why two displays of Japan's historical art in the same period read differently. The Hōōden made the whole pavilion a total environment behind roped barriers, while the Kyoto museum gave each object equal prominence as an isolated visual event. This lets her argue that the Kyoto stance, a Western building holding traditional objects, presented Japanese art to a modern exhibiting agent rather than as a period setting.

“in what can be called the contextual mode” p. 127
Hōōden national pavilion, World's Columbian Exposition, Chicago 1893Imperial Kyoto Museum

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The pair could be used to compare period rooms with classified galleries in any museum of Asian art, asking which mode a given display uses and what it leaves out of the object's setting.

Veldkamp, Elmer (2014). “Keeping It Real: The Exhibition of Artifact Replicas in National Museums of Korea”. Acta Koreana, 17.2 (December 2014): 557-581.
auraVeldkampappliestheoretical framing

Benjamin's notion that an original work has a unique presence and a distance that mechanical reproduction erodes. The article uses it to explain the National Museum of Korea's insistence on exhibiting originals, and the distance that cases create around objects. (Veldkamp 2014p. 563)

Draws on Walter Benjamin

How it is used Veldkamp reads the museum's policy of exhibiting originals in Benjaminian terms, and then uses the same idea to show that glass cases and lighting keep even a replica at a distance that creates aura. The concept lets him argue that aura is produced by display practice as well as by the object.

“withers in the age of mechanical reproduction is the aura of the work of art” p. 563
National Museum of Korea display of the replica incense burnerDisplay cases and lighting at the Kongju National Museum

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could compare the display conditions of originals and replicas (case, lighting, viewing distance) to test whether aura attaches to the object or to its arrangement.

Vergo, Peter (ed.) (1989). The New Museology. London: Reaktion Books.
aesthetic and contextual exhibitionsVergorejectstypology

Two opposed approaches to exhibition making. Aesthetic shows let the object speak with little adjunct material; contextual shows treat objects as tokens of an age or culture and surround them with text and comparison. (Vergo 1989p. 48)

Draws on Brown Goode

How it is used Vergo uses the typology to reject the aesthetic view as seriously flawed, citing a Scandinavian painting show at the Hayward Gallery that had no captions or map. Vergo also rejects over-documented display, and proposes that good exhibitions need knowledge of their audience and non-verbal means such as a costume beside paintings. The Nazi 'Degenerate Art' exhibition shows that hanging and captions can make an argument, so the typology alone does not settle the question.

“what I shall call for brevity's sake 'aesthetic' exhibitions” p. 48
Scandinavian painting show, Hayward GalleryNazi 'Degenerate Art' exhibition, Munich 1937-8

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The typology could be applied to a Chinese or Japanese gallery in a Western museum to see whether its displays let objects speak or explain them as tokens of a culture.

Yanni, Carla (1999). Nature’s Museums: Victorian Science and the Architecture of Display. Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press.
Scopic reciprocity (Bennett)Yannicriticisesanalytic concept

Bennett’s claim that museum and arcade architecture organised space and vision so that visitors became objects of each other’s inspection, a public displaying itself to itself in its own orderliness. Yanni presents it as Bennett’s argument about the museum’s architecture of looking. (Yanni 1999p. 9)

Draws on Tony Bennett

How it is used Yanni accepts that the relations of space and vision matter but denies that all acts of looking are equal. The reciprocity Bennett describes is absent from the art museums of Durand, Schinkel and Smirke, and most museums were closed on Sundays when a bourgeois promenade would have happened. He explains the resemblance of museums to arcades and department stores by the practical need for cheap natural light.

“The scopic reciprocity to which Bennett refers is not evident in many art museums,” p. 9
Durand’s ideal museumSchinkel’s Altesmuseum, BerlinSmirke’s British Museummuseums with open halls and balconies

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could check whether a given museum’s sight lines and opening hours allowed visitors to watch one another, rather than assuming it from the building type.

Museum visionYanniadaptsanalytic concept

Alpers’s proposal that museum vision is a way of seeing: once an object rests in a museum it can be viewed only as an object of visual worth, so the museum setting itself dictates vision. Yanni presents it as the starting point for his own argument. (Yanni 1999p. 19)

Draws on Alpers

How it is used Yanni agrees that the setting dictates vision and takes the point a step further by arguing that each museum’s architectural setting shapes how visitors see and understand objects. This lets him read the Oxford iron-and-glass cloister, the Edinburgh Great Hall and the Natural History Museum’s Romanesque hall as different ways of seeing comparable specimens.

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could compare two museums holding similar collections in different buildings and ask whether the buildings change what visitors are led to look at, using visitor books or contemporary guidebooks.

Architecture as participant in the construction of knowledgeYannicoinstheoretical framing

The argument that buildings did not merely house science but helped make it: architecture legitimated particular versions of science, and Victorian buildings stated their context openly instead of claiming neutrality. (Yanni 1999p. 159)

How it is used This is the book’s central claim. Yanni uses it to read the Oxford cloister and the angel over the door, and the Natural History Museum’s hall and statue of Adam, as explicit references rather than neutral settings, and to show that the Museum of Practical Geology and Edinburgh museum defined nature for a less educated audience. It lets him argue that the buildings are evidence of Victorian natural knowledge, not just its containers.

Society of spectacle (periodisation)Yannicriticisesperiodisation

The question of when a society of spectacle began. Crary places it in the late 1920s; Richards places it in 1851, with the Great Exhibition, which Yanni uses to date the spectacle in museum display. (Yanni 1999p. 94)

Draws on Foucault; Crary; Thomas Richards

How it is used Yanni rejects Foucault’s phrase that society is one of surveillance rather than spectacle as misleading, because the two regimes of power coincide. Following Richards, he links the Crystal Palace, with its goods and its light-maximising iron and glass, to the encyclopedic displays of the 1860s, and reads Huxley’s opposition to showing every object as opposition to spectacle.
