The social role of museums: inclusion, gender and difference

The new museology and after: inclusion, community, social justice, care, activism and the museum profession; feminist and queer theory and disability. 41 concepts from 21 texts

The approaches in this section treat the museum as a social institution whose public purpose can include or exclude people, and whose work depends on who is allowed to make, care for and speak through it. Their shared question is whose museum it is and for whom it is run. The family begins with Vergo's new museology, defined by dissatisfaction with an older museology that concentrated on methods (Vergo 1989p. 3). It extends to feminist theory, the split between cultural and positional difference, the ethics of care, needs-based accounts of museum benefit and the sociology of the professions (Macdonald & Fyfe 1996PDF p. 112; Sandell & Nightingale 2012; Morse 2021p. 7; Silverman 2010p. 17; Shapiro & Kemp 1990p. 312).

According to our texts, the theorists behind these approaches include Kreps, whose appropriate museology Barrett and Kamel and Gerbich apply (Barrett 2011p. 152; Sandell & Nightingale 2012); Young, Morphy and Hardin, used by Mears and Modest, Sandell and Anderson (Sandell & Nightingale 2012); Tronto and Mol, behind Morse's ethics and logic of care (Morse 2021p. 3p. 192); and Maslow, behind Silverman's needs approach (Silverman 2010p. 16). The texts at the centre are Morse on care (77), Sandell and Nightingale on rights and equality (63), Hill on women and museums (37), Silverman on the social work of museums (79) and Barrett on the public and community (58).

New museology and appropriate museology (Vergo, Kreps)

Vergo holds that every acquisition, arrangement and label places a construction on history, so museology should ask what museums are for rather than how they are run (Vergo 1989p. 3p. 43). Barrett takes Kreps's appropriate museology, in which practice is adapted to the communities served, to argue that the curator's intellectual role is strengthened rather than displaced (Barrett 2011p. 152p. 153). Kamel and Gerbich apply it to the planned Marib Museum in Yemen, calling it a "bottom-up, community-based approach that combines local knowledge and resources", and test it against visitor research at Sana'a National Museum (Sandell & Nightingale 2012). Lu tests the European ecomuseum in Guizhou, finding public ecomuseums run from above with little participation and dependent on falling funds (Lu 2014p. 144p. 162).

Ethics and logic of care (Mol, Tronto)

Morse takes the logic of care, inspired by Mol, from clinical practice and reads engagement sessions with mental health, dementia, addiction and stroke groups at Tyne & Wear Archives & Museums (Morse 2021p. 3p. 18). Set against the logic of contribution, which values participants for what they add to the museum, it judges sessions by good care (Morse 2021p. 31). Morse then draws on the ethics of care to treat care as a value across management, front-of-house and curatorial work (Morse 2021p. 7). Tronto's three areas of institutional care serve as a test of the local authority museum, which Morse finds not uncaring but not always care-ful (Morse 2021p. 192p. 193). The affective labour of sessions, read through Hochschild and Hardt and Negri, is productive yet unrecognised (Morse 2021p. 142).

Feminist museology and gendered display (Porter, Hill, Duncan)

Porter translates the relation of text, author and reader from Berger, Williamson, Coward, Rose and Tagg "into the museum forms of exhibition, curator and visitor" (Macdonald & Fyfe 1996PDF p. 112). Her reading finds women represented as passive and closed and men as active and open, and treats these assumptions as positional rather than anchored in real people (Macdonald & Fyfe 1996PDF p. 111). Hill tests Bailkin's feminist museology against women founders and donors, and against Hoberman argues that women before 1914 sought inclusion in masculine spaces rather than a separate museum (Hill 2016PDF p. 142). Hill applies Ruskin's model to Walkley and Ancoats, where women "successfully blended domestic and museum spaces, private and public" (Hill 2016PDF p. 197PDF p. 198). Duncan uses the male ritual subject to read the Museum of Modern Art's female nudes as a gendered ritual space (Duncan 1995p. 128–129p. 126–127).

Positional difference and sites of persuasion (Young, Morphy, Hardin, Shue)

Mears and Modest set Young's politics of positional difference, which concerns how a group's social position limits its opportunities, against the politics of cultural difference, and use it to test three curatorial strategies for African collections (Sandell & Nightingale 2012). Sandell applies Morphy's "sites of persuasion" to the Glasgow sh[OUT] programme, treating the controversy it caused as part of rights work (Sandell & Nightingale 2012). Anderson applies Hardin's tragedy of the commons to gallery space and combines it with Shue's basic rights to argue that museums should keep space open for public learning rather than cede it to faith groups (Sandell & Nightingale 2012).

Human needs and relationships (Maslow, Silverman)

Silverman uses the human needs perspective to argue that museum benefit meets basic requirements, and builds the structure of her survey on it (Silverman 2010p. 16p. 17). Her grid of sixteen relationship needs, drawn from Maslow and Kilpatrick, organises programmes by self, pair, family and group, and is stressed as non-hierarchical (Silverman 2010p. 141). Social capital is the route from individual meaning-making to collective benefit, in the trust sense from Putnam and the norms sense Silverman attributes to Fukayama, as the text spells it, but the link to civil society is cited rather than tested (Silverman 2010p. 19). Silverman's ten functions classify eighty-three interventions and show psychotherapy as the function museums are least prepared to offer (Silverman 2010p. 144).

Professions, labour and exhibition makers (Etzioni, Hughes, Beegan, Alberti)

Teather tests museum work against the traits sociologists use to define a profession, places it among Etzioni's semi-professions, and follows Hughes in asking how workers gain control of their work. Teather concludes: "We can be sure that occupations like museum work are at least semi-professions" (Shapiro & Kemp 1990p. 312). Guy, Williams and Wintle argue that professional status excludes people on grounds of money, class, ethnicity and gender, drawing on Beegan, and propose the inclusive term exhibition maker in place of the professional designer (Guy 2024p. 8). Longair and McAleer combine Lambert and Lester's imperial careers with Alberti's call for research on museum staff, treating the curator as mediator between empire and display (Longair & McAleer 2012p. 9).

Stewardship and organisation (Janes, Phillips, Rifkin)

Janes extends stewardship from permanent collections to societal and environmental responsibility, and tests museums by that responsibility rather than by collection quality. The core of the idea is "the care of something that doesn’t belong to you" (Janes 2009p. 27p. 33). Janes applies Phillips's three agendas to show that conferences and boards concentrate on content and neglect culture and change (Janes 2009p. 57p. 58). Rifkin's high- and low-entropy contrast serves to classify small, self-organising work cultures (Janes 2009p. 143p. 144).

Reading against the grain (Ginzburg, Davis, Habel)

Çelik adapts a method of reading archival records, photographs and reports for evidence their authors did not intend, in order to recover the voices of subordinate people (Çelik 2016p. 167). Applied to excavation reports from Sardis, Babylon and Nippur, it recovers workers' own decisions about schedules, harvests and the length of the season: "I, too, heard them on the excavation sites and was compelled to include them in my stories" (Çelik 2016p. 11). Çelik admits that the method carries risks and depends on reading each site in its political context (Çelik 2016p. 167).

Debates and limits

Several authors criticise these approaches from within. Brady sets the National Museum of the American Indian's dialogic model against residual object-centred display, dioramas and fund-raising partnerships, and argues that inclusion can become accommodation under neoliberal funding (Sleeper-Smith 2009p. 147). Barrett criticises the replacement of public by community without change of practice, and visitor metrics that treat visitors as customers (Barrett 2011p. 129p. 56). Morse argues that the critique of participation persists because participation is already framed as contribution (Morse 2021p. 4p. 31). Heinich tests the Pompidou Centre's hope of mixing audiences and finds a young, highly educated public, with manual workers at 3 per cent (Lumley 1988p. 199p. 208). Hill and Hoberman disagree over whether women's museum work was inclusion or separation (Hill 2016PDF p. 142). Bennett and Schwarzer read settlement-house museum work as patronising, a charge Silverman answers with evidence of wider class contact (Silverman 2010p. 10).

What the approaches leave out, according to the texts themselves, is the practice itself. Silverman admits that no comprehensive theory yet explains the social work of museums (Silverman 2010p. 14), and Morse notes that research on engagement practice is less developed than work on participants (Morse 2021p. 7).

Carrying it over to a new case

  • Ask which people in a museum's outreach programme do the emotional work of sessions, and whether staffing and evaluation count it. Affective labour would model this in an Asian or diaspora museum (Morse 2021p. 142).
  • Compare the curator's career with the fate of a regional museum's collections when each curator left, as Longair and McAleer did for imperial museums (Longair & McAleer 2012p. 9).
  • Read a national history museum's display of wartime or industrial labour with Porter's positional categories, asking who is shown as active and who as background (Macdonald & Fyfe 1996PDF p. 111).
  • Test a Southeast Asian ecomuseum with Lu's questions: who runs it, who speaks in it, and whether the culture persists once funds fall (Lu 2014p. 144p. 162).
  • Trace the exhibition makers behind an ethnographic gallery, such as craftswomen, mannequin makers and label writers, and set them against the credited curator (Guy 2024p. 8).
  • Apply Young's split to a display of a Chinese or Southeast Asian community, asking whether it addresses the structural position of present-day members (Sandell & Nightingale 2012).
  • Code a museum's programmes against Silverman's ten functions to see which are absent, such as advocacy or activism (Silverman 2010p. 144).

Where to start reading

  • Morse, Nuala (2021). The Museum as a Space of Social Care. London: Routledge. the engagement chapters, for the logic of care set against the logic of contribution
  • Barrett, Jennifer (2011). Museums and the Public Sphere. Chichester: Wiley-Blackwell. Barrett's critiques of community and public rhetoric and of visitor metrics
  • Sandell, Richard; Nightingale, Eithne (eds.) (2012). Museums, Equality and Social Justice. London: Routledge. how rights, controversy and positional difference are applied to specific displays
  • Hill, Kate (2016). Women and Museums, 1850–1914: Modernity and the Gendering of Knowledge. Manchester: Manchester University Press. Hill's test of feminist museology and the Ruskinian community museum
  • Macdonald, Sharon; Fyfe, Gordon (eds.) (1996). Theorizing Museums: Representing Identity and Diversity in a Changing World. Oxford: Blackwell. Porter's translation of text, author and reader into exhibition, curator and visitor
  • Silverman, Lois H. (2010). The Social Work of Museums. London: Routledge. Silverman's needs grid and the ten functions of museum social work
  • Janes, Robert R. (2009). Museums in a Troubled World: Renewal, Irrelevance or Collapse?. London: Routledge. Janes on stewardship, the three agendas and the primus model

Barrett, Jennifer (2011). Museums and the Public Sphere. Chichester: Wiley-Blackwell.
romanticised communityBarrettcriticisescritique

The view that 'community' is no more democratic than 'public', since it too can be romanticised as inherently good and unified. Barrett criticises museums that replace 'public' with 'community' while continuing to operate as before. (Barrett 2011p. 111)

Draws on Jean-Luc Nancy

How it is used Barrett uses the critique to attack museum rhetoric in which 'community' replaces 'public' without any change of practice. Drawing on Nancy's account of community without essence, she proposes a notion of community as participants in the making and management of museums, with reciprocity as the safeguard against appropriation by well-intentioned professionals.

The curator's role of speaking for the museum to the public. Barrett argues that the role has been displaced by educators and managers, but that curators are not inherently barriers between museum and public and can take it up again. (Barrett 2011p. 13)

Comparing art, social history and anthropology, she argues that curators need more intellectual emphasis, not less, and that participatory and respectful curatorial practice can reposition the museum as a public intellectual.

Janes turns the concept to organisations, using Kabat-Zinn on digital distraction and the 'museum chatter' of governance and stress, and proposes thinking orthogonally as a way of keeping practice while questioning its assumptions.

Ways of writing museum history

Institutional, biographical, transnational and comparative approaches; periodisations and typologies of museums. 55 concepts from 39 texts

Institutional, biographical, transnational and comparative approaches treat a museum's history as a sequence of decisions taken by particular people, governments and networks, not as a steady march from collection to public display. Their question is how a given museum became what it is, and which earlier dependencies, rivalries or local ties its later account smooths away (Hill 2012p. 2; Miller 1973p. 17). Our texts draw most often on Foucault, mediated through Hooper-Greenhill; on Cooper and Stoler, mediated through Longair and McAleer; and on Patel, mediated through Meyer and Savoy (Hooper-Greenhill 1992p. 10; Longair & McAleer 2012p. 7; Meyer & Savoy 2014p. 5). Hooper-Greenhill's book stands at the centre of the anti-teleological position (Hooper-Greenhill 1992p. 191); Hill's edited volume and Miller's history of the British Museum test biographical and institutional forms (Hill 2012p. 2; Miller 1973p. 17); and Meyer and Savoy's volume gives the transnational case (Meyer & Savoy 2014p. 6).

Foucault and effective history

Hooper-Greenhill takes from Foucault the method of effective history, which stresses rupture and error rather than a smooth line from past to present (Hooper-Greenhill 1992p. 10). The method lets Hooper-Greenhill reread cabinets of curiosity that earlier histories dismissed as irrational, and it supports the claim that "There is no essential museum." (Hooper-Greenhill 1992p. 191). That claim is turned against accounts of a fundamental role for museums, such as Cannon-Brookes's (Hooper-Greenhill 1992p. 191). Hooper-Greenhill also criticises a 'safe' history of Sloane that describes his collecting without asking how Jamaica accelerated it (Hooper-Greenhill 1992p. 20).

Smoothing out and biography

Hill identifies the smoothing-out effect in biographical histories of charismatic curators, institutions and buildings, which make messy processes look coherent and progressive (Hill 2012p. 2). Abt applies corporate personhood to the Metropolitan, the Boston museum, the Art Institute of Chicago and the Detroit Institute of Arts, asking what a single legal identity conceals (Hill 2012p. 133). Sandino reads seven oral histories of V&A curators through Ricoeur's narrative identity, so that the curator's self is shaped by the institution's past (Hill 2012p. 88; Hill 2012p. 98). Miller goes the other way, following the people who secured the treasures rather than the objects (Miller 1973p. 17; Miller 1973p. 340). Gardner tells the Louvre along three fronts, architectural, institutional and historical, so that one chapter can join a building phase, an institutional change and a dynastic event (Gardner 2020).

Historicising collectors and colonial metropoles

Krech and Hail ask that collectors be returned to their own day, and reject presentist critiques of collecting as colonial disinheritance: "return collectors and museum founders to their day" is the stated goal (Krech & Hail 1999). Longair and McAleer take Cooper and Stoler's call to analyse metropole and colony together and find several local metropoles, such as Madras, Zanzibar and Melbourne, whose curators corresponded across the empire (Longair & McAleer 2012p. 7). McCarthy applies Cooper's critique of doing history backward to Maori responses to the Colonial Museum in Wellington, tracing them in visitors' books rather than inferring them from an imperialist gaze (Longair & McAleer 2012p. 58). Cvetkovski and Hofmeister add a knowledge history in which village healers compete with academic medicine (Cvetkovski & Hofmeister 2014p. 7; Cvetkovski & Hofmeister 2014p. 9).

Periodisation as argument

Several texts organise their histories around successive forms. Hopkins's five forms, from Enlightenment to post-national, each draw on the one before, and the post-national museum transcends rather than negates the national museum (Hopkins 2021). MacKenzie offers five colonial stages as a comparative frame, then qualifies them by denying a progressive continuum (MacKenzie 2009p. 265; MacKenzie 2009p. 270). Aldrich's three phases of colonial patrimony in France (display, concealment and renewed boom) order the book's sites and frame the Marseille memorial as a product of the third (Aldrich 2005p. 18; Aldrich 2005p. 329). Pearce's modern European museum, framed by meta-narratives of science and progress, serves as the frame of the whole book (Pearce 1992p. 16). Arnold reverses the usual account, reading the eighteenth-century move to typical specimens as a loss, which he labels dumbing-up (Arnold 2006).

The new museology and visitor research

Barrett dates the turn to visitor studies from the "new museology" that Vergo named in the late 1980s, and reads it through Bourdieu's research on visiting (Barrett 2011p. 3; Barrett 2011p. 148). Barrett then criticises the result: visitor studies and quantitative metrics reduce complexity and treat visitors as customers, leaving the curator's role unexamined (Barrett 2011p. 148). Hudson tests the claims of visitor surveys from the 1950s onward against the surveys that exist, and concludes that curators still rely on overheard remarks (Hudson 1975p. 100). Silverman places the community museums of Le Creusot, Anacostia and Hirano-cho in this movement, where forms were "tools of the people" (Silverman 2010p. 12). Pearson argues that the label hides audience-centred debates already set out in the Miers and Markham reports (Pearson 2017).

Transfer and transnational circulation

Meyer and Savoy apply Patel's transnational history, with its flows of people, ideas and products, to museums that had been studied as national institutions, keeping national boundaries as reference points (Meyer & Savoy 2014p. 5; Meyer & Savoy 2014p. 6). Adam narrows the frame: after about 1900 transfer passed from wealthy amateurs to professional directors who carried ideas in both directions, so that the German museum-association movement of 1913 was modelled on New York (Meyer & Savoy 2014p. 112). Silina extends Gough's model of museums as flexible laboratories to interwar Soviet display, treating failures as experiments (Silina 2026p. 1; Silina 2026p. 3). Tseng rejects the claim of Valéry and Malraux that the museum was foreign to Asia, linking the Meiji Imperial Museums to late-Edo temple airings and painting gatherings (Tseng 2008p. 210; Tseng 2008p. 211).

Folk objects and history from objects

Hall takes folkloric truth, the beliefs a community holds to be facts, as an object of interpretation beside historical fact, and argues that a history museum can show through which lens each is presented (Hall & Seemann 1987p. 77). Vlach applies the representativeness of folk objects to argue for a more democratic history: "The folk object is then extremely representative because it is so typical." (Hall & Seemann 1987p. 115). Conn tests the object-based epistemology of Mercer and Ford, who held that objects convey history more objectively than texts, and finds both using evolutionary and labour-centred frameworks that resemble older natural history museums (Conn 1998p. 154; Conn 1998p. 174). Durrans applies the time-machine display to Jorvik and to ethnographic halls, arguing that every surviving society has the same time-depth (Lumley 1988p. 143; Lumley 1988p. 144).

Debates and limits

The texts disagree most over the collector's standing. Krech and Hail reject presentist critiques that judge collectors by later standards (Krech & Hail 1999). Cuno defends an encyclopedic museum that keeps unprovenanced antiquities in circulation, against national retention laws (Cuno 2009p. 28). Buckley criticises relativism as museum orthodoxy and argues that museums should seek the truth and favour less powerful groups (Kavanagh 1996p. 42; Kavanagh 1996p. 44). Barrett criticises the visitor-studies turn, and Hudson finds that much visitor research was badly done, so both doubt the metrics that followed the new museology (Barrett 2011p. 148; Hudson 1975p. 100). Miller's institutional history gives sparse treatment to object histories and art history, which the object-based strand would require (Miller 1973p. 340).

Carrying it over to a new case

  • Ask what a regional museum's founders meant to do before judging their acquisitions by present standards of provenance, as Krech and Hail do for private collectors (Krech & Hail 1999).
  • Compare a colonial museum's local correspondence with its imperial correspondents, asking whether the networks ran around the capital or through it, as Longair and McAleer do for Madras and Zanzibar (Longair & McAleer 2012p. 7).
  • Trace who carried models between museums and when they became professionals, as Adam does for American and German museums (Meyer & Savoy 2014p. 112).
  • Read an origin story against the accession registers to find the trade, colonial or missionary sources it omits, as Hooper-Greenhill does for Sloane (Hooper-Greenhill 1992p. 20).
  • Ask whether a museum's chronology of its own collections ranks regional arts against a classical yardstick, as Çelik does for Istanbul (Çelik 2016p. 60).
  • Compare the pasts that a city museum of future plans invokes with the record it leaves out, as Denton does for planning halls in China (Denton 2014p. 266).
  • Test whether an ethnographic gallery's order from simple to complex is a choice of the museum or a feature of the material, as Durrans does (Lumley 1988p. 143).
  • Check whether a museum's surveys reach the people who do not come, as Hudson's critique of surveys implies (Hudson 1975p. 100).

Where to start reading

  • Hooper-Greenhill, Eilean (1992). Museums and the Shaping of Knowledge. London: Routledge. Hooper-Greenhill, for effective history and the critique of the 'safe' history of Sloane.
  • Hill, Kate (ed.) (2012). Museums and Biographies: Stories, Objects, Identities. Woodbridge: Boydell Press. Hill, for the smoothing-out critique and the biographical case studies.
  • Longair, Sarah; McAleer, John (eds.) (2012). Curating Empire: Museums and the British Imperial Experience. Manchester: Manchester University Press. Longair and McAleer, for local metropoles and peripheral imperial museums.
  • Meyer, Andrea; Savoy, Bénédicte (eds.) (2014). The Museum Is Open: Towards a Transnational History of Museums 1750–1940. Berlin: De Gruyter. Meyer and Savoy, for the transnational introduction and its tests of particular transfers.
  • Hall, Patricia; Seemann, Charlie (eds.) (1987). Folklife and Museums: Selected Readings. Nashville: American Association for State and Local History. Hall and Seemann, for folkloric truth and the representativeness of folk objects.
  • Barrett, Jennifer (2011). Museums and the Public Sphere. Chichester: Wiley-Blackwell. Barrett, for the public-sphere argument and the critique of visitor studies.
  • Hopkins, Owen (2021). The Museum: From Its Origins to the 21st Century. Hopkins, for the five forms of the museum and their sequence.

Aldrich, Robert (2005). Vestiges of the Colonial Empire in France: Monuments, Museums and Colonial Memories. Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan.
periodisation of display, concealment and renewed boomAldrichappliesperiodisation

The material patrimony of colonialism passed through three stages: colonialists marked the French landscape from 1890 through the 1940s; empire was forgotten from the 1960s through the 1980s; and since the 1990s there has been a boom in colonial interest, with exhibitions, memorials, debate and new museum projects. (Aldrich 2005p. 18)

How it is used Aldrich applies the three phases to monuments and museums and links them to lived experience (the imperial apogee of the 1930s, decolonisation, the 1990s rediscovery) and to the workings of memory. The periodisation structures the book's ordering of sites and gives the conclusion its account of the Marseille Mémorial as a product of the third phase.

“Monuments and museums reveal three stages in France’s” p. 18
colonial monumentsmuseum collectionsMarseille Mémorial National de l'Outre-Mer

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The same three-stage pattern could be tested against the Dutch, Belgian or Portuguese case, to see whether a concealment phase followed decolonisation there and whether the renewed boom came at a similar time.

Arnold, Ken (2006). Cabinets for the Curious: Looking Back at Early English Museums. Aldershot: Ashgate.
dumbing-upArnoldcoinsperiodisation

Arnold's term for the eighteenth-century shift from odd, anomalous objects to typical specimens and systematic inventories, which he reads as a loss of the earlier museum-science rather than a maturing into science. Arnold sets it against the late twentieth-century 'dumbing-down' of museums into experience-led institutions. (Arnold 2006)

How it is used Arnold reverses the usual account of museum history, in which the move to classification marks the coming of scientific seriousness, and reads the eighteenth-century taxonomic turn as a decline that parallels the present one. The reversal supports his remedy, which is to reapply seventeenth-century attention to specific objects. The argument depends on the two declines being comparable, and the introduction presents that comparison as its central parallel.

“the “dumbing-up” of the museum mission”
eighteenth-century taxonomic museumsthe British Museumlate twentieth-century experience-led museums

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The periodisation could be tested on a regional museum's catalogue history: does the move from anecdote to inventory there look like a loss of specificity or a gain in use?

Barrett, Jennifer (2011). Museums and the Public Sphere. Chichester: Wiley-Blackwell.
new museologyBarrettcriticisesperiodisation

The movement, named by Vergo in the late 1980s, that stressed visitors, thematic display and community consultation in answer to funding cuts and charges of elitism. Barrett uses it as the turning point after which visitor studies displaced curatorial authority in museum studies. (Barrett 2011p. 3)

Draws on Peter Vergo

How it is used Barrett periodises the public museum around this shift and reads it through Bourdieu's research on visiting. Barrett then criticises its results: visitor studies and quantitative metrics reduce complexity and treat visitors as customers, and the new museology's talk of the public left the curator's role unexamined.

“One result of the new museology was a move towards visitor studies and” p. 148
visitor studies programmesmuseum studies curricula

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could date the shift in a given national museum from its annual reports, to see when visitor evaluation began to outweigh curatorial reports.

Bilsel, Can (2012). Antiquity on Display: Regimes of the Authentic in Berlin’s Pergamon Museum. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
history as a tower (Hegelian and Schellingian models)Bilselappliesperiodisation

Hegel's and Schelling's models of the history of art and mind, translated into architecture as a tower or staircase culminating in a higher stage, which Stüler's Neues Museum is read as embodying. (Bilsel 2012PDF p. 63)

Draws on Hegel; Schelling

How it is used Bilsel reads the Neues Museum's staircase imagery as an architectural form of the Hegelian scheme, with a Christian monarchy at the top, and says the scheme later gave way to a view of history as a tree. Applied to Messel's Museum Island plan, the same scheme is found only in part: Bilsel argues that Bode's programme does not offer a linear history, because the route through the museum was ruptured and rewoven by correspondences between cultures.

“If the history of art is a Tower of” PDF p. 63
Neues Museum, BerlinMuseum Island master plan of Messel and Bode

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A museum's stair or route could be read the same way, asking which history of art or culture it presents as culminating and which routes it leaves out.

Çelik, Zeynep (2016). About Antiquities: Politics of Archaeology in the Ottoman Empire. Austin: University of Texas Press.
decadence as a historicising aesthetic termÇelikcriticisesperiodisation

A late-nineteenth-century aesthetic and historical term used to rank a society’s art against Periclean Athens, and to link artistic change to social, climatic and national boundaries; the Sidon sarcophagi, admired for their colour, were placed below pure Greek art because of it. (Çelik 2016p. 60)

How it is used Çelik traces how the term judged the Alexander sarcophagus as belonging to a decline, and shows how Strzygowski’s work on the “Orient” reversed the valuation of the Middle Eastern sites by making the East the source of late antique art. The argument shows that a periodisation of art was also a political verdict on the Ottoman lands.

“a popular and primarily aesthetic term” p. 60
Sarcophagus of Alexander, IstanbulBaalbek and Palmyra

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The concept invites a question about any museum’s chronology of its own collections, namely whether a periodising word such as decline or decadence was used to rank the arts of a region against a classical yardstick.

Conn, Steven (1998). Museums and American Intellectual Life, 1876–1926. Chicago: University of Chicago Press.
history from objectsConntestsanalytic concept

The view, held by Henry Mercer and Henry Ford and described by Conn, that ordinary tools and objects convey the nation's history more directly and objectively than written texts, which are subject to interpretation. Conn treats Mercer's 'History in Implements' lecture as its fullest statement. (Conn 1998p. 154)

How it is used Conn uses the two men's object history to test an object-based epistemology against the professional historians of their day. Conn shows that both men used evolutionary and labour-centred frameworks resembling the older natural history and anthropology museums, and that both were disconnected from academic history. Ford's Greenfield Village is read as the most ambitious version, and a 1925 visitor's words that the relics 'cannot lie' are quoted. The concept lets Conn argue that their history was neither purely nostalgic nor modern, but held past and present in unresolved tension.

“to create an “objective” history instead” p. 154
Mercer Museum, DoylestownHenry Ford Museum and Greenfield Village, Dearborn

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The concept could be used on a present-day community or company museum to ask which objects it treats as truer than documents, and which parts of the past it leaves out when it does so.

Cuno, James (ed.) (2009). Whose Culture? The Promise of Museums and the Debate over Antiquities. Princeton: Princeton University Press.
encyclopedic museumCunoappliestypology

A museum that gathers objects from all cultures and periods in one place, so that they are seen beside one another and produce understanding and tolerance. Cuno presents it as the Enlightenment type, embodied by the British Museum, and as the alternative to a nationalised culture. (Cuno 2009p. 28)

How it is used Cuno uses the type as the standard for judging acquisition of unprovenanced antiquities: a museum that keeps such objects in the public domain fulfils the encyclopedic purpose, while nationalist claims to a single national culture work against it. Cuno ties the argument to the Laocoön and the Rosetta Stone, whose value has always depended on circulation and reuse rather than on the find-spot.

“It is the promise of the encyclopedic museum to counter the nation-” p. 28
Art Institute of ChicagoBritish MuseumMetropolitan Museum of Art

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could test the same claim on a regional or colonial museum in Southeast Asia that holds undocumented material: whether it can be called encyclopedic, and what its acquisition records show about the purpose it serves.

two propositions on context and periodisationWatttestsperiodisation

Archaeological context matters more the earlier a period is, and less as written records cover a period more densely. Once enough tombs of a period have been excavated, further digging adds little, so antiquities can be valued directly as art. (Cuno 2009p. 89)

How it is used Watt tests the claim on Chinese material: a Neolithic Liangzhu cong, Lady Hao’s Shang jades, a Western Zhou ding, the Marquis of Zeng’s bells and the Tang horse of Li Xian. The Tang horse is his main case for the second proposition, since Tang tombs are known well enough that the tomb adds little to the horse.

The writing of history that treats knowledge as changeable, plural and dependent on its dissemination and social setting, with competing knowledge cultures and no single line of rising rationality. The introduction gives four meanings for the term. (Cvetkovski & Hofmeister 2014p. 7)

The method lets the editors look for specific situations and contact zones between knowledge areas rather than a single master story of Russian ethnography. Histories that use the historian’s own family relations to the past to open new ways of thinking about war’s legacies, distinguished from the popular boom of family research. “gonzo” historianStanleyappliestypology

A historian who writes himself or herself into the story, with the reporter’s own reactions and emotions made part of the account. Stanley borrows the term from Hunter S. Thompson’s gonzo journalism and applies it to Thomson and Scates. (Damousi 2020p. 129)

How it is used Stanley uses the term to characterise a new kind of Australian military history that treats emotion as part of the analysis. Stanley applies it to Thomson’s Anzac Memories and to Scates’s pilgrimage books, and he treats the criticism of sentimental nationalism as the test of whether such work is sound history.

“historians who write themselves into the stories they tell” p. 129

Urban planning exhibition halls that display visions of a future city rather than the past. Denton treats them as the final form of exhibitionary culture because past, present and future are bound together. (Denton 2014p. 265)

Gardner, James (2020). The Louvre: The Many Lives of the World’s Most Famous Museum. New York: Atlantic Monthly Press.
three fronts: architectural, institutional and historicalGardnercombinesmethod

Gardner's organising method: the Louvre's history is told at once as the history of the building, of the museum as an institution, and of the French dynasties and state that used the palace. (Gardner 2020)

How it is used The method lets Gardner tie the building to the museum. He treats the architecture, the founding of the museum and royal politics as one history, so that a chapter can show a building phase, an institutional change and a dynastic event together. He uses it across the book, with the Grande Galerie and the Second Empire Cour Napoléon as cases where form, institution and power meet.

“In telling the story of the Louvre, I have proceeded simultaneously along three fronts, the architectural, the institutional and the historical.”
the Louvre complex as a wholeGrande GalerieCour Napoléon

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A study of another palace turned museum could test whether the same three-part division recovers phases that a single-campaign reading hides.

placeness (lieu-dit)Gardnerappliesanalytic concept

The sense of the Louvre as a named piece of land with a prior existence before any building, a lieu-dit with no official standing, which the palace's scale and symmetry are designed to hide. (Gardner 2020)

How it is used Gardner uses the idea to open the book from the ground up. The name le Louvre predates Philippe Auguste's fortress of 1191, and the sites of the Cour Napoléon and place du Carrousel were in use for millennia before it. He argues that the later architecture, with its claims to superhuman scale, covers this origin, and he gives the 1980s excavations as the evidence that recovers it.

“I emphasize the “placeness” of the Louvre in part because everything about it today seems designed to reject and cover up its infinitely humble, elemental origins.”
the Cour Napoléon and place du CarrouselPhilippe Auguste's fortress

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The same question could be put to another royal or imperial museum: what was on the site before the building, and which later campaign made that earlier use invisible.

Hall, Patricia; Seemann, Charlie (eds.) (1987). Folklife and Museums: Selected Readings. Nashville: American Association for State and Local History.
folkloric truthHallcombinesanalytic concept

The beliefs a community holds to be the facts, and the reasons it holds them, as distinct from verifiable historical fact. Hall treats it as a legitimate object of interpretation alongside historical fact rather than as a source of error. (Hall & Seemann 1987p. 77)

How it is used Hall uses the distinction to answer historians who reject folklife data as unreliable. Hall argues that a history museum can set folkloric truth beside historical fact and make clear through which lens each is presented. The idea lets beliefs, myths and everyday notions enter exhibits without being presented as verified fact.

“Folklorists, in their study of culture, are concerned with folkloric truth” p. 77

folk object as representativeVlachappliesanalytic concept

Folk objects belong to a class of typical things used by many people, so unlike unique elite objects they stand for a broad social segment and a longer span of years. Representativeness is the basis for Vlach's case that folk artifacts should hold a central place in museums. (Hall & Seemann 1987p. 115)

How it is used Vlach uses the idea to argue for a more democratic and detailed history than one built on elite objects. A Buncombe County potter's crocks reflect local food preferences in a way a single elite piece cannot. He sets the idea against the one-of-a-kind residues of elite culture and argues that artifacts can check the authenticity of written history when historians and folklorists work together.

“The folk object is then extremely representative because it is so typical.” p. 115

Hill, Kate (ed.) (2012). Museums and Biographies: Stories, Objects, Identities. Woodbridge: Boydell Press.
narrative identitySandinoadaptsanalytic concept

Ricoeur’s idea that a person’s identity is a story that combines continuity of character with change over time. Sandino uses it to describe how V&A curators understood their own professional selves. (Hill 2012p. 88)

How it is used Sandino uses Ricoeur’s dialectic of sameness and self-constancy to read seven oral life histories of retired and serving V&A curators. The concept lets her show continuity in the civil-service ethos and the Official Secrets Act alongside change in how cataloguing was valued as core expertise. The result is an account of the curator’s identity as shaped by the institution’s history, not as an autonomous self.

The effect by which biographical histories of museums, whether of a charismatic curator, an institution or a building, make messy processes look coherent and progressive. Hill treats it as the main problem that the volume addresses. (Hill 2012p. 2)

How it is used Hill uses the idea to criticise celebratory histories of museums and their curators, and it organises the sections, which test individual biography, institutional biography and object biography in turn. Hill argues that lives of people, things and institutions can be ‘messier, more entwined, less coherent’ and still yield meaning. The critique is applied to MacLeod’s Walker Art Gallery, Abt’s corporate histories and the curators examined in the individual section.

corporate personhood of museumsAbtcriticisesanalytic concept

The legal idea that a private non-profit museum is a corporation with a single identity before the law, even though it is run by many people. Abt uses it to ask what the single identity of a museum conceals. (Hill 2012p. 133)

Abt applies this to the Metropolitan Museum, the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston, the Art Institute of Chicago and the Detroit Institute of Arts, and uses it to criticise life-story histories of museums for celebrating milestones rather than internal disputes or local ties.

Hill, Kate (ed.) (2021). Museums, Modernity and Conflict: Museums and Collections in and of War since the Nineteenth Century. London: Routledge.

Esben Kjeldbæk's three generations of war museum, each marked by a purpose: Ethos, tradition often driven by veterans and their special interest; Logos, historical study and detailed narratives of war; and Pathos, emotion produced through design, trends and a focus on visitors' needs. How it is used Tomasiewicz uses the typology to place the IWM in time. The Logos phase under Director-General Noble Frankland, who sought an 'objective' military history of the two world wars, is set against the later Pathos phase, and the chapter traces how the museum moved between the three. The typology gives a way to explain why the same museum could both celebrate objects and claim to be a social history.

“For Esben Kjeldbæk, war museums do not remain static in terms of their” p. 217
Imperial War Museum, London

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could code other national war museums by the same three purposes and ask which generation their founding narratives belong to.

Hooper-Greenhill, Eilean (1992). Museums and the Shaping of Knowledge. London: Routledge.
effective historyHooper-Greenhillappliesmethod

A way of writing the past that stresses discontinuity, rupture and error instead of a smooth, progressive line from past to present, so that today’s museum practices are not treated as given. The author takes it from Foucault and uses it to ask how museum forms were constituted at each moment. (Hooper-Greenhill 1992p. 10)

Draws on Foucault

How it is used Hooper-Greenhill applies the method to museum history, arguing that accounts which project present relations back as ‘direct ancestors’ miss the specific conditions of each period. It lets her reread cabinets of curiosity that earlier histories dismissed as irrational. It also serves as a yardstick for museum historians, many of whom, she argues, read archival documents in ways that presuppose a centralised collector-subject.

“rejects the notion of a continuous, smooth, progressive, totalising,” p. 10
Medici Palacecabinets of curiosityBritish Museum (Sloane)Tradescant and the Ashmolean

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could take one object-rich museum and ask which of its ‘errors’, such as an early classification that later looks irrational, were the conditions under which its holdings counted as knowledge.

‘safe’ historyHooper-Greenhillcriticisescritique

Museum histories written as chronological, incremental accounts of an already fixed museum, which select details that suit the present and avoid analysing the particular conditions in which collections were formed. The author calls the result a ‘safe’ and uncontentious history. (Hooper-Greenhill 1992p. 20)

Draws on Foucault

How it is used Hooper-Greenhill applies the critique to accounts of Sloane, whose ‘passion for collecting’ is described without asking how it was accelerated in Jamaica, and to histories of the Ashmolean that read Tradescant’s documents as evidence of a transcendental collector. Hooper-Greenhill notes that a later account links Sloane’s marriage to a Jamaican heiress and his part in the slave trade to his financial ability to collect, and she calls for an effective history that assesses such elements together.

“This results in the construction of a ‘safe’ and” p. 20
British Museum (Sloane)Ashmolean (Tradescant)

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher writing a founding history of a regional museum could check whether its origin story leaves out the trade, colonial or missionary sources that appear in its accession registers.

no essential museumHooper-Greenhillcriticisescritique

The claim that museums have no fixed identity, origin or single fundamental role: what a museum is, and what its objects mean, changes with each epistemic framework and with shifting relations of advantage. (Hooper-Greenhill 1992p. 191)

Draws on Foucault

How it is used This is the book’s central claim. It is turned against accounts that trace ‘direct ancestors’ of present museums, and against the idea of a ‘fundamental role’ for museums (Cannon-Brookes), and it is applied to each case study in turn. In the final chapter it is extended to modern museums, where Hooper-Greenhill argues that the meaning of an artefact can always be reopened, which she presents as the museum’s radical potential.

“There is no essential museum.” p. 191
Medici Palacecabinet of the worldRoyal Society RepositoryLouvremodern museum

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): Applied to a single collection, the idea would ask how its meaning changed across the frameworks of its founders, colonial administrators and later curators, and which of those meanings its displays left out.

Hopkins, Owen (2021). The Museum: From Its Origins to the 21st Century.
five manifestations of the museumHopkinsappliesperiodisation

The museum's history as five successive forms (Enlightenment, public, modern, global and post-national), each drawing on what came before and reshaping what came after. The Enlightenment museum classified the world that the wunderkammer had encapsulated. (Hopkins 2021)

How it is used Hopkins makes the chapter structure follow this periodisation and uses it in the conclusion to ask what comes next. The sequence treats the museum as one institution with changing aims rather than a fixed type, and it allows him to read each form as drawing on the one before, and the post-national museum as a transcendence of the national museum rather than its negation.

“Where the wunderkammer had sought to encapsulate the world, the Enlightenment Museum aimed at classifying it”
British Museum and Louvre (Enlightenment)South Kensington Museum (public)MoMA (modern)Guggenheim Bilbao (global)Museum of Black Civilizations, Dakar (post-national)

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The sequence could be tested against a national museum system, such as one in Southeast Asia, to ask whether its phases follow the same order or are driven by different forces, such as independence or regional tourism.

Hudson, Kenneth (1975). A Social History of Museums: What the Visitors Thought. London: Macmillan.
the market research ageHudsontestsperiodisation

The period from the 1950s onward in which visitor surveys became common, though few museums commissioned them. Hudson places the change against earlier practice, when success was measured by turnstile counts and public comment was not sought. (Hudson 1975p. 100)

Draws on Duncan F. Cameron; D. S. Abbey

How it is used Hudson reads Cameron and Abbey's 1961 verdict that visitor research had yielded little against the surveys that followed, and argues that much of the research was badly done. Hudson then tests the period's claims against the surveys that exist, and concludes that curators still rely on overheard remarks.

“Their conclusions were not encouraging.” p. 100
Ulster Museum survey (1967)Belfast visitor surveyMuseum of Non-Objective Painting commentsLondon museums survey of 1973

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask what a museum's surveys measure, and whether the sample and questions allow any claim about the people who do not come.

Impey, Oliver; MacGregor, Arthur (eds.) (1985). The Origins of Museums: The Cabinet of Curiosities in Sixteenth- and Seventeenth-Century Europe. Oxford: Clarendon Press.
Mannerist museumFučíkovátestsperiodisation

Erwin Neumann's term for Rudolf II's Kunstkammer at Prague, which he read as a systematic collection built on an encyclopaedic principle rather than a mere cabinet of curiosities. (Impey & MacGregor 1985p. 67)

Draws on Erwin Neumann; Thomas DaCosta Kaufmann

How it is used Fučíková reports Neumann's conclusion and Kaufmann's stress on the diplomatic role of the collection, and then argues that the arrangement was systematic yet hard for a modern reader to decode. Fučíková uses the inventory of 1607-11 to reconstruct the rooms and cupboards, which tests the term against the layout rather than accepting it as a label.

“it was thus a Mannerist museum” p. 67
Rudolf II's Kunstkammer, Prague

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The term could be tested on other late-sixteenth-century collections by asking whether their inventories show a deliberate order or only accumulation.

Kavanagh, Gaynor (ed.) (1996). Making Histories in Museums. London: Leicester University Press.
relativism as museum orthodoxyBuckleycriticisescritique

Relativism holds that every idea is relative to the culture that holds it and that all cultures' ideas are equally valid. Buckley treats this as a complacent orthodoxy in museums that makes truthful history impossible. (Kavanagh 1996p. 42)

Draws on Thomas Kuhn; Paul Feyerabend

How it is used Buckley argues against relativism in three steps: it contradicts itself, people from different cultures can still communicate by pointing and shared categories, and theories must answer to the world. From this he concludes that museums should seek the truth and favour the histories of less powerful groups, rather than pander to what visitors want.

“Relativism states that all ideas arise out of a particular culture or sub-culture.” p. 42
museum displays in generalcommercial theme parks

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The same test could be applied to a display that presents an Asian religion or a colonial episode as several equally valid accounts without evidence.

Krech, Shepard, III; Hail, Barbara A. (eds.) (1999). Collecting Native America, 1870–1960. Washington: Smithsonian Institution Press.
collectors in their own day (against presentism)Krechrejectsmethod

A method of writing museum history that returns collectors to the intellectual and social context of their time and explains their acts by their own intentions, rather than by later critiques of collecting as licentious, disinheriting or merely hegemonic. (Krech & Hail 1999)

Draws on T. J. Jackson Lears; Richard Wrightman Fox

How it is used The Introduction sets this method against critiques of collecting as colonial disinheritance and of exhibits as systems of enforced meaning, and says that explaining consumption by external power alone ignores the intentions of people at the time. The method lets the volume treat Haffenreffer, Lummis and Jackson as agents with reasons of their own, and it is the basis for the claim that presentist strokes obscure what collectors intended.

“One of our principal goals here is to return collectors and museum founders to their day, with the intent of comprehending anew their motivations and actions.”
Haffenreffer's King Philip Museumthe collectors treated across the nine chapters

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could apply the same test to a museum in Asia founded by a private collector, asking what the founder meant to do before judging the acquisitions by present standards of provenance and consent.

Longair, Sarah; McAleer, John (eds.) (2012). Curating Empire: Museums and the British Imperial Experience. Manchester: Manchester University Press.
multiple metropolesLongair, McAleeradaptstheoretical framing

Each museum city, such as Madras, Zanzibar or Melbourne, acted as a 'local metropole' with its own networks of exchange, so the empire had several centres rather than one London centre and colonial peripheries. (Longair & McAleer 2012p. 7)

Draws on Frederick Cooper; Ann Laura Stoler

How it is used The editors take the call by Cooper and Stoler to analyse metropole and colony in one field and turn it into a picture of many centres. They apply it to Madras, Zanzibar and Melbourne, where curators corresponded with colleagues across and beyond the empire, and where objects and expertise circulated between regions. The frame lets them argue that peripheral museums were not simply subordinate to London.

“one in which multiple metropoles may be identified” p. 7
Madras MuseumZanzibar MuseumNational Museum of Victoria, Melbourne

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask whether a museum in another empire, such as the Dutch East Indies, formed a similar local metropole with its own correspondence networks, and whether those networks ran around the imperial centre or through it.

doing history historicallyMcCarthyappliesmethod

A method, drawn from Cooper, that puts coloniser and colonised in one analytical frame, takes account of the alternatives open to people at the time, and avoids reading the past through present categories. (Longair & McAleer 2012p. 58)

Draws on Frederick Cooper

How it is used McCarthy applies Cooper's critique of 'doing history backward' to museum studies, where he finds a predilection for theory over history. McCarthy argues that Maori response to museums must be traced in archives, such as the visitors' books and the proposed National Maori Museum, rather than inferred from post-colonial theory about an 'imperialist gaze'. The method is what lets him show Maori negotiating with empire rather than being simply its objects.

“that includes both coloniser and colonised in the same” p. 58
Colonial Museum, Wellington visitors' booksProposed National Maori Museum (Hamilton and Carroll)

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The method could guide a study of any museum that displayed colonised people, by asking what options the visitors and performers themselves saw at the time.

Lumley, Robert (ed.) (1988). The Museum Time-Machine: Putting Cultures on Display. London: Routledge.
ethnohistoryHoyaucriticisesmethod

A discipline concerned with ways of life in a particular locality, which takes the minor, the everyday and the trivial as its subject and absorbs history into the study of community life. (Lumley 1988p. 28)

How it is used Hoyau treats ethnohistory as the channel through which history dissolves into ethnology: conflicts, resistance and specific sequences of events fade into an unchanging local landscape. Hoyau uses this to explain how the French heritage programme could draw on academic scholarship while leaving the past uncontested. The concept links a research discipline to a state policy, which is the step his argument depends on.

“History is absorbed” p. 28
French Heritage Year 1980 and its local inventories

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The idea suggests a question for local history museums: whether a community-focused display removes the historical conflicts that a national narrative would have to address.

time-machine displayDurranscriticisesanalytic concept

A display device that arranges peoples or periods in a sequence from past to present, which implies evolutionary grades so that living societies appear more or less primitive. (Lumley 1988p. 143)

How it is used Durrans applies the idea to the Jorvik Centre, where layers of history are stripped back to reach the reconstructed bustle of Viking York, and to ethnographic displays in which modern hunter-gatherers appear more primitive than cultivators or city-dwellers. Durrans argues that every surviving society has the same time-depth, so none can be judged by intrinsic primitiveness, and asks museums to show the classifications and provenance that shape the message. The image gives the volume its title.

“Ethnographic museums are influenced by the time-machines we” p. 143
Jorvik Centre, Yorkethnographic displays of contemporary hunter-gatherers

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could check whether an ethnographic gallery on another region arranges its cases from simple to complex, and whether that order is a museum choice or a feature of the material.

MacKenzie, John M. (2009). Museums and Empire: Natural History, Human Cultures and Colonial Identities. Manchester: Manchester University Press.
five-phase model of colonial museum historyMacKenziecoinsperiodisation

A five-stage sequence of museum development in the colonies: proto-foundation, pioneering, transitional, pre-modern and modern, whose key elements can be found in most museums even though the stages do not strictly apply to all of them. (MacKenzie 2009p. 265)

How it is used MacKenzie offers the sequence as a comparative frame for the cases in the book, from economic rhetoric and metropolitan models to local and then national identities. MacKenzie then qualifies it, arguing that the changes should not be seen as a progressive continuum and that museums remain malleable. The model lets him place Singapore's move from a colonial to a national museum alongside the settler cases.

“They can perhaps be divided into five, identified” p. 265
Royal Ontario MuseumSingapore National MuseumSouth African Museum

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could test whether a museum in a Southeast Asian or Chinese colonial city, such as a Hong Kong museum that the book leaves out, passes through the same five stages or a different sequence.

McClellan, Andrew (1994). Inventing the Louvre: Art, Politics, and the Origins of the Modern Museum in Eighteenth-Century Paris. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.
art historical survey museumMcClellanappliestypology

A museum arranged to demonstrate the history of art through works grouped by national school and in chronological sequence. The term comes from de Mechel's Vienna gallery, described as a showroom for the visual demonstration of the history of art. (McClellan 1994p. 4)

How it is used McClellan uses the type as the yardstick against which the Luxembourg, d'Angiviller's plan, the Revolutionary Louvre and Lenoir's chronological period rooms are measured. It lets the author show that the school-and-chronology model was an eighteenth-century invention which the Revolution then adopted and adapted for political purposes.

“a showroom for the visual demonstration of the history of art” p. 4
Vienna Imperial Gallery (de Mechel)Musee des monuments francaisLouvre Grand Gallery

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The type can be tested on a museum of Asian art arranged by dynasty or by national school, asking whether the chronological display converts a regional collection into a narrative of decline or progress.

cyclical decline of artMcClellantestsperiodisation

The idea, drawn from Winckelmann and taken up by Quatremere, that art passes through archaic, classic, imitative and decadent phases, so that art after the Renaissance is decline. McClellan sets it against an optimistic, non-cyclical view that Denon's hang implicitly adopted. (McClellan 1994p. 146)

Draws on Winckelmann; Quatremère de Quincy

How it is used McClellan uses the cyclical model as an interpretive standard for the Louvre hang of 1803, comparing it with Cosway's etchings of Denon's arrangement of the Raphael bays. The test shows that the museum's design made a historical argument, and that the choice between cycle and progress was tied to the political need of the Empire to show France as capable of a new great art.

“consistent with what might be termed the optimistic, noncyclical view of post-Renaissance art” p. 147
Raphael bays of the Louvre, 1803 (Denon)Emeric-David's preface to Le Musee francais

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask whether a museum of Asian art arranged to show a classical peak followed by decline, or a progressive sequence, makes a political claim about the region's history, and who benefits from each sequence.

Meyer, Andrea; Savoy, Bénédicte (eds.) (2014). The Museum Is Open: Towards a Transnational History of Museums 1750–1940. Berlin: De Gruyter.
transnational history of museumsMeyer, Savoyadaptstheoretical framing

A way of writing museum history that treats exchange across borders as a formative factor, instead of telling each nation’s museums as a separate story. The national frame is kept as one term among others, with its weight varying over time. (Meyer & Savoy 2014p. 5)

Draws on Patel; Pernau; Iriye and Saunier

How it is used The introduction takes Patel’s account of transnational history, with its flows of people, ideas and products, and applies it to museums, which had been studied mainly as national institutions. It keeps national boundaries as points of reference even where they are crossed, so the national and the transnational are read together. Each chapter then tests the idea on a particular transfer, such as the Kassel gallery, the Moscow museum or the Metropolitan.

“It thus signals that national boundaries – as implied in the term “transnational” – do” p. 6
Kassel Picture GalleryPushkin Museum, MoscowMetropolitan Museum, New YorkNational Gallery, LondonLisbon national museum

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask, for any single national museum, which of its models, staff or objects came from abroad and whether its national story survives that record. The same question works for museums in Asia that were built on European or Japanese models.

professionalization of intercultural transferAdamappliesperiodisation

The shift after about 1900 from the transfer of museum models by wealthy amateurs to a systematic practice by professional directors and academics who visited museums, reported to their trustees and carried ideas in both directions. (Meyer & Savoy 2014p. 112)

How it is used Adam applies the periodisation to American museum building, using the report by A. B. Meyer on American museums and the Boston commission that toured ninety-five European museums. Meyer uses it again to argue that the German museum-association movement of 1913 was modelled on New York and earlier German associations, which Seidlitz had overlooked. The periodisation lets him show that transfer was reciprocal and that the origins of models became obscured.

“the transfer of such models was an occupation for wealthy dilettantes, it turned into” p. 112
Metropolitan Museum of Art, New YorkBoston museum commissionGerman museum-association movement, 1913

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could ask when the professional transfer of museum models began between Europe and East Asia, and who acted as the professional intermediary in that exchange.

Miller, Edward (1973). That Noble Cabinet: A History of the British Museum. London: André Deutsch.
the house-like spirit of the MuseumMillerappliestheoretical framing

The Museum has kept the intimacy and customs of the private house in which it was once lodged, such as housekeepers, house-keys, a house-list and entry by the Front Hall, and this continuity persists through change. (Miller 1973p. 17)

How it is used Miller makes the image the frame of the whole book, presenting the Museum as one institution across the move from Montagu House to later buildings and across the changes of the twentieth century. It sets the book's pace, since changes are measured against surviving customs. The image is asserted in the Author's Note and is not tested against the evidence that follows, so it works as a premise rather than an argument.

“It is this spirit of continuity, which I have endeavoured to stress” p. 17
Montagu Housethe Front Hall entrancestaff housekeepers and the house-list

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could test whether a comparable house image explains continuity in another national museum, using staff customs and entrances as evidence.

history through the people who secured the treasuresMillerappliesmethod

The treasures are touched on only as they relate to those, whether staff or not, who acquired them for the Museum, so the institutional story runs through Trustees, Keepers, benefactors and staff rather than through the objects. (Miller 1973p. 17)

How it is used Miller applies this throughout: Hawkins and the Canino vases, Elgin and his marbles, Franks and his bequests, and Eumorfopoulos in the 1930s. It keeps the book on administrative decisions, money and personal rivalry, so the reader learns why objects arrived and how they were funded, not what they mean. This accounts for the book's sparse treatment of object histories and art history.

“treasures have here been touched upon only incidentally and then for” p. 17
the Department of Antiquities 1820-1860Franks's bequests of 1897the Eumorfopoulos Chinese collection

A shift in historical scholarship from campaigns and commanders to the common soldier, the experience of war and the place of the armed forces in society. The authors date its arrival in military museum display to the 1980s. (Muchitsch 2013p. 42)

How it is used The authors use the shift as a yardstick for American military exhibitions. The 1987 Japanese-American exhibit and G.I. (1992) drew on it, but the 2002 West Point exhibit was framed around the graduates' biographies and economic development, and the Price of Freedom hall (2004) reverted to weapons and uniforms with little context. They conclude that the change came only slowly.

“illustrate how little the presentation of war mattered” p. 55
A More Perfect Union (1987)G.I. (1992)West Point in the Making of America (2002)The Price of Freedom (2004)

Naquin, Susan (2004). “The Forbidden City Goes Abroad: Qing History and the Foreign Exhibitions of the Palace Museum, 1974–2004”. T’oung Pao, 90 (2004).

Naquin's sequence of four changes in the exhibitions and the scholarship: a turn toward court life, Central Asian and Tibetan elements, China's links with Europe, and the Qianlong reign. (Naquin 2004p. 379)

How it is used The four shifts structure the closing section. Naquin ties the exhibitions to changes in the Qing field, such as the opening of Beijing archives in the 1980s and the reappraisal of Manchu identity in the 1990s, so that the catalogues become evidence of scholarship as well as of collecting.

“Looking over the whole period from 1974 to 2004” p. 379
1985 Berlin catalogue1996-97 Paris catalogue2002 Taipei and 2002 Edinburgh Qianlong shows

Paver, Chloe E. M. (2018). Exhibiting the Nazi Past: Museum Objects Between the Material and the Immaterial. Cham: Palgrave Macmillan.
object-oriented exhibitions and object renunciation (Objektbezogenheit, Objektverzicht)Paveradaptstypology

Exhibitions on 1933 to 1945 are of two basic types: those oriented towards objects and those that renounce them, with documentation centres showing documents and photographs rather than objects. The typology is drawn from Drecoll and is used as a description of the field. (Paver 2018p. 2)

Draws on Axel Drecoll

How it is used Paver takes Drecoll's typology as the starting point of her introduction and then qualifies it, arguing that the two types operate in tandem rather than in competition and that some documentation centres have moved into object collection. This lets her answer the objection that documentation centres are the new norm and justify a book about objects.

“types of exhibition about the years 1933–45, characterized either” p. 2
Dokumentation Obersalzberg, with a plan to display 350 objectsGermany's national history museums and their collections

Pearce, Susan M. (1992). Museums, Objects, and Collections: A Cultural Study. Leicester: Leicester University Press.
modern museum and the meta-narratives of modernityPearceappliesperiodisation

The museum is a modern European institution, which came to birth in the Renaissance cities and courts of Italy and spread with other European institutions. Modernity is a set of meta-narratives that claim objective reality and eternal truths, running from an early phase in the mid fifteenth to mid seventeenth centuries through classic modernity to a post-modern present. (Pearce 1992p. 16)

Draws on Habermas; Harvey; Giddens; Jameson

How it is used Pearce uses this periodisation to frame the whole book: the museum's linear European development is the case, and the modern meta-narratives of science, progress and great men are what museum collections served. The framing is set against the 1857 description of the Victoria and Albert Museum and the Apollo 17 rock at the National Air and Space Museum, and it lets her treat museums as objects of critical social theory in the present.

“Museums are a typical part of modern European cultural expression,” p. 16
Victoria and Albert MuseumNational Air and Space Museum

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The same periodisation could be tested on a non-European museum, asking whether its founding meta-narratives were nation-building or colonial rather than scientific and progressive.

structuration and Braudel's time-scalesPearcecombinesanalytic concept

Giddens's structuration, in which people make choices that both reproduce and change structures, is joined to Braudel's three time-scales of event, conjuncture and long-term structure. An object's meaning is seen as built up across its commission, its owners and its exhibitions. (Pearce 1992p. 319)

Draws on Giddens; Braudel

How it is used Pearce uses the combination to explain a Limoges reliquary of about 1200 in the Burrell Collection, Glasgow, whose meaning accumulated across its history. Pearce closes with two doubts, that the model needs real individuals with genuine choices and that object meanings are stable when they may be radically polysemic, which tests the model against the object itself.

“Giddens, who has developed the theory of structuration (e.g. 1984).” p. 319
Limoges reliquary, Burrell Collection, GlasgowChelsea porcelain tureens, Fitzwilliam Museum

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The three time-scales could be applied to a Southeast Asian object that changed hands across colonial and post-colonial display, asking which changes were conjunctural and which were long-term.

Pearson, Catherine (2017). Museums in the Second World War: Curators, Culture and Change. London: Routledge.

The claim that later curators reinvented debates about audience-centred museums and social purpose as a 'new museology' because they had lost the history that had already raised them in the inter-war years. (Pearson 2017)

Draws on Vergo

How it is used Pearson turns the new-museology label against itself. Pearson argues that audience-centred ideas were already set out in the Miers and Markham reports, that the mid-1950s retreat to collections erased them, and that museological theory has grown apart from practice, so the wartime record is lost to the profession.

“older debates as a ‘new museology’ without any recourse to the past”
Miers (1928) and Markham (1938) reportsthe post-war return to collections in the 1950s

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could check a current museum policy statement for ideas already present in older surveys, and trace which of them were dropped during a later period of retrenchment.

Rees Leahy, Helen (2012). Museum Bodies: The Politics and Practices of Visiting and Viewing. Farnham: Ashgate.
period eyeLeahyappliesanalytic concept

Baxandall's idea that the skills needed to apprehend works of art are historically and culturally acquired, so that artists respond to an attuned viewer and viewing norms vary from period to period. (Rees Leahy 2012p. 116)

Draws on Baxandall; Adrian Randolph; David Solkin

How it is used Leahy extends the idea from painting to exhibitions, asking whether the period eye can explain the operation of visuality within a display. Leahy’s example of a fifteenth-century Chinese viewer shows how expectations shape what is seen, and she tests the idea against Solkin's reconstruction of the crowded Royal Academy hang in Art on the Line.

“Baxandall’s concept of the ‘period eye’ is based on the premise that the” p. 116
Royal Academy hang reconstructed in Art on the Line (Courtauld)

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): One could ask what a visitor from a different visual tradition would make of a display of Chinese or Japanese painting, and whether the labels assume a period eye.

Sandell, Richard; Nightingale, Eithne (eds.) (2012). Museums, Equality and Social Justice. London: Routledge.
discovered identities and hidden historiesWinchestercriticisescritique

The approach of many recent exhibitions that present same-sex desire as discovered in the past through retrospective outing. Winchester regards it as a restrictive trans-historical essentialism that tells gradual stories of liberation. (Sandell & Nightingale 2012)
