Winchester applies this to the V&A's LGBTQ Network programmes and to William Beckford's collecting, arguing that the museum should be a book with its pages always open, in which exclusions are deliberate and visible. The target is a museological practice rather than particular objects.

“‘discovered’ identities and ‘hidden’ histories, telling self-consciously bright and optimistic narratives”
V&A LGBTQ Network programmes (from 2006)William Beckford's collecting and scrapbooksGran Fury's Kissing Doesn't Kill

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): One could ask whether queer or gender-variant objects in a Southeast Asian or Chinese collection are presented as discoveries, when their own contexts would support a fuller account.

Sellers, Charles Coleman (1980). Mr. Peale’s Museum: Charles Willson Peale and the First Popular Museum of Natural Science and Art. New York: W. W. Norton.
the New Museum IdeaSellerscombinesperiodisation

The British mid-nineteenth-century movement, defined by John Edward Gray in 1864 as the diffusion of instruction and rational amusement among the people together with scientific access to the specimens. Sellers treats it as the later, British form of Peale's concept, arrived at without borrowing from Philadelphia. (Sellers 1980p. 333)

Draws on John Edward Gray; Richard Owen; Edward Forbes

How it is used Sellers uses the New Museum Idea to close the book: the Peale plan was lost in America and revived through Bickmore's American Museum of Natural History, which he presents as the Peale concept in new form. Sellers treats the idea as a transatlantic movement with its own British origin, so the periodisation shows a shared pattern rather than a direct line of influence from Philadelphia.

“The New Museum Idea” was British in origin” p. 333
the American Museum of Natural Historythe British Museum (Natural History)South Kensington

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could test whether a museum in East or Southeast Asia during the same period adopted the diffusion-of-instruction language of the New Museum Idea, and whether it came from British, American or Japanese models.

Shapiro, Michael Steven (ed.); Kemp, Louis Ward (1990). The Museum: A Reference Guide. New York: Greenwood Press.
noncanonical reading of canonical textsShapiroappliesmethod

A way of reading the existing literature on museums that takes its established works as objects to be questioned, examining the assumptions beneath them rather than accepting them as authorities. The introduction borrows the phrase from Dominick LaCpra. (Shapiro & Kemp 1990PDF p. 16)

Draws on Dominick LaCpra

How it is used The introduction asks contributors to challenge the assumptions underlying the literature and to reconsider familiar episodes in museum history. Porter applies the reading to natural history museums, dismissing the view that they became inactive storehouses in the nineteenth century and reconstructing them as scientific institutions that disseminated research. The method lets the volume assess works written for different purposes and audiences rather than simply list them.

“Dismissing the view that the natural history museum became an inactive storehouse” PDF p. 16
natural history museums of the nineteenth centuryfamiliar episodes in American museum history across the chapters

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could read the standard histories of museums of Asian art in the West the same way, asking which canonical accounts of acquisition and display were written without the Asian objects or their makers in view.

Silina, Maria (2026). Soviet Museums Between the Two World Wars: Art History on Display. London: Routledge.
museum as experimental laboratorySilinaadaptstheoretical framing

Maria Gough's account of avant-garde museums as flexible laboratories for experiment and exchange, which Silina extends to most interwar Soviet displays. On this view museums were hubs of a broader cultural network open to local communities, and their failures count as experiments. (Silina 2026p. 1)

Draws on Maria Gough; Kazimir Malevich; Osip Brik; Nikolai Punin

How it is used Silina extends Gough's analysis of the avant-garde Museum of Painterly Culture to the whole range of interwar display: period rooms, children's shows and quick-response exhibitions. This lets her treat the Marxist displays and everyday-life museums as serious museum work rather than as propaganda, and it moves the question from artists' museums to professional curatorial work.

“As this book demonstrates, not only venues for contemporary art but also the majority” p. 3
Museum of Painterly Culture, Moscoweveryday-life museumsMarxist displays at the Tretyakov Gallery

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The frame could be used to ask whether early Chinese or Japanese museums that were run as experiments, as in the work the notes cite on China, reveal a similar tension between laboratory and public.

history of errorsSilinaadaptsmethod

The proposal to write the history of museums that were judged unsuccessful, vulgar or outmoded, treating their failures as a source of conceptual and creative potential rather than as a closed episode. Silina borrows the question from Eric Naiman. (Silina 2026p. 6)

Draws on Eric Naiman

How it is used Silina adapts Naiman's question, whether museums that did not survive should be judged as their critics judged them, to justify reading the everyday-life museums and Marxist displays on their own terms. The method lets her show that the criticism of the mid-1930s was itself a political act, and that abandoned projects still shaped later display.

“do we really need to think about museums that did not survive the Second” p. 6
everyday-life museumsMarxist displays at the Tretyakov Gallery

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The method could be applied to closed or reorganised display projects in other national museum systems, reading them for what they proposed as well as for why they were closed.

Silverman, Lois H. (2010). The Social Work of Museums. London: Routledge.
new museology: integrated, ecomuseum and neighbourhood museumsSilvermanappliesperiodisation

The late 1960s and 1970s movement in which museums became embedded in their communities: the integrated museum in Latin America, the ecomuseum in France and the neighbourhood museum in the United States, all with deep community involvement in operation and display. (Silverman 2010p. 12)

Draws on van Mensch; de Varine; Davis

How it is used Silverman uses the new museology as the turning point in her history of museums as social service. Placing Le Creusot, the Latin American integrated museum and the Anacostia Neighborhood Museum together, she shows that communities can shape a museum's operations, and this sets up the empowerment argument of Chapter 6.

“forms were not just for the people but tools of the people.” p. 12
Le Creusot ecomuseum, FranceAnacostia Neighborhood Museum, Washington DCHirano-cho Ecomuseum, Osaka Prefecture

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): A researcher could test whether a neighbourhood museum in a Japanese or Vietnamese city shows the same community control as the Hirano-cho case, or whether the state runs it.

Tseng, Alice Y. (2008). The Imperial Museums of Meiji Japan: Architecture and the Art of the Nation. Seattle: University of Washington Press.
the museum as a cross-cultural invention rather than a European oneTsengrejectscritique

The museum was not naturally European: analogous practices of collecting, preserving and exhibiting existed in Asian cultures, and the state-run museum is an invention that arose from particular social and cultural aspirations. (Tseng 2008p. 210)

Draws on Paul Valéry; André Malraux

How it is used Tseng rejects the claim of Valéry and Malraux that the museum was foreign to Asia. Tseng argues that the museum disoriented Valéry as much as it would any Asian visitor, that Malraux's own argument applied to Europe and non-Europe alike, and that the Meiji museums arose from aims of national display and public education, linked to late-Edo temple airings and painting gatherings. This lets her treat the Imperial Museums as one case of a general process rather than a precarious graft.

“museum, particularly the state-run museum, as an invention that arose from a” p. 211
Imperial Museums in Tokyo, Kyoto and Naralate-Edo temple airings and painting gatherings

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): One could ask whether a museum in a Southeast Asian state built under colonial or post-colonial conditions was an invention of similar aspirations, rather than an import, and what earlier practices it drew on.

Meiji self-representation and the historiography of the periodTsengadaptsmethod

Studies of Meiji must be careful not to repeat the period's own claims to newness and rupture. Tseng draws on Gluck's warning that writers on Meiji must escape the restraints of the period's self-representation and draws a clear line between the changes that took place and the claims made for them. (Tseng 2008p. 15)

Draws on Carol Gluck

How it is used Tseng uses this to argue that the Imperial Museums were both modern and rooted in older identities: modernisation heightened more than it disrupted the primacy of religion in Nara and of artistic industries in Kyoto. Tseng applies it to the museums' rhetoric of progress and to the dual-capital symbolism, so that the Kyoto and Nara museums are read as continuations rather than breaks.

“A discussion of the Imperial Museums inevitably requires treading” p. 15
Imperial Kyoto MuseumImperial Nara Museum

Possible use elsewhere (a suggestion, not the author's claim): The same caution could be applied to the official histories of museums in other Asian states, which often present a museum as the founding act of a new nation.

Each text's framing, inspirations, opponents, methods and gaps

Open a text for its overall stance, the concepts it works with, the positions it argues against, the sources and ways of working it relies on, and the gaps it names.

Alberti, Samuel J. M. M. (2009). Nature and Culture: Objects, Disciplines and the Manchester Museum. Manchester: Manchester University Press.7 concepts

The book frames the Manchester Museum as a site where nature, culture and the disciplines that study them were built and rebuilt through buildings, objects and people. Its overall argument is that disciplinary order in the museum was contingent and that people, rather than objects, drove these changes. It is an institutional and social history that draws on museum studies, the history and sociology of science, and the study of material culture.

Concepts and inspirations

  • disciplinary topography (cultural cartography) (Ken Arnold; Thomas Gieryn)
  • disciplines built from objects (Simon Knell)
  • object biography (social life of things) (Igor Kopytoff; Arjun Appadurai)
  • fivefold typology of acquisition
  • exhibitionary practices
  • museums as political instruments and machines for making meaning (Eilean Hooper-Greenhill; Susan Pearce; Tony Bennett)
  • federation of knowledge practices (John Pickstone)

Argues against

  • accounts that give museum objects an active role in shaping meanings: Objects did not act in their own right; material culture was acted upon and was a conduit for human intention. p. 189
  • object biographies that ignore the afterlife of things after accession: Chapter 5 attends to the practices that operated on objects inside the museum, including conservation, cataloguing, storage and display. p. 5
  • museum studies centred on state-level governance: The book explores an intermediary, local level of control in provincial England and its audience constituencies. p. 191
  • the apparent stability of disciplinary boundaries: Boundaries can be deceptive: objects collected under different intellectual auspices were only recently grouped as archaeology. p. 192

Sources and ways of working

  • manuscripts, publications and oral history testimony p. 191
  • Museum Committee minutes and annual reports, with staff appointments p. 60
  • oral histories of museum visiting and staff recollection p. 191
  • comparison with other university and provincial collections such as the Hunterian, Pitt Rivers and Horniman p. 2

Gaps it names

  • a comprehensive history of museums in the twentieth century p. 193
  • displaying and collecting at the end of empire, as context for post-colonial museology p. 193
  • the role of museums in the Cold War and the fate of cultural institutions under the 1980s government p. 193
  • comparative work on the processes of collection, conservation and display across museums p. 191

Contents and chapter overviews

Aldrich, Robert (2005). Vestiges of the Colonial Empire in France: Monuments, Museums and Colonial Memories. Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan.7 concepts

Aldrich frames museums, monuments and street names as 'colonial lieux de mémoire': places where the French have built, displayed, forgotten and only partly recalled their empire. The overall argument is that colonial traces are more widespread than they appear, that the French remembered selectively rather than erasing the past, and that current museum and memorial projects are a late, ambivalent attempt to come to terms with it. It is a cultural and political history of memory and heritage, with elements of art history (Orientalist painting, non-Western art) and museum studies.

Concepts and inspirations

  • colonial lieux de mémoire (sites of memory) (Halbwachs; Nora)
  • selective memory and forgetting (Renan; Marc Augé; Régis Debray)
  • culture of imperialism and culture contact (John Mackenzie)
  • ambivalence
  • Orientalism as a contested category (Edward Said; John Mackenzie; Roger Benjamin)
  • pedigree of objects
  • periodisation of display, concealment and renewed boom

Argues against

  • the view that Orientalism is simply a branch of colonialism: Orientalism and colonialism are not synonymous; much artistic influence from overseas occurred during conquest, and the works resonate with colonialist stereotypes without being identical to them p. 11
  • the view that the French simply forgot their empire: if the French tried to reject the memory of colonialism, it pushes its way to the surface, as events in France and in the former colonies provide unavoidable reminders p. 7

Sources and ways of working

  • visits to monuments and museums supplemented by published catalogues and secondary literature, with no claim to a full inventory PDF p. 9
  • reading museum labels for provenance information and for what they say about the colonial past p. 287
  • comparison of the display methods of older ethnographic museums with those of modern galleries such as the Musée Dapper p. 268

Gaps it names

  • France has no museum of colonial history; the 1990s debate on such an institution stalled until the Marseille initiative p. 328
  • little scholarship on the commemoration of the dead of the Indochinese and Algerian wars p. 11
  • the relative scarcity of monuments to the Indochinese War, which Aldrich links to the difficulty of commemorating defeat p. 124

Contents and chapter overviews

Arnold, Ken (2006). Cabinets for the Curious: Looking Back at Early English Museums. Aldershot: Ashgate.8 concepts

Arnold frames the early museum as a workshop where seventeenth-century English collectors produced factual knowledge from individual objects, and argues that the three strategies they developed (narrative, functional and taxonomic) still shape museum work. The book is a cultural and intellectual history of science, written by a practising exhibition maker, and it draws on museum studies, anthropology and philosophy mainly as analytic counterpoints in its diachronic chapters. Its overall argument is that the eighteenth-century move to classification lost the curious object, and that present-day museums should recover the seventeenth-century habit of attending to particular things.

Concepts and inspirations

  • epistemology of the hunt (William Eamon; Ginsburg; Bruce Trigger)
  • narrative, functional and taxonomic strategies
  • dumbing-up
  • objects removed from use (Baudrillard and Pomian) (Jean Baudrillard; Krystof Pomian)
  • contact zones (James Clifford)
  • wonder (Stephen Greenblatt; Marina Warner; P. Fisher)
  • authenticity (Donald Horne)
  • Renaissance episteme (Michel Foucault)

Argues against

  • Douglas Crimp and Steven Mullaney, who deny that early cabinets resemble modern museums: Arnold stresses both continuity and difference between then and now, and says the two sides are meaningfully comparable.
  • Thomas Kuhn's split between mathematical and experimental traditions in the scientific revolution: Natural historians, collectors and fact-gatherers formed a second, idiographic tradition of scientific practice that Kuhn's account leaves out.
  • Foucauldian readings of museums as discipline and confinement: The image of passive visitors shepherded through museums is not useful for seventeenth- and early-eighteenth-century England, where visitors were active investigators.
  • Baudrillard and Pomian on the sealed, virtual economy of museum objects: Museum value is in constant exchange with glamour, academia, religion and politics, so the uses of museums are more complicated than their accounts suggest.

Sources and ways of working

  • exhibition-making and curatorial practice, used to ask how objects are handled after accession
  • collection catalogues, such as Sloane's 'Miscelanies' and the Tradescant and Ashmolean catalogues, read for each object's origin and use
  • Royal Society questionnaires sent to travellers and the Society's correspondence, read as evidence of what collectors wanted to know
  • visitor diaries, such as Ralph Thoresby's account of visiting collectors and collections

Gaps it names

  • collections of mathematical, mechanical and surgical instruments, inscriptions and antiquities, manuscripts and anatomical preparations, which the book deliberately leaves out
  • the poetic, symbolic, political, emotional and experiential aspects of museum objects, which the book does not scrutinise
  • the parallel history of the emotional responses visitors have to objects, which has a large literature that the book does not cover
  • what role the collections of twentieth-century anthropology museums still play, which the author says the book cannot attempt

Contents and chapter overviews

Askew, Rie Kido (2007). “The Politics of Nostalgia: Museum Representations of Lafcadio Hearn in Japan”. museum and society, 5.3 (November 2007): 131-147.5 concepts

Askew frames the Hearn museums in Japan as sites of postwar memory, where nostalgia for 'Old Japan' depoliticises a writer whose views included approval of sacrifice for the Emperor. It is a museum-studies and cultural-politics article that reads exhibits as texts, using Porter's framework and Nora's notion of places of memory. Its argument is that the museums' nostalgia is a response to modernization and to the denial of the war, and that moving beyond it requires facing both.

Concepts and inspirations

  • places of memory (Nora)
  • Old Japan and New Japan
  • the depoliticizing of Hearn (Zolberg)
  • exhibit, curator and visitor as text, author and reader (Porter)
  • nostalgia as the function of the museums (Urry; Gerster)

Argues against

  • Öta's view that Hearn's letters reveal a real Hearn who spoke of Japan with abhorrence, so that the lover-of-Japan image is a 'myth': Askew says Öta's position is somewhat overstated, but Hearn did express occasional disgust for Japan, as in his dislike of the common people of Kumamoto. p. 137
  • Kobori's argument that Hearn's praise of Yasukuni supports the Prime Minister's visits to the shrine: Askew accepts that Hearn approved of self-sacrifice for the Emperor, and reads this as the reason the museums avoid him, not as a justification. p. 139

Sources and ways of working

  • visits to each of the three museums, examining exhibits, labels, video and the house, and identifying what is remembered and forgotten p. 132
  • museum pamphlets, official websites and written correspondence with each museum p. 132
  • comparison of the museum narratives with the Yushukan's official pictorial record p. 138

Gaps it names

  • the popular Japanese reception of Hearn, which no analysis to date has examined p. 132
  • how the Yaizu museum can attract visitors and persuade citizens to return, given few exhibits p. 136

Contents and chapter overviews

Asma, Stephen T. (2001). Stuffed Animals and Pickled Heads: The Culture and Evolution of Natural History Museums. New York: Oxford University Press.8 concepts

Asma frames natural history museums as 'three-dimensional windows into the world of ideas' whose presentation frame, the arrangement and staging around specimens, shapes what visitors learn without their noticing. Specimens take their meaning from the systems and settings that present them, so the book reads museum history through the changing organising principles of collections. It is a cultural and intellectual history of science, combining the history of anatomy and taxonomy, a narrative account of museum fieldwork and interviews, and a philosophy of display; it reads more as an intellectual memoir than as formal museum studies.

Concepts and inspirations

  • presentation frame
  • specimen as cipher
  • collecting as mastery (Freud and Baudrillard) (Sigmund Freud; Jean Baudrillard; Rheims)
  • kinds of spectacle (odd, wonderful, grotesque) (Plato; Freud)
  • function over form in arrangement (Cuvier; Hunter)
  • intuition pumps (Daniel Dennett; Plato; Descartes)
  • nonoverlapping magisteria (NOMA) (Stephen Jay Gould)
  • culture-bound classification (Jorge Luis Borges; Michel Foucault)

Argues against

  • Freud's psychoanalytic account of collecting: the Freudian analysis is too speculative and untestable to be of more value
  • the criticism of museums for offering too much show and too little substance: that criticism is frequently driven by an old cultural prejudice, with a prevalent Western prejudice against visual imagery behind it
  • Gould's NOMA settlement: Gould does not explain the source of his ontological commitments; he only identifies the domain from which they do not originate

Sources and ways of working

  • interviews with taxidermists and museum staff in the back rooms, and observation of skin preparation
  • interviews with museum designers and display developers about how exhibits are built and how associations are chosen
  • visitor feedback: talk-back boards and visitors' typed letters tacked up beside the exhibit

Gaps it names

  • the book is not an exhaustive survey of modern museums; the other collections were chosen to illustrate specific theoretical points
  • the deeper genetic and developmental mechanisms behind teratological monsters, which were not understood until the twentieth century

Contents and chapter overviews

Barrett, Jennifer (2011). Museums and the Public Sphere. Chichester: Wiley-Blackwell.9 concepts

Barrett frames museums as a cultural public sphere: sites of public address that are spatial and visual as well as discursive, and that fall short of democratic ideals because of their ties to the state and to society. The book is a critical study in museum studies that draws on social and political theory of the public sphere (Habermas and his critics), on the sociology of cultural taste (Bourdieu), and on the post-colonial and critical analysis of museum display, and it argues from the history of museums and from visitor and curatorial practice.

Concepts and inspirations

  • cultural public sphere (Habermas)
  • counter-public (Nancy Fraser)
  • disciplinary space and heterotopia (Michel Foucault; Tony Bennett; Eilean Hooper-Greenhill)
  • cultural capital (Pierre Bourdieu; Bourdieu and Darbel)
  • romanticised community (Jean-Luc Nancy)
  • contact zone (James Clifford; Eilean Hooper-Greenhill)
  • new museology (Peter Vergo)
  • public intellectual
  • appropriate museology (Kreps)

Argues against

  • Habermas's model of rational discourse as the basis of the public sphere: his demand for reason and decorum excludes women, workers and rival counter-publics; the public sphere is better understood as contested and plural p. 23
  • modernist 'public participation' that envisages a homogenised public: museums should move beyond it toward engagement with diverse communities, without romanticising community p. 111
  • treating museum visitors as audiences or customers, measured by quantitative visitor metrics: such metrics reduce complexity and, under funding pressure, treat visitors as customers; Barrett sets 'embracing complexity' and case-study methods against them p. 56

Sources and ways of working

  • visitor research (segmentation, barrier analysis, visitor counts) read critically for what its metrics leave out p. 124
  • architecture and display read as visual discourse, with photographs of museum visitors (Thomas Struth) as evidence p. 167

Gaps it names

  • how the publics of museums in China and the Gulf states differ from those of developed countries, and which notions of public and public space apply to them p. 172

Contents and chapter overviews

Bennett, Tony (1995). The Birth of the Museum: History, Theory, Politics. London: Routledge.9 concepts

Bennett frames the public museum as a cultural technology of government: an institution that regulates its visitors through culture and self-regulation rather than force, and whose displays of order and progress programme how visitors behave. The book is cultural and political history and theory, combining Foucault and Gramsci with Bourdieu and Pomian, and it is a study of museums, fairs and exhibitions in Britain, Australia and North America. Its overall argument is that museum politics must take account of the museum's own institutional rationality rather than treat its displays only as ideology.

Concepts and inspirations

  • liberal government (Foucault)
  • exhibitionary complex
  • political rationality (Foucault)
  • Gramscian hegemony and counter-hegemony (Gramsci)
  • semiophores (Krzysztof Pomian)
  • pure gaze and distinction (Pierre Bourdieu)
  • backteller (Huxley)
  • nationing history (Poulantzas; Benedict Anderson)
  • carnival (Bakhtinian reading) (Mikhail Bakhtin; Terry Eagleton)

Argues against

  • Foucault's sharp opposition between the museum and the fair as contrary heterotopias: The opposition is too starkly stated and insufficiently historical; amusement parks and the Chicago Midway blurred it. p. 3
  • Foucault's generalising conclusions from the carceral system about disciplinary surveillance: The exhibitionary complex shows power exercised through spectacle as well as surveillance, so the disciplinary account is incomplete. p. 61
  • Douglas Crimp's reading of museums as enclosing institutions on the model of Foucault's asylum, clinic and prison: Museums and prisons developed in opposite directions: museums opened to the public where prisons withdrew. p. 92

Sources and ways of working

  • reading the plans, projections and advocates' writings of museums, fairs and exhibitions, not the visitor's actual experience p. 11
  • textual reading of a memorial's inscriptions, entry court and central spaces to see how they place the visitor p. 140
  • the rhetoric of nineteenth-century museum promoters and early historians, such as Greenwood and Murray p. 2

Gaps it names

  • how far the planned effects of museum display are actually felt by visitors, or evaded and unnoticed p. 11

Contents and chapter overviews

Bilsel, Can (2012). Antiquity on Display: Regimes of the Authentic in Berlin’s Pergamon Museum. Oxford: Oxford University Press.8 concepts

Bilsel treats the Pergamon Museum as a frame that became the exhibit: the reconstructions of the Great Altar of Pergamon, the Miletus Gate and the Babylonian gates are read as successive modern frames that authenticated copies as ancient monuments. The argument is that the museum produced a 'regime of the authentic' through archaeology, museology and preservation practice, and that the museum's reception and the German excavations were parts of one modern process rather than a later abuse of antiquity. It is a study of cultural and architectural history, combining German intellectual history, the history of archaeology and museum studies, and the theory of art history from Winckelmann to Riegl.

Concepts and inspirations

  • the museum as frame of works of art
  • regimes of the authentic
  • style room (Stilraum)
  • aura (Walter Benjamin)
  • post-Orientalist critique (Edward Said; James Clifford; Partha Chattarjee)
  • reception history (Rezeptionsgeschichte)
  • history as a tower (Hegelian and Schellingian models) (Hegel; Schelling)
  • Hildebrand's criteria of high art (Adolf Hildebrand)

Argues against

  • post-Orientalist critique of museums that follows Said: the relation between the museum's displays and hegemony was neither determined nor stable, and the museum does not have one subject PDF p. 33
  • reception history (Rezeptionsgeschichte): appropriation of an ancient monument by a modern regime is not an abuse of an original; the question is why the monuments took this form in this place PDF p. 33
  • a linear, Hegelian reading of the museum's plan: Bode's programme does not offer a linear history of civilization; the presentation was frequently ruptured and woven back through unexpected correspondences PDF p. 106

Sources and ways of working

  • an archive of travel diaries, excavation reports, illustrated restoration treatises, museum commission minutes, museum guides and press reception PDF p. 31
  • reading the museum's displays in the present alongside the historical material, following the visitor's route through the building PDF p. 31
  • full-scale wooden mock-ups and photographs made during construction, which let the building commission walk into the planned displays PDF p. 151

Gaps it names

  • the material on the architects, archaeologists and museum directors introduced is not exhausted; the book is offered as a roadmap into a much larger field PDF p. 33
  • the change in the regime of the authentic between the mid nineteenth and mid twentieth century, shown by the destruction in 1955 of the V&A's Indian architectural displays for being copies PDF p. 33

Contents and chapter overviews

Black, Barbara J. (2000). On Exhibit: Victorians and Their Museums. Charlottesville: University Press of Virginia.9 concepts

On Exhibit treats the Victorian museum as the central institution of nineteenth-century culture, tied to empire, mass education and the control of the public, whose logic of gathering and ordering spreads into private homes, novels, poems and boys' fiction. Black's argument is that the museum is a political and hybrid institution that opens the world to the many while assimilating it under one aegis, and that collecting is driven by anxieties about loss and lineage. It is a work of cultural and literary history that reads fiction and poetry as museum culture, drawing on Foucault, Baudrillard, Said and Elias.

Concepts and inspirations

  • heterotopia (Michel Foucault)
  • museum as panopticon and utopia of surveillance (Jeremy Bentham; John McClure; Benedict Anderson)
  • museumification (Jean Baudrillard)
  • exotic at home: the domesticated exotic
  • Orientalism applied to the translator's own text (Edward Said)
  • collapsed significance (Susan Stewart)
  • regulating the body through civilising display (Norbert Elias)
  • museum poem (ut pictura poesis)
  • museum as cenotaph

Argues against

  • Pictorialism and the ut pictura poesis tradition in poetry about art: The museum poem exposes disorder and clutter rather than the idyll of order, so it does not follow the tradition of a single painting inspiring an occasional poem. p. 130
  • Baudrillard's dating of the simulacrum after the age of production: The Victorian museum, with its powers of reproducibility, was the true age of the emergent hyperreal and the first age of museumification. p. 37

Sources and ways of working

  • close reading of FitzGerald's letters for his purchases and the objects he gathered at home p. 50
  • reading advice manuals and trade advertisements (Haweis, Eastlake, importers) as evidence of how domestic collecting was promoted p. 72

Contents and chapter overviews

Çelik, Zeynep (2016). About Antiquities: Politics of Archaeology in the Ottoman Empire. Austin: University of Texas Press.7 concepts

The book frames museums as products of empire, rivalry and national identity from their founding, and argues that the Imperial Museum in Istanbul and the Metropolitan in New York were built on imperial and national politics as much as on science. It is a cultural and social history of archaeology in the late Ottoman Empire, combining museum studies, the history of architecture and cities, the history of periodicals and visual culture, and labour history, with a closing critique of present-day restitution debates.

Concepts and inspirations

  • alternative archaeologies (Bruce Trigger)
  • Orientalism as a discourse on local people and places
  • dual settlement as colonial template
  • decadence as a historicising aesthetic term
  • reading against the grain and hearing voices (Carlo Ginzburg; Natalie Zemon Davis; Dorothy Metzger Habel)
  • indigenous archaeologies (Yannis Hamilakis)
  • encyclopedic versus nationalistic museums (James Cuno; James F. Goode; Robin F. Rhodes)

Argues against

  • The thesis that certain peoples lack the cultural right to own antiquities, with Salomon Reinach’s 1883 article at the forefront: Çelik calls it a thesis from tired nineteenth-century precedents, and argues that the present debate over who is ‘all of us’ and who is ‘the public’ hides the question of objects illegally obtained by Western museums. p. 217
  • The view that Western museums have histories cleansed of political agendas: Çelik says such histories are not convincing: the museums and the archaeology that supplied them were deeply rooted in politics and contributed to imperial and national identity building from their beginnings. p. 216
  • James F. Goode and Robin F. Rhodes, who hold that members of traditional societies rarely approached their ancient history as scientists and that ownership should follow preservation: Çelik reports the argument as part of the case for keeping objects in Western museums, and answers it by pointing out that Western museums were shaped by the same national and imperial politics as the source states. p. 217

Sources and ways of working

  • excavation reports and notebooks read against the grain, for the names, wages and decisions of workers p. 167
  • photographs analysed for meanings their makers did not intend p. 11
  • comparison of unequal archives on two museums, Istanbul and New York, with the limits that this imposes p. 9
  • Istanbul periodicals such as Servet-i Fünun and Şehbal read for how they presented antiquities to readers p. 8

Gaps it names

  • visitor numbers to the Imperial Museum, which were not recorded p. 9
  • reports or journals by the Ottoman officials who supervised the foreign excavations p. 9
  • accounts by local visitors to the Imperial Museum, and by Ottoman women, which the author searched for in vain p. 10
  • the workers’ own voices, which the documents do not give p. 11

Contents and chapter overviews

Conn, Steven (1998). Museums and American Intellectual Life, 1876–1926. Chicago: University of Chicago Press.7 concepts

Conn frames museums of 1876 to 1926 as intellectual institutions that claimed knowledge through objects, not only as instruments of power or monuments to patrons. The overall argument is that an object-based epistemology, dominant in natural history, anthropology, commerce and history museums, was displaced by universities by the 1920s, leaving museums with popular display and an art-museum hierarchy. It is a cultural and intellectual history of museums and science, combining history of science, history of anthropology and art history, with a Foucauldian critique set against it.

Concepts and inspirations

  • object-based epistemology
  • synecdoche and metonymy of objects (Roman Jakobson; Terence Hawkes; Susan Stewart)
  • Foucauldian power-knowledge critique (Michel Foucault; Tony Bennett; Eilean Hooper-Greenhill)
  • epistemology of imperialism
  • aura and ritual in the art museum (Walter Benjamin)
  • history from objects
  • value through exchange (Georg Simmel; Arjun Appadurai; Jean Baudrillard)

Argues against

  • the older view of museums as monuments of wealthy businessmen to their connoisseurship: Conn argues that museums were charged with creating and providing knowledge to visitors, and that this is what the critics miss. p. 10
  • Foucauldian critics who read museums only as instruments of power: Power did operate through classification, but the categories were needed for understanding, so the analysis must also take up the knowledge museums produced. p. 11

Sources and ways of working

  • annual reports and museum guides, such as the Commercial Museum's 1905 Annual Report and its guides to trade p. 142
  • letters between curators, trustees and officials, such as Sellers's 1879 letter about display arrangement p. 206
  • newspaper reports and press reactions, such as the Washington Evening Star's account of Manila p. 141
  • museum displays read as texts, analysed by how their objects were arranged by region, product or period p. 124

Contents and chapter overviews

Coombes, Annie E. (1994). Reinventing Africa: Museums, Material Culture and Popular Imagination in Late Victorian and Edwardian England. New Haven: Yale University Press.8 concepts

The book treats British museums, exhibitions and missionary shows as places where an image of Africa was produced and made credible through 'scientific' anthropology, and argues that the ethnographic collection and the spectacle of African people served imperial, state and professional ends. Its central claim is that the contradiction between admiration for African art and contempt for African societies was a product of colonial knowledge rather than an oversight. It is a cultural and social history of museums and exhibitions, drawing on the history of anthropology, museum studies and theories of colonial discourse.

Concepts and inspirations

  • popular knowledge (as against 'scientific' knowledge) (Tony Bennett)
  • hegemony as maintained through negotiation (Gramsci)
  • discursive formation and regimes of truth (Foucault)
  • spectatorial lust (John Atkinson Hobson)
  • discourse of authenticity
  • degeneracy of a 'degraded' race
  • racial typology of the ethnographic collection (Keane)
  • hybridity as a post-colonial object concept

Argues against

  • histories that treat colonial power as a monolithic propaganda machine: the colonial encounter was a dynamic meeting, and colonised groups were heterogeneous and not straightforwardly oppositional p. 6
  • histories that cast anthropology as either the liberal conscience of the colonial administration or a government lackey: its relation to imperialism was a necessarily ambiguous and shifting partnership p. 4
  • art-historical accounts of primitivism that track when the European avant-garde discovered colonial art: discussions of the aesthetic value of colonial material were familiar to a far broader middle-class public p. 5

Sources and ways of working

  • accessions files, annual reports and museum bulletins, read for how donors and curators described objects p. 142
  • exhibition guides and catalogues, read for the terms used to describe performers and objects p. 115
  • steward manuals and congregational study groups in missionary exhibitions p. 175

Gaps it names

  • the African diaspora in Britain over this period, which the book sets aside p. 6
  • the relation between anthropology's academic and public image, which has received little attention p. 4

Contents and chapter overviews

Cuno, James (ed.) (2009). Whose Culture? The Promise of Museums and the Debate over Antiquities. Princeton: Princeton University Press.9 concepts

The volume frames the museum as a public repository of objects for knowledge, tolerance and the encyclopedic display of world culture, and argues against national retention laws and archaeological rules that would bar undocumented antiquities from acquisition. It is a museum-studies and cultural-policy study, drawing on art history, archaeology, Assyriology, law, philosophy and anthropology. The editor’s position is set out in the introduction and defended mainly by museum directors and curators, with archaeologists, a law professor and an anthropologist of Indigenous heritage as the main counterpoints.

Concepts and inspirations

  • encyclopedic museum
  • many contexts of an object
  • two propositions on context and periodisation
  • object-oriented policy against nation-oriented policy
  • cultural patrimony
  • trusteeship of objects for humanity
  • pedigree rule
  • intangible heritage
  • common heritage of humanity (UNESCO)

Argues against

  • Colin Renfrew, Loot, Legitimacy, and Ownership (2000): Unprovenanced antiquities, ripped from their archaeological context without record, can tell us little that is new, and museums betray their trust when they acquire them. p. 14
  • nationalist governments and their claim to ancient pedigree: Modern nations claim descent from ancient cultures, which the volume calls nationalist fantasy based on geography and enforced by sovereignty. p. 28
  • archaeologists who regard unprovenanced artifacts as of little historic value (Owen’s target): Journals and societies have banned unprovenanced cuneiform texts, though such texts have reconstructed archival groups and enlarged knowledge of Ur III history. p. 125

Sources and ways of working

  • object-by-object comparison within one museum’s collection, using a few objects in a single gallery to argue for their meaning and display p. 17
  • stylistic and technical analysis that links an object to earlier artifacts and to the collector who gathered them p. 95
  • reading the annual reports and publication records of museums and excavation projects as evidence of acquisition and conflict of interest p. 140

Gaps it names

  • why ancient artists made certain forms in jade or decorated bronze, which archaeology has yet to explain p. 30
  • unpublished excavations at sites such as Umm al-Hafriyat, whose ancient names remain unknown p. 139
  • the Chinese excavation publication record, which leaves much to be desired p. 116

Contents and chapter overviews

Cuno, James (2008). Who Owns Antiquity? Museums and the Battle over Our Ancient Heritage. Princeton: Princeton University Press.8 concepts

Cuno frames museums, especially encyclopedic ones, as cosmopolitan institutions whose collections express a shared human heritage and should be defended against nationalist cultural property laws. Cuno’s overall argument is that the dispute over unprovenanced antiquities is political rather than archaeological, and that the question of who owns antiquity should be answered by common heritage, exchange and shared access. It is a cultural and political study with strong elements of legal, museum and intellectual history, written by a former art museum director who draws on court cases, government requests and his own visits to sites.

Concepts and inspirations

  • nationalist retentionist cultural property laws
  • Merryman's triad of preservation, knowledge and access (John Henry Merryman)
  • partage
  • encyclopedic museum
  • cosmopolitanism (Diogenes; Hume; Nussbaum)
  • plural identity (identity as flowing currents) (Edward Said; Amin Maalouf; Amartya Sen)
  • nationalism as a recent elite construction (Eric Hobsbawm; Ernest Gellner; Benedict Anderson)
  • cultural purity and hybridity

Argues against

  • archaeologists, who present their support for source-nation laws as protecting sites and their work as disinterested science: their work is used by source nations for nationalist purposes, and the price of excavating in national jurisdictions is that support for national laws PDF p. 14
  • the Chinese state's claim that its antiquities belong to Chinese culture as a whole: the state decides what counts as Chinese, and Chinese culture has always been formed by exchange PDF p. 109
  • the Italian government's claim that its antiquities developed autonomously and express a unique national identity: nothing was developed autonomously anywhere, so the claim ignores the hybridity of culture PDF p. 113

Sources and ways of working

  • legal and diplomatic records, such as the US import-restriction statute and CPAC recommendations on requests PDF p. 56
  • press reports and public statements by museum and state spokesmen, read against their context PDF p. 98
  • site visits and the study of individual objects with students, such as the Dunhuang Tang sculpture PDF p. 88

Gaps it names

  • whether the cultural heritage of China's minority peoples is valued equally with Han Chinese antiquities, which the author says cannot be answered with easy answers PDF p. 109

Contents and chapter overviews

Cvetkovski, Roland; Hofmeister, Alexis (eds.) (2014). An Empire of Others: Creating Ethnographic Knowledge in Imperial Russia and the USSR. Budapest: Central European University Press.8 concepts

The volume treats ethnography as a knowledge culture produced in specific milieus, not as a neutral cultural technique or as a simple instrument of state power. Its overall argument is that ethnographic categories (narod, nationality, race, ethnogenesis) were contingent, contested and institutionally made in imperial and Soviet Russia, and that objects and classifications did not carry a fixed imperial message. It is a cultural and intellectual history of knowledge, with a museum-studies strand and anthropological and sociological input, written as an edited volume of case studies by historians and ethnographers.

Concepts and inspirations

  • ethnographic knowledge as cultural technique (Konrad Köstlin)
  • knowledge history (Peter Burke; Karin Knorr-Cetina; Lorraine Daston)
  • exhibitionary complex
  • Stockholm system
  • representation of the Other
  • mixed physical type
  • Marrist ethnogenesis (Nikolai Marr; Sergei Tolstov)
  • philosophical geography (Larry Wolff)

Argues against

  • Konrad Köstlin's view that ethnography is a neutral cultural technique separate from state politics: The introduction argues that this separation obscures European colonial and imperial experiences, since ethnic categories shaped imperial policy from the nineteenth century p. 1
  • Orientalism and colonialism as a priori analytical frames for the ethnography of Central Asia: Abashin argues for treating ethnography as an autonomous zone, open to authority but with its own rights, logics and inner dynamics p. 147
  • contemporary museum experts who treated ethnographic knowledge as imperial knowledge and the museum as an extension of ethnographic science: The chapter argues that the museum was no mirror of the imperial self, and that its objects produced equality among peoples rather than a clear imperial message p. 249

Sources and ways of working

  • museum registers and classification records (registration by collection, catalogues, the Stockholm and Copenhagen systems), read with the arrangement of the displays p. 241
  • the hall-by-hall arrangement of the 1910 trial exhibition, read as a spatial text alongside the contemporary reviewer's criticism p. 243
  • anthropometric and craniological data, court records of the Multan trial and dissertation debates, read against each other p. 113
  • visitor comment books of the 1920s, used to test what visitors took from the displays p. 248

Gaps it names

  • the epistemic situations in which ethnographic categories were modelled and prepared for wider use in Russia, which the authors say earlier studies have not examined p. 6

Contents and chapter overviews

Damousi, Joy; Tout-Smith, Deborah; Ziino, Bart (eds.) (2020). Museums, History and the Intimate Experience of the Great War: Love and Sorrow. London: Routledge.8 concepts

The volume frames the First World War in Australia as an experience sustained by families and by emotion, and argues that museums, above all the Love and Sorrow exhibition, can reopen that intimate war for audiences a century later. Its editors’ introduction presents the war as fought in the senses and emotions as well as on the battlefield. It is a study of cultural, social and military history, museum and public history, and historiography, with affect theory central to the curatorial chapters and reflexive method central to the historians’ chapters.

Concepts and inspirations

  • sticky objects (Sarah Ahmed)
  • mimetic communication (Anna Gibbs; Tomkins)
  • testimony and witness (Nanette Auerhahn; Dori Laub; Roger Simon)
  • pedagogy of feeling
  • familial histories
  • emotional communities (Barbara Rosenwein)
  • “gonzo” historian (Hunter S. Thompson)
  • postmemory (Marianne Hirsch)

Argues against

  • Revisionist military historians such as Brian Bond and Dan Todman, who distrust emotion and post-war cultural productions: Post-war cultural productions have skewed historical understanding of the war as experienced in 1914–18, and emotion is assumed to affect historical comprehension negatively. p. 137
  • Mark McKenna and Stuart Ward, who criticised Scates for “sentimental nationalism”: Stanley, though sympathetic, accepts that emotion in military history is an unstable element liable to become sentimentality unless carefully handled. p. 131
  • Critics of the Anzac legend’s masculinity: Love and Sorrow uses the family to challenge the masculinist Anzac legend, which it presents as erasing the act of killing and the war’s imperial and racist foundations. p. 172

Sources and ways of working

  • Repatriation files, read closely for the disputes over pensions and the acceptance of a physical war cause p. 101
  • Private letters between a general and his family and friends, read for anxiety and grief on the home front p. 48
  • Visitor evaluation surveys of Love and Sorrow, reporting that 97% of visitors were made to think about the war’s impact p. 165
  • Forum posts from online learners, read for emotional responses and disputes p. 209
  • Observation of visitors’ responses in galleries, which Stanley treats as evidence that emotion was being engaged p. 124

Gaps it names

  • Lighter emotions such as pleasure, comradeship and love remain largely unexplored by historians of war emotion p. 132
  • Historians cannot assume they know what silence means in the records of trauma, and recorded evidence may not contain the testimony they seek p. 147
  • Historians have so far studied mainly grief, bereavement and mourning p. 132

Contents and chapter overviews

Denton, Kirk A. (2014). Exhibiting the Past: Historical Memory and the Politics of Museums in Postsocialist China. Honolulu: University of Hawai‘i Press.8 concepts

Denton frames museums in postsocialist China as instruments of party-state memory politics whose narratives have changed under market reform without loosening the state's hold on the past. The book is a cultural and political study of exhibitions, architecture and location, read through the visual language of museums. Its overall argument is that the state remains central to popular memory even as its stories are remodelled as nostalgia, commodified revolution and national revival.

Concepts and inspirations

  • exhibitionary complex (Tony Bennett; Foucault)
  • lieux de memoire (Pierre Nora)
  • official and vernacular memory (Gillis; Susan Crane; Maurice Halbwachs)
  • invention of tradition (Eric Hobsbawm; Terence Ranger)
  • nostalgic exhibitionary mode (Svetlana Boym; Dai Jinhua; Ban Wang)
  • empire of nations (Francine Hirsch)
  • the miniature (Susan Stewart)
  • museums of the future

Argues against

  • the view that museum theory emphasizes the institution's power to impose ideology on visitors: Denton says this is too deterministic: exhibits are negotiated among curators, officials and historians, and visitors' experience varies. p. 13
  • the assumption that the Chinese state holds a monopoly over historical memory: Denton says that online, fiction and unofficial memorial spaces offer alternative forms of remembering, though she keeps a state-centred approach. p. 267

Sources and ways of working

  • narratological reading of the visual language of exhibits, architecture and location p. 14
  • a scholar's recorded exchange with a visitor, used as evidence of how official memory is held p. 83
  • first-hand visits to museums and galleries, with notes on staging and displays p. 94

Gaps it names

  • how visitors actually receive museum narratives, which the book raises as a larger question p. 94

Contents and chapter overviews

Dudley, Sandra H. (ed.) (2010). Museum Materialities: Objects, Engagements, Interpretations. London: Routledge.8 concepts

The volume frames museums as places where objects are experienced through the body and the senses, not only read as carriers of information, and argues that this physical engagement should shape museum practice and museum studies. Dudley's introduction sets the agenda, and the chapters, written by curators, artists, anthropologists, psychologists and museum educators, test it through case studies of Western museums and galleries. It is a museum studies and material culture study that draws on the anthropology of the senses, phenomenology, affect theory and art history, presented as an edited collection rather than a single argument.

Concepts and inspirations

  • object-subject engagement (Tilley; Pearce; Gosden)
  • affect (pre-rational response) (Tomkins; Best; Deleuze)
  • darsan (being seen by the image) (Eck)
  • object biography (Janet Hoskins; Kopytoff; Tilley)
  • object knowledge (MacDougall)
  • metaphorical association (Tilley; Golding)
  • agent of change (Moyle; Hooper-Greenhill)
  • authenticity as a relation to the audience (Auslander; Jones)

Argues against

  • The view that the museum object is an object-information package, in which the physical thing matters only as one element in institutional meaning (Parry; Kavanagh): The object is also an object-subject engagement whose sensory and emotional force that framing neglects p. 3
  • The assumption that physical and emotional engagement with museum objects is non-existent or restricted to an elitist, detached aesthetic response: The possibilities of engagement are wider, and textual information can inhibit them p. 3
  • Susan Stewart's account of miniatures as freezing time, erasing history and framing it through nostalgia: The Treblinka model condenses the camp's history into one moment, but it links past and present and invites affect rather than nostalgia p. 49

Sources and ways of working

  • Visitor studies and focus groups on what visitors want from displays, used to plan the Australian Journeys gallery p. 153
  • Visitor studies at Bristol City Museum showing that visitors are least interested in technical qualities of ceramics p. 191

Gaps it names

  • What the physicality of museum objects may imply for the museum experience, which the editor says has been surprisingly little explored p. 6
  • Whether mobile eye trackers in galleries would show differences from originals and reproductions that laboratory settings, resembling the white cube, do not p. 98

Contents and chapter overviews

Duncan, Carol (1995). Civilizing Rituals: Inside Public Art Museums. London: Routledge.7 concepts

Duncan frames public art museums as ritual sites: their buildings, rooms and collections form a 'script or score' that visitors perform, and that script conveys values about social, sexual and political identity. It is a cultural and art-historical study that borrows from anthropology (ritual, liminality) and from feminist critique of modernism, and it argues against both the educational and the aesthetic museum as the terms of debate. Its overall argument is that Western public art museums were staged as civic rituals of the bourgeois state and, in the modern case, as a male ritual space that now bends toward consumerism.

Concepts and inspirations

  • art museum as ritual structure (civic ritual) (Arnold van Gennep; Victor Turner; Mary Douglas)
  • liminality (liminal zone of the museum) (Arnold van Gennep; Victor Turner)
  • Bourdieu's account of cultural distinction (Pierre Bourdieu; Alain Darbel)
  • art/artifact distinction (Raymond Williams)
  • male ritual subject (gendered museum)
  • advertising as parallel ritual of the consumer self (Raymond Williams)
  • donor memorial

Argues against

  • sociological accounts that treat the art museum only as an instrument of class distinction: Museums are not only socially distinguishing forms but also structures with substantive cultural content not always reducible to sociological or political description. p. 5–6
  • advocates of the educational museum who present it as the democratic alternative to the aesthetic museum: The educational museum is no less a ritual space than the aesthetic museum, and in its way generates as much ideology. p. 5–6
  • treatments that see the museum as a neutral sheltering space for objects or as a work of architecture: Art museums are complex entities in which art and architecture are parts of a larger whole, to be understood as a script or score. p. 1–2

Sources and ways of working

  • museum instructions to visitors, such as the Hirshhorn's sign, read as evidence of ritual comportment p. 11–12
  • donors' terms of gift and installation read as evidence of how a collection was staged p. 61–62
  • installations and architecture read as text, treating the whole museum as a script or score p. 1–2
  • comparison across museums and their organising arrangements, such as the civilisation sequence in Boston p. 71–72

Gaps it names

  • how Western museums represent non-Western and minority cultures, which the study explicitly sets aside p. 3–4
  • what real visitors make of museum rituals; the visitors discussed are hypothetical ideal types p. 5–6

Contents and chapter overviews

Findlen, Paula (1994). Possessing Nature: Museums, Collecting, and Scientific Culture in Early Modern Italy. Berkeley: University of California Press.6 concepts

Findlen frames the early modern museum as the place where old and new knowledge met: collecting let naturalists modify Aristotelian and Plinian natural history rather than overturn it, and the museum made natural philosophy a tactile, sociable and courtly practice. The book is a cultural and social history of natural history in Italy, 1500 to 1700, combining the history of collecting, intellectual history of natural philosophy and a sociology of patronage and brokerage. It treats the museum as a microcosm of elite society and reads the collector's identity and the visitor's access as part of the science.

Concepts and inspirations

  • theater of nature (teatro di natura)
  • wonder and sign (Lorraine Daston)
  • curiosity (Krzysztof Pomian)
  • saved appearances
  • distinction and access (Pierre Bourdieu)
  • book of nature (Hans Blumenberg; Michel Foucault)

Argues against

  • Francis Bacon's call for a natural history based on experience rather than erudition: Findlen says Aldrovandi and Kircher treated experience as complementing ancient authority, not competing with it, so the collectors dissolved none of the boundaries of their world. p. 4
  • Galileo's and Descartes' critique of curiosity and of the disorderly culture of the marvelous: Findlen says Baroque collectors' musings should not be judged unscientific, since they reflect a scientific culture that had no clear criteria for truth yet. p. 94

Sources and ways of working

  • museum inventories and catalogues, university and academy archives, correspondence between naturalists, travel journals, and the publications that resulted from collecting p. 8

Gaps it names

  • the many lesser patrons, brokers and collectors between Aldrovandi and Kircher, such as Mattioli, Calzolari, Imperato and Mercati, whose contributions have not been reassessed p. 5
  • the historiography of the scientific revolution, which has paid little attention to natural history p. 10

Contents and chapter overviews

Fromm, Annette B.; Golding, Viv; Rekdal, Per B. (eds.) (2014). Museums and Truth. Newcastle upon Tyne: Cambridge Scholars Publishing.9 concepts

The volume treats museums, especially ethnographic ones, as institutions that present partial and situated truths, and asks them to expose the contested nature of their narratives while taking firm stands against injustice. Its overall argument is that museums should show complexity and disagreement, dialogue with source communities and visitors, and engagement with difficult histories, rather than retreat into celebration or relativism. It is an anthology in museum studies and heritage studies, whose chapters draw on hermeneutics, discourse analysis, anthropology, memory studies and political philosophy rather than building one sustained theory.

Concepts and inspirations

  • fusion of horizons (Gadamer)
  • cultural translation (Talal Asad; Wittgenstein; Winch)
  • discourse and subject positions (Laclau; Laclau and Mouffe; Althusser)
  • public space as space of appearance (Judith Butler; Barrett; Habermas)
  • pluriversality (Ziauddin Sardar; Tariq Ramadan; Mignolo)
  • denial of coevalness (Johannes Fabian)
  • intangible reparations
  • art-party and context-party
  • sacred objects and the museum taboo (Kohl; Derlon)

Argues against

  • Relativism and celebratory tolerance, which Golding calls 'excessive tolerance' or charitable cultural translation: Understanding must be paired with firm stands against injustice and human rights abuses, not left at tolerance. p. 11
  • Religious items displayed as pure art, judged by European or art-market standards: The relational approach of the context-party is needed, since the art-party's aesthetic universalism repeats colonial collecting. p. 132
  • War memorials and celebratory peace messages: Rekdal says such messages may be emotionally deep but intellectually shallow, and museums should show complexity and scholarly disagreement. PDF p. 23
  • The Trieste memorial project for the Istrian exodus and the foibe: Buletić argues that the project reflects a post-fascist political agenda, and offers dialogue and oral history as an alternative. p. 96

Sources and ways of working

  • discourse analysis of the public debate: the forty-one most decisive contributions, mostly newspaper pieces and letters, examined for who speaks and with what authority p. 104
  • oral history: life histories of ordinary people, used for multi-voiced displays and to recover silenced memories p. 96
  • reading a museum's annual report as evidence of its existing peace and reconciliation work p. 23

Gaps it names

  • theoretical reflection on the concepts used to theorize museums, which Grinell says is too rare compared with case studies p. 170
  • the decline of central American memory museums: national museums of memory have not been built there as they have in South America p. 77

Contents and chapter overviews

Gardner, James (2020). The Louvre: The Many Lives of the World’s Most Famous Museum. New York: Atlantic Monthly Press.7 concepts

Gardner frames the Louvre as a building, an institution and a symbol of the French crown and state, and argues that its present form is the product of many building campaigns, some of them hidden by a long-standing claim to unity. The book is a cultural and architectural history of one site, written by an author who describes himself as a cultural critic rather than an archival researcher (preface), and it combines architectural, museum and dynastic history. It makes no sustained theoretical argument and names almost no theorists; its concepts are the author's own framings and historical terms.

Concepts and inspirations

  • three fronts: architectural, institutional and historical
  • placeness (lieu-dit)
  • the Louvre as a work of art
  • encyclopedic museum and arbiter of collective visual culture
  • restitution
  • the triumphal spoils parade
  • export of French culture (André Malraux)

Argues against

  • Stendhal's view that the French, not the Italians, were the true victims of the restitution of works from Italy: The text calls this an astounding display of moral obtuseness and sets it against the treaty basis of the Italian claims and Canova's retrieval of the works

Sources and ways of working

  • architecture read as the record of successive building campaigns, with the surviving fabric and its stylistic disparities used as evidence
  • archaeological excavation of the site before the palace, including the 1980s digs in the open spaces
  • the visitor's view of the complex from the Pyramide and across the Tuileries site

Gaps it names

  • space for the collection: the thirty-six thousand works on view are under a tenth of the holdings, and the author expects curators to claim more of the complex

Contents and chapter overviews

Genoways, Hugh H.; Andrei, Mary Anne (eds.) (2008). Museum Origins: Readings in Early Museum History and Philosophy. Walnut Creek, CA: Left Coast Press.2 concepts

The editors frame the book as a teaching resource and source of inspiration on museum history and philosophy, arranged in seven sections (origins, philosophy, the new museum, education, exhibition, museums and universities, living collections) that group the readings by theme and chronology, and each section has an editorial introduction. The readings are practical and philosophical essays by administrators, educators and critics (mostly natural history curators, 1850-1925), so the book's overall argument is that museums should serve the public through education and that their research and display functions must be separated. It is a museum-history and museum-studies anthology of sources, not an argued study, and it has no single theory of its own.

Concepts and inspirations

  • the new museum idea (William Henry Flower; John Edward Gray; Charles Coleman Sellers)
  • museum education as informal education

Argues against

  • George A. Dorsey's criticism of the American Museum of Natural History's reorganised ethnological halls (1907): Boas replies that the large museum is chiefly justified by preserving long series for science, that exhibits should present single ideas against a plain background, and that anthropological objects cannot be arranged in one scheme without distortion p. 231
  • George Brown Goode's dictum that an educational museum is a collection of instructive labels, each illustrated by a well-selected specimen: Gilman argues that art objects are unica valued for their individuality, so the formula fails for art museums and a fine art museum is an artistic institution with educational uses p. 129

Sources and ways of working

  • comparing earlier and later installations of the same ethnographic collections, read as evidence of how a museum's arrangement shapes what visitors learn p. 225

Contents and chapter overviews

Greenhalgh, Michael (2019). Plundered Empire: Acquiring Antiquities from Ottoman Lands. Leiden: Brill.7 concepts

Plundered Empire frames museums as the end point of a long removal of antiquities from the Ottoman Empire and Greece by travellers, diplomats, consuls and excavators, and argues that the museums' claim to have rescued objects is part of the plunder. It is a history of antiquarian collecting and early archaeology in the field, documentary and empirical in method, drawing on travel books, consular papers and firmans. Its critical stance is against imperial, nationalist and colonial archaeology, and it treats the collecting as a question of acquisition, funding and shipping rather than of the travellers' attitudes.

Concepts and inspirations

  • plunder
  • the rescue defence (Jenkins)
  • Orientalism (Bernard Lewis)
  • trophy (Encyclopaedia Britannica 1911, s.v. trophy)
  • shopping list
  • partage (Anderson 2017)
  • removal from setting (Quatremère de Quincy; Willis)

Argues against

  • recent books defending the retention of antiquities in Western museums, such as Jenkins's Keeping their marbles (2016): Greenhalgh calls their arguments old and tired and a continuing alibi for the West, and says looting has continued and arguably increased since 1918, as the 2003 invasion of Iraq shows. p. 560
  • nineteenth-century archaeology as a disinterested pursuit of Truth: Greenhalgh places it in Trigger's categories of nationalist, colonialist or imperialist, so it was not disinterested. p. 56
  • commentators such as Sterrett who blamed the Turks who hammer and deface inscriptions: Greenhalgh notes the number of ancient column shafts in mosques that still bear crosses, so the damage is unlikely to have been a hostility to Christian signs. p. 554

Sources and ways of working

  • compass-and-pace itineraries recording every mile, used to map country that existing maps had not recorded; Hamilton's 1842 maps of Asia Minor were judged useless p. 88
  • guidebooks by Murray and Baedeker, read as sources in their own right, since they carried the identifications and authorities of established scholars p. 100
  • museum labels and storerooms read for provenance, which the book finds often missing or reduced to the name of a country p. 27

Gaps it names

  • Asia Minor's interior and unrecorded sites, which Greenhalgh says were still partly terra incognita in 1889 p. 90
  • a regular scientific survey of the whole country, which he says for Asia Minor lay in the distant future p. 91
  • European behaviour after the First World War, which the book leaves to another study PDF p. 16

Contents and chapter overviews

Guy, Kate; Williams, Hajra; Wintle, Claire (eds.) (2024). Histories of Exhibition Design in the Museum: Makers, Process, and Practice. London: Routledge.9 concepts

The volume frames museums as places where exhibitions are continually made, unmade and revised by many workers, not as finished statements of institutional or state power. Its overall argument is that the history of exhibition design (designers, technicians, label writers, carpenters, curators and administrators) has been obscured by studies that treat exhibitions as polished end products, so that labour, process and collaboration need to be written back in. It is a social and cultural history of museum practice, with contributions from museum studies, design history, anthropology, art history and heritage studies, and it mixes archival case studies with interviews and reconstructions.

Concepts and inspirations

  • exhibitionary complex (Tony Bennett; Michel Foucault)
  • exhibition in process as an experiment (Calum Storrie)
  • exhibition maker
  • professionalisation as exclusion (Gerry Beegan; Paul Atkinson)
  • embodied and emotional labour of exhibition making (Andrea Witcomb; Rachael Minott)
  • ethnographic perspective and thick design (Clifford Geertz; Renato Rosaldo; Hal Foster)
  • one nation and one people (Preziosi)
  • visual intervention
  • re-materialisation of economic knowledge (Bruno Latour)

Argues against

  • Scholarship that studies museum exhibitions as finished, static and fully formed statements of institutional agendas: Exhibitions are complex, unfinished processes whose making and remaking must be studied, not only their final form. p. 3

Sources and ways of working

  • Interviews and surveys with exhibition designers, conservators and curators (Pyun's chapter on Korean and Japanese mannequins) p. 170
  • Participant observation in the field, and thick description of design practice (Zhang and Francis on the Dali Project) p. 140

Gaps it names

  • The history of museum exhibition design across collections, disciplines and institutions is yet to be told, according to the editors p. 6
  • Multi-ethnic descendants and multicultural families are rarely considered valid audiences for national museum mannequins p. 181

Contents and chapter overviews

Hall, Patricia; Seemann, Charlie (eds.) (1987). Folklife and Museums: Selected Readings. Nashville: American Association for State and Local History.7 concepts

An applied museum-studies anthology: fourteen essays by folklorists, museum professionals, historians and anthropologists, framed by an editors' preface that says why folklife and museums need each other. Its overall argument is that folk objects and performances, understood in their context and process, can make museums more representative, authentic and interpretive. The study draws on folkloristics, social history, anthropology and historic-site interpretation rather than on social theory, so its frames are mostly folklore-internal.

Concepts and inspirations

  • interpretation as metaphor (Fath Davis Ruffins)
  • folkloric truth
  • performance-centered approach
  • ethnographic model
  • folk object as representative
  • authenticity and context of live presenters
  • contagious magic (Sir James G. Frazer)

Argues against

  • historians who deny that folklife materials are reliable historical data: Folkloric truth is a different category from historical fact; history museums can use both, provided they say which lens they use. p. 77
  • museum presentations of Judaism as normative and outside time and place, such as the American Museum of Natural History's Jews section: Variation, provenance and period should be identified, and the community's own categories and context kept in view. p. 152
  • one-dimensional exhibits that show a single interpretation of an event: Exhibits should show multiple interpretations, including those of makers and users, and the losses as well as the gains. p. 102
  • elite artifacts as the basis of museum history: Elite objects are one-of-a-kind and represent only isolated individuals; folk objects reach a broader social segment and a longer span of years. p. 115

Sources and ways of working

  • probate inventories read room by room to reconstruct household furnishings and the clutter of earlier living spaces p. 93
  • live presentations and interviews with the people who carry the traditions, letting them speak without curators' texts p. 153
  • interviews with miners and mine owners to build an exhibit's storyline and its physical details p. 112
  • fieldwork documentation of living communities before exhibiting them p. 152

Gaps it names

  • American anthropologists have seldom studied American Jews as a culture, so museums lack a collection comparable to those of Tibet or North American Indians and few studies exist to consult p. 152

Contents and chapter overviews

Hicks, Dan (2020). The Brutish Museums: The Benin Bronzes, Colonial Violence and Cultural Restitution. London: Pluto Press.7 concepts

Hicks frames the British sacking of Benin City in February 1897 and the objects looted from it as an ongoing act of colonial violence, so that anthropology museums are 'brutish' institutions and weapons rather than neutral containers, and must be returned to restitution. The book is a political and historical study of British corporate-militarist colonialism, combining museum studies, anthropology and archaeology in a sustained critique of existing theories of material culture (object biography, entanglement). Its overall argument is that the museum must be turned from a space of representation into one of action and conscience, with restitution as the first step.

Concepts and inspirations

  • theory of taking (Marcel Mauss; Karl Marx; Rosa Luxemburg)
  • object biography (Kopytoff)
  • entanglement (Alfred Gell; Nick Thomas; Bruno Latour)
  • necrography (Achille Mbembe; Foucault)
  • chronopolitics (Achille Mbembe; Johannes Fabian; Frantz Fanon)
  • white projection
  • corporate-militarist colonialism (Max Weber; Rosa Luxemburg)

Argues against

  • Object-biographical and entanglement theories of museum objects, including Hartwig Fischer's defence of the Parthenon marbles and the Pitt Rivers relational project: The theft of an object by a European museum is a negative act, and telling its losses and deaths is required rather than an upbeat life-history.
  • The universal museum defence in James Cuno's 'Culture War' against repatriation: The encyclopaedic museum is presented as a western inheritance, which the text calls improbable myth-making.
  • Foucauldian museum studies: Museum studies has taken up Foucault in a purely contemplative critique standing outside the institution, which the text rejects as not a Foucauldian study.

Sources and ways of working

  • Officers' album-diaries and photographs, read as devices that measure duration rather than frozen moments
  • Press and newspaper reports (Daily Mail, The Times), read against official accounts
  • Archival excavation of museum records, treating the museum as an archaeological site to be reshaped by excavation
  • A provisional census of collections worldwide, compiled from museum records and open to correction

Gaps it names

  • No anthropological theory of looting, plunder or dispossession has been written
  • Many holdings of Benin loot are unknown or uncertain, including private collections and possible gifts or sales by the Wellcome Collection; the list is provisional and readers are asked to correct it
  • The death histories of objects, as against their life histories, remain to be written

Contents and chapter overviews

Hill, Kate (ed.) (2012). Museums and Biographies: Stories, Objects, Identities. Woodbridge: Boydell Press.9 concepts

The editor frames museums as arenas where people, things, buildings and institutions are entangled, and argues that museum histories written as the life of a charismatic curator or institution smooth out that mess. The volume is a museum-history and museum-studies collection with strands of cultural and social history, art history, architectural history, anthropology and material culture theory, and its overall argument is that biography is useful for museums only if it is critical of its own tendency to celebrate its subjects.

Concepts and inspirations

  • object biography (Igor Kopytoff)
  • Bourdieu’s distinction and the donor’s legitimacy (Pierre Bourdieu)
  • narrative identity (Paul Ricoeur)
  • smoothing out
  • contaminated collections (Nick Stanley)
  • period eye (Baxandall; Gide; Carrier)
  • communicative and cultural memory (Aleida Assmann; Jan Assmann; Maurice Halbwachs)
  • empathy as historical experience
  • corporate personhood of museums (Bayle St John; Blackstone)

Argues against

  • Celebratory museum histories told as the life of an institution or of its charismatic curators: These are too celebratory and not critical or reflexive enough to help museums understand themselves p. 2
  • Taking individual biographies, such as Lady Eastlake’s own account, at face value: Curators are not always to be taken at their own valuation, and other people have an important role in museums too p. 4

Sources and ways of working

  • Oral life-history interviews with curators, used to show how professional identity is built and changed p. 88
  • Accession registers, paper slips and departmental records, read to trace how an object was classified p. 175
  • Letters and archives of the National Gallery, read against a posthumous published journal to test claims of influence p. 66
