  • Oral history and video testimony, read as a route by which communicative memory becomes cultural memory in museums p. 299

Gaps it names

  • Collective biography built from fragments of evidence, which Cowman argues could be a productive method for feminist historians, is not tried in the volume p. 4
  • Histories of collective labour such as the Women’s Society in Edmonton, which left almost no individual trace, need to trace the institution’s discourses as well as its individuals p. 84

Contents and chapter overviews

Hill, Kate (ed.) (2021). Museums, Modernity and Conflict: Museums and Collections in and of War since the Nineteenth Century. London: Routledge.9 concepts

An edited volume of historical case studies, mainly from museum studies, history and art history, on how European conflicts from the 1870s to the 1940s shaped museum collections, displays and war museums. The introduction argues that museums and war are linked within modernity itself: imperial conquest and 'total war' drove museum development as much as secularisation did, and museums were both instruments of state power and places of personal memory. The chapters work mainly from archives (inventories, consignment books, personnel and service files, committee minutes) and from close reading of displays.

Concepts and inspirations

  • total war (Chickering; Förster; Strachan)
  • circulations culturelles in times of strife
  • wartime heritage protection as a test bench (International Museums Office, La Protection des Monuments et Oeuvres d'Art en Temps de Guerre (1939))
  • nation-building museum
  • peopling
  • Ethos, Logos and Pathos (Esben Kjeldbæk)
  • celebratory, sanitised and realistic display (Scott)
  • indexicality of memorial landscapes (Violi)
  • private and public memory (Caroline Winter)

Argues against

  • the view that museums are part of a benign process of modernisation, cited from Aronsson: imperial conquest and total war were at least as important in driving the development of museums in the modern period p. 2
  • the view that modern museums are mainly about peace, justice and mutual understanding: their modern forms were created by, and focused on, conflict p. 8
  • conventional institutional histories of museums: conflict and revolution were catalysts for the consolidation, relocation and dispersal of collections, processes that such histories have often failed to acknowledge p. 17
  • the GDR's account of Ravensbrück as a site of communist antifascist struggle: the memorial now presents two memorial landscapes side by side, the GDR's path from dark to light and the present focus on responsibility p. 182

Sources and ways of working

  • Christie's consignment books and Agnew's stock books, read with annotated catalogues to identify the consigners behind wartime sales p. 20
  • close reading of museum plans, room arrangements, wall panels, labels, handouts and audio guides, which the author calls forensic p. 40
  • inventories, correspondence and committee minutes of wartime museum administration, cross-referenced to complete the record p. 62
  • personnel files, medical records and service files used to date objects and verify their makers' histories p. 247

Gaps it names

  • the history of imperial collecting and conflict, which the chapters do not generally engage with p. 8
  • the link between the art market and internal European conflicts and crises, and the transformation of the global art market in the heyday of European imperialism, which are only just beginning to be mapped p. 30
  • an exhibition that juxtaposes official war art with trench art and explores the experiences of official war artists alongside the soldiers they painted p. 250

Contents and chapter overviews

Hill, Kate (2005). Culture and Class in English Public Museums, 1850–1914. Aldershot: Ashgate.9 concepts

Hill treats municipal museums as local and negotiated institutions in which middle-class elites sought status, distinction and civic legitimacy, and argues against reading them as a single project of discipline, modernity or working-class reform. The book is social and cultural history of English towns, 1850 to 1914, which tests the theories of museum studies and social theory (Foucault, Bennett, Bourdieu, DiMaggio, Habermas) against donation records, building plans, displays and visitor evidence from several museums. Its argument is that municipal museums were not as modern or efficient as their rhetoric claimed, and that their main effect by 1914 was to make the middle classes more secure in their exclusive status.

Concepts and inspirations

  • negotiated power in the museum (Tony Bennett)
  • disciplinary space and self-surveillance (Tony Bennett; Thomas Markus; Michel Foucault)
  • rational recreation (Peter Bailey; Tony Bennett)
  • public sphere (Habermas; Eley)
  • cultural capital (Pierre Bourdieu; Paul DiMaggio)
  • modes of collecting: souvenir, fetishistic, systematic, trophy (Susan Pearce)
  • realistic display as magical revelation (Donna Haraway)
  • racial ordering of man-made objects (Melanian, Mongolian, Caucasian) (Annie Coombes)
  • objects as metonym and metaphor (Susan Pearce; Lévi-Strauss)

Argues against

  • Studies of national museums that see a shift from juridico-discursive to disciplinary power: There are grounds for questioning that switch; municipal museums were not necessarily as efficient and progressive as their rhetoric suggested. p. 5
  • Habermas's idealised account of the public sphere: Recent commentators show that the public sphere was bound up with middle-class identities and hegemony, that competing publics existed and that some groups were excluded altogether. p. 10
  • Writers who relate museums to capitalism in a schematic way: The broad schema does not change over time or place, so chronologically and geographically specific studies are needed. p. 10
  • Treating municipal museums as the same phenomenon as national museums: Municipal museums had their own births, social constituencies, acquisition patterns, display practices and visitors, so they cannot be lumped together with national museums. p. 145

Sources and ways of working

  • room-and-route analysis of ground plans, following Markus and Hillier and Hanson p. 93
  • donation records and the curator's solicitation of gifts through official channels, such as consuls and the Foreign Secretary p. 62
  • newspaper reports and letters about the museum and its visitors p. 137
  • comparison across municipal museums of different size and resources, from Liverpool to the one-room Scunthorpe museum p. 146

Gaps it names

  • how far the museums' messages were accepted and internalised by visitors, which the evidence cannot show p. 145
  • chronologically and geographically specific studies to fill in the broad schema linking museums and capitalism p. 11
  • the museums of other parts of Britain, particularly Scotland, where the rate-supported museum was less common p. 13

Contents and chapter overviews

Hill, Kate (2016). Women and Museums, 1850–1914: Modernity and the Gendering of Knowledge. Manchester: Manchester University Press.9 concepts

Hill frames museums as distributed institutions, shaped by donors, dealers, fieldworkers, visitors and committees as well as curators, so that women's agency inside them can be recovered from donations, visits, patronage and fieldwork. The book is a social and cultural history of gender, museums and modernity in Britain, 1850-1914, drawing on museum studies, the history of collecting, and women's history. Its argument is that women made museums modern and museums made women modern, though neither reached a single settled form.

Concepts and inspirations

  • distributed museum (Gosden and Larson)
  • cultural capital and prestige (Tony Bennett; Pierre Bourdieu)
  • collective object biography (Arjun Appadurai; Igor Kopytoff)
  • authenticity and the domestic object (John Ruskin; William Morris; Chris Miele)
  • visiting script (Carol Duncan; Alan Wallach; Helen Rees Leahy)
  • feminist museology (Jordanna Bailkin)
  • Ruskinian community museum (John Ruskin; William Morris)
  • feminine public sphere (Jürgen Habermas; Megan Smitley; Simon Morgan)
  • cumulative agency

Argues against

  • Ruth Hoberman's account of women's interwar move towards a separate feminine museum space: Hill argues that before 1914 women sought inclusion within masculine museum spaces, and that the attempt to develop a distinct, separate museum space for women only really emerged after the First World War. PDF p. 142
  • late twentieth-century views of the museum as an impersonal apparatus of power: Hill argues that these gave far too much weight to the museum's power to produce a unified effect on visitors, since museums were aggregations of groups with different agendas. PDF p. 19
  • the view that museums suppressed all the non-museum meanings of objects: Hill is sceptical that museums could do this, and argues that donated domestic objects kept their earlier meanings in the museum. PDF p. 91

Sources and ways of working

  • accession registers and annual reports of nine museums, counted by discipline, with donation events as the unit PDF p. 93
  • collective object biography built from scraps of documentation, since most gifts have a sentence or two of record PDF p. 91
  • the diaries and letters of individual women visitors, read for how they used the museum PDF p. 129
  • accession registers and annual reports from a dozen museums, 1880-1914, for donors and sellers PDF p. 63

Gaps it names

  • The author says work on women and museums has mainly concerned art museums and visitors, and calls for looking beyond visitors, art and national institutions PDF p. 18
  • The author calls women's involvement in the interwar period ambiguous and leaves the shape of the later period open PDF p. 231

Contents and chapter overviews

Ho, Denise Y.; Li, Jie (2016). “From Landlord Manor to Red Memorabilia: Reincarnations of a Chinese Museum Town”. Modern China.8 concepts

The article frames museums in China as living, dynamic public spaces that continually redefine the past, against the view that they are static, museal mausoleums. It is a cultural and political history of one site, a museum town in Sichuan, combining the history of exhibition with fieldwork, archives and the study of ritual, theatre and the market. Its argument is that the museum's power lies in its material things and their afterlives, not in material permanence.

Concepts and inspirations

  • museal (museums as mausoleums) (Theodore Adorno; Joseph Levenson; Mayfair Yang)
  • living spaces (after Robson) (James Robson)
  • object lesson
  • museum as temple (Robson; ter Haar; Teiser)
  • model theatrical work (museum as stage) (Clark)
  • museum as courtroom
  • guerilla exhibits
  • commodity form (Denton; Dutton)

Argues against

  • the view that Chinese museums are static, museal spaces, as in Levenson's 'museumified' temples and Adorno's 'museal': far from being museumified or museal, museums in China have been dynamic and vital public spaces p. 4
  • the view that the market has commodified the Maoist past and so erased it (Denton; Dutton): the commodity form is more complex; marketing Mao memorabilia can offer alternative, even subversive, understandings p. 25
  • the official Mao-era account of Liu Wencai and the water dungeon: at the height of the Mao years the authorities fabricated evidence like the water dungeon p. 20

Sources and ways of working

  • fieldwork in Anren, with interviews of museum staff, the Liu family and Fan Jianchuan p. 4
  • archival sources, including Shanghai Municipal Archive files and directives found in archives p. 17
  • close reading of exhibit booklets, children's readers, comic books, films and songs as texts, including the manor's floor plan and labels p. 7

Gaps it names

  • how Liu Wencai is taught in school textbooks; the authors' survey of contemporary textbooks did not confirm the accounts they heard p. 32
  • whether the case of Liu Wencai will be resolved; the authors describe it as still unresolved p. 22

Contents and chapter overviews

Hooper-Greenhill, Eilean (1992). Museums and the Shaping of Knowledge. London: Routledge.8 concepts

The book treats museums as historically variable systems of knowing rather than fixed institutions with a single origin, and it argues that the museum’s rationality, objects and visitors have changed with each epistemic framework and with shifting relations of power. It is a critical intellectual and cultural history addressed to museum practitioners and museum studies, drawing on Foucault’s ‘effective history’ and epistemes. Its final argument is that the contemporary turn to experience, participation and pleasure may be a new form of control.

Concepts and inspirations

  • effective history (Foucault)
  • episteme (Foucault)
  • disciplinary museum (Foucault)
  • cabinet of the world (Foucault; Yates)
  • ‘safe’ history (Foucault)
  • no essential museum (Foucault)
  • producing and consuming subjects
  • experience and pleasure as control (Foucault)

Argues against

  • accounts that project present museum relations back in time as ‘direct ancestors’ of modern museums (Taylor; Whitehead): Such histories are blind to present practices and to the plurality of museum forms; the text holds that no essential museum or direct ancestor can be identified. p. 8
  • the Medici Palace as ‘the first museum of Europe’ (Taylor; Alsop): The label projects a later museum back onto the palace; its older forms of knowledge, magic included, were integral rather than superseded, and the collection served the Medici family alone. p. 11
  • normal histories that describe cabinets of curiosity as ‘irrational’, ‘miscellaneous’ and ‘confused’: The cabinets were rational within their own episteme, and their logic becomes visible only when their conditions of truth are reconstructed. p. 11

Sources and ways of working

  • archival documents read against the grain: inventories, letters, catalogues and commission reports, interrogated for the conditions under which objects were valued p. 21
  • reconstruction of a lost cabinet from surviving drawings, a contemporary description and a sale catalogue (the Bonnier de la Mosson cabinet, after Hill) p. 21

Gaps it names

  • the curatorial aim of ‘completing the collection’ and ‘filling the gaps’ assumes that a complete classification is possible; the author calls for analysis of how such classifications were constituted p. 165
  • an effective history of the British Museum that selects a time-frame and assesses together the slave trade, travel, financial resources and other elements of the museum’s identity p. 20
  • a series of documents showing how colonisation enabled particular subject positions and technologies of collecting at a specific geo-historical site p. 21

Contents and chapter overviews

Hopkins, Owen (2021). The Museum: From Its Origins to the 21st Century.8 concepts

Hopkins frames the museum as an institution whose authority has survived every critique, from Broodthaers and Crimp onward, and whose history passes through five forms: the Enlightenment, public, modern, global and post-national museum. Hopkins’s overall argument is that each form was shaped by power, empire and the symbolic building, and that the museum now has to be reinvented around decolonisation and inclusion. The book is a general cultural and architectural history of the museum, written for a broad readership, with some museum-studies and heritage concerns in its final chapter.

Concepts and inspirations

  • institutional critique
  • heterotopia (Michel Foucault)
  • cabinet of curiosities as microcosm
  • five manifestations of the museum
  • public museum as moral improvement
  • post-national museum (Edward Said)
  • decolonize is to decontextualise
  • building transcends the collection

Argues against

  • Gertrude Stein's view that a museum of modern art is an 'oxymoron': Hopkins argues the chapter has shown this was far from the case, because Modernism changed and reinvented the museum.
  • Le Corbusier's earlier view that the museum is a liar that sanctifies its objects: Hopkins notes that Le Corbusier had been very critical of museums, and then records that he designed the National Museum of Western Art in Ueno in 1955.
  • the claim that museums are neutral and can rise above debates about their objects (as put by the British Museum's director): The #MuseumsAreNotNeutral campaign argues that museums are political constructs rooted in colonial power.
  • the view on the political left that museums are agents of colonialism and all their objects were stolen: Hopkins argues this ignores the nuances of each object's history, and that each needs its own assessment.

Sources and ways of working

  • visitor numbers and national counts of museums, such as China's 349 museums in 1978 against about 5,100 now
  • reading the building as the embodiment of its contents, by comparing the Parthenon with the Acropolis Museum
  • comparison across regions, placing Chinese building beside Western museum outposts in Abu Dhabi and Shenzhen
  • press releases, news reports and web sources for recent cases, cited in the end notes

Gaps it names

  • decolonisation requires treating every object differently, assessing its origin, provenance and meaning today; this is described as a long and complex project
  • workforce diversity: the staff of museums must reflect the public in class, ethnic background and gender
  • how a museum collects digital objects such as apps, which Hopkins raises as an open question
  • the decisions about what to display and what to keep in storage are seldom acknowledged

Contents and chapter overviews

Hudson, Kenneth (1975). A Social History of Museums: What the Visitors Thought. London: Macmillan.7 concepts

Hudson writes a social history of the visitor: how museums in Europe and North America came to admit a broad public, and how far their owners and directors treated visitors as privileged guests, as learners or as subjects of research. It is cultural and social history with elements of museum studies and of the history of visitor research, and it relies on letters, press comment, catalogues and survey reports more than on theory. Its overall argument is that museums stayed run for the taste of their makers until visitor research began, and that the main obstacle to change has been curators' attitudes towards the public.

Concepts and inspirations

  • visitors admitted as a privilege, not a right
  • the museum as temple and the director as priest
  • the market research age (Duncan F. Cameron; D. S. Abbey)
  • class differences in how visitors see museums (Pierre Bourdieu; Alain Darbel)
  • several publics and the chief reasons for a visit (Peter H. Pott)
  • the visitor as guest, not child (Peter H. Pott)
  • participation and closing the interval (Marshall McLuhan; Harley W. Parker)

Argues against

  • museum directors and curators who see visitor surveys as frivolous and value the public less than the collections: Hudson records a Vienna director who thought surveys of visitors a frivolous use of museum funds and accepted that the public should be grateful for access; Hudson treats this as the attitude he is criticising p. 3
  • curators who believe they learn as much by listening to visitors as by commissioning research: Hudson grants that overheard remarks are a useful supplement but says a survey is needed to know what kind of person is speaking p. 101

Sources and ways of working

  • turnstile counts and attendance figures as the measure of success p. 6
  • overheard remarks and unsolicited written comments from visitors p. 101
  • questionnaires put to visitors, reported partly as statistics and partly as quotations p. 114
  • visitor letters, press comment and reports of exhibitions as the only evidence for earlier periods p. 7

Gaps it names

  • visitor surveys are rare and the author says that comparable figures for other countries are lacking p. 122
  • how visitors of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries actually responded, since no visitor survey of their period was made p. 7

Contents and chapter overviews

Impey, Oliver; MacGregor, Arthur (eds.) (1985). The Origins of Museums: The Cabinet of Curiosities in Sixteenth- and Seventeenth-Century Europe. Oxford: Clarendon Press.8 concepts

The volume treats the cabinet of curiosities as a serious, if miscellaneous, early form of the museum rather than a whimsical precursor, and it sets out to revise von Schlosser's 1908 account. It is a collection of case studies in the history of collecting: reconstructions of named collections and their inventories, with art-historical, scientific-historical, archaeological and anthropological strands. Its theory is historiographical (Schlosser, Bacon, Fludd, Quiccheberg) rather than social theory, so its concepts are mostly terms of art and museum history.

Concepts and inspirations

  • Kunst- and Wunderkammer (terminology and typology) (Julius von Schlosser)
  • universal programme (universal Kunstkammer) (Francis Bacon)
  • microcosm (Robert Fludd; Thomas DaCosta Kaufmann)
  • Mannerist museum (Erwin Neumann; Thomas DaCosta Kaufmann)
  • trade goods versus curious objects
  • migration of objects between cabinet categories
  • 'Indian' as a catch-all label for Asian and other goods
  • cabinet as working resource

Argues against

  • Julius von Schlosser's 1908 north-south distinction between Kunst- and Wunderkammer mentalities: Schepelern holds that collecting principles were the same everywhere: the prince aimed at totality and the natural philosopher at systematic order, so the difference is one of purpose, not of region p. 175
  • the view that the cabinet of curiosities was a whimsical precursor of the museum: the introduction argues that the miscellany of the cabinet was a serious programme aimed at universality PDF p. 17
  • the founders' assumption that private cabinets would pass easily into public museums: the move from private to public was by no means straightforward, as the Royal Society's Repository shows p. 226

Sources and ways of working

  • visitors' reports and travel accounts used to reconstruct a treasury cupboard by cupboard (Distelberger, Vienna) p. 53
  • dated inventories read against surviving objects, for example the Ambras inventories of 1596 and 1621 p. 38
  • comparison of identical objects across English country-house collections to infer a common dealer or auction source (Impey) p. 371

Gaps it names

  • the typology of Brazilian clubs and axes, which needs a closer look (Feest) p. 332
  • fuller systematic studies of collections and records for Asian material, with each object tied to dated inventories (Ayers) p. 355

Contents and chapter overviews

Janes, Robert R. (2009). Museums in a Troubled World: Renewal, Irrelevance or Collapse?. London: Routledge.9 concepts

Janes frames museums as trustees of collections that have turned inward: captured by market ideology, business 'tribalism' and self-inflicted habits, they have stopped asking why they exist. Janes’s argument is that museums must take up 'stewardship' of communities and the biosphere, moving from temple to forum. The book is a practitioner's polemic rather than a theoretical study, and the author says it 'lacks a theoretical stance'; it sits between museum studies, organisational and leadership writing, and environmental and social critique, with ideas borrowed from ecology, complexity and Buddhist meditation.

Concepts and inspirations

  • stewardship (Eric Hoffer)
  • temple, not forum (Duncan Cameron)
  • civil society and the public sphere
  • the three agendas (Will Phillips)
  • fallacy of authoritative neutrality
  • primus inter pares (Robert Greenleaf)
  • linear exhibition as a book (Kathleen McLean)
  • mindfulness (Jon Kabat-Zinn)
  • high-entropy and low-entropy culture (Jeremy Rifkin)

Argues against

  • the Universal Museum Declaration, signed by the Louvre, the Rijksmuseum and the British Museum: Janes calls it an ethnocentric and colonial relic that refuses repatriation claims on the ground that universal museums are best placed to act for the world, violating the anthropological principle of not deciding other people's best interests p. 85
  • Adam Gopnik's object-centred idea of the mindful museum: the preoccupation with objects and collections is one of the primary obstacles to museums becoming truly mindful p. 147
  • the lone museum director model: the primus inter pares tradition offers a collective and shared executive authority as an alternative p. 62
  • the Bilbao Effect as a model of culture-led regeneration: Janes treats the Guggenheim Bilbao effect as a seductive poster child and cites critics who show that the regeneration was not culturally led p. 110

Sources and ways of working

  • fieldwork and apprenticeship among the Willow Lake Dene hunters in the Canadian subarctic, used as a model of adaptation p. 46
  • career-based observation at the Glenbow Museum, including budgets, deaccessioning and reorganisation p. 72
  • interviews and reports from practitioners such as exhibit planner Kathleen McLean on visitor response and exhibition design p. 78
  • admissions and attendance figures as measures of museum performance and market pressure p. 79

Gaps it names

  • the role of museums as agents of the collective good and civil society, which the author says has received little attention beyond education and entertainment p. 21
  • how far the Universal Museum Declaration is harming public perceptions of the museum community is unknown p. 85
  • the stewardship of the ethnosphere, the diversity of human cultures, which the author says seems to be going the way of biodiversity p. 46

Contents and chapter overviews

Jasanoff, Maya (2005). Edge of Empire: Conquest and Collecting in the East, 1750–1850. London: Fourth Estate.7 concepts

Jasanoff treats collecting as a lens on the British empire in India and Egypt between 1750 and 1850, reading the objects and collectors who gathered them as evidence of an empire that was piecemeal, collaborative and still contested by indigenous powers and by France. Museums appear mainly as the destinations of imperial collections (the East India Company's Oriental Repository, the British Museum, the Louvre, the Townley Gallery), not as institutions studied in their own right. The study is cultural and political history with strong biographical and material-culture methods, written against triumphalist and purely oppositional accounts of empire.

Concepts and inspirations

  • collecting as self-fashioning
  • Orientalism as the collecting of knowledge (Edward Said)
  • the British Empire as a collection
  • crossing and mixing (collaborative empire) (Edward Said; Subaltern Studies)
  • trophy of war
  • know-thy-enemy approach
  • demonized enemy

Argues against

  • postcolonial scholarship that treats European expansion as a one-sided, oppositional imposition of Western power (Said, Subaltern Studies): Stories of crossing and mixing show that encounters involved accommodation as well as division, and that others changed and challenged imperial power. p. 7
  • triumphal accounts of British expansion as heaven's command and a sure thing: The expansion was contingent and hotly contested by indigenous powers and by France, and depended on continental Europeans and imperial subjects. p. 8
  • the division of the British empire into a first Atlantic empire and a second Asian one: The Seven Years War created an empire that was both Atlantic and Asian, commercial and conquering, so the opposition misleads. p. 21
  • the chauvinistic imperial ethos read back onto earlier expansion in the East: The ethos hardened only after Europeans had gained influence for generations, and it was partly wishful thinking that compensated for British vulnerability. p. 11

Sources and ways of working

  • biographies of individual collectors, traced through wills, inventories and receipts, such as the lists of lost trunks of de Boigne's household p. 95
  • prize agents' accounts and valuations of captured libraries and palaces after a war p. 185
  • reading the collected objects themselves as hard evidence of contact, and following where they were later displayed p. 12

Gaps it names

  • the fate of Tipu's manuscript library: of perhaps 3,500 volumes, only about three hundred reached London and the rest are lost p. 185
  • the experiences of camp followers, interpreters, common soldiers, women and children on imperial frontiers, which the author says warrant research p. 8

Contents and chapter overviews

Karp, Ivan; Lavine, Steven D. (eds.) (1991). Exhibiting Cultures: The Poetics and Politics of Museum Display. Washington: Smithsonian Institution Press.8 concepts

The volume treats the museum as a contested site where every display carries the cultural assumptions of its makers, and it argues that exhibitions should make those assumptions visible, especially when they show other cultures. Most chapters are case studies of American, European and Native American displays, and the argument is a practical one about how exhibitions can admit their own point of view. The volume is an edited collection mixing art history, anthropology, folklore studies and curatorial reflection, so its overall argument is set by the editors' introduction and by Karp's framing of Part I rather than by any single author.

Concepts and inspirations

  • museum effect (Svetlana Alpers)
  • exhibition as a field of three agents
  • resonance and wonder (Thomas Greene; Louis Montrose; new historicism)
  • museum as ceremonial monument and secular ritual (Victor Turner; Alan Wallach)
  • mitate (Masakatsu Gunji; Jean Baudrillard; Claude Levi-Strauss)
  • rasa (Bharata Muni (Natyasastra))
  • ethnographic object: excision, in situ and in context
  • frame analysis of festival participation (Erving Goffman)

Argues against

  • the universal aesthetic values claimed by the great survey museums: Greenblatt's historicising approach makes it the exhibitors' responsibility to show continuities and differences between aesthetic evaluations and the contexts in which objects are appreciated
  • the view that art museums are a neutral and transparent sheltering space: A museum is not the neutral and transparent sheltering space that it is often claimed to be; it is a ceremonial monument
  • the exhibitor as a spokesman who represents a culture: Exhibitors cannot represent cultures; they should set up nonmisleading and stimulating conditions for the viewer
  • the museum as a temple offering an objective model: Few serious museum practitioners would claim that a museum could be anything but a forum

Sources and ways of working

  • fieldwork with participants at a festival, observing and interviewing them about how they understood what they were doing
  • reading the architecture, decoration and installation of a museum as a ceremonial text
  • visitor research with novice viewers and multisensory exhibition trials
  • comparison of the labels, placement and storage of several museums from one region

Gaps it names

  • experiments in which artworks are organised according to the aesthetic categories of the cultures from which they derive
  • the expansion of the expertise of established museums in presenting non-Western and minority cultures
  • experiments in exhibition design that present multiple perspectives or admit the contingent nature of interpretations
  • the sensory dimension of ethnographic displays, since smells, temperature and sound are generally left out

Contents and chapter overviews

Kavanagh, Gaynor (ed.) (1996). Making Histories in Museums. London: Leicester University Press.9 concepts

An edited volume of 21 chapters by museum practitioners, mainly historians and anthropologists working in museums, arguing that history made in museums is constructed, political and plural, and must engage material evidence, visitors and the present. Kavanagh's preface frames it as a call for braver, object-rich histories. It is practice-led museum studies, drawing on cultural history, historiography and a few anthropological and sociological sources, rather than a theoretical monograph.

Concepts and inspirations

  • symbolic spaces: cognitive, social and dream spaces (Sheldon Annis)
  • memory as construction, set against history (Halbwachs)
  • relativism as museum orthodoxy (Thomas Kuhn; Paul Feyerabend)
  • a montage of memories (E.P. Thompson)
  • interpretative flexibility of technology (SCOT) (Bijker; Pinch)
  • museum narrative as the present author's account (Hodder; Shanks; Tilley)
  • folklore as oral-assumptive symbolic behaviour
  • the loss of the West as the centre of civilisation (George Steiner)
  • the 'Other' and 'One of Us'

Argues against

  • relativism in museum practice, including the views of Kuhn and Feyerabend: Truth is not wholly relative to culture: people from different cultures can communicate, and their theories must answer to the world p. 45
  • the folk museum tradition that tidies rural poverty into a harmonious past: Folk museums such as Skansen served dominant needs for a placid, secure past; curators should instead record the contexts in which objects were made and used p. 34
  • internalist and celebratory technology exhibitions: Technology should be shown as shaped by social groups, with its failures and costs visible p. 125

Sources and ways of working

  • oral history and recollection of people who lived or worked the past, to add to objects p. 5
  • reconstruction of objects from documents, tested in use, as with the Ulster plough p. 37
  • front-end evaluation of exhibition ideas with visitors, quantitative and by gender p. 119

Gaps it names

  • few museums have established posts for minority audiences; such posts are the exception rather than the norm p. 178

Contents and chapter overviews

Kirshenblatt-Gimblett, Barbara (1998). Destination Culture: Tourism, Museums, and Heritage. Berkeley: University of California Press.9 concepts

Kirshenblatt-Gimblett frames museums, world's fairs, festivals and tourist sites as agencies of display: objects gain meaning at their destination, and heritage is a new mode of production that takes the past as its resource. The overall argument is a political economy of showing, in which the work of exhibition, tourism and the 'consciousness industry' shapes what is shown and what value it acquires. It is a cultural and anthropological study that draws on ethnography, performance and avant-garde theory, museum studies and the history of world's fairs, with each essay treating a different site.

Concepts and inspirations

  • the ethnographic object as fragment (detachment)
  • in situ and in context display
  • heritage as new production in the present
  • display as interface
  • heritage that forecloses what it shows (Steven Mullaney)
  • alienability of inalienable possessions
  • authenticity located in reception (undoing the ethnographic) (Bertolt Brecht; Antonin Artaud)
  • 'multicultural' and 'international' as euphemisms
  • bad taste and kitsch as circulating categories (Clement Greenberg; Theodor Adorno; Mikhail Bakhtin)

Argues against

  • Modernist and Greenbergian accounts of kitsch as a defence of high culture against mass audiences: Kitsch is a category produced by the arbiters of taste and is unstable; whether the erosion of high and low leads to kitsch or to liberating pluralism is left open p. 278
  • The heritage industry's discourse of conservation, preservation and reclamation: Heritage is not lost and found, stolen and reclaimed; it produces something new in the present p. 149
  • Festival organisers' claim that the labels used in the Los Angeles Festival were benign: Ethnic, national and cultural designations are not unproblematic; they reduce performers to a geopolitical identity p. 242

Sources and ways of working

  • reading press reviews of the festival, to see how critics wrote about performances from Asia and the Pacific p. 247
  • observation of heritage sites and tourist promotional material in New Zealand, Australia and the United States p. 7
  • interviews with festival organisers, here an associate artistic director of the Los Angeles Festival p. 208
  • archival correspondence and fair reports, such as a special correspondent's account of the Benguiat collection in 1904 p. 108

Gaps it names

  • whether the erosion of distinctions between high and low leads to a world of kitsch or to a liberating pluralism, which the chapter leaves open p. 281

Contents and chapter overviews

Knell, Simon J.; Aronsson, Peter; Amundsen, Arne Bugge; et al. (eds.) (2011). National Museums: New Studies from Around the World. London: Routledge.8 concepts

The volume treats national museums as places where nations are performed, anchored in objects and memory, and negotiated among states, professionals and publics, rather than as neutral records of national history. Its overall argument, set out in the introductions by Knell, Aronsson and Preziosi, is that these museums are poetic and political, and that comparison should complicate generalisations about them. It is a museum studies and cultural history collection, with chapters drawing on art history, postcolonial criticism, anthropology and the sociology of memory.

Concepts and inspirations

  • the nation performed in the museum (Benedict Anderson; Bourdieu)
  • exhibitionary complex (Tony Bennett)
  • cultural nation (Kulturnation) set against the state nation (Halbwachs; Smith)
  • Orientalism in the display of Chinese art (Said)
  • third space (Bhabha; Pratt; Spivak)
  • aesthetics as belief enhancer (Greenblatt; Preziosi; Shanks and Tilley)
  • symbolic capital transferred through looted objects (Bourdieu)
  • palimpsest of colonial and postcolonial history

Argues against

  • Postmodern museologists who treat the nation as an imagined construction and cite Anderson without his historical basis: Knell argues that Anderson was not writing through a postmodern lens, and that his account is more historically specific than the constructed-nation idea that his disciples borrow. p. 3
  • Museum professionals who present the museum as neutral and authoritative: Knell argues that this is a moral positioning produced through professionalisation, and that museums are poetic and political spaces rather than purveyors of objective truth. p. 4
  • Forum-style museum models that offer only cultural diversity: Choi argues that a forum-like museum cannot address the legacy of colonialism in Korea, and that cultural diversity without deconstructing power justifies social dominance. p. 298
  • Heritage management that treats culture as something to protect: Preziosi argues that serious care for culture entails its de-sanctification, that museums should expose the faith in artefacts as witnesses of a national essence. p. 66

Sources and ways of working

  • autoethnography, with the author's own visits to a national museum as the main research material, read against the museum's interpretive approach p. 291
  • exhibition lists, annual reports and loan records of a national museum, read as evidence of its political purposes p. 188
  • architecture and building history read as a record of colonial power p. 374
  • visitor surveys and interviews with tourists on a guided tour, taken as evidence of how visitors read a museum's ideology p. 369

Gaps it names

  • a comparative study of the origins of European national museums and their uses of history, which the editors plan under the follow-on Eunamus project PDF p. 20

Contents and chapter overviews

Krech, Shepard, III; Hail, Barbara A. (eds.) (1999). Collecting Native America, 1870–1960. Washington: Smithsonian Institution Press.9 concepts

The volume treats private collecting of Native American artifacts as a historical process. It argues that collectors' motives must be understood in their own time, not through presentist critique or an account of imposed hegemony alone. Its overall argument is that these collectors, many of whom believed Native cultures were vanishing, shaped the public museums and university anthropology of North America, and that in Hearst's case professionalization erased alternative modes of acquisition. It is museum history and history of anthropology, with elements of cultural, social and intellectual history, resting on archival, documentary and object-based research.

Concepts and inspirations

  • collectors in their own day (against presentism) (T. J. Jackson Lears; Richard Wrightman Fox)
  • missionary discourse (Nicholas Thomas)
  • recontextualization of sacred objects (Nicholas Thomas)
  • cabinet to public museum (Carol Duncan)
  • salvage and the vanishing Indian
  • professionalizing anthropological museum and erasure of alternative acquisition (Henry May)
  • educational collecting as cultural production (Margery Akin; Pierre Bourdieu; Belk et al.)
  • authenticity of re-created objects
  • the typological exhibit

Argues against

  • critical museum studies that read collecting as colonial dispossession, judge collectors by present methods, or read exhibits as enforced meaning: the editors seek to return collectors to their day and understand their motives without presentist judgement
  • judging missionary collectors by present standards of culture and church-state separation: wholesale condemnation of Jackson's conversion aims amounts to a form of presentism, since the Great Chain of Being informed the whole missionary crusade
  • the museum as a neutral public education institution: McCord's displays decontextualized objects and perpetuated an idealized, timeless image of aboriginal people

Sources and ways of working

  • printed, manuscript and oral sources on collectors, used to fill gaps in museum catalogues and accession records
  • correspondence and family papers, including McCord's letters kept as dossiers of transactions
  • photographs of exhibition halls read for their typological arrangement
  • exchange records and systematic field collections in university and museum holdings

Gaps it names

  • the collector who housed artifacts in a private museum is seldom the focus of studies of indigenous collections
  • the link between gender, occupation and collecting, which the authors suggest is worth exploring
  • Native responses to collecting, which survive mainly as isolated rebukes and oral accounts

Contents and chapter overviews

Logan, William; Nic Craith, Máiréad; Kockel, Ullrich (eds.) (2016). A Companion to Heritage Studies. Chichester: Wiley Blackwell.8 concepts

The volume frames heritage as a present-centred cultural practice and a form of cultural politics, not a technical or managerial task, and argues that the field has changed through evolution since the late 1980s rather than through a paradigm shift. Its chapters are mostly by heritage scholars and practitioners, so it is an interdisciplinary companion combining critical heritage studies, anthropology, law, tourism studies, museum studies and architecture, with a strong ethical and human-rights strand. Its overall argument is that heritage should serve communities and that expert and state authority over it needs critical scrutiny.

Concepts and inspirations

  • heritagescaping
  • exoticlandia (Said; Salazar)
  • authorised heritage discourse (Laurajane Smith)
  • memory ecology (Latour; Ingold; Meskell)
  • World Heritage as a discursive tool of nation-building (Nora; Tunbridge and Ashworth; Duara)
  • embodiment (Yanagi Soetsu; John Collins; Taylor)
  • registers of engagement
  • stability, justice and reconciliation trade-off in post-conflict heritage (Ciorciari; Bloomfield, Barnes and Huyse)

Argues against

  • Claims that heritage studies has undergone a paradigm shift (Araoz, Silberman): Change has been evolutionary rather than revolutionary, in Kuhn's sense, building on the past rather than sweeping it aside
  • David Lowenthal's distrust of empathy and of emotion in heritage and museum practice: Emotion and affect are constitutive of heritage-making and should be built into interpretive practice and research
  • The simplistic East/West binary in heritage scholarship and practice: Western and Asian ideas have long intermingled, and a creolized hybrid culture overcomes the binary

Sources and ways of working

  • Critical discourse analysis of official tourism promotion videos, read for scripts and stereotypes
  • Visitor interviews at museums and heritage sites, coded as registers of engagement
  • Close reading of official Chinese documents, state media and nomination dossiers, set against historians' accounts

Gaps it names

  • Whether UNESCO should keep separate lists for tangible and intangible heritage, or bring them together
  • Research on the affective moment of visiting, on memory, imagination and emotional regulation

Contents and chapter overviews

Longair, Sarah; McAleer, John (eds.) (2012). Curating Empire: Museums and the British Imperial Experience. Manchester: Manchester University Press.9 concepts

The volume treats museums in the British Empire as individual, fragile and peripheral projects, shaped by the curators who ran them, rather than as instruments of a planned imperial policy. Its argument is that a museum's purpose and the meaning of its objects depended on local circumstances, audiences and personalities, and that these museums formed networks of 'multiple metropoles' that bypassed London. It is a work of cultural and museum history in an imperial-history framework, drawing on archives, newspapers, visitors' books and object histories; the editors say its authors range across anthropology, archaeology, history, museum studies and the histories of art, design and material culture.

Concepts and inspirations

  • multiple metropoles (Frederick Cooper; Ann Laura Stoler)
  • museums as tools of empire (John MacKenzie)
  • curator as cultural mediator (Susan Sheets-Pyenson; David Lambert; Alan Lester)
  • visitor agency (Michael Baxandall; Eilean Hooper-Greenhill)
  • cultural technologies of rule (Bernard Cohn; Nicholas Dirks)
  • recolonisation (James Belich)
  • doing history historically (Frederick Cooper)
  • meanings of objects inflected by display context (Tim Barringer)
  • automata and the Orient (Simon Schaffer)

Argues against

  • Museums as monolithic instruments of imperial control, or the products of a central imperial plan: Museums in the empire were vulnerable and fragile institutions, rarely bastions of insurmountable imperial control, often founded by peripheral initiatives p. 5
  • Museum studies that prefer theory over history and present museums as synonymous with empire: Museums should be assessed in their original historical contexts, not by present-day standards, using archival evidence p. 5
  • Post-colonial readings of Maori artefacts as objects of an imperialist gaze: The literature on the Pacific is enthusiastic about post-colonial theory without historical method or an understanding of museum practice p. 59
  • The 'invention of tradition' school, which dismisses indigenous attempts at cultural maintenance and revival: Indigenous people survive and construct their own modernities p. 58

Sources and ways of working

  • Newspaper reports, personal correspondence, education department records and funding applications, used to reconstruct visitors' responses where visitor books give only numbers p. 13
  • Visitors' books, such as the Colonial Museum in Wellington, read for the names and visits of Maori leaders p. 63
  • Comparison across museums in different settings, from King's Lynn and Brighton to Freetown, Christchurch and Colombo p. 7
  • Bazaar and fair programmes and local press reports as evidence of how audiences encountered empire p. 45

Gaps it names

  • The relationship between museums and their audiences, which needs more research; visitors are the great unknowns p. 13
  • The significance of museum architecture as an expression of intellectual and social aims, flagged for further study PDF p. 12
  • The careers, roles and practices of museum staff, especially in smaller institutions p. 9

Contents and chapter overviews

Lu, Tracey L-D (2014). Museums in China: Power, Politics and Identities. London: Routledge.9 concepts

The book frames Chinese museums as instruments of competing stakeholders (foreign elites, missionaries, the Republican government, the Communist state, local communities and private founders), each using museums to promote its own values and interests. Its overall argument is that Chinese museums have served political, religious and economic ends from the start, and that ecomuseums and tourism sites have often weakened the communities they claim to serve. It is a cultural and political history of museums, written within museum studies and heritage studies and drawing on some anthropological fieldwork.

Concepts and inspirations

  • museum as selective institution serving particular social segments (Bennett; Bourdieu and Darbel)
  • agency of stakeholders and curators (Bourdieu; Byrne et al.)
  • cultural capital of collectors and curators (Bourdieu)
  • habitus of curators and scholars (Bourdieu)
  • heritage museumised as regalia for a colonial state (Anderson B.)
  • civilizing ritual (Duncan)
  • ecomuseum as a model of community heritage (Davis P.)
  • actor-network theory (Latour; Byrne et al.)
  • dichotomised discourse of advanced West and antique China

Argues against

  • the ICOM definition of a museum as a non-profit institution in the service of society: Heritage is defined in different contexts and museums serve the interests of particular social groups, so the definition is not always true in reality PDF p. 16
  • the Louvre and the British Museum as models of national museums: Chinese national museums have much greater ideological and political missions, since the Louvre was built to glorify the French state and the British Museum to enlighten the British p. 138

Sources and ways of working

  • the visitor signature book of the Heude Museum, 1932 to 1946, analysed as a list of visitors and their affiliations p. 35
  • receipts and letters on specimen sales and publications, used to trace the museum’s role as a supplier to Western institutions p. 36
  • interviews with curators, docents and villagers in the ecomuseums, translated by the author p. 145
  • the author’s own observation in villages in 2005 and 2012, and of museum staff at work p. 151

Gaps it names

  • how local communities engaged with the Shanghai and Nantong museums is largely undocumented, so visitors’ reception of the displays is unknown p. 88
  • the lack of community participation has left many museums alienated from the public, and private museums are financially fragile p. 214

Contents and chapter overviews

Lumley, Robert (ed.) (1988). The Museum Time-Machine: Putting Cultures on Display. London: Routledge.9 concepts

The volume treats the museum as a 'time-machine' that represents the past, and argues that the spread of open-air museums, period reconstructions and media-influenced displays has made it a central arena for national history and nostalgia. Its overall argument is that heritage and museum display are political and commercial constructions, that museums should expose their own classifications and the partiality of their records, and that they should help visitors orient themselves where inherited ideas of time and place are losing their force. It is a cultural and political study of heritage and display, with museum studies, sociology of culture (Bourdieu) and cultural studies behind it.

Concepts and inspirations

  • effective nostalgia
  • ethnohistory
  • countryside of the mind (Martin Wiener)
  • picturesque representation of subordinate classes (Gramsci)
  • time-machine display
  • SHIC classification
  • authority effect
  • Utopian site (Pierre Bourdieu)
  • realism and the real thing (Umberto Eco; Jean Baudrillard)

Argues against

  • curatorial empiricism, which treats museum work as factual, non-theoretical and objective: Empiricism alone is no guarantee of objectivity; curators must acknowledge that their structures of thought help form the reality they re-present p. 118
  • heritage policy presented as neutral preservation of the monumental past: nostalgia is a prescriptive and prospective matter, serving political ends p. 30
  • the display that claims this is how it was: a more honest statement would say what might have been, for these people, at this time p. 120

Sources and ways of working

  • visitor survey data broken down by gender, age, education and occupation, used to test a museum's audience against the population p. 200
  • reading the tape-slide scripts and guidebooks at the visitor centre, to see how a site presents its people and region p. 64
  • reading government reports and ministerial statements against the programmes they describe p. 29

Gaps it names

  • how visitors make sense of exhibitions, from the organisers' intentions through the display to the public's reading, which the volume says is rarely studied p. 9
  • how women's historical experience appears in areas where change is slow and measured by objects, and so is hard to display p. 118

Contents and chapter overviews

Macdonald, Sharon; Fyfe, Gordon (eds.) (1996). Theorizing Museums: Representing Identity and Diversity in a Changing World. Oxford: Blackwell.9 concepts

The volume frames museums as contextualizing and contextualized, contested, and constituted by their own institutional practice, and rejects accounts that read them as transparent reflections of dominant interests or as simple agencies of control. It is a collection of social and cultural theory applied to museums: social theory of time and memory (Urry), class and visiting (Fyfe and Ross), the sociology of the Tate as an agency of classification (Fyfe), feminist and poststructuralist readings of display (Porter, Riegel), and ethnographic and historical studies of institutional practice (Gable, Prösler, Zolberg). Its overall argument is that museums should be theorised as a distinctive cultural complex rather than used as a neutral vantage point.

Concepts and inspirations

  • context, contest and content
  • symbolic violence and the cultural arbitrary (Bourdieu; Bourdieu and Darbel)
  • heterotopia and utopies (Foucault; Marin; Malraux)
  • dialogic irony (Babcock; Hutcheon; Kathleen Stewart)
  • exhibition, curator and visitor as text, author and reader (John Berger; Judith Williamson; Ros Coward)
  • grid and group (Mary Douglas; Bourdieu; Urry)
  • incorporating and inscribing practices (Connerton; Bergson; Mead)
  • cosmological ordering of museum space (Cicero; Yates; Foucault)
  • vernacular historiography (new social history)

Argues against

  • Accounts that treat museums only as agencies of social control or as sites of distinction: Too simple; museums are also processes and creative agencies, and their role in consumption is wider than distinction. PDF p. 11
  • Bourdieu's account of museums in social reproduction: Qualified: subordinate groups partly penetrate the cultural arbitrary, reproduction occurs through fragmentation as well as incorporation, and institutions must be included; critics read the account as a covert determinism, a charge Fyfe takes seriously while keeping Bourdieu's framework. PDF p. 207
  • Museum studies that read displays as unproblematic reflections of dominant ideological interests: Too clear-cut a manipulation by exhibitors and too passive a public; the analyst's own reading should be acknowledged as a positioned act of interpretation. PDF p. 11
  • Urry's view that Connerton's account of bodily memory is general enough to stand alone: Too general; memory is socially structured, collective and artefact-based, so more localised processes must be added. PDF p. 55

Sources and ways of working

  • in-depth household interviews on visiting, read against class and place PDF p. 136
  • ethnographic study of frontline guides, taped tours and performances PDF p. 180
  • reading exhibitions through their poetics: layout, juxtaposition, visitor paths and the mirror and costume device PDF p. 88
  • close study of inquiry records and press campaigns over commissions and purchases PDF p. 224

Gaps it names

  • the social scientific study of museums is still relatively under-developed PDF p. 10
  • how people conceptualise museum visiting and how it articulates with their identity and locality PDF p. 18
  • how visitors' alternative readings are socially and culturally positioned PDF p. 17
  • how museums deal, or should deal, with controversial subjects PDF p. 18

Contents and chapter overviews

MacKenzie, John M. (2009). Museums and Empire: Natural History, Human Cultures and Colonial Identities. Manchester: Manchester University Press.9 concepts

MacKenzie frames the colonial museum as a tool of empire that ordered nature and peoples, displayed a Western vision of the world and justified expansion, yet also stimulated respect for indigenous cultures and layered identities that were imperial, colonial, provincial and national at once. The book is a comparative cultural and social history of museums in the settler colonies and Asia, written as a critical narrative with museum theory used sparingly. Its overall argument is that colonial museums were locally driven but tied together by networks of collecting and exchange, and that their claims to economic and moral benefit were largely rhetoric.

Concepts and inspirations

  • imperial archive (Benedict Anderson; Thomas Richards)
  • exhibitionary complex and surveillance (Tony Bennett; Foucault)
  • social life of things and object biography (Arjun Appadurai; Barringer and Flynn)
  • layered identities
  • view from below: visitors and reception
  • museum as theatre of identity
  • five-phase model of colonial museum history
  • scramble and othering
  • museum memory as a source of power

Argues against

  • Benedict Anderson's account of the museum within the colonial state's totalising classificatory grid: The statement is the pure vision of the social scientist and only partly grounded in reality: museums lived in the real world, the visibility Anderson imagined was seldom achieved, and funding and staff fell short. p. 8
  • The so-called new museology's claim that museums functioned as a metonym of the state itself: Museums should not be claimed to do too much, and colonial museums were not the instruments of state control that this view implies. p. 8
  • The early protagonists who argued that museums were vital to the economic and cultural health of colonies: Colonies strapped for funds did not see museums as the vital resource their advocates claimed, and budgets were always vulnerable. p. 9
  • John Ruskin's idealism about the museum as a didactic and aesthetic institution: Ruskin's idealism, skewed towards didactic and aesthetic ends, seems unrealistic when applied to the phases through which museums passed in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. p. 265

Sources and ways of working

  • Correspondence between collectors and curators, such as the letters between White and Currelly about Chinese purchases, read as evidence of motive and of how collectors justified their work p. 54
  • Annual reports and attendance figures, especially festival-period counts, read with awareness that reported visitor numbers were often dubious p. 256
  • Museum architecture read as an expression of colonial, civic and national power, alongside the displays it housed p. 7
  • A critical narrative built from territorial case studies rather than from museum theory p. 16

Gaps it names

  • Visitor reception and the view from below, which the author says is much less documented than the view from above p. 277
  • The class systems of the metropole recreated in colonies, which the author says need a more nuanced and technical analysis p. 16
  • The influence of Darwin's theory of evolution on colonial museums and the social and intellectual context of colonial science p. 15
  • Areas left out of the study, including Hong Kong, the Caribbean, West and East Africa and the Indian Ocean islands p. 16

Contents and chapter overviews

McClellan, Andrew (1994). Inventing the Louvre: Art, Politics, and the Origins of the Modern Museum in Eighteenth-Century Paris. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.7 concepts

The book frames the Paris art museum of 1750-1816 as a political and pedagogic institution rather than a neutral space of aesthetic display: the Crown, the Revolution and later the Empire each used the museum to project authority, and the classification and hanging of pictures carried that symbolic load. It is a cultural and political history grounded in architecture, hanging plans, catalogues and the reactions of visitors, with the history of art and museum studies as its frame.

Concepts and inspirations

  • transparency (Michel Foucault; Barbara Stafford)
  • comparative viewing (André Félibien; Roger de Piles)
  • art historical survey museum
  • conservation as good government
  • displacement and aura (Quatremère de Quincy; Louis-Pierre Deseine)
  • cyclical decline of art (Winckelmann; Quatremère de Quincy)
  • politico-historical model of art (Winckelmann)

Argues against

  • Quatremere de Quincy's cyclical and pessimistic view that post-Renaissance art declined and that a museum full of confiscated art would make no difference: The text says Denon's hang rejected the cyclical view and that the Louvre created a new historical insight, so that the museum did more than Quatremere allowed. p. 147
  • Quatremere de Quincy's view that great art must serve a useful and noble purpose and that the picture gallery is fit only for lesser genres: McClellan says that Quatremere's argument disregards the pleasure and intellectual stimulation of close visual engagement with a work in a well-tempered environment. p. 201

Sources and ways of working

  • visitors' accounts of the hang and of the museum public, such as the 1799 description of a village family in the Grand Gallery in La Decade philosophique p. 11
  • reconstructing the lost arrangement of a gallery from plans, catalogues and administrative records, such as Hubert's 1797 plan for the antique sculpture galleries p. 150
  • reconstructing eighteenth-century viewing habits from period treatises (Felibien, de Piles) so that the collection is read through contemporary eyes p. 31

Gaps it names

  • the Louvre under Vivant-Denon after 1803 and the museum's expansion, which the author says would need a different kind of study p. 2
  • early visitor responses to the Louvre and the Musee des monuments, which the author says lies beyond this study p. 201

Contents and chapter overviews

Meyer, Andrea; Savoy, Bénédicte (eds.) (2014). The Museum Is Open: Towards a Transnational History of Museums 1750–1940. Berlin: De Gruyter.8 concepts

The volume treats museums as products of transnational circulation rather than as containers of national identity, and asks what objects, casts, photographs, architectural models and experts carried from one institution to another. Its overall argument, set out in the editors’ introduction, is that national rhetoric about museums was real but incomplete, and that transfer, comparison and competition shaped museum form in Europe and across the Atlantic. It is a transnational cultural and art history of museums, with elements of museum studies, the history of collecting and the history of museum professionals, and some postcolonial criticism in the chapters on Istanbul and Algiers.

Concepts and inspirations

  • transnational history of museums (Patel; Pernau; Iriye and Saunier)
  • canonization and decanonization of objects (Krzysztof Pomian)
  • photographic connoisseurship (Hubert Locher)
  • national affirmation through transnational means
  • museum visit as transnational ritual (Carol Duncan)
  • contact sphere of art
  • systematic series versus the Cluny method
  • professionalization of intercultural transfer

Argues against

  • The view of the nation as a container without contacts or networks, which made national museum histories separate stories: Transnational history attends to the dependencies and transfers that cross political boundaries, and the editors reject the container idea p. 5
  • Pomian’s account of the museum object, with its stable life before and after the museum: Objects in transit are unstable, and how meaning is constituted during transit is not explained by that account p. 20

Sources and ways of working

  • Museum correspondence and reports by officials and advisers, such as Vachon’s reports on European museums of industrial arts and the Valentiner letters to Bode p. 139
  • Archive correspondence and committee records of the League of Nations’ International Museums Office, cited by Kott from the UNESCO archives p. 205
  • Museum reviews and reporting columns in journals, such as the museum chronicle of Museumskunde, which reported openings and guidebooks worldwide p. 183

Gaps it names

  • The shift from displayed to stored collections in the first decades of the twentieth century, through the Madrid conference and its handbook, which Kott says deserves a case study p. 216
  • A study of the museum’s establishment that argues beyond national borders, which the introduction says did not yet exist for the eighteenth century p. 3
  • How objects acquire meaning during the times of transit between cultures p. 20

Contents and chapter overviews

Miller, Edward (1973). That Noble Cabinet: A History of the British Museum. London: André Deutsch.5 concepts

Miller writes an institutional history of the British Museum: its founding, growth, buildings, staff and disputes with the Trustees, Treasury and Parliament, from 1753 to the separation of the library in the early 1970s. It names no theorist and states no theoretical framework; it is an administrative and intellectual history in the tradition of museum history, with a strong sense of the Museum as one continuous institution. Its overall argument is that the collections grew haphazardly, shaped by money, space and personalities, and that they should be understood through the people who secured them.

Concepts and inspirations

  • the house-like spirit of the Museum
  • history through the people who secured the treasures
  • classical taste of the Trustees
  • ethnography as the plaything of administrative convenience
  • national collection and national library

Argues against

  • the view that collecting is a product merely of artistically sterile ages: Collecting has graced almost every civilisation, from Hellenic temples to Roman private and public collections, so it is no new thing. p. 19
  • books that centre on the treasures of the Museum: Such treasures are touched upon only incidentally, in relation to the people who secured them. p. 17

Sources and ways of working

  • Trustees' committee minutes and parliamentary accounts and papers, cited for decisions on purchases and staff p. 221
  • parliamentary select committee evidence, read as testimony on the Museum's management and the ethnographical collections p. 222
  • private correspondence in the Add. MS. collections, such as letters between Keepers and excavators p. 308

Gaps it names

  • the ethnographical collections, whose objects in Sloane's catalogue largely remain unidentified p. 356
  • a separate ethnographical museum, which was not created and was not even contemplated nearly fifty years after the 1929 Royal Commission p. 327
  • the Museum's relation to the public libraries and the other national libraries, from which the author says it has tended to stand apart p. 362

Contents and chapter overviews

Morse, Nuala (2021). The Museum as a Space of Social Care. London: Routledge.8 concepts

Morse frames museums as institutions whose community engagement work is shaped by a 'logic of contribution' that treats communities as sources of something for the museum, and argues for a 'logic of care' as the alternative, with the museum as a space of social care. The book is an empirical practice study, grounded in ethnography of community engagement workers at a single local museum service, that draws on museum studies, cultural and feminist geography, care ethics and affective labour theory to recast the participatory turn and the institutional life of museum staff.

Concepts and inspirations

  • logic of care (Annemarie Mol)
  • logic of contribution
  • non-performative (Sara Ahmed; John Austin)
  • ethics of care (Virginia Held; Joan Tronto; Berenice Fisher)
  • affective labour (Michael Hardt; Antonio Negri; Hochschild)
  • museumness of care (Morse and Munro (2015))
  • care-ful museology (Joan Tronto)
  • institutional care (purpose, power, particularity) (Joan Tronto)

Argues against

  • the critical literature on participation, which redeems participation by calling for more and better forms of it (Graham, 2012): The cycle of critique followed by optimism for better participation is a critical impasse that persists because participation is framed as contribution to the museum; the logic of care is offered as a way out p. 4
  • the institutional claim that 'everything we do is community engagement': Such a statement lets a museum claim a commitment without changing practice, because naming the commitment comes to stand in for the action p. 81

Sources and ways of working

  • long-term ethnography in the Outreach team of a local authority museum, following engagement workers into sessions and out into the community p. 16
  • interviews, organisational documents and informal discussions with museum staff across departments p. 16
  • observation of community sessions with mental health, dementia, addiction and stroke groups, with snapshots of practice in narrative form p. 17
  • analysis of staff discourse and quotation of practitioners' voices, combined with the author's own interpretation p. 17

Gaps it names

  • research about the actual professional practice of community engagement is far less developed than work on participants or on the political ramifications p. 7
  • care-ful museology is left as an agenda for future research and conversation p. 212

Contents and chapter overviews

Muchitsch, Wolfgang (ed.) (2013). Does War Belong in Museums? The Representation of Violence in Exhibitions. Bielefeld: transcript.8 concepts

The volume frames war museums as ambivalent sites, at once museums and memorials, that cannot represent 'the war' and must either interrogate how war can be represented or slide into pseudo-realism. Its editor and keynote speaker argue that war museums are sites of contestation that should point visitors to the battlefields and memorials around them. It is a museum studies and heritage studies collection, combining military history, memory studies, art and architecture criticism, and reports on museum reform by practitioners.

Concepts and inspirations

  • pseudo-realism (Joan Scott)
  • semi-sacred war museum (museum and memorial)
  • memory and history (Nora) (Pierre Nora; Maurice Halbwachs)
  • technical aura
  • documentation, mise en scene and ensemble (Gottfried Korff; Martin Roth)
  • military-nation (Ayşe Gül Altınay)
  • foundation myth (Dieter Langewiesche)
  • new military history

Argues against

  • Ernst Jünger's essentialist view of war experience (Kriegserlebnis): War experience is not in the body unless one was wounded; for everyone else it is in the mind and in memories that never remain fixed. p. 37
  • The view that visitors can get near the thrill of battle by getting near weaponry: Stylised fascination with combat is the fantasy of stunted imaginations; war museums should offer alternative ways to approach the terror of the battlefield. p. 37
  • The claim that a war museum can describe war itself: All war museums fail to represent 'the war', since there was never consensus on what it was; they show the traces of collisions that happened long ago. p. 23

Sources and ways of working

  • Object case studies: conserved personal items set within a narrative and read against their wartime history p. 146
  • Comparison of the same photograph across museums with different captions, panels and visitor preconceptions p. 158
  • Typology of exhibitions sorted by presentation style, applied to a documented set of city-museum displays p. 132
  • Biographies of selected individuals used as the organising device of a military exhibition p. 56

Gaps it names

  • The normality of violence, the everyday acceptance of cruelty across history, which Rekdal admits he avoided and finds the hardest theme p. 128
  • The Holocaust in Belarusian museum display, which the author says is neglected though not taboo p. 194
  • Critical memorial work that goes further than Tur's Unknown Knight in questioning the image of the enemy p. 181
  • The gender balance of representations of populations at war, with women's traces left out of war museums p. 37

Contents and chapter overviews

Naquin, Susan (2004). “The Forbidden City Goes Abroad: Qing History and the Foreign Exhibitions of the Palace Museum, 1974–2004”. T’oung Pao, 90 (2004).5 concepts

Naquin frames the Beijing Palace Museum's foreign exhibitions of 1974 to 2004 as a history of how one museum packaged its collection for overseas audiences as the Forbidden City and the Qing court. It is an article of museum and exhibition history with a cultural-historical reading of the Qing, drawing on catalogues, museum publications and recent Qing scholarship. Its argument is that the packaging was made possible by diplomacy and enlarged by competition with Taipei and Shanghai, and that the catalogues record a Qing picture that lagged behind the scholarship.

Concepts and inspirations

  • the Forbidden City as an absent presence
  • the formulaic Forbidden City exhibit
  • the Qing Forbidden City as the museum's identity
  • four shifts in focus, 1974 to 2004
  • identity as situational and constructed (Rawski 1996 (note 119))

Argues against

  • the 'dismissive nationalist view' of the Qing rulers as assimilated invaders, which most historians still held: Naquin says that by the late 1980s the Manchuness of the court was being approached more directly and positively, though the Chinese scholarship and most catalogues had not yet taken this up. p. 381

Sources and ways of working

  • close reading of thirty-five exhibition catalogues as the lasting record of each show, with their photographs, captions, essays and bibliographies p. 344
  • comparison of the Beijing shows with those of the Taipei, Shanghai and Shenyang museums p. 370
  • reading the Palace Museum's own journals and glossy magazines as the context of the foreign shows p. 375

Gaps it names

  • the inner history of the exhibitions, including selection, negotiation, payment, reception and profitability, which the author leaves to others p. 344
  • technological exchange between Europe and the Qing, such as clocks, glass, enamels and instruments, which the Palace Museum could show but has not p. 387

Contents and chapter overviews

Outka, Elizabeth (2009). Consuming Traditions: Modernity, Modernism, and the Commodified Authentic. New York: Oxford University Press.8 concepts

Outka frames museums only obliquely. The book is about British commodity culture around 1880 to 1922: model towns, the Ideal Home Exhibition, the Selfridges department store, shop windows, and the modernist novel. Its overall argument is that the “commodified authentic,” the sale of noncommercial values (rural England, originality, aesthetic purity) with their commercial origin in view, was intrinsic to the making of modernity and literary modernism, and should be understood rather than unmasked. It is a cultural and literary history that combines architecture, advertising and literary criticism, with commodity culture and performance as its main lenses.

Concepts and inspirations

  • commodified authentic
  • commodified nostalgia (nostalgic authentic) (Alun Howkins)
  • originary authentic
  • performing authenticity (Jon McKenzie; Richard Schechner)
  • the great divide (Andreas Huyssen; Fredric Jameson)
  • cultural capital (Pierre Bourdieu)
  • window gazing (window shopping as performance) (Bowlby; Anne Friedberg; Walter Benjamin)
  • tableau of the authentic dead (Thomas Richards)

Argues against

  • critics who unmask the selling of authenticity as fraud, the inauthentic masquerading as the authentic: Such exposure is important, but the rush to condemn or smirk has limited investigation of the marketing’s history and allure; the book aims to understand rather than debunk p. 5
  • Baudrillard, who might take marketed models to the logical extreme of simulacra, so that the authentic term shifts out altogether: Without defining what an authentic object is, it is still possible to distinguish more and less substantive versions of the commodified authentic, as Bournville shows p. 44
  • recent modernist critics who dismantle the great divide from the modernist side: They neglect how commercial ventures deployed and dismantled the high-low relation, and how modernism moved between the two impulses p. 12

Sources and ways of working

  • newspaper article-advertisements laid out like news, read against the news columns they mimic (Selfridges in The Times, 1909) p. 111
  • store exhibitions and in-store demonstrations of production, such as Old-time Industry p. 112
  • reading literary scenes and commercial material together, pairing James and Wells with Selfridges p. 20
  • built environments read as texts that record the passage of time, such as houses mixing styles from different eras p. 19

Gaps it names

  • how the commodified authentic developed within Britain, which the impulse to criticise and dismiss has kept from investigation p. 14

Contents and chapter overviews

Paver, Chloe E. M. (2018). Exhibiting the Nazi Past: Museum Objects Between the Material and the Immaterial. Cham: Palgrave Macmillan.7 concepts

Paver frames museums as places where everyday objects from 1933 to 1945 and after are displayed to communicate a critical, morally framed account of National Socialism and post-war memory in Germany and Austria. Paver’s argument is that such history exhibitions have become routine, and that an object's meaning shifts across its life phases, from use through disuse and storage to museum display. It is a study in cultural and public history and museum studies, with strong strands of memory studies and material culture theory.

Concepts and inspirations

  • object as signifier and the rhetorical figures of synecdoche, metonymy and metaphor (Korff and Roth; Pomian; Mieke Bal)
  • object as conduit for experience, emotions and mentalities (Alon Confino; Lucien Febvre)
  • object life cycle and the rubbish phase (Michael Thompson; Krzysztof Pomian; Igor Kopytoff)
  • passive cultural forgetting (Aleida Assmann)
  • testimonial object and the punctum of time (Marianne Hirsch; Leo Spitzer; Roland Barthes)
  • exhibitionary routine
  • object-oriented exhibitions and object renunciation (Objektbezogenheit, Objektverzicht) (Axel Drecoll)

Argues against

  • Michael Thompson and Krzysztof Pomian, who assume that objects pass through a rubbish state on the way to the museum: Neither account can quite explain the display of discarded items in German and Austrian history museums, which were kept in storage after 1945 and are now shown in those containers p. 175
