  • Thompson and Igor Kopytoff, who assume that objects enter a safe and neutral ground once they cross the museum threshold: Charles Saumarez Smith argues that in the museum objects continue to circulate and be revalued or reinterpreted depending on contingent needs p. 54
  • the paradigm of post-war forgetting, cited through Wolfgang Benz's claim of collective silence and widespread amnesia: Confino shows that National Socialism was regularly talked about in the post-war private sphere, so Germans did not only forget and the Nazi past was not hermetically sealed p. 45
  • the liberal narrative that German and Austrian museums tell about the post-war years: Not every museum follows it: the Celle documentation centre plan was abandoned, the Celler Garnison-Museum shows Wehrmacht objects without political context, and the Nienburg permanent display is broad-brush p. 276

Sources and ways of working

  • reading exhibition captions and paratexts for the meaning they fix for objects p. 29
  • photographs, letters and diaries read as objects through their making, purchase, sharing and storage p. 62
  • asking Kopytoff-style questions of an object's biography, such as what its life phases are and what happens at the end of its usefulness p. 54
  • inspecting the containers in which donated objects arrived, such as cardboard boxes, carrier bags and bubble wrap p. 175

Gaps it names

  • a study of the transition to a second democratic generation of exhibitions about National Socialism and the Holocaust p. 278
  • testimony, generations, postmemory and trauma, which generate large scholarship in memory studies but remain secondary in German and Austrian history exhibitions p. 278
  • the feelings of the bureaucrats involved in restitution, which Grossmann calls for p. 49

Contents and chapter overviews

Pearce, Susan M. (1992). Museums, Objects, and Collections: A Cultural Study. Leicester: Leicester University Press.8 concepts

Pearce frames museums as cultural expressions in their own right, built on collections and objects, and holds that theory and practice in museums cannot be separated. The book is a museum-studies text written from inside curatorship and positions museums within a critical social theory of meaning. It draws on material culture studies, anthropology, semiotics and the philosophy of knowledge, and argues that objects make meaning through selection, collecting, classification, function, structure, history, lived experience and power, so curators must justify their interpretations to a critical community.

Concepts and inspirations

  • modern museum and the meta-narratives of modernity (Habermas; Harvey; Giddens)
  • souvenir, fetishistic and systematic collecting (Stewart; Ellen; Marx)
  • objectification (Hegel; Miller)
  • cognitive processes of collecting (Ellen) (Ellen; Barthes)
  • power and knowledge (Foucault, Marx) (Marx; Foucault; Hooper-Greenhill)
  • third world of objective knowledge (Popper) (Popper; Collingwood; Kuhn)
  • structure and binary opposition (Saussure, Barthes, Leach) (Saussure; Barthes; Leach)
  • structuration and Braudel's time-scales (Giddens; Braudel)

Argues against

  • post-structuralist denial of the possibility of meaning or reality: Pearce accepts that meanings are not fixed but argues that some interpretations are better than others, citing Popper's third world and Gombrich's rejection of relativism p. 369
  • Marxist accounts of museums as instruments that legitimate the capitalist order: the critique is powerful but drains meaning away, so curators need conceptual justifications for their work p. 330

Sources and ways of working

  • reading exhibition catalogues, labels and posters as texts whose claims to value and authority can be examined, for example the catalogue of The Genius of China p. 363
  • accession records and collection documentation, where the unique accession name is the museum identity of an object p. 195
  • visitor responses and studies of how people see museums, gathered alongside theory p. 381

Gaps it names

  • more work about the history and nature of museums and collections p. 380
  • more work upon the material from a range of standpoints p. 381
  • more information about how people see museums and respond to them p. 381

Contents and chapter overviews

Pearson, Catherine (2017). Museums in the Second World War: Curators, Culture and Change. London: Routledge.8 concepts

Pearson frames the Second World War as a productive period for British museums, which stayed open, engaged audiences and built education services, and whose wartime record was erased by the post-war return to collections and the failure of the Museums Association's campaign for a national service. The book is a historical study of policy, the museum profession and visitor experience, built from government and Museums Association records, the Museums Journal, curators' diaries and interviews, and Mass-Observation material. Its argument is directed against the accepted view of the war as a hiatus in museum history.

Concepts and inspirations

  • museum as mausoleum (Markham)
  • museum as 'dream space' (Kavanagh)
  • visitors' own meanings against the museum's authority (Samuel; Lowenthal)
  • social control through municipal museums (Bennett)
  • 'new museology' as a repetition of older debates (Vergo)
  • museum as mouseion, a temple of the arts (Frank Lambert)
  • museum of ideas (Markham)
  • layers of meaning in the object (Pearce; Monti and Keene)

Argues against

  • the view that the Second World War was a hiatus in museum history, with few significant developments: wartime museums were popular, engaged audiences successfully and were valued for their educational services
  • Renaissance in the Regions (2001), which overlooked the legacy of the past: museum histories should be reconnected with present policy rather than erased

Sources and ways of working

  • first-hand interviews with retired curators and wartime visitors, recruited by word of mouth, appeals in the Museums Journal and local and airbase history groups
  • Mass-Observation studies made inside museum galleries, read with caution because they reflect the observer's interpretation
  • visitor-number records, treated as weak evidence of visitors' reactions

Gaps it names

  • little critical assessment of the museum's past within the profession, which tends to present its development as uncontroversial
  • the principles of wartime experiments, which post-war specialist groups did not know about
  • surviving local records, which are often limited in regional museums

Contents and chapter overviews

Rees Leahy, Helen (2012). Museum Bodies: The Politics and Practices of Visiting and Viewing. Farnham: Ashgate.8 concepts

Leahy frames the art museum as a site of learned bodily practice: from the 1750s onward, visitors acquire habits of walking, looking, sitting and behaving that make them legible to the institution, and the museum's rules and displays script those habits. The book is a cultural and social history of spectatorship in English art museums and exhibitions, drawing on museum history, art history, anthropology and fiction. It reads documentary sources (guidebooks, press reports, visitor accounts, caricatures, novels) for the embodied visitors behind the regulations, and uses performance theory to argue that visitors are both performers and interpreters of the exhibition script.

Concepts and inspirations

  • performing museology (Barbara Kirshenblatt-Gimblett)
  • techniques of the body and social habitus (Marcel Mauss; Pierre Bourdieu)
  • exhibitionary complex (Tony Bennett)
  • performatives and the museum's script (Judith Butler; Barbara Kirshenblatt-Gimblett)
  • gaze and glance (Norman Bryson; De Bolla)
  • museum fatigue (Benjamin Ives Gilman; Edward S. Robinson; Arthur W. Melton)
  • constructed situation
  • period eye (Baxandall; Adrian Randolph; David Solkin)

Argues against

  • The curators' model of attentive, disinterested looking: Museum looking in practice oscillates between gaze and glance, and distraction is part of it p. 47
  • Gilman's idea of 'good seeing' as the norm against which fatigue is measured: Good seeing is itself a normative practice that needs to be examined p. 61

Sources and ways of working

  • documentary sources: admission rules, guidebooks, press reports, visitors' accounts and caricatures (Rowlandson, Alken, the Cruikshanks) p. 9
  • fiction read as evidence of museum bodies (Zola, Dickens, Forster's Maurice) p. 10
  • reconstruction of past hangs and displays to test how they were viewed p. 46

Gaps it names

  • touching, tasting and smelling in the museum, which the author says receive less attention than looking and walking p. 3
  • the book is not an exhaustive history of bodily practices in the museum p. 9

Contents and chapter overviews

Sandell, Richard; Nightingale, Eithne (eds.) (2012). Museums, Equality and Social Justice. London: Routledge.8 concepts

The volume frames museums as constitutively social institutions that can either reproduce or challenge inequality, and argues that equality, diversity and social justice have moved from the margins of museum practice towards its core, though unevenly. It is a collection of mostly applied, practitioner-informed studies (museum studies, cultural policy, critical legal studies, social anthropology and disability studies), with the editors calling for museums to realise their untapped potential for a more equal society.

Concepts and inspirations

  • politics of positional difference (Iris Marion Young)
  • epidermalization (Frantz Fanon; Kobena Mercer)
  • interpretive community (Stanley Fish; Anderson (imagined communities))
  • sites of persuasion (Morphy)
  • constituent and constituted power (critical legal studies)
  • cultural rights as commons (Hardin; Henry Shue)
  • discovered identities and hidden histories
  • appropriate museology (Christina Kreps; Macdonald; Karp et al.)

Argues against

  • policy targeting of BAME audiences combined with market segmentation at Tate Britain: it produces separated segments that reproduce existing social divisions, with no coming together of cultures; diversity became managed as a risk to the museum's core values
  • the view that multiculturalism has failed (David Cameron, as quoted): the chapter asks whether museums can pursue inclusion in a political climate unsupportive of it, treating the claim as a sentiment rather than a settled verdict
  • critics who dismiss equality work as socially divisive or box-ticking: the Commission aimed to democratise the heritage sector and to serve as a template for other communities
  • exhibitions that present sexual identity as trans-historical essentialism: desire is chaotic and cannot be confined to neat binaries; the museum must show its gaps and exceptions

Sources and ways of working

  • organisational study of staff and networks at Tate Britain, with a survey of over 200 students
  • nearly 500 individual interviews at Sana'a National Museum, plus consultations with blind people, disabled women, teachers and guides
  • quantitative and qualitative analysis of visitor comment cards and interviews, including with transgender activists
  • good-practice case review drawn from interviews with museum staff in the UK and United States

Gaps it names

  • little empirical research on how museums' human rights work affects visitors and rights activists
  • no agreed list or classification of cultural rights, which has slowed their provision
  • contemporary material after 1900 in the British Museum's Asian gallery, despite recent collecting

Contents and chapter overviews

Sellers, Charles Coleman (1980). Mr. Peale’s Museum: Charles Willson Peale and the First Popular Museum of Natural Science and Art. New York: W. W. Norton.7 concepts

Sellers frames Peale's Museum in Philadelphia as a new kind of popular science institution, one that combined scientific order (Linnaean classification and a total view of each natural form) with 'rational amusement' for a general public. The argument is that the museum shaped American natural history and the Peale family's collecting, but that commercial imitators, Barnum above all, eventually undermined its model. It is a museum and institutional history with strong intellectual history alongside, drawing on the history of science and the American Enlightenment, and it is more narrative and archival than theoretical.

Concepts and inspirations

  • rational amusement (Rousseau)
  • the total concept
  • chain of nature
  • American degeneracy (Buffon's thesis) (Buffon; Jefferson)
  • the races of mankind (wax group)
  • moral effect of a museum
  • the New Museum Idea (John Edward Gray; Richard Owen; Edward Forbes)

Argues against

  • the commercial imitators of Peale's museum, such as Barnum's shows: a collection of oddities without scientific purpose was good business, and the imitators drew the public away from the museum's aims p. 2
  • Buffon's degeneracy thesis: Peale's comparisons showed different species, so the claim that American life was smaller and weaker was a ridiculous idea p. 103
  • Federalist critics of the wax figures, led by Cobbett: Peale's racial wax show was declared not worth the price of admission p. 94

Sources and ways of working

  • auction and sale catalogues, read item by item to reconstruct what a collection held (the 1848 sale catalogue) p. 316
  • surviving objects with their original museum labels and donor records, used to trace what passed to Boston and Harvard collections p. 324
  • letters and correspondence, including Peale's letters to donors and naturalists p. 30

Gaps it names

  • the printed catalogue of a c.1840-1845 Pacific collection has never been located and is known only through labels p. 324
  • no source is given for forty-four cases of Chinese insects, which the text attributes to William Wood's 1831 shipment p. 321
  • whether the Salem museum copied Peale's wax figures of mankind is unknown p. 2

Contents and chapter overviews

Shapiro, Michael Steven (ed.); Kemp, Louis Ward (1990). The Museum: A Reference Guide. New York: Greenwood Press.3 concepts

The volume treats museums in the United States as civic institutions whose published literature has been neglected, partisan and disorganised, mostly written by directors and insiders for a small readership. Its overall argument is that this literature should be assessed critically, with each museum type's history set against its sources and against the professional debates around it. It is a reference and bibliographic work in museum studies, with chapters that combine institutional history, historiography and, in the professionalism chapter, sociology of occupations; no single theoretical framework governs the twelve chapters.

Concepts and inspirations

  • collective memory
  • semi-profession (Amitai Etzioni; Nina Toren; Everett Hughes)
  • noncanonical reading of canonical texts (Dominick LaCpra)

Argues against

  • the older literature on museums, written by directors and insiders for a small readership: the literature has been disorganised and unevaluated, and it is less accessible to general readers than it should be PDF p. 15
  • the view that natural history museums became inactive storehouses in the nineteenth century: they were important scientific institutions that stored collections and also helped to disseminate information essential to research PDF p. 16

Sources and ways of working

  • a historical narrative followed by a critical survey of sources and a bibliographic checklist PDF p. 15
  • annotated lists of museum directories, archives and periodicals used as finding aids PDF p. 18

Gaps it names

  • no single comprehensive history of natural history museums exists; the literature is fragmented p. 12
  • museum education still lacks a theory to guide it, despite useful visitor research PDF p. 17

Contents and chapter overviews

Sherman, Daniel J.; Rogoff, Irit (eds.) (1994). Museum Culture: Histories, Discourses, Spectacles. Minneapolis: University of Minnesota Press.9 concepts

The volume treats museums as sites where objects, contexts, publics and reception are historically constructed, so that display naturalises history and nation rather than presenting neutral evidence. It is a cultural and political history of museums and exhibitions, combining the editors' critical theory of the museum with art history, sociology of audiences, feminist and postcolonial criticism, and studies of national cultural festivals. Its overall argument is that museums and spectacular exhibitions legitimate states, elites and corporations, and that critical practice can expose that work.

Concepts and inspirations

  • the four structuring concepts of object, context, public and reception
  • museum classification and cultural master narratives (Foucault)
  • collecting as an act that defies use and capital (Adorno; Walter Benjamin)
  • the museum as manager of consciousness (Hans Haacke; Hans Magnus Enzensberger; Daniel Buren)
  • habitus and cultural capital in museum audiences (Pierre Bourdieu; Alain Darbel)
  • fabricated exhibits among authentic objects
  • the museum's loss of context and moral purpose (Quatremere de Quincy; Marx; Walter Benjamin)
  • national allegory in cultural festivals (Benedict Anderson)
  • self-Orientalizing in national display (Edward Said)

Argues against

  • the view that a national festival is simply art, not politics, as an Indonesian foundation chairman argued: Wallis argues that the festival's promotional function, its omission of human rights and environmental issues, and the sponsors' interests make it political p. 276
  • the view that national culture can be shown as a whole and neutral: Whose version of the national culture is being shown? What is not shown? And why? p. 267

Sources and ways of working

  • close reading of exhibition catalogues and wall labels p. 276
  • interviews with festival organisers and sponsors, with press reports on sponsorship and protests p. 275

Gaps it names

  • the contemporary political, environmental and cultural issues that the Festival of Indonesia failed to address p. 275

Contents and chapter overviews

Siegel, Jonah (ed.) (2008). The Emergence of the Modern Museum: An Anthology of Nineteenth-Century Sources. New York: Oxford University Press.3 concepts

This is an anthology of nineteenth-century British sources on the museum, arranged thematically in two parts (From Collection to Museum; Rationalizing the National Collections) rather than a monograph with its own thesis. The editor's introduction frames the modern museum as having emerged from revolution, empire and a mass public, as a compromise among preservation, study, display and instruction whose meaning remains unresolved. It is a study of cultural and institutional history, with the selections (parliamentary testimony, periodicals, catalogues) doing the work of evidence.

Concepts and inspirations

  • the public museum as a compromise
  • loss and fragmentation of the museum's objects (Heidegger; Walter Benjamin)
  • objects do not speak for themselves

Argues against

  • the assumption that a museum's display conveys the lesson its collectors and planners intended: Objects do not necessarily say what their collectors intended, and the viewer's imagination is what museum planners find hardest to control. p. 8

Sources and ways of working

  • parliamentary select committee testimony and debates, read as the record of how museums were run and argued over p. 41
  • published visitor counts and admission figures from official reports and periodicals p. 67

Gaps it names

  • provincial and imperial museums, which the editor regrets not treating at length PDF p. 12
  • libraries, zoos, botanic gardens, sales galleries and the international exhibition, which are left out PDF p. 12

Contents and chapter overviews

Siegel, Jonah (2020). Material Inspirations: The Interests of the Art Object in the Nineteenth Century and After. Oxford: Oxford University Press.7 concepts

Siegel frames museums and art as sites where the materiality of artworks, their reproduction and their display never stabilised, so that nineteenth-century writers kept returning to art to think about the relation between matter and idea. It is a cultural and intellectual history that combines art history, literary criticism and institutional history, reading criticism, fiction, handbooks and reproductions together. Its overall argument is against demystifying materialism and against the experiential school of objecthood, and for the view that nineteenth-century art was work toward binding society together.

Concepts and inspirations

  • demystification (Baxandall; Bourdieu; Marx)
  • the experiential encounter with the thing (Heidegger; Jane Bennett; Michael Fried)
  • realism (against network) (Bruno Latour)
  • the classical canon as images on paper (Spence; Tooke; Winckelmann)
  • allegory against symbol (Walter Benjamin; Warburg)
  • the museum as symbol and cause
  • the ruined cathedral and the responsibility of caretaking (John Ruskin)

Argues against

  • demystificatory materialism (Baxandall, Bourdieu) that explains art by the social or economic interests behind it: it is a willfully limited approach even to the material; its 'follow the money' stops short of matter itself p. 15
  • mercantile exchange as the explanation of the nineteenth-century culture of art: the culture of art was work toward binding society together, not bound to reflect an already fated set of material or social conditions p. 33
  • the assumption that visual and literary art relate directly, held by Spence and Winckelmann: Lessing's argument that the restraint of the Laocoön is 'due entirely to the peculiar nature of Art and its necessary limits' p. 166

Sources and ways of working

  • reading compendia and reference works (Spence, Tooke, Rees's Cyclopaedia) as the medium through which classical objects were known p. 162
  • close reading of fiction and essays that stage a visitor's encounter with a museum (Eliot, Vernon Lee) p. 209
  • reading the handbook text of Baedeker across its editions p. 225
  • reading the illustrated and popular press (Penny Magazine, Illustrated London News) for how images circulated p. 256

Gaps it names

  • earlier sources of antiquarianism, going back to the Renaissance, which would deepen the historical argument p. 308

Contents and chapter overviews

Silina, Maria (2026). Soviet Museums Between the Two World Wars: Art History on Display. London: Routledge.8 concepts

Silina presents Soviet museums of 1914 to 1945 as experimental display and museum work that was part of an international museum culture (Bode's Berlin reforms, the Office international des musées, American educators), not as isolated avant-garde collections or as propaganda. The argument is historiographical: the 1920s and 1930s displays, including the everyday-life museum and the Marxist displays, were serious projects that were later condemned or forgotten, and the book revises the totalitarian model of Soviet culture. It is a study in museum history and art history, with elements of intellectual history and the history of display theory.

Concepts and inspirations

  • unique present (authenticity as an isolated moment) (Bergson; Husserl; Heidegger)
  • ostranenie (estrangement of objects) (Viktor Shklovsky)
  • Marxist comprehensive display (marksistskaia opytnaia kompleksnaia ekspozitsiia) (Mikhail Pokrovsky)
  • gaze-appeal (nagliadnost') (Serguei Oushakine)
  • perezhivanie (experiencing) (Lichtwark)
  • vulgar sociology (vulgarny sotsiologizm)
  • museum as experimental laboratory (Maria Gough; Kazimir Malevich; Osip Brik)
  • history of errors (Eric Naiman)

Argues against

  • the totalitarian model of Soviet culture, which treats museums only as avant-garde collections or as propaganda: the book follows the trend that revises the model and its actors, looking at networks and agents of the cultural industry rather than at unified state control p. 5
  • the view that Marxist art-historical projects and writings are mechanistic: this tendency still prevails, but the Marxist displays rested on a complex formal and conceptual base p. 7
  • cybernetic accounts of museums as neutral information carriers: the content and paths of information in Soviet museums were controlled by ideological bodies, so the neutrality they assume is not available p. 7
  • the distrust that museology was possible in the USSR at all: the theory and practice of Soviet museums can be recovered and belongs to international museum history p. 7

Sources and ways of working

  • reconstruction of lost displays from models, plans, catalogues and press reports where no images survive, as with Simon's models for the Oriental museum project p. 104
  • archival documents from the State Tretyakov Gallery and state archives, cited in the notes p. 187
  • comparison of Soviet practice with Western and North American museum practice, following Chlenova's comparative study of Barr and Fedorov-Davydov p. 2
  • reading of visual sources, such as iconography, to recover the ordinary background of everyday life, as Shaposhnikov did p. 44

Gaps it names

  • Soviet display and museology after 1950, including the transfer of Soviet display methods to China, Cuba and the German Democratic Republic, which the book treats only in passing p. 7
  • the work of Fedorov-Davydov and Kovalenskaya on the class value of art and the sociology of patronage, which has been largely overlooked p. 7
  • the perspective of local communities on Soviet museum policy, which should be studied alongside the critique of Russian-imposed narratives p. 5

Contents and chapter overviews

Silverman, Lois H. (2010). The Social Work of Museums. London: Routledge.9 concepts

Silverman frames museums as institutions of social service that already meet the relationship needs of selves, close pairs, families and groups, though they seldom name this work as social work. The book is a social and cultural study with a museum-studies base, combining a historical survey, a synthesis of visitor-studies theory and a survey of programmes from many countries. Its overall argument is that museum communication, through objects, relationships and meaning-making, produces beneficial change in individuals and social conditions, and that museums and social work should share an ethics base, an evidence base and collaboration.

Concepts and inspirations

  • interactive experience model (Falk and Dierking)
  • communication as meaning-making (Hooper-Greenhill; Roberts)
  • the meaning of things (Pearce; Csikszentmihalyi; Rochberg-Halton)
  • human needs (Annis; Graburn; Maslow)
  • social capital (Putnam; Fukayama)
  • cultural inclusion and exclusion (Karp and Lavine; Hooper-Greenhill; Sandell)
  • new museology: integrated, ecomuseum and neighbourhood museums (van Mensch; de Varine; Davis)
  • relationship needs framework (Maslow; Kilpatrick)
  • ten functions of social work intervention (Barker; Kirst-Ashman)

Argues against

  • the museum field's earlier linear transmission model of communication, in which professionals send messages and visitors receive them: visitors are actively involved in making sense of what they encounter, so the product of communication is meaning, not receipt of a message p. 15
  • critics (Bennett, Schwarzer) who read early settlement-house and public museum work as patronising attempts to teach the lower classes elite ways without changing class power: many positive benefits did result, such as increased interaction across class lines and an expansion of the public that attended museums p. 10

Sources and ways of working

  • visitor conversations and comment-book remarks as evidence of meaning-making p. 16
  • outcome-based evaluation of changes in knowledge, skill, attitude and behaviour, such as the UK generic learning outcomes and US IMLS model p. 17
  • exploratory small-group studies in a university gallery, reporting participants' personal responses p. 121

Gaps it names

  • no comprehensive theory yet explains the social work of museums; the literature is scattered p. 14
  • a shared ethics base for museums and social work, which existing codes do not provide p. 149
  • an empirical body of knowledge and evidence, including which museum resources are more effective for particular interventions p. 147

Contents and chapter overviews

Sleeper-Smith, Susan (ed.) (2009). Contesting Knowledge: Museums and Indigenous Perspectives. Lincoln: University of Nebraska Press.9 concepts

The volume treats museums as institutions that displayed Indigenous peoples through colonial ethnography and asks how Native communities now contest that legacy in national and tribal museums. It is an edited collection of cultural and political studies that combines museum studies, anthropology, history and Indigenous studies. Its overall argument, set out in the editor's introduction, is that 'Indian' was a European construction, and that Indigenous voice, sovereignty and community knowledge have to be built into museum practice rather than assumed to follow from new buildings.

Concepts and inspirations

  • problematization (Michel Foucault)
  • dialogic model of the museum (James Carey)
  • contact zone (Mary Louise Pratt; James Clifford)
  • denial of coevalness (Johannes Fabian)
  • collections as complete outcomes of colonial practice (Chris Gosden; Chantal Knowles; Brian Durrans)
  • aesthetic of controlled heterogeneity (Annelise Riles)
  • cultural sovereignty (Amanda Cobb; Scott Lyons)
  • Indigenous space
  • ethnography as scientific justification

Argues against

  • the view that the inclusive, dialogic museum is an unambiguous advance: Brady calls it a real advance, but inclusion can mean accommodation under neoliberal funding and nation building p. 147

Sources and ways of working

  • reading a collection through what its collector intended and what the collector and museum said and recorded about it p. 68

Contents and chapter overviews

Stewart, Susan (1984). On Longing: Narratives of the Miniature, the Gigantic, the Souvenir, the Collection. Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press.8 concepts

Stewart treats museums and collections as objects of narrative desire: the miniature, the gigantic, the freak, the souvenir and the collection are read as ways in which the bourgeois subject and the state invent, distance and possess the world. The overall argument is that exaggeration, scale and nostalgia expose the ideology of narrative closure, and that the museum's claim to represent the world is a fiction built on fragment-for-totality displacement. It is a cultural and semiotic study that draws on literary history, popular culture and anthropology.

Concepts and inspirations

  • nostalgia as the desire of narrative
  • the miniature as figure for the interior self
  • the gigantic as figure for the state and the collective
  • the freak as a freak of culture (Leslie Fiedler)
  • the souvenir as partial sample of lost experience
  • the collection as containment of experience (Bunn)
  • the museum as the central metaphor of the collection (Eugenio Donato)
  • decontextualization in museum acquisitions

Argues against

  • the view that realist narrative represents the world as it is: Narrative 'seeks to realize' a formulation of the world, a world which works, so every narrative is a miniature and every book a microcosm; the text treats this as ideological desire rather than access to the real. PDF p. 12
  • the non-Western tradition of experiments with scale and the fantastic: The author sets it aside and treats the Japanese netsuke and the Persian, Indian and Chinese forms as outside the study's scope. PDF p. 14
  • the museum as a neutral representation of the world: The museum's representational universe is a fiction sustained by metonymic displacement and classification, following Donato. p. 161

Sources and ways of working

  • collectors' advice literature and handbooks, such as Vallois's First Steps in Collecting and Booth Tarkington's parody of collectors p. 157
  • handbills and advertisements for freak and side-show exhibitions p. 108
  • a book-club museum of art in miniature read as a distributed object, with its categories and arrangement p. 65
  • architectural experiments with scale models and the perception of scale p. 66

Gaps it names

  • non-Western traditions of miniature and giant forms (netsuke, Persian and Indian miniatures, Indonesian and Chinese giants), which the author leaves out as too context-bound to treat here PDF p. 14

Contents and chapter overviews

Stocking, George W., Jr. (ed.) (1985). Objects and Others: Essays on Museums and Material Culture. Madison: University of Wisconsin Press.9 concepts

Stocking frames the volume as a history of anthropological museums, the 'Museum Period', and as a philosophical question about what museums do to the objects of 'others'. Most essays are institutional and archival history of American, British, French and Dutch collections, with one essay on Rockefeller philanthropy and one on Quebec heritage law; the theory is largely implicit in them and is stated in Stocking's introduction and in Clifford's afterword, which reads collecting as a cultural-theory problem. The study is best described as museum studies and the history of anthropology, with cultural and political theory in the framing.

Concepts and inspirations

  • museum as archive of material objects of 'others'
  • expropriation and appropriation of objects (Foster)
  • principle of continuity and typological arrangement (Herbert Spencer)
  • contextual display (objects in their cultural setting) (Stocking (1974))
  • object orientation of museum anthropology
  • possessive individualism and the possessive self (C. B. Macpherson)
  • fetishism of collections (Susan Stewart; Marx; Baudrillard)
  • art and artifact as two classifications of non-Western objects
  • cultural property and the typology of ownership claims

Argues against

  • O. T. Mason's typological evolutionary arrangement of artifacts at the U.S. National Museum: Boas held that human artifacts cannot be sorted like biological specimens into families, genera and species, because their connections depend on their cultural setting. p. 77
  • the view that great collections should stay intact in museums, as Lurie (1981) put it: Stocking records that repatriation has been an international concern since the 1970 UNESCO convention, so museum anthropologists can no longer treat the objects of others without considering their rightful ownership. p. 11
  • the charge that Rockefeller philanthropy was colonially complicit in the end of museum anthropology: Stocking weighs the charge against the Kirchhoff affair and finds it secondary; the main effect was that field-based funding moved work out of museums. p. 136

Sources and ways of working

  • visitor studies, including the time-and-motion study of museum visitors and audience demographics p. 10
  • surveys of journal articles and museum acquisitions, counted by source p. 9
  • archival correspondence of museum directors, trustees and patrons, cited by archive and date p. 84
  • hall layouts and case arrangements read against the plan of a given scheme, as in the Northwest Coast Hall p. 93

Gaps it names

  • a systematic history of Western notions of the object, the icon and the fetish, and of the savage and civilised relation to material things p. 13
  • the actual processes of collection of objects, and the recent movement for their repatriation p. 13
  • the anthropology of world's fairs and of modern touristic cultural performances p. 13
  • the historical criteria by which an authentic cultural or artistic product is validated p. 240

Contents and chapter overviews

Tseng, Alice Y. (2008). The Imperial Museums of Meiji Japan: Architecture and the Art of the Nation. Seattle: University of Washington Press.8 concepts

Tseng frames the Imperial Museums of Meiji Japan as state monuments whose architecture and collections were planned together to show a constructed national identity: modern in means, traditional in meaning. Tseng’s overall argument is that the museums made Japan's art lineage visible as a national achievement while using Western architecture and organisation, so that the buildings and the objects must be read together. It is an architectural and art-historical study that draws on museum studies, world's-fair scholarship, the historiography of Meiji and anthropological accounts of the museum as a space of ritual and visibility.

Concepts and inspirations

  • Kyoto and Tokyo as the paired progressive and sacred capitals (Takashi Fujitani)
  • the museum setting as a ritual space of visitor performance (Carol Duncan; Alan Wallach)
  • visibility and limited visibility in museum display (Eilean Hooper-Greenhill)
  • the Saidian framework applied to Conder's Saracenic style (Said)
  • contextual and classificatory modes of display
  • the museum as a cross-cultural invention rather than a European one (Paul Valéry; André Malraux)
  • the icon-to-art-object shift (John Rosenfield; Bernard Faure; Gregory Levine)
  • Meiji self-representation and the historiography of the period (Carol Gluck)

Argues against

  • Art-historical and architectural studies that treat the museum's content and its building as separate events: the original buildings of the Imperial Museums have not been analysed as designs for object exhibition, so the building and the collection must be read together p. 13
  • Valéry and Malraux, who held that the museum was alien to China and the Far East: the museum was as unnatural to European eyes as to Asian ones; the claim that Asia lacked the museum is a familiar Orientalist trope p. 211
  • Western scholarship that reads Japanese architecture as the expression of an essential Japanese identity: this expectation devalues Western-style buildings as derivative; Tseng reads them as the Meiji state's chosen means of national representation p. 14
  • Meiji histories that present the period as a rupture with the past: modernisation heightened more than disrupted the religious identity of Nara and the artistic industries of Kyoto p. 15

Sources and ways of working

  • institutional records and centennial histories of the three successor National Museums, read critically for their separation of the three museums into distinct stories p. 8
  • comparison of a museum building with a contemporary exposition pavilion, read as an exhibition event and as a display strategy p. 126
  • architecture read with its building debates, its critics' reviews and the collections housed in it p. 12
  • close reading of period interiors and of display methods to see how objects were grouped p. 127

Gaps it names

  • the mid-Meiji state projects of about 1880 to 1900 have a tremendous scholarly void, and Conder and Katayama have been studied mainly as developments in Japanese architectural history p. 14
  • the role of Western conventions, specifically the museum, in enforcing the Kyoto and Tokyo symbolism, which Fujitani does not explore p. 135

Contents and chapter overviews

Veldkamp, Elmer (2014). “Keeping It Real: The Exhibition of Artifact Replicas in National Museums of Korea”. Acta Koreana, 17.2 (December 2014): 557-581.5 concepts

The article frames museums in Korea as places where the visitor's perception of the past matters as much as the object's material originality. Its argument is that replicas can carry 'pastness' and real value for a general public, while specialists still need the original. It is a museum studies and heritage studies article with a cultural-theoretical base, using the author's own observation of two national museums and one overseas display.

Concepts and inspirations

  • pastness (Cornelius Holtorf)
  • margins of authenticity (Holtorf; Crew and Sims)
  • aura (Walter Benjamin)
  • singularization (cultural biography of things) (Kopytoff)
  • mythicization and banalization of heritage icons

Argues against

  • the doctrine in archaeological heritage management that ancient objects are authentic and have an aura that fakes and copies lack: there is nothing special about an original ancient artifact: it is the assumption of antiquity that matters, not its veracity p. 558
  • the Eurocentric definition of authenticity as preservation of fabric and original materiality: in Asia, preserving the spiritual message of a heritage item is not as important as preserving its fabric p. 561

Sources and ways of working

  • the author's own observation of exhibition spaces, labels and figures at the National Museum of Korea and Kongju, with reflection on his own experience as a visitor p. 561
  • personal communication with museum staff on the replacement of one object by another for display p. 565
  • reading wall labels and digital information screens as evidence of whether a display presents an object as original or replica p. 573

Gaps it names

  • the manufacturing process of exhibition-grade replicas and of the Cultural Heritage Administration's certified display replicas, which the author says is undocumented p. 578
  • studies of authenticity and museum display in the Korean context, which are scarce p. 561

Contents and chapter overviews

Vergo, Peter (ed.) (1989). The New Museology. London: Reaktion Books.9 concepts

Vergo's volume argues that museums are never neutral: every acquisition, arrangement, label and display places a construction on history, and museology should ask what museums are for rather than how they are run. It is a critical collection of essays on British museums that mixes museum history, exhibition criticism, cultural studies, the sociology of leisure and legal analysis. Its frame is the 'new museology' as a critique of the museum profession rather than a general theory of museums.

Concepts and inspirations

  • new museology
  • meaning transformed within the museum
  • knowing through looking (Donna Haraway; James Clifford)
  • fetish (Marx; Freud)
  • aesthetic and contextual exhibitions (Brown Goode)
  • neutrality as fiction
  • cultural capital (Pierre Bourdieu)
  • lex situs rule
  • denial of time in theme parks (L. P. Hartley)

Argues against

  • Donald Horne's The Great Museum, which contrasts an Australia without history with a Europe turned into a museum (Bann): Horne's account tells us virtually nothing, because it gives no attention to how people experience the past; any relationship to the past is constructed. p. 104
  • Bourdieu's account of museum visiting, which rests on French art galleries (Merriman): Class alone cannot explain visits to general museums, and visiting depends also on life-cycle, structural factors and individual history. p. 163
  • the claim that museums can be politically objective (Greenhalgh): This striving towards objectivity has no philosophical platform, and curators always present a world-view. p. 95
  • the aesthetic view of exhibitions, in which objects speak for themselves (Vergo): The aesthetic view is a view seriously flawed in a number of obvious ways, since it treats contemplation as unmediated. p. 49

Sources and ways of working

  • close study of a few problematic objects and their displays, chosen as not representative (Victoria and Albert Museum case studies) p. 9
  • comparison of visiting patterns in general museums with results of a national attitudes survey p. 163
  • close reading of a legal case and of the rules it applies (Winkworth) to test the law of title p. 190
  • analysis of a museum display in relation to the realist representation it uses (American Museum of Natural History primate hall) p. 33

Gaps it names

  • why people who never visit museums stay away; visitor-only surveys give no direct information on deterrents p. 163
  • museum theory and practice outside the United Kingdom, which the volume does not attempt to cover p. 4
  • administration, conservation, registration and corporate sponsorship, which the volume leaves to other literature p. 4
  • gender, race and class in museum display, and the public display of subject peoples, which the editor says are conspicuous by their absence p. 4

Contents and chapter overviews

Yallop, Jacqueline (2011). Magpies, Squirrels and Thieves: How the Victorians Collected the World. London: Atlantic Books.7 concepts

Yallop treats museums as the product of private collecting, dealing and connoisseurship in the Victorian period, and argues that the private collector and the public museum were entangled rather than separate. The book is a cultural and social history of collecting, with elements of museum history, art-historical method and the history of the art trade, told through five collectors' archives. Its theory is light: the preface poses questions about what a collection is and what drives the collector, and the argument is carried by the cases rather than by named theorists in the body of the text.

Concepts and inspirations

  • objects as cultural evidence
  • ethnographic objects as art or cultural curiosity
  • museum as moral instruction (Ruskin) (John Ruskin)
  • the 'Chinese character' in museum display
  • objects from intransigent states as spoils
  • looted relics in circulation
  • 'stay what is fleeting' (Ruskin) (John Ruskin)

Argues against

  • the view that Victorian museum display of Chinese objects was a neutral presentation of knowledge: Bushell and Franks tried to replace that contempt with understanding of the objects, not to show the Chinese as degenerate
  • the view that collecting from the Empire was an assertion of imperial supremacy: Franks's collecting of Indian pieces 'had little to do with asserting imperial supremacy or showing off the bizarre accomplishments of a heathen race'

Sources and ways of working

  • collectors' own archives: letters, journals and account records of purchases
  • a collector's journal, as used for Charlotte Schreiber's buying trips
  • careful notes on objects, kept by Bushell and used for later publication
  • correspondence with museum staff and loan and sale negotiations

Gaps it names

  • science and natural history collections, which the book says it cannot cover
  • the loan-based display of Bushell's Chinese objects, few of which remained on public display

Contents and chapter overviews

Yanni, Carla (1999). Nature’s Museums: Victorian Science and the Architecture of Display. Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press.9 concepts

Yanni frames the natural history museum as a building that expresses and helps legitimize a particular knowledge of nature, and argues that Victorian Britain never settled on one building type because naturalists disagreed about what nature was. The book is architectural history written between architectural history and the sociology of science, reading plans, competitions and built interiors alongside the clients’ and scientists’ debates. It takes issue with Foucauldian readings of museums while using their questions about power, vision and display.

Concepts and inspirations

  • Foucauldian reading of museums (power, master narratives, visuality) (Foucault; Sherman and Rogoff)
  • Scopic reciprocity (Bennett) (Tony Bennett)
  • Cabinet of curiosities as precursor of the museum (Pomian; Hooper-Greenhill; Crimp)
  • Museum vision (Alpers)
  • Architecture as participant in the construction of knowledge
  • Museums present knowledge as neutral (Sherman and Rogoff; Sharon MacDonald)
  • Society of spectacle (periodisation) (Foucault; Crary; Thomas Richards)
  • Authenticity of specimens (aura) (Gould; Secord)
  • Meanings of nature (creation, natural resource, secular science)

Argues against

  • Foucauldian readings that treat classification as inherently hierarchical and museum narratives as unified: Some museums might present a single master narrative, but this is rare; there are usually several co-existing theories, and displays and architecture resist such analysis. p. 8
  • Bennett’s conflation of museums with arcades, department stores and the Familistère: The similarities can be explained by the perceived need for cheap natural lighting, which let architects fit more items under a skylight. p. 9
  • Crimp’s rejection of the cabinet of curiosities as the origin of the museum: A Wunderkammer could have a different system of classification and still illustrate the origins of museums, because master narratives change over time. p. 20

Sources and ways of working

  • reading competition entries alongside the recorded debates among the building clients p. 74
  • contemporary press reviews of the buildings, such as the Edinburgh Evening Courant p. 93
  • reading Victorian descriptions of earlier museums as evidence of how they were seen, such as Greenwood on Bullock’s Museum p. 27
  • building plans, lighting and ornament read against the institution’s programme and the later reception of the design p. 160

Gaps it names

  • Steven Conn’s point that much more historical detail is needed before making grand claims about museums and power p. 9
  • how visitors received the buildings, which the author admits architects could not always control p. 8

Contents and chapter overviews

Yoshida, Takashi (2014). From Cultures of War to Cultures of Peace: War and Peace Museums in Japan, China, and South Korea. Portland, ME: MerwinAsia.7 concepts

Yoshida presents museums as sites where Japanese postwar peace culture has been contested from the 1950s to the present, and argues that peace museums should show human suffering rather than national self-justification. It is a historical and museum-studies account of war and peace museums in Japan, China and South Korea, with critical analysis of memory, nationalism and the politics of exhibition. The central argument is that peace museums need not show Japanese atrocities, but on no account should they glorify aggression.

Concepts and inspirations

  • victimizer consciousness
  • multi-layered pacifism
  • peace museum (narrow and broad definitions) (Johan Galtung; Anzai Ikuro)
  • history wars
  • innocent-us and savage-them
  • sanitized view (the war museum's display)
  • patriotism as a problematic term

Argues against

  • Japanese critics who call exhibits of Japanese atrocities self-flagellating and disgracing the martyrs: Yoshida reports this view and implies it is wrong. Its supporters regard the war museums and the kamikaze museums as the only account of Imperial Japan that citizens need, which he does not accept. p. 233
  • Chinese and South Korean museums that use vivid images of Japanese atrocities to promote peace: Following Anzai, Yoshida says such exhibits tend to provoke hatred and offer little encouragement to visitors seeking peace and reconciliation. PDF p. 23
  • The Yushukan's position that the Pacific War was a just and honorable war of liberation: Yoshida says the museum disregards the negative aspects of the Imperial Army and the empire, and he judges it less acceptable than the Kyoto museum. p. 235
  • Galtung's narrow definition, under which many institutions calling themselves peace museums do not qualify: Yoshida records this view but uses a loose definition of his own, so that the selection can include the war-dead and kamikaze museums. PDF p. 23

Sources and ways of working

  • visitor comments and letters, and the letters of kamikaze pilots on display, read as evidence of how museums are received p. 133
  • victims' testimonies gathered by curators, followed up by researchers who visited the sites of events and checked the accounts against other sources p. 109
  • committee deliberations and the revision of captions and video commentaries, compared as original and revised versions p. 168
  • checking a photograph's original caption in a wartime publication against the museum's caption p. 177

Gaps it names

  • whether the museums of China can promote both patriotism and peace among children and adults, which the author says remains to be determined p. 215
  • understanding of the war from the viewpoints of the people of the countries Japan invaded or colonised, which the exhibits of the Tokyo war-memory museums are said to offer only in scant form p. 196

Contents and chapter overviews

Gaps the authors name

Things the authors themselves say are neglected, unknown or worth further research: a list of openings for new work.

  • a comprehensive history of museums in the twentieth century (Alberti 2009p. 193)
  • displaying and collecting at the end of empire, as context for post-colonial museology (Alberti 2009p. 193)
  • the role of museums in the Cold War and the fate of cultural institutions under the 1980s government (Alberti 2009p. 193)
  • comparative work on the processes of collection, conservation and display across museums (Alberti 2009p. 191)
  • France has no museum of colonial history; the 1990s debate on such an institution stalled until the Marseille initiative (Aldrich 2005p. 328)
  • little scholarship on the commemoration of the dead of the Indochinese and Algerian wars (Aldrich 2005p. 11)
  • the relative scarcity of monuments to the Indochinese War, which Aldrich links to the difficulty of commemorating defeat (Aldrich 2005p. 124)
  • collections of mathematical, mechanical and surgical instruments, inscriptions and antiquities, manuscripts and anatomical preparations, which the book deliberately leaves out (Arnold 2006)
  • the poetic, symbolic, political, emotional and experiential aspects of museum objects, which the book does not scrutinise (Arnold 2006)
  • the parallel history of the emotional responses visitors have to objects, which has a large literature that the book does not cover (Arnold 2006)
  • what role the collections of twentieth-century anthropology museums still play, which the author says the book cannot attempt (Arnold 2006)
  • the popular Japanese reception of Hearn, which no analysis to date has examined (Askew 2007p. 132)
  • how the Yaizu museum can attract visitors and persuade citizens to return, given few exhibits (Askew 2007p. 136)
  • the book is not an exhaustive survey of modern museums; the other collections were chosen to illustrate specific theoretical points (Asma 2001)
  • the deeper genetic and developmental mechanisms behind teratological monsters, which were not understood until the twentieth century (Asma 2001)
  • how the publics of museums in China and the Gulf states differ from those of developed countries, and which notions of public and public space apply to them (Barrett 2011p. 172)
  • how far the planned effects of museum display are actually felt by visitors, or evaded and unnoticed (Bennett 1995p. 11)
  • the material on the architects, archaeologists and museum directors introduced is not exhausted; the book is offered as a roadmap into a much larger field (Bilsel 2012PDF p. 33)
  • the change in the regime of the authentic between the mid nineteenth and mid twentieth century, shown by the destruction in 1955 of the V&A's Indian architectural displays for being copies (Bilsel 2012PDF p. 33)
  • visitor numbers to the Imperial Museum, which were not recorded (Çelik 2016p. 9)
  • reports or journals by the Ottoman officials who supervised the foreign excavations (Çelik 2016p. 9)
  • accounts by local visitors to the Imperial Museum, and by Ottoman women, which the author searched for in vain (Çelik 2016p. 10)
  • the workers’ own voices, which the documents do not give (Çelik 2016p. 11)
  • the African diaspora in Britain over this period, which the book sets aside (Coombes 1994p. 6)
  • the relation between anthropology's academic and public image, which has received little attention (Coombes 1994p. 4)
  • whether the cultural heritage of China's minority peoples is valued equally with Han Chinese antiquities, which the author says cannot be answered with easy answers (Cuno 2008PDF p. 109)
  • why ancient artists made certain forms in jade or decorated bronze, which archaeology has yet to explain (Cuno 2009p. 30)
  • unpublished excavations at sites such as Umm al-Hafriyat, whose ancient names remain unknown (Cuno 2009p. 139)
  • the Chinese excavation publication record, which leaves much to be desired (Cuno 2009p. 116)
  • the epistemic situations in which ethnographic categories were modelled and prepared for wider use in Russia, which the authors say earlier studies have not examined (Cvetkovski & Hofmeister 2014p. 6)
  • Lighter emotions such as pleasure, comradeship and love remain largely unexplored by historians of war emotion (Damousi 2020p. 132)
  • Historians cannot assume they know what silence means in the records of trauma, and recorded evidence may not contain the testimony they seek (Damousi 2020p. 147)
  • Historians have so far studied mainly grief, bereavement and mourning (Damousi 2020p. 132)
  • how visitors actually receive museum narratives, which the book raises as a larger question (Denton 2014p. 94)
  • What the physicality of museum objects may imply for the museum experience, which the editor says has been surprisingly little explored (Dudley 2010p. 6)
  • Whether mobile eye trackers in galleries would show differences from originals and reproductions that laboratory settings, resembling the white cube, do not (Dudley 2010p. 98)
  • how Western museums represent non-Western and minority cultures, which the study explicitly sets aside (Duncan 1995p. 3–4)
  • what real visitors make of museum rituals; the visitors discussed are hypothetical ideal types (Duncan 1995p. 5–6)
  • the many lesser patrons, brokers and collectors between Aldrovandi and Kircher, such as Mattioli, Calzolari, Imperato and Mercati, whose contributions have not been reassessed (Findlen 1994p. 5)
  • the historiography of the scientific revolution, which has paid little attention to natural history (Findlen 1994p. 10)
  • theoretical reflection on the concepts used to theorize museums, which Grinell says is too rare compared with case studies (Fromm 2014p. 170)
  • the decline of central American memory museums: national museums of memory have not been built there as they have in South America (Fromm 2014p. 77)
  • space for the collection: the thirty-six thousand works on view are under a tenth of the holdings, and the author expects curators to claim more of the complex (Gardner 2020)
  • Asia Minor's interior and unrecorded sites, which Greenhalgh says were still partly terra incognita in 1889 (Greenhalgh 2019p. 90)
  • a regular scientific survey of the whole country, which he says for Asia Minor lay in the distant future (Greenhalgh 2019p. 91)
  • European behaviour after the First World War, which the book leaves to another study (Greenhalgh 2019PDF p. 16)
  • The history of museum exhibition design across collections, disciplines and institutions is yet to be told, according to the editors (Guy 2024p. 6)
  • Multi-ethnic descendants and multicultural families are rarely considered valid audiences for national museum mannequins (Guy 2024p. 181)
  • American anthropologists have seldom studied American Jews as a culture, so museums lack a collection comparable to those of Tibet or North American Indians and few studies exist to consult (Hall & Seemann 1987p. 152)
  • No anthropological theory of looting, plunder or dispossession has been written (Hicks 2020)
  • Many holdings of Benin loot are unknown or uncertain, including private collections and possible gifts or sales by the Wellcome Collection; the list is provisional and readers are asked to correct it (Hicks 2020)
  • The death histories of objects, as against their life histories, remain to be written (Hicks 2020)
  • The author says work on women and museums has mainly concerned art museums and visitors, and calls for looking beyond visitors, art and national institutions (Hill 2016PDF p. 18)
  • The author calls women's involvement in the interwar period ambiguous and leaves the shape of the later period open (Hill 2016PDF p. 231)
  • how far the museums' messages were accepted and internalised by visitors, which the evidence cannot show (Hill 2005p. 145)
  • chronologically and geographically specific studies to fill in the broad schema linking museums and capitalism (Hill 2005p. 11)
  • the museums of other parts of Britain, particularly Scotland, where the rate-supported museum was less common (Hill 2005p. 13)
  • Collective biography built from fragments of evidence, which Cowman argues could be a productive method for feminist historians, is not tried in the volume (Hill 2012p. 4)
  • Histories of collective labour such as the Women’s Society in Edmonton, which left almost no individual trace, need to trace the institution’s discourses as well as its individuals (Hill 2012p. 84)
  • the history of imperial collecting and conflict, which the chapters do not generally engage with (Hill 2021p. 8)
  • the link between the art market and internal European conflicts and crises, and the transformation of the global art market in the heyday of European imperialism, which are only just beginning to be mapped (Hill 2021p. 30)
  • an exhibition that juxtaposes official war art with trench art and explores the experiences of official war artists alongside the soldiers they painted (Hill 2021p. 250)
  • how Liu Wencai is taught in school textbooks; the authors' survey of contemporary textbooks did not confirm the accounts they heard (Ho & Li 2016p. 32)
  • whether the case of Liu Wencai will be resolved; the authors describe it as still unresolved (Ho & Li 2016p. 22)
  • the curatorial aim of ‘completing the collection’ and ‘filling the gaps’ assumes that a complete classification is possible; the author calls for analysis of how such classifications were constituted (Hooper-Greenhill 1992p. 165)
  • an effective history of the British Museum that selects a time-frame and assesses together the slave trade, travel, financial resources and other elements of the museum’s identity (Hooper-Greenhill 1992p. 20)
  • a series of documents showing how colonisation enabled particular subject positions and technologies of collecting at a specific geo-historical site (Hooper-Greenhill 1992p. 21)
  • decolonisation requires treating every object differently, assessing its origin, provenance and meaning today; this is described as a long and complex project (Hopkins 2021)
  • workforce diversity: the staff of museums must reflect the public in class, ethnic background and gender (Hopkins 2021)
  • how a museum collects digital objects such as apps, which Hopkins raises as an open question (Hopkins 2021)
  • the decisions about what to display and what to keep in storage are seldom acknowledged (Hopkins 2021)
  • visitor surveys are rare and the author says that comparable figures for other countries are lacking (Hudson 1975p. 122)
  • how visitors of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries actually responded, since no visitor survey of their period was made (Hudson 1975p. 7)
  • the typology of Brazilian clubs and axes, which needs a closer look (Feest) (Impey & MacGregor 1985p. 332)
  • fuller systematic studies of collections and records for Asian material, with each object tied to dated inventories (Ayers) (Impey & MacGregor 1985p. 355)
  • the role of museums as agents of the collective good and civil society, which the author says has received little attention beyond education and entertainment (Janes 2009p. 21)
  • how far the Universal Museum Declaration is harming public perceptions of the museum community is unknown (Janes 2009p. 85)
  • the stewardship of the ethnosphere, the diversity of human cultures, which the author says seems to be going the way of biodiversity (Janes 2009p. 46)
  • the fate of Tipu's manuscript library: of perhaps 3,500 volumes, only about three hundred reached London and the rest are lost (Jasanoff 2005p. 185)
  • the experiences of camp followers, interpreters, common soldiers, women and children on imperial frontiers, which the author says warrant research (Jasanoff 2005p. 8)
  • experiments in which artworks are organised according to the aesthetic categories of the cultures from which they derive (Karp & Lavine 1991)
  • the expansion of the expertise of established museums in presenting non-Western and minority cultures (Karp & Lavine 1991)
  • experiments in exhibition design that present multiple perspectives or admit the contingent nature of interpretations (Karp & Lavine 1991)
  • the sensory dimension of ethnographic displays, since smells, temperature and sound are generally left out (Karp & Lavine 1991)
  • few museums have established posts for minority audiences; such posts are the exception rather than the norm (Kavanagh 1996p. 178)
  • whether the erosion of distinctions between high and low leads to a world of kitsch or to a liberating pluralism, which the chapter leaves open (Kirshenblatt-Gimblett 1998p. 281)
  • a comparative study of the origins of European national museums and their uses of history, which the editors plan under the follow-on Eunamus project (Knell et al. 2011PDF p. 20)
  • the collector who housed artifacts in a private museum is seldom the focus of studies of indigenous collections (Krech & Hail 1999)
  • the link between gender, occupation and collecting, which the authors suggest is worth exploring (Krech & Hail 1999)
  • Native responses to collecting, which survive mainly as isolated rebukes and oral accounts (Krech & Hail 1999)
  • Whether UNESCO should keep separate lists for tangible and intangible heritage, or bring them together (Logan 2016)
  • Research on the affective moment of visiting, on memory, imagination and emotional regulation (Logan 2016)
  • The relationship between museums and their audiences, which needs more research; visitors are the great unknowns (Longair & McAleer 2012p. 13)
  • The significance of museum architecture as an expression of intellectual and social aims, flagged for further study (Longair & McAleer 2012PDF p. 12)
  • The careers, roles and practices of museum staff, especially in smaller institutions (Longair & McAleer 2012p. 9)
  • how local communities engaged with the Shanghai and Nantong museums is largely undocumented, so visitors’ reception of the displays is unknown (Lu 2014p. 88)
  • the lack of community participation has left many museums alienated from the public, and private museums are financially fragile (Lu 2014p. 214)
  • how visitors make sense of exhibitions, from the organisers' intentions through the display to the public's reading, which the volume says is rarely studied (Lumley 1988p. 9)
  • how women's historical experience appears in areas where change is slow and measured by objects, and so is hard to display (Lumley 1988p. 118)
  • the social scientific study of museums is still relatively under-developed (Macdonald & Fyfe 1996PDF p. 10)
  • how people conceptualise museum visiting and how it articulates with their identity and locality (Macdonald & Fyfe 1996PDF p. 18)
  • how visitors' alternative readings are socially and culturally positioned (Macdonald & Fyfe 1996PDF p. 17)
  • how museums deal, or should deal, with controversial subjects (Macdonald & Fyfe 1996PDF p. 18)
  • Visitor reception and the view from below, which the author says is much less documented than the view from above (MacKenzie 2009p. 277)
  • The class systems of the metropole recreated in colonies, which the author says need a more nuanced and technical analysis (MacKenzie 2009p. 16)
  • The influence of Darwin's theory of evolution on colonial museums and the social and intellectual context of colonial science (MacKenzie 2009p. 15)
  • Areas left out of the study, including Hong Kong, the Caribbean, West and East Africa and the Indian Ocean islands (MacKenzie 2009p. 16)
  • the Louvre under Vivant-Denon after 1803 and the museum's expansion, which the author says would need a different kind of study (McClellan 1994p. 2)
  • early visitor responses to the Louvre and the Musee des monuments, which the author says lies beyond this study (McClellan 1994p. 201)
  • The shift from displayed to stored collections in the first decades of the twentieth century, through the Madrid conference and its handbook, which Kott says deserves a case study (Meyer & Savoy 2014p. 216)
  • A study of the museum’s establishment that argues beyond national borders, which the introduction says did not yet exist for the eighteenth century (Meyer & Savoy 2014p. 3)
  • How objects acquire meaning during the times of transit between cultures (Meyer & Savoy 2014p. 20)
  • the ethnographical collections, whose objects in Sloane's catalogue largely remain unidentified (Miller 1973p. 356)
  • a separate ethnographical museum, which was not created and was not even contemplated nearly fifty years after the 1929 Royal Commission (Miller 1973p. 327)
  • the Museum's relation to the public libraries and the other national libraries, from which the author says it has tended to stand apart (Miller 1973p. 362)
  • research about the actual professional practice of community engagement is far less developed than work on participants or on the political ramifications (Morse 2021p. 7)
  • care-ful museology is left as an agenda for future research and conversation (Morse 2021p. 212)
  • The normality of violence, the everyday acceptance of cruelty across history, which Rekdal admits he avoided and finds the hardest theme (Muchitsch 2013p. 128)
  • The Holocaust in Belarusian museum display, which the author says is neglected though not taboo (Muchitsch 2013p. 194)
  • Critical memorial work that goes further than Tur's Unknown Knight in questioning the image of the enemy (Muchitsch 2013p. 181)
  • The gender balance of representations of populations at war, with women's traces left out of war museums (Muchitsch 2013p. 37)
  • the inner history of the exhibitions, including selection, negotiation, payment, reception and profitability, which the author leaves to others (Naquin 2004p. 344)
  • technological exchange between Europe and the Qing, such as clocks, glass, enamels and instruments, which the Palace Museum could show but has not (Naquin 2004p. 387)
  • how the commodified authentic developed within Britain, which the impulse to criticise and dismiss has kept from investigation (Outka 2009p. 14)
  • a study of the transition to a second democratic generation of exhibitions about National Socialism and the Holocaust (Paver 2018p. 278)
  • testimony, generations, postmemory and trauma, which generate large scholarship in memory studies but remain secondary in German and Austrian history exhibitions (Paver 2018p. 278)
  • the feelings of the bureaucrats involved in restitution, which Grossmann calls for (Paver 2018p. 49)
  • more work about the history and nature of museums and collections (Pearce 1992p. 380)
  • more work upon the material from a range of standpoints (Pearce 1992p. 381)
  • more information about how people see museums and respond to them (Pearce 1992p. 381)
  • little critical assessment of the museum's past within the profession, which tends to present its development as uncontroversial (Pearson 2017)
  • the principles of wartime experiments, which post-war specialist groups did not know about (Pearson 2017)
  • surviving local records, which are often limited in regional museums (Pearson 2017)
  • touching, tasting and smelling in the museum, which the author says receive less attention than looking and walking (Rees Leahy 2012p. 3)
  • the book is not an exhaustive history of bodily practices in the museum (Rees Leahy 2012p. 9)
  • little empirical research on how museums' human rights work affects visitors and rights activists (Sandell & Nightingale 2012)
  • no agreed list or classification of cultural rights, which has slowed their provision (Sandell & Nightingale 2012)
  • contemporary material after 1900 in the British Museum's Asian gallery, despite recent collecting (Sandell & Nightingale 2012)
  • the printed catalogue of a c.1840-1845 Pacific collection has never been located and is known only through labels (Sellers 1980p. 324)
  • no source is given for forty-four cases of Chinese insects, which the text attributes to William Wood's 1831 shipment (Sellers 1980p. 321)
  • whether the Salem museum copied Peale's wax figures of mankind is unknown (Sellers 1980p. 2)
  • no single comprehensive history of natural history museums exists; the literature is fragmented (Shapiro & Kemp 1990p. 12)
  • museum education still lacks a theory to guide it, despite useful visitor research (Shapiro & Kemp 1990PDF p. 17)
  • the contemporary political, environmental and cultural issues that the Festival of Indonesia failed to address (Sherman & Rogoff 1994p. 275)
  • earlier sources of antiquarianism, going back to the Renaissance, which would deepen the historical argument (Siegel 2020p. 308)
  • provincial and imperial museums, which the editor regrets not treating at length (Siegel 2008PDF p. 12)
  • libraries, zoos, botanic gardens, sales galleries and the international exhibition, which are left out (Siegel 2008PDF p. 12)
  • Soviet display and museology after 1950, including the transfer of Soviet display methods to China, Cuba and the German Democratic Republic, which the book treats only in passing (Silina 2026p. 7)
  • the work of Fedorov-Davydov and Kovalenskaya on the class value of art and the sociology of patronage, which has been largely overlooked (Silina 2026p. 7)
  • the perspective of local communities on Soviet museum policy, which should be studied alongside the critique of Russian-imposed narratives (Silina 2026p. 5)
  • no comprehensive theory yet explains the social work of museums; the literature is scattered (Silverman 2010p. 14)
  • a shared ethics base for museums and social work, which existing codes do not provide (Silverman 2010p. 149)
  • an empirical body of knowledge and evidence, including which museum resources are more effective for particular interventions (Silverman 2010p. 147)
  • non-Western traditions of miniature and giant forms (netsuke, Persian and Indian miniatures, Indonesian and Chinese giants), which the author leaves out as too context-bound to treat here (Stewart 1984PDF p. 14)
  • a systematic history of Western notions of the object, the icon and the fetish, and of the savage and civilised relation to material things (Stocking 1985p. 13)
  • the actual processes of collection of objects, and the recent movement for their repatriation (Stocking 1985p. 13)
  • the anthropology of world's fairs and of modern touristic cultural performances (Stocking 1985p. 13)
  • the historical criteria by which an authentic cultural or artistic product is validated (Stocking 1985p. 240)
  • the mid-Meiji state projects of about 1880 to 1900 have a tremendous scholarly void, and Conder and Katayama have been studied mainly as developments in Japanese architectural history (Tseng 2008p. 14)
  • the role of Western conventions, specifically the museum, in enforcing the Kyoto and Tokyo symbolism, which Fujitani does not explore (Tseng 2008p. 135)
  • the manufacturing process of exhibition-grade replicas and of the Cultural Heritage Administration's certified display replicas, which the author says is undocumented (Veldkamp 2014p. 578)
  • studies of authenticity and museum display in the Korean context, which are scarce (Veldkamp 2014p. 561)
  • why people who never visit museums stay away; visitor-only surveys give no direct information on deterrents (Vergo 1989p. 163)
  • museum theory and practice outside the United Kingdom, which the volume does not attempt to cover (Vergo 1989p. 4)
  • administration, conservation, registration and corporate sponsorship, which the volume leaves to other literature (Vergo 1989p. 4)
  • gender, race and class in museum display, and the public display of subject peoples, which the editor says are conspicuous by their absence (Vergo 1989p. 4)
  • science and natural history collections, which the book says it cannot cover (Yallop 2011)
  • the loan-based display of Bushell's Chinese objects, few of which remained on public display (Yallop 2011)
  • Steven Conn’s point that much more historical detail is needed before making grand claims about museums and power (Yanni 1999p. 9)
  • how visitors received the buildings, which the author admits architects could not always control (Yanni 1999p. 8)
  • whether the museums of China can promote both patriotism and peace among children and adults, which the author says remains to be determined (Yoshida 2014p. 215)
  • understanding of the war from the viewpoints of the people of the countries Japan invaded or colonised, which the exhibits of the Tokyo war-memory museums are said to offer only in scant form (Yoshida 2014p. 196)
